### PAGE 9
**[Title Page]**

# OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS OF TORUŃ
## SIX BOOKS ON THE REVOLUTIONS
### of the celestial spheres.

You have in this work, now newly born and published, studious reader, the motions of the stars—both the fixed and the wandering—restored [reconstructed] from both ancient and recent observations: and, moreover, adorned with new and wonderful hypotheses. You also have most convenient Tables, from which you will be able to calculate the same [motions] for any time with the greatest ease. Therefore: buy, read, enjoy.

**[Greek Motto:]** Let no one untrained in geometry enter.

**[Printer’s Mark of Johannes Petreius]**

**At Nuremberg, at the house of Johannes Petreius,**
**In the Year 1543.**

**[Note in margin:]** 17:3
**[Ownership mark in margin:]** From the library of [unclear: Master Michaelis]

### PAGE 10
**[Preface]**

# TO THE READER CONCERNING THE HYPOTHE-
### SES OF THIS WORK.

**[N]** I do not doubt that certain learned men—the report of the novelty of the hypotheses of this work having already been spread, namely that it establishes the Earth to be mobile and the Sun indeed to be stationary in the middle of the universe—will be vehemently offended, and will think that the liberal disciplines, long ago correctly established, ought not to be thrown into confusion. However, if they wish to weigh the matter exactly, they will find that the author of this work has committed nothing that deserves reproach. 

For it is the property of the Astronomer to collect the history of the celestial motions with diligent and skilled observation. Then, to conceive and devise the causes of these [motions], or hypotheses—since he can by no method attain the true ones—of whatever kind they may be, which being assumed, the same motions may be correctly calculated from the principles of Geometry, both for the future and for the past. This craftsman [the author] has remarkably excelled in both. For it is not necessary that these hypotheses be true, nor even probable, but this one thing suffices: if they provide a calculation consistent with observations. 

Unless, perhaps, someone is so ignorant of Geometry and Optics that he considers the epicycle of Venus to be probable, or believes it to be the cause why it [Venus] sometimes precedes the Sun and sometimes follows it by forty degrees and more. For who does not see that, this being assumed, it necessarily follows that the diameter of the star [planet] appears more than four times larger, and the body itself more than sixteen times larger, in the perigee (*περιγείῳ*) than in the apogee (*ἀπογείῳ*); yet the experience of every age contradicts this? There are also other things in this discipline no less absurd, which it is not necessary to examine at present. For it is sufficiently clear that this art is completely and simply ignorant of the causes of the apparent unequal motions. And if it devises any by imagining them (as it certainly devises many), it does not devise them so that it may persuade anyone that it is so, but only so that they may establish a correct calculation. Since, however, various hypotheses sometimes offer themselves for one and the same motion (as in the motion of the Sun: eccentricity and the epicycle), the Astronomer will seize that one which is easiest to grasp. The Philosopher, perhaps, [seeks] more for the appearance of truth...

**[Marginalia:]** XE. 5020A. 53; Feb 10, 1902; 55762

---

### Scholarly Notes on the Translation:

1.  **Authorship of the Preface:** Although the title page credits **NICOLAI COPERNICI**, the preface *Ad Lectorem* was written anonymously by the Lutheran theologian **Andreas Osiander**. He added it without Copernicus's permission to soften the blow of the heliocentric theory by claiming it was merely a mathematical tool (instrumentalism) rather than a physical reality.
2.  **Abbreviations:** The OCR text contains standard Renaissance printing abbreviations which I have expanded in the translation:
    *   *immobilẽ* → *immobilem*
    *   *putẽtꝙ* → *putentque* (the *q;* or *qꝙ* symbol denotes the enclitic *-que*)
    *   *nõ* → *non*
    *   *inueniẽt* → *inuenient*
    *   *utrunqꝙ* → *utrunque* (standard variant of *utrumque*)
    *   *quãplurimas* → *quamplurimas*
3.  **Technical Terms:** 
    *   *Stellarum fixarum, quàm erraticarum:* Refers to "fixed stars" and "wandering stars" (planets).
    *   *Hypothesibus:* In this context, it refers to the mathematical models or geometric constructs used to predict planetary positions.
    *   *Artifex:* Lit. "artisan" or "craftsman," here referring to Copernicus as the master of the "art" of astronomy.
    *   *Calculum:* Refers to the mathematical result or "computation" derived from the tables.
4.  **Greek:** The motto *Ἀγεωμέτρητος οὐδεὶς εἰσίτω* is a famous Platonic injunction emphasizing that geometry is the prerequisite for higher philosophy/astronomy.

# OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS OF TORUŃ
## SIX BOOKS ON THE REVOLUTIONS
### of the celestial spheres.

You have in this work, now newly born and published, studious reader, the motions of the stars—both the fixed and the wandering—restored <note>In this context, "restored" or "reconstructed" refers to the correction of astronomical data.</note> from both ancient and recent observations: and, moreover, adorned with new and wonderful hypotheses. You also have most convenient Tables, from which you will be able to calculate the same motions for any time with the greatest ease. Therefore: buy, read, enjoy.

Let no one untrained in geometry enter. <note>original Greek: "Αγεωμέτρητος οὐδεὶς εἰσίτω." This is a traditional warning famously associated with the entrance to Plato's Academy, emphasizing that mathematics is the foundation of higher knowledge.</note>

# BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS OF THORN
<note>original: "Torinensis" refers to Copernicus’s birthplace, Thorn, now Toruń in modern-day Poland.</note>

## ON THE REVOLUTIONS OF THE HEAVENLY SPHERES,
## In Six Books.

->You have in this work, now recently born and published, diligent reader, the motions of the stars, both fixed and wandering <note>original: "erraticarum"; a reference to the planets, which appear to "wander" across the sky compared to the fixed background stars</note>, restored from both ancient and recent observations: and furthermore adorned with new and wonderful hypotheses. You also have most convenient tables, from which you will be able to calculate these same motions most easily for any given time. Therefore buy, read, and enjoy.<-

->Let no one untrained in geometry enter.<-
<note>original: "Αγεωμέτρητος οὐδεὶς εἰσίτω." This Greek phrase was famously inscribed above the entrance to Plato's Academy in Athens, signaling that mathematical understanding is a prerequisite for higher knowledge.</note>

### At Nuremberg, by Johannes Petreius,
### In the year 1543.

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>Following the title page of the 1543 Nuremberg edition. This page contains the unsigned foreword "To the Reader," now known to have been written by the Lutheran theologian Andreas Osiander rather than Copernicus himself. # TO THE READER CONCERNING THE HYPOTHESES OF THIS WORK
<note>The term "hypothesis" here refers to a mathematical assumption used to model planetary paths, which in the 16th century was often distinguished from "physical truth."</note>

I have no doubt that certain learned men, now that the report of the novelty of the **hypotheses** of this work has spread abroad—which sets the Earth in motion and puts the Sun motionless in the center of the universe—will be greatly offended, and will think that the liberal arts, established long ago on a correct basis, should not be thrown into confusion. 

However, if they are willing to weigh the matter carefully, they will find that the author of this work has done nothing worthy of blame. For it is the duty of an astronomer to compose the history of the celestial motions through careful and expert study. Then he must conceive and devise the causes of these motions or **hypotheses** <note>original: "hypotheses"; here meaning mathematical models</note>—since he cannot by any means attain to the true causes—from which, if they are assumed, these same motions can be calculated correctly from the principles of geometry, for both the future and the past. 

This author has performed both of these duties excellently. For these hypotheses need not be true nor even probable; it is enough if they provide a **calculus** <note>original: "calculum"; referring to a method of mathematical computation</note> which fits the observations. Unless, perhaps, someone is so ignorant of geometry and optics that he regards the epicycle of Venus as probable, or believes that it is the cause why Venus sometimes precedes and sometimes follows the Sun by forty degrees or more. 

->For who does not see that from this assumption it follows of necessity that the diameter of the planet in the **perigee** <note>The point in an orbit where a body is closest to the Earth.</note> should appear more than four times greater, and the body itself more than sixteen times greater, than in the **apogee**? <note>The point in an orbit where a body is furthest from the Earth.</note><-

Yet the experience of all ages contradicts this. There are other things in this discipline that are no less absurd, which it is quite unnecessary to examine for the present. For it is sufficiently clear that this art is absolutely and profoundly ignorant of the causes of the apparent unequal motions. And if it constructs and thinks up any causes—and it certainly thinks up a great many—it does not think them up in order to persuade anyone that they are even true, but only that they may provide a correct basis for calculation. 

<margin>The astronomer accepts the easiest model.</margin>

Therefore, let us permit these new hypotheses to be made known along with the ancient ones, which are no more probable; especially as they are admirable and easy, and bring with them a vast treasury of most learned observations. And let no one expect anything certain from astronomy, which cannot furnish it, lest he accept as the truth ideas conceived for another purpose, and depart from this study a greater fool than when he entered it. Farewell.

# TO THE READER CONCERNING THE HYPOTHESES OF THIS WORK
<note>The term "hypothesis" here refers to a mathematical assumption used to model planetary paths, which in the 16th century was often distinguished from "physical truth."</note>

I have no doubt that certain learned men, now that the report of the novelty of the **hypotheses** of this work has spread abroad—which sets the Earth in motion and puts the Sun motionless in the center of the universe—will be greatly offended, and will think that the liberal arts, established long ago on a correct basis, should not be thrown into confusion. 

However, if they are willing to weigh the matter carefully, they will find that the author of this work has done nothing worthy of blame. For it is the duty of an astronomer to compose the history of the celestial motions through careful and expert study. Then he must conceive and devise the causes of these motions or **hypotheses** <note>original: "hypotheses"; here meaning mathematical models</note>—since he cannot by any means attain to the true causes—from which, if they are assumed, these same motions can be calculated correctly from the principles of geometry, for both the future and the past. 

This author has performed both of these duties excellently. For these hypotheses need not be true nor even probable; it is enough if they provide a **calculus** <note>original: "calculum"; referring to a method of mathematical computation</note> which fits the observations. Unless, perhaps, someone is so ignorant of geometry and optics that he regards the **epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex paths of planets.</note> of Venus as probable, or thinks that it is the reason why Venus sometimes precedes and sometimes follows the Sun by forty degrees and even more. 

For who does not see that it necessarily follows from this assumption that the diameter of the planet in its **perigee** <note>The point in an orbit where the planet is closest to the Earth.</note> should appear more than four times greater, and the body of the planet more than sixteen times greater, than in its **apogee** <note>The point in an orbit where the planet is furthest from the Earth.</note>? Yet the experience of all the ages contradicts this. There are other things, no less absurd, in this discipline, which there is no need to examine at this time. 

For it is clear enough that this art is completely and simply ignorant of the causes of the seemingly irregular motions. And if it devises any causes through the imagination (and it certainly does devise many), it does not do so in order to persuade anyone that they are true, but only that they might provide a correct basis for calculation. Since different hypotheses are sometimes offered for one and the same motion (such as an **eccentric** <note>A circular orbit where the Earth is not at the exact center.</note> or an epicycle for the Sun's motion), the astronomer will take as his first choice that which is easiest to grasp. The philosopher may perhaps seek more after the appearance of truth; but neither of them will understand or state anything certain unless it has been divinely revealed to him. 

Therefore, let us permit these new **hypotheses** to become known alongside the ancient ones, which are no more probable; especially since they are wonderful and easy, and bring with them a vast treasury of most learned observations. And as far as hypotheses go, let no one expect anything certain from astronomy, which cannot provide it, lest he accept as truth things devised for another purpose, and leave this study a greater fool than when he entered it. Farewell.

<meta>This page is the formal title page of Nicolaus Copernicus’s masterpiece. It follows the anonymous "To the Reader" preface (by Andreas Osiander) which attempted to frame the work as a mathematical tool rather than physical reality. This page introduces the author and the scope of his work, which would eventually trigger the Scientific Revolution.</meta>

# BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS OF TORUŃ
## ON THE REVOLUTIONS OF THE CELESTIAL
### spheres, in Six Books.

You have in this work, which has been newly born and published, diligent reader, the motions of the stars—both the fixed and the wandering <note>original: "erraticarum"; this refers to the planets, which appear to "wander" across the sky compared to the fixed stars.</note>—restored from both ancient and also recent observations. Furthermore, these motions are adorned with new and wonderful <term>hypotheses</term> <note>original: "hypothesibus"; here meaning the foundational mathematical assumptions or models, specifically the heliocentric arrangement.</note>. You also have very convenient <term>tables</term> <note>original: "Tabulas"; these are the data sets and calculation tools used by astronomers to predict the positions of heavenly bodies.</note>, from which you will be able to calculate these same motions for any given time with the greatest of ease. Therefore: buy, read, and enjoy!

->Let no one untrained in geometry enter.<- 
<note>original Greek: "Ἀγεωμέτρητος οὐδεὶς εἰσίτω"; this is a famous motto said to have been inscribed over the entrance to Plato's Academy in Athens, emphasizing that mathematics is the essential prerequisite for understanding the universe.</note>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page serves as the famous, originally anonymous preface to Nicolaus Copernicus's "De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium" (1543). It follows the title page and was written by the Lutheran theologian Andreas Osiander without Copernicus's permission. Osiander’s goal was to soften the controversial impact of the book by suggesting that the "moving Earth" was merely a mathematical convenience rather than a physical reality.</meta>

# TO THE READER CONCERNING THE HYPOTHE-
### SES OF THIS WORK.

[[image: Large decorative initial 'N' showing a scholar at a desk.]]

**I** do not doubt that certain learned men, now that the rumor has spread about the novelty of the <term>hypotheses</term> <note>original: "hypotheseon"; in this context, it refers to the foundational mathematical assumptions of the system.</note> of this work—which posits that the Earth moves and that the Sun stays stationary in the center of the universe—are deeply offended and believe that the liberal disciplines, having been correctly established long ago, ought not to be thrown into confusion. However, if they are willing to weigh the matter exactly, they will find that the author of this work has committed nothing that deserves reproach. For it is the duty of an astronomer to gather the history of the celestial motions through diligent and skillful observation. Then he must conceive and devise causes for them, or hypotheses—since he cannot by any means attain the true causes—of such a kind that, if they are assumed, these same motions can be correctly calculated from the principles of geometry, both for the future and for the past. This artist <note>The author uses "artist" (artifex) here to mean a skilled practitioner of a mathematical or technical craft.</note> has excelled in both these requirements. For it is not necessary that these hypotheses be true, nor even probable; rather, this one thing is sufficient: that they provide a calculation consistent with the observations. 

Unless, perhaps, someone is so ignorant of geometry and optics that he considers the <term>epicycle</term> <note>original: "epicyclium"; a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle, used in ancient astronomy to explain the apparent "looping" paths of planets.</note> of Venus to be probable, or believes it to be the reason why Venus sometimes precedes and sometimes follows the Sun by forty degrees or more. For who does not see that, if this were assumed, it would necessarily follow that the diameter of the star would appear more than four times larger, and its body more than sixteen times larger, in <term>perigee</term> <note>original Greek: "περιγείῳ"; the point in an orbit where a celestial body is closest to the observer.</note> than in <term>apogee</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπογείῳ"; the point in an orbit where a celestial body is farthest from the observer.</note>? Yet the experience of every age argues against this. There are other things in this discipline no less absurd, which it is not necessary to examine at this time. For it is clear enough that this art is simply and entirely ignorant of the causes of the apparent unequal motions. And if it devises any by imagination—as it certainly devises many—it does not devise them so that it may persuade anyone that it is so, but only so that they may establish a correct calculation. Since different hypotheses are sometimes offered for one and the same motion (such as eccentricity and the epicycle for the motion of the Sun), the astronomer will preferably grab hold of that which is easiest to grasp. A philosopher, perhaps, might seek more after the semblance of truth...

<margin>XE. 5020A. 53</margin>
<margin>handwritten notes: Feb 10, 1902; 55762</margin>

It uses the visual size of Venus to illustrate the logical difficulties inherent in traditional astronomical models.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the anonymous preface by Andreas Osiander and presents a formal letter of encouragement from Cardinal Nikolaus von Schönberg to Nicolaus Copernicus. The transition shows the contrast between Osiander’s cautious "mathematical fiction" approach and the high-level ecclesiastical interest in Copernicus's actual findings.</meta>

...requires <note>This sentence continues from the previous page, discussing why one should not seek physical "truth" in astronomical models.</note> more logic, yet neither will comprehend or pass on anything certain unless it has been divinely revealed to him. Let us therefore permit these new <term>hypotheses</term> <note>original: "hypotheses"; here meaning the underlying mathematical assumptions of the system.</note> to become known alongside the old ones, which are no more probable—especially since these are both wonderful and easy to use, and bring with them a vast treasure of most learned observations. Nor should anyone expect anything certain from astronomy regarding its underlying assumptions, since the discipline itself cannot provide such a thing. Otherwise, if a student seizes as true those things fashioned for another purpose <note>i.e., for the purpose of easier calculation rather than physical reality.</note>, he may depart from this discipline a greater fool than when he first approached it. Farewell.

# NIKOLAUS VON SCHÖNBERG, CARDINAL
### of Capua, to Nicolaus Copernicus, Greetings.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'C' containing a figure, possibly a scholar or clerical figure, seated at a desk or holding a book.</image-desc>

**W**hen reports of your talent had been brought to me by the constant talk of everyone some years ago, I began at that time to hold you in the highest regard and to congratulate our countrymen, among whom you flourished with such great glory. For I had learned that you were not only remarkably skilled in the discoveries of the ancient mathematicians, but that you had also established a new system of the world. In this system, you teach that the Earth moves; that the Sun occupies the lowest <note>In the Aristotelian view, the center of the universe was considered the "lowest" point.</note> and thus the central place of the universe; that the **eighth heaven** <note>The sphere of the "fixed stars," which was the outermost boundary of the universe in traditional astronomy.</note> remains motionless and fixed forever; and that the Moon, together with the **elements** <note>original: "elementis"; referring to the four sublunary elements (earth, air, fire, water) which were thought to travel with the Earth.</note> included in its sphere, situated between the heavens of Mars and Venus, revolves around the Sun in an annual course. 

I also learned that you have composed commentaries on this entire system of astronomy and have compiled the motions of the **wandering stars** <note>The planets.</note> into tables calculated with great effort, to the universal admiration of all. Therefore, most learned man, unless I am a bother to you, I beg you again and again most earnestly that you communicate this discovery of yours to scholars, and that you send to me at the earliest possible time your late-night labors concerning the sphere of the world, together with the Tables and whatever else you have pertaining to this same subject. 

I have, moreover, charged Theodoric of Reden to have everything transcribed there at my expense and sent to me. If you grant me this favor, you will understand that you have dealt with a man who is devoted to your name and eager to do justice to such great talent. Farewell. 

At Rome, the Kalends of November, in the year 1536.

# TO THE MOST HOLY LORD, PAUL III, SUPREME PONTIFF,

## Preface by Nicolaus Copernicus to the Books of the Revolutions.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'S' depicting a scholar or clerk seated at a desk with an open book, with a second figure standing behind him in a study setting.</image-desc>

I can well enough estimate, Most Holy Father, that as soon as some people learn that in these books of mine, which I have written regarding the revolutions of the spheres of the world, I attribute certain motions to the terrestrial globe, they will immediately shout that I and such an opinion ought to be hissed off the stage <note>original: "explodendum"; a theatrical term meaning to be booed or driven off by clapping and hissing.</note>. For my own works do not please me so much that I do not weigh what others will judge of them. And although I know that the thoughts of a philosopher are far removed from the judgment of the common people—because his study is to seek the truth in all things, insofar as God has permitted this to human reason—nevertheless, I think that opinions utterly foreign to what is right must be avoided. Therefore, when I considered with myself how absurd a recital <note>original: "ἀκρόαμα" (akroama); a Greek term for a lecture, performance, or something heard.</note> it would be considered by those who know that the judgment of many centuries has confirmed the opinion that the Earth is placed motionless in the middle of the heavens as their center, if I, to the contrary, asserted that the Earth moves; I hesitated with myself for a long time as to whether I should bring my commentaries, written to demonstrate its motion, into the light of day, or whether it would be better to follow the example of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for keeping their mathematical and philosophical discoveries secret within their own community.</note> and certain others, who were accustomed to hand down the mysteries of philosophy not through writings, but by hand <note>Meaning orally or through personal instruction.</note>, and only to relatives and friends. This is testified by the letter of Lysis to Hipparchus <note>Lysis and Hipparchus were Pythagoreans; Lysis's letter famously scolded Hipparchus for sharing secret teachings with the uninitiated.</note>. And indeed, they seem to me to have done this not, as some think, out of a certain jealousy of sharing their doctrines, but so that things of such great beauty, investigated with much effort by great men, should not be held in contempt by those who are either too lazy to spend any honest effort on literature (unless it is profitable), or who, even if they are stirred to the liberal study of philosophy by the exhortations and example of others, are nevertheless, on account of 

<meta>catchword: stupidity</meta>

<summary>In this formal dedication, Copernicus expresses his fear that his theory of the Earth's motion will be mocked by those accustomed to the traditional geocentric model. He explains that he nearly kept his findings secret, following the Pythagorean tradition of oral transmission, to protect his work from the contempt of the unlearned.</summary>
<keywords>Nicolaus Copernicus, Pope Paul III, heliocentrism, Earth's motion, Pythagoreans, secrecy of knowledge, scientific reception, Lysis, Hipparchus</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s dedication to Pope Paul III. He describes his fear of ridicule from those he considers "drones"—pseudophilosophers—and lists the influential friends who convinced him to publish his long-delayed work. He begins to explain his motivation: the inconsistency of current mathematical models.</meta>

...the stupidity of their minds among philosophers, moving like drones among bees. When I weighed these things with myself, the contempt that I had to fear because of the novelty and absurdity of my opinion almost drove me to abandon the work I had begun entirely.

But my friends, while I was hesitating and even resisting for a long time, pulled me back. First among these was **Nicolaus Schönberg**, Cardinal of Capua, renowned in every branch of learning. Closest to him was a man who holds me in great affection, **Tiedemann Giese**, Bishop of Culm <note>Culm is the Latin name for Chełmno, a city in Poland where Giese served as bishop and supported Copernicus.</note>, a most devoted student of sacred and all fine literature. For he often urged me, sometimes even adding reproaches, demanding that I publish this book and finally allow it to come into the light, which had lain hidden with me not just for nine years <note>This is a reference to the Roman poet Horace’s advice in *Ars Poetica* to keep a manuscript for nine years before publishing it to ensure its quality.</note>, but now into a fourth nine-year period <note>Copernicus reveals he has been refining his theory for nearly thirty-six years.</note>. Not a few other most eminent and learned men urged the same upon me, exhorting me that I should no longer refuse, because of the fear I had conceived, to contribute my labor for the common benefit of students of **Mathematics**. They argued that the more absurd my doctrine of the Earth's motion seemed to most people now, the more admiration and favor it would earn once they saw the "fog of absurdity" cleared away by the most transparent demonstrations through the publication of my commentaries. Thus, led by these persuaders and by this hope, I finally allowed my friends to proceed with the publication of the work they had so long requested of me.

Perhaps **Your Holiness** will not wonder so much that I have dared to bring these "night-labors" <note>original: "lucubrationes"; a term referring to scholarly work produced late at night by lamplight.</note> of mine into the light, after I have spent so much effort in elaborating them that I did not hesitate to commit my thoughts regarding the motion of the Earth even to writing. Rather, what you likely expect to hear from me is how it entered my mind to dare to imagine any motion of the Earth, contrary to the accepted opinion of Mathematicians and almost contrary to common sense. Therefore, I do not wish it to be hidden from **Your Holiness** that I was moved to think of another method of calculating the motions of the spheres of the world for no other reason than that I realized Mathematicians are inconsistent with themselves in their investigations of them. First, they are so uncertain regarding the motion of the Sun and Moon that they cannot even [determine the length of] the returning year...

<meta>This page continues the "Preface by the Author" (Copernicus's dedication to Pope Paul III). # AUTHOR'S PREFACE.

...they might be able to demonstrate and observe your greatness. Next, in establishing the motions of these, as well as the other five **wandering stars** <note>original: *errantium stellarum*; this refers to the five planets known since antiquity: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, they use neither the same principles and assumptions, nor the same demonstrations of apparent revolutions and motions. For some use **homocentric** circles only, others **eccentrics** and **epicycles**, by which, however, they do not fully achieve the desired results. For those who relied on <term>homocentrics</term> <note>These are spheres that share a common center, specifically the Earth, a system favored by Aristotle.</note>, although they demonstrated that some diverse motions could be composed from them, they could establish nothing certain that would correspond precisely to the phenomena. Those, however, who devised <term>eccentrics</term> <note>A circle whose center is "off-center" from the Earth to account for varying planetary speeds.</note>, although they seem for the most part to have resolved the apparent motions with matching numbers, nevertheless admitted many things in the meantime which seem to contradict the first principles regarding the equality of motion. Nor could they find or gather from them the principal thing—that is, the **form of the world** and the certain symmetry of its parts. But it happened to them just as if someone were to take hands, feet, a head, and other limbs from different places—painted excellently indeed, but not in comparison to a single body—with no part corresponding to the others, so that a **monster** rather than a human being would be composed from them. Thus, in the process of demonstration, which they call the <term>method</term> <note>original: μέθοδον (*methodon*)</note>, they are found either to have passed over something necessary or to have admitted something alien and hardly pertaining to the matter. This would surely not have happened to them if they had followed certain principles. For if the hypotheses they assumed were not fallacious, everything following from them would undoubtedly be verified. Although these things I am saying now may be obscure, they will nevertheless become clearer in their proper place.

When I had revolved this uncertainty of mathematical traditions regarding the calculation of the motions of the world's spheres in my mind for a long time, it began to weary me that no more certain reason for the motions of the **machine of the world** <note>original: *machinae mundi*; a metaphor suggesting the universe is a divinely designed mechanism.</note>—which was created for our sake by the best and most orderly Maker of all—was clear to the **philosophers**, who otherwise scrutinize the smallest details with such exquisite care in respect to that universe. Therefore, I took up the task of rereading the books of all the philosophers I could obtain, to search whether anyone had ever been of the opinion that there were other motions...

<meta>This page continues the "Preface by the Author" addressed to Pope Paul III. # AUTHOR'S PREFACE.

...the motions of the world's spheres were different from those established by those who teach mathematics in the schools. And indeed, I first found in the writings of **Cicero** that **Nicetas** <note>original: *Nicetum*; Copernicus refers to Hicetas of Syracuse, a 4th-century BCE philosopher who believed the Earth rotated on its axis.</note> had sensed that the earth moves. Afterward, I also found in **Plutarch** that others were of the same opinion. I have chosen to write down his words here, so that they may be available to everyone:

->Others say that the earth stands still, but **Philolaus the Pythagorean** says that it travels in a circle around the fire in an oblique path, similar to the sun and the moon. **Heraclides of Pontus** and **Ecphantus the Pythagorean** also grant motion to the earth, not in the sense of changing its position, but like a wheel turning from west to east around its own center.<- <note>Copernicus provides this quote in the original Greek from Plutarch’s *Opinions of the Philosophers*. It highlights that the idea of a moving Earth was not a new "heresy" but a rediscovered ancient theory.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Taking the opportunity from this, I too began to think about the **mobility of the earth**. And although the opinion seemed absurd, yet because I knew that others before me had been granted this liberty—to imagine any circles they wished to explain the phenomena of the stars—I thought it might easily be permitted to me as well to test whether, by assuming some motion of the earth, more reliable demonstrations of the revolutions of the celestial spheres could be found than those produced by others.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And so, having assumed the motions which I attribute to the earth later in this work, I finally found—after many long observations—that if the motions of the rest of the **wandering stars** <note>The planets.</note> are compared to the <term>circulation</term> <note>The orbital revolution.</note> of the earth, and calculated according to the revolution of each star, not only do their phenomena follow as a result, but the orders and sizes of all the stars and spheres, and the heaven itself, are so linked together that in no part can anything be moved without throwing the other parts and the whole universe into confusion. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, in the course of this work, I have followed this order: in the first book I describe all the positions of the spheres, together with the motions I attribute to the earth, so that this book contains what is essentially the general constitution of the universe. In the remaining books, I then compare the motions of the rest of the stars and all the spheres with the mobility of the earth, so that it can be gathered from them to what extent the motions and appearances of the rest of the stars and spheres can be <term>saved</term> <note>In astronomy, "saving the appearances" means creating a mathematical model that matches observed data.</note> if they are compared to the motions of the earth. Nor do I doubt that ingenious and learned mathematicians will agree with me, if they...

<meta>This page concludes Copernicus’s preface to Pope Paul III for his landmark work, *On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres*. Having established that ancient philosophers also considered the Earth’s motion, he now addresses the potential backlash from non-scientists and explains the practical utility of his work for the Church’s calendar reform.</meta>

# AUTHOR'S PREFACE.

...philosophy especially requires that those who wish to know and weigh these matters should examine the demonstrations I have presented in this work, not just in passing, but thoroughly. So that both the learned and the unlearned might see that I do not shrink from anyone's judgment, I preferred to dedicate these labors of mine to Your Holiness rather than to anyone else. This is because, even in this most remote corner of the earth where I live, you are considered the most eminent both in the dignity of your office and in your love for all literature and even **mathematics**. Thus, by your authority and judgment, you can easily suppress the bites of slanderers—even though, as the proverb says, there is no remedy against the bite of a sycophant.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If perhaps there be any **babblers** <note>original Greek: *ματαιολόγοι* (mataiologoi); meaning idle talkers or those who speak nonsense.</note> who, although they are ignorant of all mathematics, yet take it upon themselves to pass judgment on these things, and because of some passage of Scripture miserably distorted to their purpose, dare to find fault with and attack my undertaking; I do not worry about them—so much so that I even despise their judgment as reckless. For it is not unknown that **Lactantius** <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author who famously argued against the existence of the Antipodes and the spherical shape of the Earth.</note>, an otherwise famous writer but a poor mathematician, speaks quite childishly about the shape of the Earth when he mocks those who declared that the Earth has the form of a globe. Therefore, it should not seem strange to the studious if such people mock us as well.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Mathematics is written for mathematicians** <note>original: *Mathemata mathematicis scribuntur*.</note>, to whom these labors of mine, if I am not mistaken, will appear to contribute something even to the Commonwealth of the Church, over which Your Holiness now holds the leadership. For not so long ago, under **Leo X**, when the question of reforming the **Ecclesiastical Calendar** <note>The reform of the Julian calendar was a major issue because the dates of festivals like Easter were drifting away from their astronomical seasons.</note> was being discussed in the **Lateran Council** <note>The Fifth Council of the Lateran (1512–1517).</note>, it remained undecided for the sole reason that the lengths of the years and months and the motions of the Sun and Moon were not yet considered to be measured accurately enough. From that time on, I turned my mind to observing these things more precisely, encouraged by that most distinguished man, **Lord Paul, Bishop of Fossombrone** <note>original: *D. Paulo episcopo Semproniensi*; Paul of Middelburg, who headed the committee on calendar reform.</note>, who was then in charge of that business. What I have achieved in this matter I leave to the judgment of Your Holiness especially, and to all other learned mathematicians. And lest I seem to promise Your Holiness more regarding the utility of this work than I can perform, I now pass on to the undertaking.

### PAGE 23

# FIRST BOOK OF THE REVOLUTIONS
## OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS.

### That the universe is spherical. Chapter I.

[[image: Historiated initial P showing a scholar]]
FIRST we must observe that the universe is globular, either because that very form is the most perfect of all, needing no joint, being a complete whole; or because it is the most capacious of figures, which most suits that which is to contain and preserve all things; or even because the most absolute parts of the universe—I mean the Sun, the Moon, and the stars—are observed in such a form; or because all things seek to be bounded by this form, which appears in drops of water and other liquid bodies, when they desire to be bounded by themselves. Therefore, no one should doubt that such a form has been attributed to the celestial bodies.

### That the earth also is spherical. Chapter II.

[[image: Historiated initial T showing a landscape]]
The Earth also is globular, since from every part it rests upon its center. Although a perfect sphere is not immediately seen in such great height of mountains and descent of valleys, these nevertheless vary the universal roundness of the earth the least bit. This is manifest thus: for to those traveling toward the North from any direction, that pole of the diurnal revolution is gradually raised, while the other is lowered by just as much on the opposite side, and more stars about the North are seen not to set, and in the South certain stars no longer rise. Thus Italy does not see Canopus, which is visible to Egypt. And Italy sees the last star of the River [Eridanus], which our region of a colder climate does not know. On the contrary, to those passing toward the South, those stars are raised, while those which are high to us sink. Meanwhile, the very inclinations of the poles have the same ratio everywhere relative to the measured spaces of the earth, which happens in no other figure than a spherical one. From which it is manifest that the earth also is enclosed by poles, and for this reason is globular. Add also, that the evening eclipses of the Sun and Moon are not perceived by the inhabitants of the East, nor the morning ones by those living in the west; while those in the middle see them, the former indeed later, the latter truly earlier. Navigators also perceive that the waters rest upon the same form, since land which is not seen from a ship is frequently viewed from the top of the mast. And conversely, if something shining is placed on the top of the mast, as the ship moves away from land, it seems to those remaining on the shore to gradually descend, until at last it is hidden as if setting. It is also certain that waters, flowing by their nature, always seek lower places—the same as the earth—and do not strive further from the shore than its convexity allows. For which reason, it follows that the earth is so much higher wherever it rises out of the Ocean.

***

### PAGE 24

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

### How the earth with water forms one globe. Chapter III.

[[image: Historiated initial H showing a face]]
Therefore the surrounding Ocean, pouring forth seas everywhere, fills its deeper descents. And so it was necessary that there be less water than earth, so that the water would not absorb the whole earth—both contending toward the same center by their weight—but so that it might leave some parts of the earth for the safety of living things, and so many islands open here and there. For what else is the continent itself and the world of lands but an island larger than the others? Nor should certain of the Peripatetics be heard, who declared that the universal water is ten times greater than the whole earth. Namely, because in the transmutation of elements, ten parts of water are made from the resolution of one part of earth; taking this conjecture, they say that the earth juts out to some extent because, being cavernous, it is not balanced everywhere according to its weight, and that the center of gravity is one thing, and the center of magnitude another. But they are deceived by ignorance of the geometric art, not knowing that water cannot be even seven times greater so that some part of the earth might remain dry, unless the earth vacated the center of gravity entirely and gave place to the waters as being heavier than itself. Since spheres are to one another in the triple ratio of their diameters [i.e., volume is proportional to the cube of the diameter]. If therefore the earth were the eighth part to seven parts of water, its diameter could not be greater than that which extends from the center to the circumference of the waters; much less could the water be even ten times greater. That there is also no difference between the center of gravity of the earth and the center of its magnitude can be taken from this: that the convexity of the earth extending from the ocean does not continually swell in its withdrawal, for otherwise it would keep back the sea waters as much as possible, and would in no way allow the internal seas and such vast gulfs to break in. Again, the increased depth of the abyss would not cease as one moves from the shore of the ocean, whereby neither an island, nor a rock, nor any bit of land would be encountered by sailors who had progressed further. Now indeed it is certain that between the Egyptian Sea and the Arabian Gulf, scarcely fifteen stadia remain in almost the middle of the world. And conversely, Ptolemy in his *Cosmography* extended the habitable land to the middle circle [the equator], leaving moreover unknown land, where more recent authors have added Cathay and very ample regions even to 60 degrees of longitude: so that now the earth is inhabited for a greater longitude than what remains for the ocean. This will be clearer if the islands found in our age under the Princes of Spain and Portugal are added, and especially America—named after the ship's captain who discovered it—which they consider to be another world of lands because of its size still unknown, whereby we should even less wonder that there are Antipodes or Antichthones. For geometric reason compels us to believe that America itself is diametrically opposite to that part of India on the Ganges, based on its location. From all these things at last, I think it is manifest that the earth and water together rest upon one center of gravity, and that there is no other center of magnitude for the earth; which [earth], since it is heavier, has its gaping parts filled with water, and therefore the water is modest in comparison with the earth, even if perhaps more water appears on the surface. For it is necessary that the earth with the surrounding waters have such a figure as its shadow shows: for it makes the Moon fail [in eclipse] with the circumferences of a perfect circle. Therefore the earth is not flat, as Empedocles and Anaximenes thought; nor drum-shaped, as Leucippus; nor boat-shaped, as Heraclitus; nor hollow in another way, as Democritus. Nor again cylinder-shaped as Anaximander; nor extending from its lower part with an infinite thickness of roots, as Xenophanes, but with an absolute roundness, as the Philosophers believe.

***

### PAGE 26

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

### That the motion of the celestial bodies is uniform, circular, and perpetual, or composed of circular motions. Chapter IIII.

[[image: Historiated initial P]]
After these things we shall recall that the motion of the celestial bodies is circular. For the mobility of a Sphere is to be turned in a circle, expressing its form by that very act, in the simplest body, where it is not possible to find a beginning nor an end, nor to distinguish one from the other, while it moves through the same things into itself. There are, however, several motions according to the multitude of orbs. The most manifest of all is the daily revolution, which the Greeks call *nychthēmeron*, that is, the space of a day and night. By this, the whole universe is thought to glide from east to west, the earth excepted. This is understood as the common measure of all motions, since we also measure time itself chiefly by the number of days. Then we see other revolutions as if struggling against it, that is, from west to east—namely, those of the Sun, the Moon, and the five wandering stars. Thus the Sun dispenses the year to us, and the Moon the months, the most common times; so each of the other five planets makes its own circuit. They are nevertheless in manifold difference: first, because they are not turned around the same poles as that first motion, running through the obliquity of the zodiac [signiferi]. Then, because in their own circuit, they are not seen to be carried uniformly; for the Sun and Moon are detected to be sometimes slow, sometimes swifter in their course. The other five wandering stars, however, we see sometimes even to go backward, and to make stations here and there. And while the Sun always proceeds on its own direct path, they wander in various ways, straying now to the South, now to the North, whence they are called "planets." Add also that sometimes they become nearer to the earth, and are called Perigee, at other times more remote, and are called Apogee. One must nevertheless confess that the motions are circular, or composed of several circles, because these types of inequalities observe a certain law and fixed restitutions, which could not happen if they were not circular. For it is the circle alone that can bring back what has been completed, just as, for example, the Sun, by a motion composed of circles, brings back to us the inequality of days and nights and the four seasons of the year.

***

### PAGE 27

# REVOLUTIONS LIB. I.

In which [the year] several motions are understood. Since it cannot be that a simple celestial body moves irregularly in a single orb. For that would have to happen either because of the inconstancy of the moving power—whether it be derived from without or from an intimate nature—or because of a disparity in the revolved body. Since the intellect shrinks from both, and it is unworthy that such a thing be imagined in those things which are constituted in the best order: it is consistent that their uniform motions appear to us as irregular, either because of the different poles of those circles, or even because the earth is not in the middle of the circles in which they revolve; and to us looking from the earth, it happens because of the unequal distances of these stars that the things nearer to themselves seem larger than those more remote (as is demonstrated in optics); thus in equal circumferences of an orb, because of the different distance of sight, the motions will appear unequal in equal times. For which cause I think it is necessary above all that we carefully observe what the relationship [habitudo] of the earth to the heaven is, lest while we wish to scrutinize the highest things, we are ignorant of those closest to us, and by the same error attribute to celestial things that which belongs to the earth.

### Whether circular motion belongs to the earth, and concerning its location. Chapter V.

[[image: Historiated initial T]]
Now because it has been demonstrated that the earth also has the form of a globe, I think we must see whether motion also follows its form, and what place in the universe it occupies, without which it is not possible to find a certain reason for the appearances in the heaven. Although it is generally agreed among authors that the earth rests in the middle of the universe, so that they think it unthinkable and even ridiculous to feel the contrary. If nevertheless we consider the matter more attentively, it will be seen that this question is not yet settled, and for that reason is by no means to be despised. For every change of place that is seen is either because of the motion of the thing observed, or of the observer, or certainly a disparate change of both. For between things moved equally toward the same things, motion is not perceived—I mean between the thing seen and the observer. The earth, however, is that from which that celestial circuit is viewed and reproduced to our sight. If therefore some motion is assigned to the earth, it will appear the same in all things which are outside it, but in the opposite direction, as if they were passing by; such is the daily revolution first of all. For this seems to snatch the whole universe, except for the earth and those things which are around it. But if you allow the heaven to have nothing of this motion, but that the earth revolves from west to east, if you seriously consider it as far as the apparent rising and setting in the Sun, Moon, and Stars, you will find these things to be so. Since it is the heaven which contains and covers all things, the common place of the universe, it does not immediately appear why motion should not be attributed to the thing contained rather than the container, the located rather than the locater. Certainly Heraclides and Ecphantus the Pythagoreans were of this opinion, and Nicetas of Syracuse in Cicero, revolving the earth in the middle of the universe. For they thought that the stars set by the obstruction of the earth, and rose by its withdrawal. This being assumed, there follows also another, and no less a doubt concerning the location of the earth, although it has now been received and believed by almost everyone that the earth is the middle of the universe. Because if someone denies that the earth occupies the middle or center of the universe, yet does not confess that the distance is so great that it would be comparable to the sphere of the non-wandering stars [fixed stars], but is significant and evident to the orbs of the Sun and other stars, and thinks for that reason their motion appears different, as if they were regulated to another center than the center of the earth, he might perhaps be able to bring forth a not inept reason for the different apparent motion. For that the wandering stars are seen nearer to the earth and the same ones further away, necessarily proves that the center of the earth is not the center of those circles. Whereby it is even less clear whether the earth approaches and recedes from them, or they from the earth. Nor would it be so surprising if someone, besides that daily revolution, should imagine another motion for the earth; namely, that the earth revolves, and even wanders with several motions, and is one of the stars, as Philolaus the Pythagorean is said to have felt—a mathematician of no common sort, since for the sake of visiting him, Plato did not delay to seek Italy, as those who wrote the life of Plato relate. Many indeed have thought it could be demonstrated by geometric reason that the earth is in the middle of the universe, and like a point to the immensity of the heaven, occupying the role of the center, and for that reason is immobile, because when the universe is moved, the center remains unmoved, and those things which are nearest to the center are carried slowest.

***

### PAGE 29

# REVOLUTIONS LIB. I.

### On the immensity of the heaven compared to the size of the earth. Chapter VI.

[[image: Historiated initial Q/V]]
That so great a mass of the earth, however, has no estimation compared to the magnitude of the heaven can be understood from this. Since the limiting circles (for so *horizontes* are interpreted among the Greeks) bisect the whole sphere of the heaven, which could not happen if the size of the earth were significant compared to the heaven, or its distance from the center of the universe. For a circle bisecting a sphere passes through the center of the sphere, and is the greatest of the circumscribable circles. For let the horizon be the circle *A B C D*, while the earth from which our sight is, be *E*, and let *E* itself be the center of the horizon in which the visible things are defined from the non-visible. Let there be observed through a Dioptra or a Horoscopium, or a Chorobates placed in *E*, the beginning of Cancer rising at point *C*, and at that moment the beginning of Capricorn appears to set at *A*. Since therefore *A E C* were in a straight line through the Dioptra, it is certain that it is the diameter of the zodiac, because six Signs terminate a semicircle, and the center *E* is the same as that of the horizon. Again, the revolution being changed, so that the beginning of Capricorn rises in *B*, then also the setting of Cancer will be seen in *D*; and *B E D* will be a straight line and itself the diameter of the zodiac. Now indeed it has appeared that *A E C* is also a diameter of the same circle; it is clear therefore that in the common section, that *E* is the center. So therefore the horizon circle always bisects the zodiac, which is the greatest circle of the sphere. But in a sphere, if a circle bisects any of the greatest circles, it is itself also a greatest circle; therefore the horizon is one of the greatest circles, and its center the same as that of the zodiac, as it appears, although it is nevertheless necessary that the line which is from the surface of the earth be different from that which is from the center; but because of the immensity with respect to the earth, they become in a certain way similar to parallels, which because of excessive distance of the limit appear to be one line, when the mutual space which contains them is made incomparable to their length in sense, in the way that is demonstrated in Optics.

[[image: Geometrical diagram of a circle A B C D with center E]]

***

### PAGE 30

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

By this argument it appears clearly enough that the heaven is immense compared to the earth, and presents the appearance of infinite magnitude, but by the estimation of the senses the earth is with respect to the heaven as a point to a body, and the finite to the infinite in magnitude, nor does it seem to have demonstrated anything else. For it does not follow that the earth must rest in the middle of the universe. Rather, we might even more wonder if such a vastness of the universe should revolve within the space of 24 hours, instead of its smallest part, which is the earth. For as they say the center is immobile, and those things nearest to the center move less, this does not prove that the earth rests in the middle of the universe: no differently than if you say that the heaven revolves but the poles rest, and those things nearest to the poles move least. Just as Cynosura [the Little Bear] is seen to move much more slowly than Aquila or Canicula [Sirius], because it describes a smaller circle nearest the pole; since all those things belong to one sphere, whose mobility ending at its own axis does not allow an equal motion for all its parts, which nevertheless the revolution of the whole brings back in equality of time but not equality of space. To this, therefore, the reason of the argument leans: as if the earth were a part of the celestial sphere, and of the same species and motion, so that being nearest the center it would move little. It will therefore be moved itself, being a body, and not the center, in the same time through similar circumferences of the celestial circle, although smaller. How false this is, is clearer than light: for it would be necessary that it always be noon in one place, and always midnight in another, so that neither the daily risings nor settings could happen, since there would be one and inseparable motion of the whole and the part. But of those things which the difference of nature separates, the reason is far different, so that those which are enclosed in a shorter circuit are revolved more quickly than those which encompass a larger circle. Thus Saturn, the highest of the wandering stars, is revolved in the thirtieth year; and the Moon, which is undoubtedly nearest to the earth, completes its monthly circuit; and finally the earth itself will be thought to circle in the space of a day and night. Therefore the same doubt about the daily revolution will rise again. But even its location is still sought, even less certain from the things said above. For that demonstration contains nothing else than the indefinite magnitude of the heaven to the earth. But to what extent this immensity extends is by no means certain.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the main text of Copernicus's "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium." Following the errata list from the previous page, we now move into Book One, where Copernicus establishes the fundamental geometric principles of his universe. He begins with the classical Aristotelian and Ptolemaic arguments for the sphericity of the universe and the Earth before later introducing his radical heliocentric theory.</meta>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS ON THE REVOLUTIONS
## BOOK ONE.

### That the universe is spherical. Chapter I.

[An ornate initial letter P, decorated with the figure of a scholar at his desk]
IN THE BEGINNING we must observe that the universe <note>original: "mundus"; in this context, Copernicus refers to the entire cosmos or the heavens.</note> is spherical, either because that form is the most perfect of all, needing no joints and being a complete whole; or because it is the most capacious of shapes, which is most fitting for that which is to contain and preserve all things; or even because the most finished parts of the universe—I mean the Sun, the Moon, and the stars—are observed to have such a shape; or because all things seek to be bounded by this form, which is apparent in drops of water and other liquid bodies when they desire to be bounded by themselves. Therefore, no one should doubt that such a form has been assigned to the celestial bodies.

### That the earth is also spherical. Chapter II.

[An ornate initial letter T, decorated with a landscape showing hills and trees]
That the earth is also spherical, since it presses upon its center from every side. Although a perfect sphere is not immediately apparent because of such great height of mountains and the depth of valleys, these nevertheless do not significantly alter the overall roundness of the earth. This is manifest in this way: for to those traveling anywhere toward the North, that pole of the daily revolution is gradually raised, while the other pole sinks by the same amount in the opposite direction; and many stars around the North are seen not to set, while in the South some stars no longer rise. Thus Italy does not see Canopus, which is visible in Egypt. And Italy sees the last star of the River <note>the constellation Eridanus</note>, which our region of a colder climate <note>Copernicus refers here to his home in Warmia, Poland/Prussia.</note> does not know. Conversely, for those traveling South, those stars are raised, while those which are high for us sink down. Meanwhile, the inclinations of the poles have everywhere the same ratio to the distances measured on the earth, which [occurs...]

<summary>In these opening chapters, Copernicus argues for the spherical nature of both the universe and the Earth, citing geometric perfection, the behavior of liquids, and astronomical observations made during travel.</summary>

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus's physical proofs for the Earth’s shape. The previous page ended mid-sentence, discussing how the North Pole rises and the South Pole sinks by the same amount as one travels, proving the Earth's curvature from North to South. This page extends that proof to the East and West and then transitions to Chapter III, which discusses the relationship between land and water.</meta>

BY THE SAME amount <note>Completing the thought from the previous page: as one moves North or South, the celestial poles change altitude proportionally.</note> as in no other shape but the spherical. Whence it is manifest that the Earth is also enclosed between poles and is, for this reason, a globe. Add also that the inhabitants of the East do not perceive evening eclipses of the Sun and Moon, nor do those living in the West perceive morning ones; while those in between see the former later and the latter earlier. <note>Copernicus is arguing that if the Earth were flat, everyone would see an eclipse at the same time. The time difference proves the Earth's curvature from East to West.</note>

That the waters also rest upon this same shape is perceived by sailors; for land which is not visible from the ship itself is often sighted from the top of the mast. Conversely, if something shining is placed on the top of the mast, as the ship moves away from land, it seems to descend little by little to those remaining on the shore, until finally it is hidden as if setting. It is also certain that waters, flowing by their nature, always seek lower places, just as the earth does, and do not push further from the shore than the convexity of the shore allows. Wherefore, the land is necessarily that much higher wherever it rises out of the Ocean.

### How the earth with the water forms a single globe. Chapter III.

[An ornate initial letter H, decorated with a face]
Hence the surrounding Ocean, pouring out its seas everywhere, fills the deeper descents of the Earth. Therefore it was necessary that there be less water than land, lest the water swallow the whole earth—since both strive toward the same center by their weight—but rather that it might leave some parts of the earth for the safety of living creatures, and so many islands scattered here and there. For what else is the continent itself, the orb of lands, but an island larger than the others? 

Nor should we listen to certain of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> who declared that the whole volume of water is ten times larger than the whole earth. They base this conjecture on the idea that in the transformation of the elements, one part of earth creates ten parts of water when it dissolves. They say the earth projects to some extent in such a way that it is not balanced everywhere according to gravity, being full of caves, and that the center of gravity is one thing, while the center of magnitude <note>The geometric center.</note> is another. 

But they are deceived by ignorance of the art of Geometry. They do not realize that water cannot even be seven times greater without the entire earth being submerged, unless the earth moved away from the center of gravity and gave place to the waters as being heavier than itself. For the volumes of spheres are to one another in the triplicate ratio <note>The ratio of the cubes; for example, if a diameter is doubled, the volume increases eightfold.</note> of their diameters. If therefore the earth were [composed of] seven parts of water...

<summary>Copernicus provides observational evidence for the Earth's roundness using eclipses and the "ship's mast" proof, then argues against the Aristotelian view that water vastly outweighs land.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Chapter III, providing physical and geographical evidence that the Earth and its waters share a single center of gravity and together form a perfect sphere. It concludes with a list of ancient theories on the Earth's shape that Copernicus rejects in favor of a globe.</meta>

->ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK I.<-

...but if it were an eighth, its diameter could not be greater than the distance from the center to the surface of the waters. So far is it from the truth that the water is ten times larger <note>Copernicus is refuting a common medieval belief, often attributed to a misunderstanding of Aristotle or Esdras, that water was ten times more voluminous than land.</note>. That there is no difference between the center of gravity of the Earth and the center of its magnitude can be understood from this: the convexity of the land spreading out from the ocean does not continuously swell as it moves further away; otherwise, it would block the sea waters as much as possible and would not allow internal seas or such vast gulfs to break through. Conversely, the depth of the abyss would not stop increasing from the shore of the ocean, so that no island, reef, or any bit of land would be encountered by those sailing further out. 

Now, indeed, it is well known that between the Egyptian Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note> and the Arabian Gulf <note>The Red Sea</note>, barely fifteen <term>stades</term> <note>original: "stadia"; an ancient unit of length, roughly 600 feet, though the exact length varied. Copernicus uses it to describe the narrow Isthmus of Suez.</note> remain, located nearly in the middle of the world. On the other hand, Ptolemy in his *Cosmography* <note>Referring to the *Geography* of Claudius Ptolemy, the standard geographical text of the time.</note> extended the habitable land as far as the middle circle, leaving beyond it unknown land where more recent authors have added <term>Cathay</term> <note>original: "Cathagyam"; an archaic name for Northern China.</note> and most extensive regions as far as 60 degrees of longitude. Thus, the land is now inhabited over a greater longitude than what remains for the ocean. 

This will be even clearer if we add the islands found in our own time under the Princes of Spain and Portugal, and especially <term>America</term> <note>Named after Amerigo Vespucci. This is a very early mention of America in a scientific text (published 1543).</note>, named after the discoverer who was the captain of the ships. Because of its size, which is still not fully known, they think it is another world, besides many other islands previously unknown. Therefore, we should not be surprised that there are <term>Antipodes</term> or <term>Antichthones</term> <note>People who live on the opposite side of the Earth.</note>. For geometric reasoning forces us to believe that America itself is diametrically opposite to India near the Ganges. 

From all these facts, I think it is manifest that the land and the water together rest upon a single center of gravity, and that this is no different from the center of the Earth’s magnitude. Since the earth is heavier, its gaping parts are filled with water; and therefore, compared to the earth, the amount of water is modest, even though more water may perhaps appear on the surface. For it is necessary that the Earth, along with its surrounding waters, has the same shape that its shadow shows: for it produces a lunar eclipse with the arcs of a perfect circle. 

Therefore, the Earth is not flat, as Empedocles and Anaximenes thought; nor drum-shaped <note>original: "Tympanoides"</note>, as Leucippus; nor boat-shaped <note>original: "Scaphoides"</note>, as Heraclitus; nor hollow in some other way, as Democritus. Nor, again, is it cylinder-shaped <note>original: "Cylindroides"</note> as Anaximander; nor is it an infinite thickness extending downward from its lower part, as Xenophanes; but it is of an absolute roundness, as the Philosophers hold.

->a ij<- <note>This is a signature mark, used by early printers to help binders assemble the book in the correct order.</note>

<summary>Copernicus uses geographical evidence, including the discovery of America and Cathay, to prove that Earth is a sphere where land and water share a single center of gravity. He concludes by rejecting various ancient theories of a flat or shaped Earth in favor of a perfect globe, as evidenced by the round shadow cast during lunar eclipses.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the physical shape of the Earth (Chapter III) to the nature of celestial movement. Copernicus begins to establish the geometric principles—specifically the necessity of circular motion—that underly his entire system.</meta>

NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

### That the motion of the heavenly bodies is uniform, circular, and perpetual, or composed of circular motions. Chapter IV.

**A**fter this, we shall recall that the motion of the heavenly bodies is circular. For the natural property of a sphere is to turn in a circle; by this very act, it expresses its own form as the simplest of bodies, wherein one can find neither a beginning nor an end, nor distinguish one part from another, as it moves through the same path back into itself. However, there are multiple motions because of the vast number of spheres. The most obvious of all is the daily revolution, which the Greeks call *nychthēmeron* <note>original: "νυχθήμερον"; a period of twenty-four hours, encompassing both a full day and a full night.</note>. By this motion, the entire universe—excepting the Earth—is thought to be carried from east to west. This is understood as the common measure of all motions, since we measure time itself primarily by the number of days.

Then, we see other revolutions that seem to move in the opposite direction—that is, from west to east; I am speaking of the Sun, the Moon, and the five wandering stars <term>planets</term> <note>From the Greek "planētēs," meaning "wanderer." In the 16th century, the Sun and Moon were often grouped with the five visible planets as "seven wanderers."</note>. In this way, the Sun regulates our year and the Moon our months, which are the most common divisions of time. Likewise, each of the other five planets completes its own circuit.

Yet, these motions differ in many ways. First, they do not revolve around the same poles as the primary daily motion, but instead travel through the obliquity of the zodiac <term>signifer</term> <note>original: "signiferi"; literally the "sign-bearer," the Latin name for the belt of the heavens containing the twelve constellations of the zodiac.</note>. Secondly, in their own circuits, they do not appear to move uniformly. We find that the Sun and Moon are sometimes slow and at other times faster in their courses. As for the other five wandering stars, we perceive them sometimes even moving backward <note>original: "repedare"; this refers to "retrograde motion," where a planet appears to move in reverse against the background of stars.</note> and coming to a standstill in various places. And while the Sun always proceeds along its own direct path, the planets wander in various ways, straying sometimes toward the South and sometimes toward the North; it is for this reason they are called "planets." Add to this that they are sometimes nearer to the Earth, called <term>perigee</term> <note>From the Greek, meaning "near the Earth."</note>, and at other times further away, called <term>apogee</term> <note>From the Greek, meaning "away from the Earth."</note>.

Nevertheless, we must admit that these motions are circular, or composed of several circles. This is because these irregularities observe a fixed law and occur at regular intervals, which could not happen if they were not circular. For only a circle can bring back what has already passed; for example, the Sun, through a motion composed of circles, restores to us the inequality of days and nights and the four seasons of the year. 
restores...

<summary>Copernicus explains that celestial bodies must move in circles because their cycles repeat predictably over time. He acknowledges that while planets appear to speed up, slow down, or move backward, these complex appearances are actually caused by combinations of uniform circular motions.</summary>
<keywords>circular motion, uniform motion, planets, zodiac, retrograde motion, perigee, apogee, nychthemeron</keywords>

--- Page 27 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument for the uniformity of celestial motion. Copernicus concludes Chapter IV by explaining why movements appear irregular to us (due to perspective and the Earth’s position) before transitioning to Chapter V, where he begins his revolutionary argument that the Earth itself might be in motion.</meta>

->ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK I<-

brings it back to its starting point, in which several motions are understood. For it is impossible that a simple celestial body should move irregularly in a single sphere. For such a thing would have to happen either because of an inconstancy in the moving power—whether it be derived from an external source <note>original: "asciticia"; referring to an external force acting upon the body</note> or from its own internal nature—or because of some unevenness in the revolving body itself. Since the intellect shrinks from both of these explanations, and it is unworthy to imagine such a flaw in those things which are established in the most perfect order, it is reasonable that their uniform motions appear non-uniform to us. This happens either because they have different poles for their circles, or because the Earth is not in the center of the circles in which they revolve. To us, looking from the Earth, the passage of these stars appears to vary because of their unequal distances; those closer to us seem larger than those further away (as has been demonstrated in the study of optics). Thus, on equal arcs of a circle, the motions will appear unequal in equal amounts of time due to the different distances of the observer's sight. For this reason, I think it is necessary above all that we carefully observe the relationship <term>habitudo</term> <note>Copernicus uses "habitudo" to describe the geometric and spatial relationship between the Earth and the heavens.</note> of the Earth to the heavens, so that while we wish to examine the highest things, we do not remain ignorant of what is closest to us, and by the same error attribute to the celestial bodies that which belongs to the Earth.

### Whether a circular motion belongs to the Earth, and concerning its location. Chapter V.

**N**ow <note>The historiated initial "T" combined with the text "am" forms "Tam," a transition meaning "So" or "Now."</note> because it has been demonstrated that the Earth also has the form of a globe, I believe we must see whether a motion also follows from its form, and what place in the universe <term>universitatis</term> it occupies. Without these facts, it is impossible to find a certain explanation for the appearances in the heavens. Although authors generally agree that the Earth remains at rest <term>quiescere</term> in the middle of the universe, so much so that they think the contrary is unbelievable and even ridiculous; yet, if we consider the matter more closely, it will be seen that this question is not yet settled, and therefore by no means to be despised. 

For every change in place that is perceived is due either to the motion of the object seen, or to the motion of the observer, or certainly to an unequal movement of both. For between things moving equally in the same direction, motion is not perceived—I mean between the object seen and the observer. Now, the Earth is the place from which that celestial circuit is observed and reproduced for our sight. If, therefore, some motion is...

...assigned <note>The text "depu-" at the bottom of the page is a catchword for "deputetur" (assigned/attributed) on the following page.</note>

<summary>Copernicus argues that apparent irregularities in planetary motion are optical illusions caused by the observer's position. He then introduces the radical possibility that the Earth itself might be moving, despite the prevailing opinion that it remains stationary at the center of the universe.</summary>
