--- Page 28 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from Chapter IV to Chapter V of Book I. Having established that celestial motions appear irregular due to our perspective, Copernicus now begins his famous argument for the motion of the Earth, citing ancient Pythagorean philosophers to support his radical hypothesis.</meta>

->BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS<-

assigned to the Earth, that same motion will appear in all things that are outside it, but in the opposite direction, as if they were passing by. This is especially true of the daily revolution. For this motion seems to carry away the whole universe, except for the Earth and those things that are around it. But if you were to grant that the heavens have nothing of this motion, and that the Earth instead turns from the west to the east, you will find—if you seriously consider it—that this is indeed the case regarding the apparent rising and setting of the Sun, Moon, and stars. 

Since the heavens are what contain and cover all things, acting as the common place of the universe, it is not immediately clear why motion should not be attributed to the contained rather than the container, or to that which is located rather than to that which provides the location. Indeed, Heraclides and Ecphantus the Pythagoreans, as well as Nicetas of Syracuse (as mentioned in Cicero), were of this opinion, believing that the Earth rotated in the center of the universe. For they thought that the stars set because the Earth’s obstruction <note>original: "obiectu"; the physical bulk of the Earth casting a shadow or blocking the line of sight</note> stood in their way, and that they rose when the Earth moved out of the way. 

Once this is assumed, there follows another doubt about the Earth’s location, no less serious than the first, even though almost everyone has now accepted and believed that the Earth is the center of the universe. For if someone were to deny that the Earth occupies the middle or center of the universe, yet does not admit that the distance is so great as to be comparable to the sphere of the fixed stars <note>meaning the stars are so far away that the Earth's position doesn't change their appearance</note>, but is nonetheless significant and evident relative to the orbits <term>orbes</term> of the Sun and other stars—and if they think that the motion of those stars appears different because they are regulated by a center other than the center of the Earth—they might be able to provide a reasonable explanation for why these motions appear so diverse. 

For the fact that the wandering stars <note>The "planets," from the Greek "planētēs" meaning wanderers.</note> are seen closer to the Earth at some times and further away at others, necessarily proves that the center of the Earth is not the center of their circular orbits. From this, it is even less clear whether the Earth approaches and recedes <note>original: "annuant & abnuant"; literally to nod toward and away from</note> from them, or they from the Earth. 

Nor would it be so strange if someone supposed another motion for the Earth besides that daily revolution. In fact, Philolaus the Pythagorean—a mathematician of no common sort, and one whom Plato traveled to Italy specifically to visit, as his biographers record—is said to have believed that the Earth rotates, wanders with several motions, and is one of the stars. 

However, many have thought it can be demonstrated by geometric reasoning that the Earth is in the center of the universe; that compared to the immensity of the heavens it holds the place of a mere point, acting as the center; and for that reason it is immobile, because when the universe moves, the center remains...

<summary>Copernicus argues that the daily rotation of the heavens may actually be the rotation of the Earth and suggests that the Earth might not be the center of all planetary orbits.</summary>
<keywords>daily revolution, Heraclides, Philolaus, planetary orbits, Pythagorean philosophers, relative motion, central Earth</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from Chapter V, where Copernicus discussed the possibility of Earth’s motion. Having suggested the Earth might rotate or move from its central position, he now transitions into Chapter VI to address the massive scale of the universe, arguing that the Earth is effectively a mere point in comparison to the vastness of the heavens.</meta>

->OF THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK I.<-

...remains unmoved, and those things which are closest to the center are carried along most slowly.

### On the immensity of the heavens compared to the size of the Earth. Chapter VI.

**T**hat the mass <note>original: "moles"</note> of the Earth, though so great, is of no account compared to the magnitude of the heavens can be understood from this: the "limiting circles" (for that is how *horizons* <note>original: "ὁρίζοντες" (horizontes)</note> are translated among the Greeks) cut the entire sphere of the sky into two equal parts. This could not happen if the size of the Earth were significant compared to the heavens, or if its distance from the center of the world were notable. For a circle that cuts a sphere into two equal parts must pass through the center of that sphere, and it is the greatest of the circles that can be drawn around it. 

Let the circle of the horizon be **A B C D**, and let the Earth, from which our sight originates, be **E**, which is also the center of the horizon that divides the things that are visible from those that are not. Let the beginning of Cancer <note>The zodiac sign of the summer solstice</note> be observed rising at point **C** through a <term>Dioptra</term> <note>A classical sighting instrument used for measuring angles and leveling</note>, or a <term>Horoscopium</term> <note>An instrument for observing the positions of the stars, not to be confused with a modern astrological chart</note>, or a <term>Chorobates</term> <note>A long wooden level used by Roman engineers for surveying</note> placed at **E**, and at 그 same moment the beginning of Capricorn <note>The zodiac sign of the winter solstice</note> is seen setting at point **A**. Since **A**, **E**, and **C** are in a straight line according to the sighting instrument, it is certain that this line is the diameter of the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi"; literally "the sign-bearer," the circle of the sky containing the twelve constellations</note>, because six signs of the Zodiac mark out a semicircle, and the center **E** is the same as that of the horizon. 

Again, after the revolution has changed so that the beginning of Capricorn rises at **B**, the setting of Cancer will then also be seen at **D**. The line **B E D** will be a straight line and itself a diameter of the Zodiac. Now, it has already been shown that **A E C** is also a diameter of the same circle; it is therefore clear that the point **E** at their intersection is the center. Thus, the circle of the horizon always bisects the Zodiac, which is a "great circle" <note>A circle on a sphere's surface that has the same circumference as the sphere itself</note> of the celestial sphere. However, on a sphere, if a circle cuts any of the great circles through the middle, the cutting circle itself must also be a great circle. Therefore, the horizon is one of the great circles, and its center is the same as that of the Zodiac as it appears to us. 

Nevertheless, the line originating from the surface of the Earth must be different from the line originating from its center. But because of the immense distance of the heavens compared to the Earth, these lines become effectively like parallel lines; due to the excessive distance of the point they reach, they appear to be a single line, because the space between them is...

<summary>Copernicus uses geometric proofs and astronomical sightings of the Zodiac to demonstrate that the Earth is effectively a point of no size when compared to the vastness of the celestial sphere.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the geometric argument from Chapter VI. Copernicus has been demonstrating that because the horizon always bisects the celestial sphere exactly in half, the Earth must be a mere point in comparison to the vastness of the heavens. He is now concluding that mathematical proof and moving toward the physical implications of a rotating Earth.</meta>

->BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS<-

...the distance <note>Refers to the distance between the Earth's center and its surface</note> becomes incomparable to the length of the lines of sight, in the same way that is demonstrated in the field of Optics. By this argument, it appears clearly enough that the heavens are immense in comparison with the Earth, and present the appearance of an infinite magnitude. Moreover, by the estimation of our senses, the Earth is to the heavens as a point is to a body, and as the finite is to the infinite in magnitude. Yet, nothing else seems to have been demonstrated. For it does not follow from this that the Earth must necessarily rest in the middle of the universe. Indeed, we should wonder all the more if such a vastness of the world should revolve in the space of twenty-four hours, rather than its smallest part, which is the Earth.

For as for the claim that the center is immobile and that things closest to the center move the least, this does not prove that the Earth rests in the middle of the world. It is no different than if you were to say that the sky turns, but the poles stay still, and those things closest to the poles move the least. Just as the **Little Bear** <note>original: "Cynosura"</note> is seen to move much more slowly than the **Eagle** <note>original: "Aquila"</note> or the **Dog Star** <note>original: "Canicula" (Sirius)</note>, because it describes a smaller circle being closest to the pole. Since all these things belong to a single sphere, the movement of that sphere—which vanishes at its axis—does not allow all its parts an equal motion; nonetheless, the revolution of the whole brings them back around in the same amount of time, even if not across the same distance of space.

The logic of their argument, therefore, relies on the assumption that the Earth is a part of the celestial sphere, sharing the same nature and motion, so that, being close to the center, it moves very little. Therefore, the Earth itself—existing as a body and not the center—will also move across similar (though smaller) arcs of a celestial circle in the same amount of time. How false this is, is clearer than light! For it would follow that it would always be noon in one place and always midnight in another, so that the daily sunrises and sunsets could not occur, since the motion of the whole and the part would be one and inseparable.

However, for things that are distinct and separate, the logic is very different: those enclosed in a smaller circuit revolve faster than those which encompass a larger circle. Thus **Saturn**, the highest of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>, revolves in its thirtieth year, and the **Moon**, which is undoubtedly closest to the Earth, completes its monthly circuit; and finally, the Earth itself will be thought to travel around in the space of a day and a night. Therefore, the same doubt about the daily revolution rises again. Furthermore, the Earth's place is still sought, rendered even less certain by what was said above. For that demonstration <note>regarding the horizon</note> establishes nothing other than the indefinite magnitude of the heavens compared to the Earth. But how far this immensity extends is not at all clear.

Why...

<summary>Copernicus argues that the Earth's apparent position at the center of the universe is a matter of scale, not physical necessity. He challenges the traditional view by suggesting it is more logical for the small Earth to rotate than for the entire vast universe to revolve around it every 24 hours.</summary>

### REVOLUTIONS, BOOK I.

#### Why the ancients thought the earth rested in the middle of the universe as a center. Chapter VII.

Wherefore, by certain other reasons, the ancient Philosophers attempted to affirm that the earth stands together in the middle of the universe. They allege gravity and levity as the most powerful cause. Forsooth, the element of earth is the heaviest, and all weighty things are carried toward it, striving toward its innermost center. For since the earth is spherical, into which heavy things are carried from all sides [abbrev: *undequaque*] at right angles to the surface by their own nature, they would fall together toward its center unless they were held back at the surface itself; since a straight line, which conforms at right angles to the boundary plane that touches the sphere, leads to the center. Those things, indeed, which are carried toward the middle, it seems to follow that they should rest in the middle. Therefore, the whole earth will rest all the more in the middle, and since it receives all falling things into itself, it will remain immobile by its own weight.

In the same way, they also [abbrev: *quoque*] strive to prove it by the reason of motion and its nature. For Aristotle says that the motion of one and a simple body is simple: and of simple motions, one is rectilinear, the other circular. Of rectilinear motions, one is upward, the other downward. Wherefore, every simple motion is either toward the middle (which is downward), or away from the middle (which is upward), or around the middle, and this is circular. Now, it is fitting for earth and water indeed, which are considered heavy, to be carried downward, which is to seek the middle. For air and fire, which are endowed with levity, to be moved upward and away from the middle: it seems consistent [abbrev: *consentaneum*] that a rectilinear motion be granted to these four elements, but that celestial bodies are turned in a circle around the middle [abbrev: *medium*]. These things Aristotle says. 

If therefore, says [abbrev: *inquit*] Ptolemaeus of Alexandria, the earth were turned, at least by a daily revolution, the opposite of the aforementioned things would necessarily happen. For the motion would have to be most rapid [abbrev: *concitatissimum*], and its speed [abbrev: *acceleritatem*] insuperable, which in twenty-four hours would traverse the whole [abbrev: *totum*] circuit [abbrev: *ambitum*] of the earth. But those things which are stirred by a sudden rotation seem altogether unfit for collection, and rather dispersed when united, unless they are contained by some cohesive firmness: and long ago, he says, the scattered earth would have fallen out of the heaven itself (which is quite ridiculous)

***

### PAGE 32

and even more so, living creatures and any other loose weights would by no means remain unshaken [abbrev: *inconcussa*]. But neither would things falling in a straight line reach the place destined for them and to the perpendicular, which would have been withdrawn in the meantime by such great swiftness. Clouds also [abbrev: *quoque*] and whatever [abbrev: *quaecunque*] other things are hanging in the air, we would always see being carried toward the west.

#### Solution to the said reasons, and their insufficiency. Chapter VIII.

By these surely and similar causes they say the earth [abbrev: *terram*] rests in the middle of the universe, and without a doubt [abbrev: *procul dubio*] it is so. But if anyone should think that the earth is turned, he will certainly say that the motion is natural, not violent [abbrev: *violentum*]. Those things which are according to nature, however, produce effects contrary to those which are according to violence. For those things to which force or impetus is applied must be dissolved, and cannot long subsist: but those which happen by nature are rightly disposed and preserved in their best composition. 

In vain, therefore, does Ptolemaeus fear that the earth and all terrestrial things would be dispersed in a revolution made through the efficacy of nature, which is far different from that of art, or what human genius could attain. But why does he not also suspect this even more concerning the universe, whose motion must be as much swifter as the heaven is greater than the earth? Or has the heaven become immense for the reason that it is driven away from the middle by an ineffable vehemence of motion, destined to collapse otherwise if it stood still? Certainly, if this reason held place, the magnitude of the heaven would also go on to infinity. For the more the motion itself is carried into the heights by impetus, the swifter the motion will be, on account of the ever-increasing circumference, which it must traverse in the space of twenty-four hours: and in turn, as the motion increases, the immensity of the heaven would increase. Thus velocity would promote magnitude, and magnitude velocity, unto infinity. But according to that physical axiom, that which is infinite cannot be traversed, nor moved by any reason [abbrev: *ratione*]: the heaven will necessarily stand still. 

But they say that outside the heaven there is no body, no place, no vacuum, and absolutely nothing, and therefore there is nowhere the heaven could escape to: then it is truly a wonder if something can be held back by nothing. Yet if the heaven were infinite, and finite only by an internal concavity, perhaps it will be more truly verified that there is nothing outside the heaven, since everything [abbrev: *uniquodque*]

***

### PAGE 33

which may be in it, whatever magnitude it occupies, yet the heaven will remain immobile. For the most powerful reason by which they strive to prove the world [abbrev: *mundum*] is finite is motion. Whether, therefore, the world be finite or infinite, let us leave it to the dispute of the natural philosophers [*physiologorum*]: holding this as certain, that the earth, enclosed by poles, is bounded by a spherical surface. 

Why therefore do we still hesitate to grant to it a mobility consistent with its form by nature, rather than that the whole world should slide, whose end is ignored and cannot be known, and why should we not admit that there is an appearance of daily revolution in the heaven, but the reality is in the earth? And that these things are just as if the Virgilian Aeneas were saying: "*We are carried forward from the port, and lands and cities recede.*" For since a ship floats under tranquility, all things which are outside are seen by the sailors to be moved according to the image of that motion, and in turn they think themselves to be at rest with all things that are with them. So indeed it can happen in the motion of the earth, that the whole world is thought to go around. 

What then should we say of the clouds and other things in any way hanging in the air, or subsiding, and again tending toward the heights? Unless that not only the earth with the aqueous element joined to it is thus moved, but also a not insignificant part of the air, and whatever things in the same way have kinship [abbrev: *habent*] with the earth. Either because the nearby air, mixed with earthy or watery matter, follows the same nature as the earth, or because the motion of the air is acquired, which it participates in from the earth through contiguity by perpetual revolution and without resistance. 

In turn, with equal wonder, they say the highest region of the air follows the celestial motion [abbrev: *motu*], which those sudden stars—I mean Comets and those called *Pogonias* [bearded comets] by the Greeks—indicate, to whose generation they assign that very place, and which like other stars rise and set. We can say that part of the air, on account of its great distance from the earth, is deprived of that terrestrial motion. Hence the air which is closest to the earth will appear tranquil [abbrev: *tranquillus*], and things suspended in it likewise, unless they are agitated to and fro by wind or any other impetus, as happens. For what else is wind in the air than a wave in the sea? We must admit that the motion of falling and ascending things is twofold in comparison to the world, and altogether composed [abbrev: *compositum*] of rectilinear and circular. Since those things which are pressed down by their weight,

***

### PAGE 34

since they are mostly earthy, there is no doubt but that the parts preserve the same [abbrev: *eandem*] nature as their whole. Nor does it happen otherwise in those things which are carried into the heights by fiery force. For even this terrestrial fire is nourished mostly by earthy matter, and they define flame as nothing other than burning smoke. It is the property of fire, however, to extend what it has invaded, which it does with such force that by no reason and by no machines can it be restrained from completing its work after breaking its prison. 

The extensive motion, however, is from the center to the circumference; and accordingly, if anything in the outer parts is ignited, it is carried from the middle into the height. Therefore, what they say—that the motion [abbrev: *motum*] of a simple body is simple—is verified in the first place concerning circular motion, as long as the simple body remains in its natural place and in its unity. For in that place, there is no other motion than circular, which remains entirely in itself, similar to one at rest. Rectilinear motion, however, supervenes upon those things which wander from their natural place, or are extruded, or in any way are outside it. Nothing, however, is so repugnant to the order of the whole and the form of the world as to be outside one's place. Rectilinear motion, therefore, does not happen except to things not rightly disposed, nor perfect according to nature, while they are separated from their whole and desert its unity. 

Furthermore, those things which are moved upward and downward, even without circular motion, do not make a simple uniform [abbrev: *uniformem*] and equal motion [abbrev: *motum*]. For they cannot be tempered by levity or the impetus of their weight: and whatever things fall, making a slow motion at the beginning, increase their velocity by falling. Where, in turn, we see this terrestrial fire (for we see no other) once snatched into the height immediately grow weak [abbrev: *languescere*], as if the cause of the violence of the terrestrial matter were confessed. But circular motion is always rolled equally: for it has an unfailing cause; whereas those other motions have a cause that hastens to cease, through which, having attained their place, they cease to be heavy or light, and that motion ceases. 

Since, therefore, circular motion belongs to universes, but rectilinear also to parts, we can say that circular remains with rectilinear, just as the animal remains with the sick [part]. Surely even this, that Aristotle distributed simple motion into three kinds—away from the middle, toward the middle, and around the middle [abbrev: *medium*]—will be thought of only as an act of reason, just as we distinguish a line, a point [abbrev: *punctum*], and a surface, although one cannot subsist without the other, and none of them without 

***

### PAGE 35

a body. To these things is also added, that the condition of immobility is considered nobler and more divine than that of change and instability, which for this reason would be more fitting for the earth than for the universe. I add also, that it would seem quite absurd for motion to be ascribed to the containing or locating [body], and not rather to the contained and located, which is the earth. 

Since finally [abbrev: *denique*] it is manifest that the wandering stars [planets] become nearer to the earth and more remote, there will also be a motion of one body which is both around the middle (which they want to be the center of the earth) and from the middle toward it. It is necessary, therefore, to take the motion which is around the middle more generally, and for it to be enough that each motion rests upon its own middle. You see, therefore, that from all these things, the mobility of the earth is more probable than its rest, especially in the daily revolution, as if most proper to the earth.

#### Whether several motions can be attributed to the earth, and concerning the center of the universe. Chapter IX.

Since therefore nothing prohibits the mobility of the earth, I think it must now be seen whether several motions also fit [abbrev: *conveniunt*] it, so that it can be considered one of the wandering stars. For that it is not [abbrev: *non*] the center of all revolutions, the apparent unequal motion of the wanderers and their variable distances from the earth declare, which cannot be understood in a circle concentric to the earth. 

Therefore, since there are several centers, one will not rashly doubt also concerning the center of the universe, whether namely it be that of terrestrial gravity, or another. For my part, I think that gravity is nothing other than a certain natural appetency [abbrev: *appetentiam*] instilled into the parts by the divine providence of the Architect of the universes, so that they may confer themselves into their unity and integrity by coming together into the form of a globe. Which affection it is credible is also present in the Sun, the Moon, and the other [abbrev: *caeterisque*] splendors of the wanderers, so that by its efficacy they remain in that roundness in which they represent themselves, which nevertheless effect their circuits [abbrev: *circuitus*] in many ways. 

If therefore the earth also performs others, as for example according to a center [abbrev: *centrum*], it will be necessary that they be those which similarly appear outwardly in many ways, among which we find the annual circuit. Since if it were changed from the solar to the terrestrial, with immobility granted to the Sun,

***

### PAGE 36

the rising and setting of the signs and fixed stars [abbrev: *stellarum*], by which they become morning and evening [abbrev: *uespertinaeque*], will appear in the same way: the stations, retrogradations [abbrev: *retrogradationes*], and progressions of the wanderers will also [abbrev: *quoque*] appear to be not their motions, but those of the earth, which it borrows for their appearances. Finally, the Sun itself will be thought to possess the middle of the world [abbrev: *mundi*], all of which the reason of the order in which they succeed one another and the harmony [abbrev: *harmonia*] of the whole world teaches us, if only we look at the matter with (as they say) both eyes.

#### Concerning the order of the celestial orbs. Chapter X.

I see that no one doubts that the highest of all visible things is the heaven of the fixed stars [abbrev: *fixarum*]. But we see that the ancient Philosophers wanted to take the series of the wanderers according to the magnitude of their revolutions, assuming the reason that of things carried with equal celerity, those which are further distant seem to be carried more slowly, as is shown in Euclid’s *Optics*. And therefore they think the Moon circles in the shortest space of time because, being nearest to the earth, it is turned in the smallest circle. But the highest is Saturn, which circles the greatest circuit in the most time. Below it, Jupiter. After this, Mars. 

Concerning Venus, however, and [abbrev: *atque*] Mercury, diverse opinions are found, for the reason that they are not moved away [abbrev: *elongantur*] from the Sun in every direction as the former are. Wherefore [abbrev: *Quamobrem*] some place them above the Sun, as in Plato’s *Timaeus*, others below it, as Ptolemaeus and a good part of the more recent [authors]. Alpetragius makes Venus higher than the Sun and Mercury lower [abbrev: *inferiorem*]. Therefore, those who follow Plato, since they think all stars—otherwise dark bodies—shine with conceived solar light, if they were below the Sun, they would be seen as halves or certainly deficient from roundness on account of their not great separation from it. For they would refer the light they received almost upward, that is, toward the Sun, as we see in the new or waning Moon. They say it would also be necessary that, by their opposition, the Sun would sometimes be hindered, and according to their magnitude, its light would fail: which, since it never appears, they think those stars by no means go below the Sun. 

On the contrary, those who place Venus and Mercury below the Sun claim their reason from the amplitude of the space which they find between the Sun and the Moon.

***

### PAGE 37

For they found the maximum distance of the Moon from the earth—of sixty-four parts and one-sixth, of which the one from the center of the earth is one—to be contained almost eighteen times up to the minimum interval of the Sun, and to be 1160 of those parts. Therefore, between it and the Moon there are 1096 [parts]. Accordingly, lest such a vastness should remain empty, they find from the intervals of the apsides [abbrev: *absidum*], by which they calculate the thickness of those orbs, that they nearly complete those same numbers, so that the lowest of Mercury succeeds the highest of the Moon, which [Mercury] then the highest Venus follows, which finally by its highest apsis almost reaches the lowest of the Sun. For they calculate between the apsides of Mercury nearly 177.5 of the aforementioned parts, then the remaining space is nearly completed by the interval of Venus of 910 parts. 

Therefore, they do not admit that there is any opacity in the stars similar to the lunar, but they shine either by their own light or soaked in their whole bodies with solar light, and therefore the Sun is not hindered, because it is a very rare event that they are interposed in the sight of the Sun, for the most part deviating in latitude. Furthermore, because they are small bodies in comparison to the Sun, since Venus, though larger than Mercury, can hardly cover a hundredth part of the Sun, as Machometus Arescenfis [Al-Battani] maintains, who thinks the diameter of the Sun is ten times larger. And therefore, so small a spot would not easily be seen under such a pre-eminent light. Although Averroes, in his Ptolemaic paraphrase [abbrev: *paraphrasi*], remembers having seen something blackish when he found by numbers the conjunction of the Sun and Mercury was displayed: and thus they decide these two stars are moved below the solar circle. 

But how weak and uncertain this reason also is, is manifest from this: that although there are 38 of those parts from the center of the earth to the surface up to the nearest Moon according to Ptolemaeus, but according to a truer estimation more than 52 (as will be clear below), yet we know of nothing else contained in so great a space than air, and if you please, also what they call the fiery element [abbrev: *elementum*]. Moreover, that the diameter [abbrev: *dimetientem*] of the circle of Venus, which departs from the Sun on this side or that by 45 degrees more or less, must be six times larger than that which goes from the center of the earth to its lowest apsis, as will be demonstrated in its place. What then will they say is contained in all that space, so much larger than what would hold the earth [abbrev: *terram*], air, ether, Moon, and [abbrev: *atque*] Mercury, and besides that, which the huge

***

### PAGE 38

epicycle [abbrev: *epicyclus*] of Venus would occupy if it were turned around a quiet earth [abbrev: *terram*]? 

That argumentation of Ptolemaeus also—that it was necessary for the Sun to be carried in the middle between those moving away [abbrev: *digredientes*] from it in every direction and those not so moving—is unconvincing [abbrev: *impersuasibilis*] as is clear from the fact that the Moon, which itself moves away in every direction, betrays its falsehood. But what cause will they allege, those who place Venus and then Mercury below the Sun, or separate them in another order, why they do not likewise make separate circuits and different from the Sun as the rest of the wanderers do, if indeed the reason of velocity and slowness does not fail the order? It will be necessary, therefore, either that the earth is not the center to which the order of the stars and orbs [abbrev: *orbiumque*] is referred, or certainly that there is no reason for the order, nor does it appear why a higher place is owed to Saturn rather than to Jupiter or any other. 

Wherefore I think it is by no means to be despised what Martianus Capella, who wrote the *Encyclopedia*, and indeed some other Latins, were well aware of. For they think that Venus and Mercury run around the Sun existing in their middle, and for that cause they think they do not move further away from it than the convexity [abbrev: *convexitas*] of their orbs permits, because they do not go around the earth like the others, but have converted apsides. What else therefore do they mean to signify than that the center of those orbs is around the Sun? Thus indeed the Mercurial orb will be enclosed within the Venerean, which it is fitting is twice and more larger, and will obtain a place sufficient for itself in that very amplitude. 

If anyone, taking this occasion, refers Saturn also, Jupiter, and Mars to that same center, provided he understands the magnitude of those orbs to be such that it contains and surrounds the earth staying with them, he will not err—which the canonical reason of those motions declares. For it is certain that they are always nearer to the earth around their evening rising, that is, when they are opposed to the Sun, with the earth being between them and the Sun; but most remote from the earth at their evening setting, when they are hidden around the Sun, namely while we have the Sun between them and the earth. Which things indicate sufficiently that their center pertains more to the Sun, and is the same as that to which Venus and Mercury also refer their revolutions [abbrev: *obvolutiones*]. 

But indeed, with all these relying on one middle, it is necessary that the space which is left between the convex orb of Venus and the concave of Mars be distinguished also as an orb or

***

### PAGE 39

sphere concentric [abbrev: *homocentrum*] with them according to both surfaces, which receives the earth with its attendant Moon and whatever is contained [abbrev: *continetur*] below the lunar globe. For by no means can we separate the Moon from the earth, since it is beyond controversy closest to it, especially since in that space we find a place quite fitting and abundant for it. 

Therefore, we are not ashamed to confess that this whole, which the Moon encircles, and the center of the earth, passes through that great orb among the other wandering stars in an annual revolution around the Sun, and that around it is the center [abbrev: *centrum*] of the universe: and also with the Sun remaining immobile, whatever appears concerning the motion of the Sun, this is rather verified in the mobility of the earth. So great indeed is the magnitude of the world [abbrev: *mundi*] that although that distance of the earth from the Sun has a magnitude in relation to any other orbs of the wandering stars, quite evident according to the reason of those amplitudes, yet compared to the sphere of the non-wandering stars, it is as nothing. Which I think is easier to grant than that the intellect [abbrev: *intellectum*] be distracted into an almost infinite multitude of orbs, which those were forced to do who detained the earth in the middle of the world [abbrev: *mundi*]. 

But the sagacity of nature is rather to be followed, which, just as it especially avoided producing something superfluous or useless, so rather it often enriched one thing with many effects. All of which, though they be difficult and almost unbelievable [abbrev: *inopinabilia*], namely against the opinion of many, yet in the process, with God favoring, we shall make clearer than the Sun itself, at least to those not ignorant of the Mathematical art. Wherefore, with the first reason [abbrev: *ratione*] remaining safe—for no one will allege a more fitting one than that the multitude of time measures the magnitude of the orbs—the order of the spheres [abbrev: *sphaerarum*] follows in this manner, taking its beginning from the highest.

The first and highest of all is the sphere of the fixed stars, containing itself and all things: and therefore immobile, namely the place of the universe, to which the motion and position of all other stars are referred. For as to what some think that it also changes in some way: we shall assign another cause in the deduction [abbrev: *deductione*] of the terrestrial motion why it so appears. There follows the first of the wanderers, Saturn, which completes its circuit in the 30th year. After this, Jupiter, mobile in a twelve-year revolution. Then Mars, which circles in two years. The fourth place in order is held by the annual revolution,

***

### PAGE 40

in which we said the earth is contained with the lunar orb as if by an epicycle. In the fifth place Venus is brought back in the ninth month [abbrev: *nonimestris*]. Finally, the sixth place Mercury holds, running around in the space of eighty days. In the middle of all, however, resides the Sun. 

For who in this most beautiful temple would place this lamp in another or better place than from whence he can illuminate the whole at once? Since indeed some not inaptly call it the lantern of the world, others the mind, others the ruler. [Hermes] Trimegistus calls it the visible God, Sophocles’ Electra the one seeing all things. So indeed the Sun, residing as if on a royal throne, governs the family of Stars circling around. The Earth also [abbrev: *quoque*] is by no means defrauded of the lunar ministry, but as Aristotle says concerning animals, the Moon has the greatest kinship [abbrev: *cognationem*] with the earth. Meanwhile, the earth conceives from the Sun and is impregnated with an annual birth. We find therefore under this

...it would have fallen out), and even more so animals and any other loose weights would by no means remain **unshaken**. But neither would falling things descend in a straight line to their destined place and perpendicularly, since it <note>The Earth, if it were moving.</note> would have been moved away from underneath with such **swiftness**. We would also see clouds and any other things hanging in the air always being carried toward the west.

### Solution to the stated arguments, and their insufficiency. Chapter VIII.

->**H**is sane & similibus causis<-
<note>The initial **H** in the original features a woodcut of a winged figure holding an armillary sphere or globe.</note>
For these and similar reasons, they say the Earth rests in the middle of the universe, and that it is undoubtedly so. But if anyone should think that the Earth rotates, he would certainly say that the motion is natural, not **forced** <note>original: "violentum"; in the Aristotelian physics of the time, "violent" or "forced" motion was that which was imposed upon an object against its nature, whereas "natural" motion was inherent and stable.</note>. Those things which are according to nature produce effects contrary to those which are according to force. For things to which force or impetus is applied must necessarily be dissolved, and they cannot endure for long; but things that happen by nature are in a right state and are preserved in their best composition. Therefore, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greek-Roman mathematician whose geocentric model dominated astronomy for over a millennium.</note> fears in vain that the Earth and all earthly things would be dissipated in a revolution produced by the power of nature, which is far different from **art** <note>original: "artis"; refers to human craft, technology, or mechanical devices as opposed to natural processes.</note>, or what can be achieved by human ingenuity. 

But why does he not suspect even more for the universe, whose motion must be so much swifter as the heavens are greater than the Earth? Or has the heaven been made immense because it is driven away from the center by an **inexpressible** vehemence of motion, whereas it would otherwise collapse if it stood still? Certainly if this reasoning held, the magnitude of the heavens would also go on to infinity. For the more the motion itself is carried upward by its impetus, the swifter the motion will be, because of the ever-increasing circumference which must be traversed in the space of 24 hours; and conversely, as the motion increases, the immensity of the heaven would increase. Thus velocity would promote magnitude, and magnitude velocity, unto infinity. 

But according to that physical **axiom**, that which is infinite cannot be traversed, nor moved by any means; therefore the heaven will necessarily stand still. But they say that outside the heaven there is no body, no place, no **vacuum**, and absolutely nothing, and therefore there is nowhere the heaven could expand to; but then it is truly strange if something can be contained by nothing. But if the heaven were infinite, and finite only in its inner concavity, it would perhaps be more verified that there is nothing outside the heaven, since everything...

He points out the logical absurdity in the traditional view, where the massive heavens must move at infinite speeds to revolve around a tiny Earth.</summary>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK I

...and whatever might be in it, no matter what size it occupies, while the heavens remain immobile. For the strongest argument they use to try to prove the universe is finite is motion. Whether the universe is finite or infinite, let us leave to the debate of the natural philosophers <term>physiologorum: natural philosophers or physicists who study the laws of nature</term>; holding this for certain: that the Earth is bounded by its poles and finished with a spherical surface. Why then do we still hesitate to grant it the mobility that fits its shape by nature, rather than saying the whole universe is sliding <note>original: "labatur"; Copernicus suggests that it is more logical for the small Earth to rotate than for the massive, possibly infinite universe to slide or rotate around it.</note>, whose limit is unknown and cannot be known? And why do we not admit that the appearance of a daily revolution belongs to the heavens, but the reality is in the Earth? 

And this is just as if Virgil’s Aeneas said: 
*We sail forth from the harbor, and lands and cities recede.* 
<note>original Latin: "Prouehimur portu, terraeque urbesque recedunt." Copernicus is quoting the poet Virgil's Aeneid (Book III, line 72) to explain the principle of relative motion: just as a sailor feels the shore is moving away while they are at rest, we perceive the stars moving while the Earth rotates.</note>

Since when a ship floats in calm weather, everything outside is seen by the sailors to move in the image of that motion, and in turn, they think they are at rest along with everything with them. Thus, certainly, in the motion of the Earth, it can happen that the whole universe is thought to go around. 

What then should we say about the clouds and other things hanging in the air in any way, or sinking, or rising again into the heights? Except that not only the Earth with the water element joined to it moves this way, but also a significant part of the air, and whatever has a kinship <term>cognationem: kinship or connection</term> with the Earth in the same way. Either because the nearby air, mixed with earthy or watery matter, follows the same nature as the Earth, or because the motion of the air is acquired, sharing in the Earth's perpetual revolution through contact and without resistance. 

Conversely, with different wonder, they say that the highest region of the air follows the heavenly motion, which those sudden stars indicate—I mean Comets and those called "Bearded Stars" <term>Pogoniae: from the Greek word for "bearded," referring to a type of comet with a tail that looks like a beard</term> by the Greeks—for which they assign that very place for their generation, and which rise and set just like the other stars. We can say that part of the air is deprived of that terrestrial motion because of its great distance from the Earth. Consequently, the air that is closest to the Earth will appear calm <term>tranquillus: calm or still</term>, as well as things suspended in it, unless it is agitated this way and that by wind or some other force, as happens. For what else is wind in the air but a wave in the sea? 

We must admit that the motion of falling and rising things is double in comparison with the universe, and is entirely composed of straight and circular motion. Since those things which by their own weight...

<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s argument in Chapter VIII of Book I. In the previous section, he argued that it is more reasonable for the Earth to rotate than for the massive universe to revolve around it. Here, he counters the Aristotelian objection that a rotating Earth would fly apart or that objects would not fall straight down. He explains that "natural" motion is circular and that straight-line motion is only a sign of something being out of its proper place.</meta>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...are pressed down, since they are mostly earthy, there is no doubt that the parts keep the same nature as their whole. Nor does it happen differently in those things which are snatched into the heights by fiery force. For this terrestrial fire is nourished chiefly by earthy matter, and they define flame as nothing other than burning smoke. Moreover, it is the property of fire to expand what it has invaded, which it does with such force that by no means, and by no machines, can it be restrained from finishing its work once its prison is broken. 

The motion of expansion is from the center to the circumference; accordingly, if any part of the exterior is ignited, it is carried from the middle to the heights. Therefore, what they <note>Aristotle and his followers.</note> say—that the motion of a simple body is simple <term>simple motion: in Aristotelian physics, this refers to motion in a single direction, either straight (up/down) or circular.</term>—is verified primarily regarding circular motion, as long as the simple body remains in its natural place and in its unity. 

Indeed, in its proper place, the motion is none other than circular, which remains entirely within itself, similar to a body at rest. But rectilinear <note>original: "rectus"; straight-line motion.</note> motion happens to those things which wander from their natural place, or are thrust out <term>extruduntur: forced out of a position by an external power</term>, or are outside it in any way. Nothing is so contrary to the order of the whole and the form of the world as for something to be out of its place. Therefore, straight-line motion occurs only in things that are not rightly disposed, nor perfect according to nature, while they are separated from their whole and abandon its unity. 

Furthermore, things that are moved upward and downward, even without circular motion, do not perform a simple, uniform, and equal motion. For they cannot be controlled by their lightness or by the force <note>original: "impetu"; the momentum or "impetus" of a moving object.</note> of their weight. Whatever things fall, making a slow motion at the beginning, increase their velocity as they fall. On the other hand, we see this earthly fire (for we see no other) snatched into the heights immediately grow weak <term>languescere: to lose its strength or vitality</term>, as if the cause of the violence to the earthy matter were admitted. 

Circular motion, however, always rolls equally, for it has an unfailing <term>indeficientem: a cause that does not run out or fail</term> cause; while those other motions have a cause that hastens to cease, for when the objects have reached their proper place, they cease to be heavy or light, and that motion stops. Since, therefore, circular motion belongs to wholes, and rectilinear also to parts, we can say that the circular remains with the rectilinear, just as the "animal" remains with one who is sick <note>Copernicus uses a medical metaphor: just as a sick animal is still an animal despite its illness, a part of the Earth (like a falling stone) still shares the Earth’s natural circular motion even while moving in a straight line.</note>. 

Surely this too—that Aristotle distributed simple motion into three kinds: from the center, toward the center, and around the center—will be thought of only as an act of reason. This is just as we distinguish <term>secernimus: to mentally separate or categorize</term> a line, a point, and a surface, even though one cannot exist without the other, and none of them without...

<summary>Copernicus argues that circular motion is the "natural" state of whole bodies in equilibrium, while straight-line motion is merely a temporary correction for objects out of their proper place. He uses this to reconcile the Earth's rotation with the observed behavior of falling or rising objects.</summary>

To these arguments, it is also added that the state of immobility is considered a nobler and more divine condition than that of change and instability; for this reason, instability would belong more to the Earth than to the universe. I add also that it would seem quite absurd to assign motion to that which contains or provides the space, rather than to that which is contained and occupies the space, which is the Earth. Since, finally, it is manifest that the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note> are seen to become closer to the Earth and then more remote, there will then be—even according to those who wish the center of the Earth to be the center of the universe—a motion of a single body <note>The planet in question.</note> both toward the center and away from the center. It is necessary, therefore, to understand motion around a center in a more general way, and it is enough that each motion rests upon its own center. You see, therefore, that from all these points, the mobility of the Earth is more probable than its rest, especially regarding the daily revolution, as if it were a property most belonging to the Earth itself.

### Whether Multiple Motions Can Be Attributed to the Earth, and Concerning the Center of the World. Chapter IX.

**S**ince, therefore, nothing prevents the mobility of the Earth, I believe we must now see whether several motions might belong to it, so that it can be considered one of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>. For that it is not the center of all revolutions is demonstrated by the apparent unequal motion of the wandering stars and their variable distances from the Earth, which cannot be understood as happening in circles centered on the Earth. Therefore, since there are several centers, one will not rashly doubt whether the center of the world is actually this center of terrestrial gravity, or something else. 

Indeed, I think that gravity is nothing other than a certain natural appetite <term>appetentiam: a natural tendency or "desire" for parts to join their whole</term> instilled in the parts by the divine providence of the Maker of all things, so that they might gather themselves into their own unity and wholeness by coming together in the form of a globe. It is believable that this same affection <note>original: "affectionem"; meaning a physical property or inclination.</note> is also present in the Sun, the Moon, and the other wandering lights <note>the planets</note>, so that by its power they remain in that roundness in which they show themselves, even though they perform their circuits in many ways. If, therefore, the Earth also performs other motions—for instance, around a center—it is necessary that these are those which similarly appear outside in many phenomena, among which we find the annual circuit. For if this motion is shifted from the Sun to the Earth, with immobility granted to the Sun...

...ceased, the risings and settings of the signs <note>The constellations of the Zodiac.</note> and the fixed stars, which occur in the morning and evening, will appear in the same way. Likewise, the stations, retrogradations <term>retrogradation: the appearance of a planet moving backward in the sky as the Earth passes it</term>, and progressions of the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note> will be seen as motions not of the planets themselves, but of the Earth, which lends its own motion to their appearances. Finally, the Sun itself will be thought to occupy the center of the world. All these things are taught to us by the logic of order in which they succeed one another, and by the harmony of the entire universe, if only we look at the matter with "both eyes" (as the saying goes) <note>original: "ambobus (ut aiunt) oculis" — a Latin idiom meaning to look at something clearly or with full attention.</note>.

### Concerning the order of the celestial spheres. Chapter X.

**A**s for the highest of all visible things, I see that no one doubts it is the heaven of the fixed stars. We see that the ancient philosophers wished to determine the sequence of the wandering stars <note>planets</note> according to the magnitude of their revolutions. They adopted the principle that, among objects carried at an equal speed, those which are further away appear to move more slowly, as is demonstrated in Euclid’s *Optics* <note>original: "Euclidem in Opticis" — Euclid’s work on geometry and vision explains that distant objects seem to move slower because they cover a smaller visual angle.</note>. Therefore, they think the Moon completes its circuit in the shortest space of time because, being closest to the Earth, it revolves in the smallest circle. The highest, however, is Saturn, which circles the largest circuit in the greatest amount of time. Beneath it is Jupiter. After this, Mars. 

Regarding Venus and Mercury, however, different opinions are found, because they do not move away from the Sun in every direction as the others <note>the outer planets</note> do. For this reason, some place them above the Sun, such as in Plato’s *Timaeus*, while others place them below the Sun, such as Ptolemy and a good portion of the moderns. Alpetragius <note>Al-Bitruji, a 12th-century Spanish-Arab astronomer.</note> makes Venus higher than the Sun and Mercury lower. Therefore, those who follow Plato—since they believe all stars are otherwise dark bodies that shine by reflecting solar light—argue that if these planets were below the Sun, they would be seen as half-full, or certainly lacking a full circular shape, because of their proximity to it. For the light they receive would be reflected mostly upward, that is, toward the Sun, as we see in the new or waning Moon. Furthermore, they say that the Sun would sometimes be blocked by their obstruction, and its light would fail in proportion to their size; since this never appears, they think these planets can by no means pass beneath the Sun. On the contrary, those who place Venus and Mercury below the Sun justify their reasoning by the vastness of the space they find between the Sun and the Moon.

<vocabulary>
**Retrogradations:** The apparent backward motion of a planet.
**Harmony:** The proportional and logical arrangement of the universe.
**Of things carried:** Referring to the celestial bodies moved by their spheres.
**Move away:** The angular distance (elongation) of a planet from the Sun.
**Separation:** The distance or pulling away of a body from the Sun's position.
</vocabulary>

They found that the maximum distance of the Moon from the Earth—which is sixty-four and one-sixth parts, where the Earth's radius is one part—is contained almost eighteen times within the minimum distance of the Sun, amounting to 1,160 of those parts. Therefore, between the Sun and the Moon, there are 1,096 parts. Furthermore, so that such a vastness would not remain empty, they calculate from the intervals of the apsides <term>apsides: the points in an orbit where a celestial body is at its furthest (apogee) or closest (perigee) from the center of its motion</term> (by which they determine the thickness of those spheres) that these distances nearly complete the numbers. Thus, the lowest point of Mercury succeeds the highest point of the Moon, and the highest point of Mercury is followed by the lowest of Venus, which finally, at its highest point, reaches almost to the lowest point of the Sun. Indeed, they calculate nearly 177.5 of the aforementioned parts between the apsides of Mercury, and the remaining space is filled by the interval of Venus, which is nearly 910 parts.

Therefore, they do not admit that the stars <note>In the 16th century, planets were often called "wandering stars."</note> have any opacity similar to the Moon's, but rather that they shine either with their own light or are saturated throughout their entire bodies with solar light. Because of this, they argue the Sun is not blocked—a very rare event anyway, since the planets usually pass to the side in latitude <note>Meaning they usually pass above or below the Sun's disk from our perspective.</note>. Furthermore, they argue the bodies are small compared to the Sun; even Venus, which is larger than Mercury, can hardly cover a hundredth part of the Sun, according to Mohammed al-Battani <note>original: "Machometus Arescenfis" — a 9th-century Arab astronomer whose data Copernicus frequently used.</note>, who estimates the Sun's diameter to be ten times larger than that of Venus. And therefore, they say such a tiny spot is not easily seen against that most brilliant light. Nevertheless, Averroes <note>The 12th-century philosopher and polymath Ibn Rushd.</note>, in his *Paraphrase of Ptolemy*, recalls having seen something blackish when he found by calculation that a conjunction of the Sun and Mercury was occurring. Based on this, they decree that these two planets move below the solar circle. 

But how weak and uncertain this reasoning is! This is manifest from the fact that, according to Ptolemy, the distance from the center of the Earth to the nearest point of the Moon is 38 radii; but according to a truer estimation, it is more than 52 (as will be shown below). Yet, we know of nothing else contained in such a vast space except air and, if you like, what they call the element of fire. Furthermore, the diameter of the circle of Venus—which wanders about 45 degrees to either side of the Sun—must be six times larger than the distance from the center of the Earth to its lowest point, as will be demonstrated in its proper place. What, then, will they say is contained in all that space, which is so much larger than what would be required to hold the Earth, the air, the ether, the Moon, and Mercury combined, and which moreover is a vast

...that huge epicycle of Venus would occupy, if it revolved around a stationary Earth. Furthermore, Ptolemy’s argument—that the Sun must be placed in the middle between those planets that move away from it in every direction and those that do not—is shown to be unconvincing. This is evident because the Moon, which also moves away from the Sun in every direction, proves that argument is false <note>Ptolemy argued the Sun should be a "boundary" between planets that can appear opposite the Sun (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) and those that always stay near it (Mercury, Venus). Copernicus points out that the Moon violates this logic.</note>. 

Indeed, what reason will those people give who place Venus below the Sun, and then Mercury, or separate them in some other order? Why do they not make their circuits separate and distinct from the Sun, like the other wandering stars <note>original: *errantium*, the common term for planets at the time</note>, if the ratio of speed and slowness does not fail the order? Therefore, one of two things must be true: either the Earth is not the center to which the order of the stars and their spheres is referred, or there is simply no logic to the order at all, nor any clear reason why a higher place should be owed to Saturn more than to Jupiter or any other planet.

For this reason, I think we should by no means despise the view of Martianus Capella—who wrote the *Encyclopedia* <note>A famous 5th-century textbook on the Seven Liberal Arts</note>—and certain other Latin writers who were very well-versed in these matters. For they believe that Venus and Mercury run around a Sun that exists in their center. They believe these planets do not move further away from the Sun than the convexity <term>convexity: the outward-curving boundary of a celestial sphere</term> of their spheres allows, because they do not circle the Earth like the others, but have their apsides <note>The highest and lowest points of an orbit</note> turned toward the Sun. What else do they mean to signify, then, but that the center of those spheres is around the Sun? 

Thus, surely the sphere of Mercury will be enclosed within that of Venus, which must be more than twice as large, and it will find a place within that vast space sufficient for itself. Taking this as an opportunity, if someone were to also relate Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars to that same center—provided they understand the magnitude of those spheres to be so great as to contain and circle the Earth which remains within them—they will not be in error. This is what the mathematical rule <note>original: *canonica ratio*</note> of those motions declares. 

For it is established that these planets are always closer to the Earth around the time of their evening rising (that is, when they are opposite the Sun with the Earth positioned between them and the Sun). Conversely, they are furthest from the Earth at the time of their evening setting, when they are hidden near the Sun, specifically when we have the Sun positioned between them and the Earth. These facts sufficiently indicate that their center belongs more to the Sun, and is the same center to which Venus and Mercury also refer their revolutions <note>original: *obvolutiones*</note>. 

But since all these spheres rely on a single center, it is necessary that the space left between the convex sphere of Venus and the concave sphere of Mars also be a sphere or...

For we can by no means separate the Moon from the Earth, as it is beyond controversy nearest to it, especially since we find a sufficiently suitable and abundant space for it in that area. Therefore, we are not ashamed to confess that this whole volume which the Moon circles, and the center of the Earth, travel through that <term>Great Orb</term> <note>original: *orbem illum magnum*; Copernicus’s specific term for the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun</note> among the other wandering stars <note>original: *errantes stellas*, the classical term for planets</note> in an annual revolution around the Sun; and that the center of the world is near the Sun. 

Moreover, since the Sun remains stationary, whatever appears to be a motion of the Sun is instead more truly verified as the mobility of the Earth. Furthermore, the magnitude of the world is so great that although the distance from the Earth to the Sun is significant in proportion to the size of the other planetary orbits—and indeed quite evident according to the logic of those dimensions—when compared to the sphere of the fixed stars, it is as nothing. I believe it is easier to concede this than to allow the mind to be distracted by a nearly infinite multitude of spheres, which those who kept the Earth in the middle of the world were forced to do. Instead, we should follow the wisdom <note>original: *sagacitas*, or sagacity</note> of Nature, which, just as she has most carefully avoided producing anything superfluous or useless, often prefers to endow a single thing with many effects. 

All these things are difficult and nearly unbelievable <note>original: *inopinabilia*</note>, being contrary to the opinions of many; however, in the process—God willing—we shall make them clearer than the Sun itself, at least to those who are not ignorant of the mathematical art. Therefore, while the first principle remains safe (for no one will allege a more suitable one than that the magnitude of the orbits be measured by the length of time), the order of the spheres follows in this manner, beginning from the highest.

The first and supreme of all is the sphere of the fixed stars, containing itself and all things, and for that reason it is immobile. It is indeed the place of the universe to which the motion and position of all the other stars are compared. As for the fact that some think it also changes in some way, we shall assign another cause for why it appears to do so in our deduction of the Earth's motion. 

There follows the first of the wandering stars, Saturn, which completes its circuit in thirty years. After this is Jupiter, moving in a twelve-year revolution. Then Mars, which circles in two years. The fourth place in the order is held by the annual revolution,

Indeed, some not inaptly call it the lantern of the world, others the mind, others the ruler. [Hermes] Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and the "Hermetic" tradition</note> calls it the visible God, and Sophocles’s *Electra* calls it the one who sees all things. Thus, indeed, as if sitting upon a royal throne, the Sun governs the family of stars circling around it. The Earth, moreover, is by no means deprived of the Moon's service, but as Aristotle says in his work *On Animals*, the Moon has the closest kinship with the Earth. This translation covers pages 41 through 50 of the OCR text provided, which encompasses the conclusion of Book I, Chapter 10, the entirety of Chapter 11, and the beginning of Chapter 12 of Nicolaus Copernicus's *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium*.

### PAGE 41
**ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK I.**

In this arrangement, therefore, we find an admirable symmetry of the world and a certain harmonious link between the movement and the magnitude of the orbs, such as cannot be found in any other way. For here one may observe, if they contemplate not sluggishly, why the progression and regression appear greater in Jupiter than in Saturn, and smaller than in Mars; and again greater in Venus than in Mercury. And why such reciprocation [retrograde motion] appears more frequent in Saturn than in Jupiter, yet rarer in Mars and in Venus than in Mercury. Furthermore, why Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are closer to the earth when they are at opposition [*acronychti*] than near the time of their occultation and reappearance. Especially indeed Mars, when it is visible all night [*pernox*], seems to equal Jupiter in magnitude, distinguished only by its ruddy color; yet otherwise it is scarcely found among stars of the second magnitude, being recognized only by those who follow it with diligent observation. All these things proceed from the same cause, which resides in the motion of the earth.

However, that none of these things appear in the fixed stars argues for their immense height, which causes even the circle of annual motion, or its image, to vanish from our eyes. For every visible object has a certain length of distance beyond which it is no longer seen, as is demonstrated in Optics. That there is still a very great distance from Saturn, the highest of the wandering stars, to the sphere of the fixed stars, is demonstrated by their twinkling lights. By this indication they are chiefly distinguished from the planets, and it was necessary that there be a very great difference between that which moves and that which does not move. So great, indeed, is this divine handiwork of the Best and Greatest [God].

**Demonstration of the Triple Motion of the Earth. Chapter XI.**

Since, therefore, so many and such great testimonies of the wandering stars agree with the mobility of the earth, we shall now explain the motion itself in summary, insofar as the appearances are demonstrated by it as a hypothesis; which [motion] it is necessary to admit is entirely triple. The first is that which we said is called *nychthemeron* [νυχθήμερον—a night and a day] by the Greeks, the proper circuit of day and night, around the axis of the earth, turning from west to east, just as the world is thought to be carried in the opposite direction, describing the equinoctial circle, which some call the *equidial* [equal-day], imitating the meaning of the Greeks,

**c ij** [Note: Signature mark] **among** [Note: Catchword: *rum*]

### PAGE 42
**NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**

**among** whom it is called *isēmerinos* [ἰσημέρινος]. The second is the annual motion of the center, which describes the circle of the signs [the Zodiac] around the Sun, likewise from west to east, that is, proceeding in order [*in consequentia*], between Venus and Mars, as we said, with those things resting upon it. By this it happens that the Sun itself seems to traverse the zodiac with a similar motion; as, for example, when the center of the earth passes through Capricorn, the Sun seems to pass through Cancer; from Aquarius, Leo, and so on, as we said. To this circle, which is through the middle of the signs, and its surface, it must be understood that the equinoctial circle and the axis of the earth have a changeable inclination. For if they remained fixed, and followed only the motion of the center simply, no inequality of days and nights would appear, but it would always be either the solstice, or midwinter, or the equinox, or summer, or winter, or whatever quality of time would remain similar to itself. 

There follows, therefore, a third motion of declination, also in an annual revolution, but in reverse [*in precedentia*], that is, reflecting against the motion of the center. And so, with both being nearly equal to each other and mutually opposite, it happens that the axis of the earth, and the equinoctial—the greatest of the parallels upon it—look toward nearly the same part of the world, just as if they remained immobile; meanwhile the Sun is seen to move through the obliquity of the sign-bearer [the Zodiac], by that motion with which the center of the earth [moves], not otherwise than if the earth itself were the center of the world, provided you remember that the distance of the Sun and the earth has already exceeded our sight in the sphere of the fixed stars. Since these things are such that they desire to be placed before the eyes rather than spoken of, let us describe the circle ABCD, which represents the annual circuit of the center of the earth in the surface of the sign-bearer, and let E be the Sun around its center. I will cut this circle into four parts by the subtended diameters AEC and BED. Let point A hold the beginning of Cancer, B of Libra, C of Capricorn, and D of Aries. 

Let us assume the center of the earth first at A, upon which I will designate the terrestrial equinoctial FGHI, but not in the same plane, except that the diameter GAI is the common section of the circles—the equinoctial, I say, and the sign-bearer. Having also drawn the diameter FAH at right angles to GAI itself, let F be the limit of the greatest declination to the South, and H truly to the North. These things being thus proposed, the inhabitants of the earth will see the Sun near the center E making its winter turning [solstice] under Capricorn, which the greatest northern declination H turned toward the Sun effects. For the slope of the equinoctial toward the line AE, through the diurnal revolution, marks out for itself the winter tropic parallel according to the distance which the angle of inclination EAH encompasses.

**On the Magnitude of Straight Lines in a Circle. Chapter XII.**

Since the demonstrations which we shall use in nearly the whole work are concerned with straight lines and arcs, and with plane and spherical triangles, about which although many things are already clear in the elements of Euclid, they do not yet have what is most sought here: how sides can be obtained from angles, and angles from sides. For an angle does not measure a subtended straight line [a chord], just as the line does not measure the angle, but the arc does. Wherefore a method has been found by which the subtended lines for any arc may be known, by whose help one may take the arc itself corresponding to the angle, and conversely through the arc, the straight line which subtends the angle. 

Therefore, it seems not out of place if we treat of these lines. Also of the sides and angles of both plane and spherical triangles, which Ptolemy handed down dispersedly and through examples, so that they may be completed in this place once and for all, and then what we are about to hand down may be made clearer. Now, by the common consensus of Mathematicians, we distribute the circle into 360 parts. The ancients assigned 120 parts to the diameter. But later [mathematicians], so that they might avoid the entanglement of fractions [*scrupulorum*] in the multiplications and divisions of numbers concerning these lines—which for the most part are incommensurable in length, and often even in power—some established the rational diameter as 1,200,000, others 2,000,000, others otherwise, from the time when the Indian figures of numbers [Hindu-Arabic numerals] were received into use. This number indeed surpasses any other, whether Greek or Latin, with a certain singular...

***

### PAGE 46
**NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**

...singular readiness, and accommodates itself most aptly to every kind of calculation. We also for that reason have accepted 200,000 parts of the diameter as sufficient, which can exclude manifest error. For in those things which do not have the ratio of number to number, it is enough to attain the nearest [approximation]. This, moreover, we shall explain in six Theorems and one Problem, following Ptolemy for the most part.

**First Theorem.**
The diameter of a circle being given, the sides of the triangle, square, hexagon, pentagon, and decagon which the same circle circumscribes are also given. Since the line from the center [the radius] is equal to half the diameter and to the side of the hexagon. Truly, the square of the side of the triangle is triple, and of the square [side] double, that which is formed from the side of the hexagon, as demonstrated in Euclid's *Elements*. Therefore, there are given in length: the side of the hexagon as 100,000 parts; of the square 141,422 parts; of the triangle 173,205 parts. 

Now let the side of the hexagon be AB, which by the 11th of the 2nd book, or the 30th of the 6th book of Euclid, is cut in mean and extreme ratio at point C, and let the greater segment be CB, to which let BD be placed as equal. Therefore, the whole ABD will be divided in extreme and mean ratio, and the smaller segment added [BD] is the side of the decagon inscribed in the circle, of which AB was the side of the hexagon; which is manifest from the 5th and 9th of the 13th book of Euclid. 

[Note: Geometrical diagram of a line AC E B D]

Indeed, BD itself will be given in this way: let AB be cut in half at E. It is clear by the 3rd of the same book of Euclid that the square of EBD is five times the square of EB. But EB is given in length as 50,000 parts; from which is given the five-fold power, and EBD itself in length as 111,803 parts; from which if 50,000 are taken (which is EB), there remains BD as 61,803 parts, the sought side of the decagon. The side of the pentagon also, whose square equals the square of the side of the hexagon plus the square of the side of the decagon, is given as 117,557 parts. Therefore, the diameter of the circle being given, the sides of the triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, and decagon inscribable in the same circle are given, which was to be demonstrated.

**Second Theorem.**
If a quadrilateral is inscribed in a circle, the rectangle encompassed by the diagonals is equal to those which are contained under the opposite sides. For let there be a quadrilateral ABCD inscribed in the circle; I say that the rectangle contained under the diagonals AC and DB is equal to those contained under AB, CD and under AD, BC. For let us make the angle ABE equal to that which is under CBD. Therefore, the whole angle ABD will be equal to the whole EBC, the angle EBD being assumed as common to both. Also, the angles under ACB and BDA are equal to each other in the same segment of the circle, and therefore the two similar triangles BCE and BDA will have proportional sides, as BC is to BD, so EC is to AD, and the rectangle under EC and BD is equal to that under BC and AD. 

But also triangles ABE and CBD are similar, because the angles under ABE and CBD were made equal, and those under BAC and BDC, subtending the same arc of the circle, are equal. It follows again that AB is to BD as AE is to CD, and the rectangle under AB and CD is equal to that under AE and BD. But it has already been declared that the rectangle under AD, BC is as great as that under BD and EC. Therefore, joined together, the rectangle under BD and AC is equal to those under AD, BC and under AB, CD. Which it was opportune to have shown. [Note: This is Ptolemy’s Theorem].

...having completed a semicircle, the Sun will appear to enter **Cancer** <note>The zodiac sign marking the summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere</note>. But when F, the southern declination of the equatorial circle, is turned toward the Sun, it will make the Sun appear northern and in its summer phase, traversing the <term>tropic</term> <note>The Tropic of Cancer</note> according to the ratio of the angle of inclination ECF. Again, as F turns away toward the third quadrant of the circle, the common intersection G-I will fall once more upon the line E-D; from there, the Sun, viewed in **Libra**, will be seen to have reached the autumnal equinox. And thereafter, following the same process as H-F gradually turns back toward the Sun, it will cause a return to the conditions from which we began.
