**Another way.** Let there be, likewise, a diameter A-E-C in the underlying plane, which is the common intersection of a circle standing upright to that plane. In this, around A and C—that is, at the points of **Cancer** and **Capricorn**—let the circle of the Earth be designated in turns through its poles, which shall be D-G-F-I, and let the Earth's axis be D-F: the North Pole D, the South Pole F, and G-I the diameter of the equatorial circle. Therefore, when F turns toward the Sun (which is at E), and the northern inclination of the equatorial circle is according to the angle formed by I-A-E, then the rotation around the axis will describe a southern parallel to the equator along the diameter K-L, and at the distance L-I, the <term>Tropic of Capricorn</term> <note>The southernmost latitude where the Sun can be directly overhead</note> appearing in the Sun. Or, to put it more accurately: that motion around the axis, relative to the line of sight A-E, forms a <term>conic surface</term> <note>Copernicus describes the axis "sweeping" a cone to explain how it maintains its orientation while the Earth moves</note>, having its peak at the center of the Earth and its base as a circle parallel to the equator. At the opposite sign, C, all these things happen in the same way, but in reverse. It is clear, then, how these two motions—of the center and of the inclination—occurring together, force the Earth's axis to remain in the same **equilibrium** <note>original: *libramento*; a state of steady balance or consistent orientation</note> and in a similar position, making everything appear as if they were motions of the Sun. We stated, however, that the annual revolutions of the center and of the declination are almost equal; for if they were exactly equal, the points of the equinoxes and solstices, and the entire tilt of the **zodiac** <note>original: *signiferi*; the "sign-bearer" or the path of the Sun through the constellations</note> under the sphere of the fixed stars, would not change at all. But because there is a slight difference—

# BOOK I OF THE REVOLUTIONS

The difference, becoming visible only with the passage of time, has been revealed: from Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the preeminent astronomer of antiquity</note> even to us, it is nearly 21 degrees, by which those [the equinoxes] now anticipate <note>A reference to the precession of the equinoxes, where the positions of the equinoxes move backward along the ecliptic over time</note> their former positions. For this reason, some believed that the sphere of fixed stars also moves, and therefore they favored a ninth superior sphere. When this was not sufficient, more recent scholars added a tenth; nevertheless, they have not yet attained the goal, which we hope to reach through the motion of the earth. We shall use this as a principle and hypothesis in the demonstrations of other matters.

## Chapter XII. On the Magnitude of Straight Lines in a Circle.

**Q**uoniam <note>original: "Since"</note> since the demonstrations, which we shall use in nearly the entire work, deal with straight lines and arcs, and with plane and spherical triangles—concerning which much is already clear in Euclid’s *Elements*—yet they do not have that which is most sought here: how sides may be obtained from angles, and angles from sides. Since an angle does not measure the subtended straight line—nor does the line measure the angle—but the arc does. Therefore, a method has been found through which the subtended lines <term>chords</term> <note>Copernicus is describing the foundations of trigonometry; he uses the lengths of chords in a circle where modern mathematicians would use sines</note> for any arc may be known. With the help of these chords, it is possible to obtain the arc corresponding to the angle, and conversely, through the arc, to find the straight line which subtends the angle. 

Therefore, it seems not out of place if we treat these lines. We shall also discuss the sides and angles of both plane and spherical triangles, which Ptolemy handed down scattered and through examples, so that they may be completed here all at once, and thereafter the things we are about to present may become clearer. By the common consent of mathematicians, we divide the circle into 360 parts. The ancients adopted 120 parts for the diameter. But later writers—to avoid the entanglement of <term>scruples</term> <note>Fractions or small parts of a unit, equivalent to minutes and seconds of a degree</note> in the multiplication and division of numbers regarding these lines, which for the most part are <term>incommensurable</term> <note>Lines that cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of whole numbers, such as the relationship between a side and the diagonal of a square</note> in length, and often even in power—some established the diameter as 1,200,000, others as 2,000,000, and others defined the <term>rational diameter</term> <note>A whole number chosen to represent the diameter to simplify calculations and avoid decimals</note> differently, from the time when Indian figures of numbers <note>The Hindu-Arabic numeral system (0–9), which was more efficient for calculation than Roman or Greek alphabetic numerals</note> were received into use. This number indeed [surpasses] any other, whether Greek or Latin, with a certain singular...

### Theorem I.

**G**iven the diameter of a circle, the sides of the triangle, square <term>tetragon</term>, hexagon, pentagon, and decagon which the same circle circumscribes are also given. Since the radius <note>original: quæ ex centro, "that which is from the center"</note>, which is half of the diameter, is equal to the side of the hexagon. Truly, the square of the side of the triangle is triple, and the square of the side of the square is double the square of the hexagon's side, as demonstrated in Euclid's *Elements*. Therefore, in length, the side of the hexagon is given as 100,000 parts; the square as 141,422 parts; and the triangle as 173,205 parts. Now, let the side of the hexagon be A B, which, according to the 11th [proposition] of the second [book], or the 30th of the sixth book of Euclid, is cut in "mean and extreme ratio" <note>This is the geometric construction of the "Golden Ratio"</note> at point C; let the larger segment be C B, to which B D is added as an equal. Therefore, the whole line A B D will be divided in mean and extreme ratio, and the smaller segment added [B D] will be the side of the decagon inscribed in the circle in which A B was the side of the hexagon. This is manifest from the 5th and 9th [propositions] of Euclid's 13th book.

A —— C —— E —— B —— D
<note>Representation of the geometrical diagram showing the division of the line segment</note>

But B D itself will be given in this way: let A B be bisected <note>cut into two equal parts</note> at E. It is clear from the 3rd [proposition] of the same book of Euclid that the square of E B D is five times the square of E B. But E B is given in length as 50,000 parts; from this, the fivefold power is given, and E B D itself is 111,803 parts in length. If the 50,000 parts of E B are subtracted from this, there remains B D at 61,803 parts, which is the sought side of the decagon. Also, the side of the pentagon, the square of which is equal to the squares of the sides of the hexagon and decagon combined, is given as 117,557 parts. Therefore, given the diameter of the circle, the sides of the triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, and decagon inscribable in the same circle are given, which was to be demonstrated.

### Second Theorem.

**I**f a quadrilateral <term>quadrilaterum</term> is inscribed in a circle, the rectangle contained by the diagonals <note>meaning the product of the lengths of the two diagonals</note> is equal to the [sum of the] rectangles contained by the opposite sides. For let the quadrilateral inscribed in the circle be $A B C D$; I say that the [rectangle] contained by the diagonals $A C$ and $D B$ is equal to those contained by $A B$ and $C D$, and by $A D$ and $B C$. For let us make the angle $A B E$ equal to the angle $C B D$. Therefore, the whole angle $A B D$ will be equal to the whole $E B C$, by assuming $E B D$ as common to both. The angles $A C B$ and $B D A$ are also equal to each other, as they are in the same segment of the circle <note>Both angles subtend the same arc $AB$</note>, and for that reason, the two triangles $B C E$ and $B D A$ will have proportional sides, such that as $B C$ is to $B D$, so $E C$ is to $A D$, and the [rectangle] under $E C$ and $B D$ is equal to that under $B C$ and $A D$. But also triangles $A B E$ and $C B D$ are similar, because the angles $A B E$ and $C B D$ were made equal, and the angles $B A C$ and $B D C$ are equal because they subtend the same circumference of the circle. Again, $A B$ is to $B D$ as $A E$ is to $C D$, and the [rectangle] under $A B$ and $C D$ is equal to that under $A E$ and $B D$. But it has already been shown that the [rectangle] under $A D$ and $B C$ is as much as that under $E D$ <note>original: $ED$. This is likely a scribal error in the Latin text for $BD$ or a specific segment; the logic follows that $BD \times AC = (AD \times BC) + (AB \times CD)$</note> and $E C$. Therefore, joined together, the [rectangle] under $B D$ and $A C$ is equal to those under $A D$ and $B C$, and under $A B$ and $C D$. This was the appropriate thing to have shown.

...given the diameter $A D$ and the chords $A B$ and $A C$ of unequal arcs. Since we wish to find the chord $B C$, the chords of the remaining arcs of the semicircle, $B D$ and $C D$, are given from the principles stated above. These form the inscribed quadrilateral $A B C D$ within the semicircle.

[[image: Geometrical diagram showing a semicircle with diameter AD and inscribed chords AB, BC, CD and diagonals AC, BD.]]

The diagonals of this quadrilateral, $A C$ and $B D$, are given, along with the three sides $A B, A D$, and $C D$. In this figure, as has just been demonstrated, the product of $A C$ and $B D$ is equal to the sum of the products of $A B$ times $C D$ and $A D$ times $B C$. Therefore, if the product of $A B$ and $C D$ is subtracted from the product of $A C$ and $B D$, the remainder is the product of $A D$ and $B C$. Thus, by using $A D$ as a divisor <note>original: "per A D divisorem"; Copernicus is explaining that dividing the remaining product by the diameter AD isolates the length of the chord BC</note>, the length of the sought-after chord $B C$ is calculated. Furthermore, since the sides of the pentagon and hexagon are known from the previous sections, this method provides the chord of 12 degrees—the difference by which the hexagon's arc exceeds the pentagon's arc <note>A hexagon side subtends 60°, and a pentagon side subtends 72°. The difference is 12°</note>. This is found to be 20,905 parts of the diameter.

### Fourth Theorem.

**G**iven the chord <term>subtendens</term> subtending any arc, the chord subtending half of that arc is also given. Let us describe a circle $A B C$, whose diameter is $A C$. Let $B C$ be the given arc with its chord. From the center $E$, let the line $E F$ intersect $B C$ at right angles. Therefore, according to the third [proposition] of the third [book] of Euclid <note>Euclid’s Elements III.3 states that a line from the center perpendicular to a chord bisects that chord</note>, it will bisect $B C$ at $F$, and when extended to the circumference at $D$, it will bisect the arc. Let the chords $A B$ and $B D$ also be drawn. Since triangles $A B C$ and $E F C$ are right-angled, and moreover share the angle $E C F$, they are similar. Therefore, just as $C F$ is half of $B F C$ <note>original: "B F C"; likely a reference to the chord BC</note>, so $E F$ is half of $A B$. But $A B$ is given, as it subtends the remaining arc of the semicircle; therefore $E F$ is also given, as is the remaining segment $D F$ from the half-diameter <note>The radius ED minus EF equals DF</note>. Let the diameter be completed as $D B G$, and let $B G$ be joined. In triangle $B D G$, from the right angle $B$, the perpendicular $B F$ descends to the base. Therefore, the product of $G D$ and $D F$ is equal to the square of $B D$. Thus, the length of $B D$ is given, which subtends half the arc $B D C$. Since the chord for 12 degrees has already been given, the chord for 6 degrees is also given as 10,467 parts; for three degrees, 5,235 parts; for one and a half degrees <note>original: "sesqui gradus"</note>, 2,618 parts; and for three-quarters of a degree <note>original: "dodrantis", meaning 3/4 or 45 minutes of arc</note>, 1,309 parts.

### Fifth Theorem.

**A**gain, when the chords of two arcs have been given, the chord which <term>subtends</term><note>To "subtend" an arc means to be the straight line (chord) that connects the two endpoints of that curved arc.</note> the arc composed of them both is also given. For, drawing the diameters $AFD$ and $BFE$, the straight lines $BD$ and $CE$ are also subtended, which are given from the preceding rules because $AB$ and $BC$ are given, and $DE$ is equal to $AB$. ...at point E, the segments of the base $EC$ to $AE$ will be as $BC$ to $AB$. And since $BC$ is greater than $AB$, $EC$ is also greater than $EA$. And since in every triangle, the larger angle is <term>subtended</term><note>A chord "subtends" an arc or angle by stretching across it like the string of a bow.</note> by the larger side, in triangle $DEF$, the side $DE$ is greater than $DF$, and furthermore $AD$ is greater than $DE$. Since, therefore, the <term>sector</term><note>A "sector" is a pie-slice shape of a circle, bounded by two radii and an arc.</note> $EDI$ is greater than triangle $BDF$, while triangle $DEA$ is greater than sector $DEH$, triangle $DEF$ will have a smaller ratio to triangle $DEA$ than sector $DEI$ has to sector $DEH$. But sectors are proportional to their arcs (or the angles at the center), while triangles having the same <term>vertex</term><note>The "vertex" is the highest point or corner; here, the center of the circle D.</note> are proportional to their bases. For this reason, the ratio of angles $EDF$ to $ADE$ is greater than the ratio of the bases $EF$ to $AE$. Therefore, by addition, angle $FDA$ to $ADE$ is greater than $AF$ to $AE$; and in the same way, angle $CDA$ to $ADE$ is greater than $AC$ to $AE$. And by subtraction, the ratio of angle $CDE$ to $EDA$ is also greater than $CE$ to $EA$.

Moreover, the angles $CDE$ to $EDA$ are in the same ratio as arc $CB$ to arc $AB$. But the base $CE$ to $AE$ is as the chord $CB$ to chord $AB$. Therefore, the ratio of arc $CB$ to arc $AB$ is greater than the ratio of chord $BC$ to chord $AB$, which was to be demonstrated.

<meta>This page continues the demonstration of how the ratio of arcs compares to the ratio of their chords. Having established that for very small arcs, the ratio of the chords is nearly identical to the ratio of the arcs themselves, Copernicus now calculates the specific values for his trigonometric table.</meta>

# THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK I.

From the arc **AB** to **AC**, the **AB** <term>subchord</term><note>Copernicus uses the term "subtensa" (literally 'stretched under') to refer to a chord—the straight line connecting the two endpoints of an arc.</note> is nevertheless less than double the **AC** subchord, which adds only a single small part to those <margin>2617</margin> parts. If, however, we take **AB** as one and a half degrees, and **AC** as three-quarters of one degree, we will have the **AB** subchord consisting of 2618 parts, and **AC** of 1309 parts. Although **AC** ought to be greater than half of the **AB** subchord itself, it nonetheless seems to differ not at all from the half; rather, the ratio of the circular arcs and the straight lines now appears to be the same. Since, therefore, we see that we have reached that point where the difference between the straight line and the curve entirely escapes the senses, as if they had become a single line, we do not hesitate to apply the 1309 parts of the <term>three-quarters</term><note>Original: "dodrans". A Roman fraction representing three-fourths.</note> of a degree, by the same ratio, to the full degree and the remaining parts. Thus, by adding a fourth part to the three parts, we establish one degree at 1745 parts, a half degree at 872½ parts, and a <term>third</term><note>Original: "trientis". A Roman fraction representing one-third (20 minutes of a degree).</note> of a part at approximately 582.

Nevertheless, I think it is sufficient if we record in the <term>table</term><note>Original: "canon". Copernicus uses this word to refer to a mathematical table or rule-set.</note> only the halves of the lines subtending double the arc. By this shortcut, we can encompass within a quadrant [90°] what would otherwise have to be spread out over a semicircle [180°]. This is especially useful because these halves occur more frequently in demonstrations and calculations than the whole lines. We have set forth the table increased by <term>sixths</term><note>Original: "sextantes". One-sixth of a degree is equal to 10 minutes.</note> of a degree, having three rows. In the first are the degrees (or parts of the circumference) and the sixths. The second contains the number of the half-line subtending double the arc. The third has the difference between these numbers which lies between each degree; by these, one may proportionally add what fits the individual <term>minutes</term><note>Original: "scrupulis". Literally 'scruples' or small stones, used here to mean the small fractional parts (minutes) of a degree.</note> of the degrees. This, then, is the table.

->d iij<-
<meta>catchword: Table</meta>

<summary>Copernicus explains how he calculates chords for very small angles (like 1°) and justifies his decision to create a table of half-chords (sines) rather than full chords for ease of calculation.</summary>
<keywords>chords, trigonometry, sine table, geometry, units of measurement, calculations, arc ratio</keywords>

<meta>This page follows the extensive trigonometric tables (the "Canon") from the previous sections. Having established the numerical values for chords and sines, Copernicus now moves into Chapter 14, where he applies these values to the geometry of triangles. This section is fundamental to his work, as celestial movements are calculated using the ratios of sides and angles in triangles.</meta>

NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

## On the sides and angles of plane rectilinear triangles. Chapter 14.

### I.

<image-desc>Geometrical diagram of a circle with an inscribed triangle. The vertices of the triangle are labeled A on the left horizontal axis, B at the top, and C on the right horizontal axis.</image-desc>

The sides of a triangle with given angles are given. Let us consider, I say, triangle ABC. By the fifth problem of the fourth book of <note>Euclid was an ancient Greek mathematician, the "Father of Geometry." His *Elements* was the standard textbook for nearly 2,000 years.</note> Euclid, a circle is circumscribed about it. Therefore, the arcs AB, BC, and CA will also be given, according to the system where 360 degrees <note>original: "partes"</note> are equal to two <term>right angles</term> <note>Copernicus is referencing a geometric convention where the sum of the angles in a triangle is 180 degrees, or two right angles.</note>. When the arcs are given, the sides of the triangle inscribed in the circle are also given as <term>chords</term> <note>original: "subtensæ," meaning lines that stretch under an arc.</note>, by means of the published <term>Table</term> <note>original: "Canonem." This refers to the trigonometric table provided in the previous chapters.</note>, in units where the <term>diameter</term> <note>original: "dimetiens."</note> is assumed to be 200,000.

### II.

<image-desc>Geometrical diagram of a triangle with vertex A at the top, vertex B at the bottom left, and vertex C at the bottom right. A vertical altitude line is drawn from vertex A to the base BC.</image-desc>

If, however, two sides of the triangle are given along with one of the angles, the remaining side and the remaining angles will be known. For either the given sides are equal, or they are unequal. Furthermore, the given angle is either right, acute, or obtuse. Again, the given sides either <term>contain</term> <note>i.e., the angle is located between the two known sides.</note> the given angle or they do not. First, therefore, let the two sides AB and AC in triangle ABC be given as equal, and let them contain the given angle A. Thus, the remaining angles at the base BC, being equal to each other, are also given as half of the remainder of angle A subtracted from two right angles. And if any angle at the base was given first, its companion is immediately given, and from these, the remainder of the two right angles is found. But when the angles of the triangle are given, the sides are given; and the base BC itself is given from the Table in those units where AB or AC, acting as the <term>radius</term> <note>original: "ex centro," meaning the distance from the center.</note>, is 100,000 units, or the diameter is 200,000 units.

### III.

<image-desc>Geometrical diagram of a right-angled triangle. Vertex A is at the top, vertex B is at the bottom left (forming the right angle), and vertex C is at the bottom right.</image-desc>

But if the angle BAC, contained by the given sides, is a right angle, the same result will follow. Since it is most clear that the <term>squares</term> <note>original: "quadrata."</note> which are formed from AB and AC are equal to the square of

<meta>catchword: of,</meta>

<summary>In this page, Copernicus transitions from trigonometric tables to the practical geometry of triangles, explaining how to calculate unknown sides and angles using the laws of circles and the Pythagorean theorem.</summary>
<keywords>plane triangles, Euclid, geometry, chords, diameter, right angles, trigonometry</keywords>

--- Page 61 ---
<meta>This page continues Chapter 14 of Book I, transitioning from the general rules of triangles inscribed in circles to the specific methods for solving plane triangles using the trigonometric tables (the "Canon") and the properties of right-angled triangles.</meta>

->REVOLUTIONS BOOK I.<-

to that which is from the base bc; therefore bc is given in length, and the sides themselves are given in ratio to one another. But the segment of a circle which contains a <term>right-angled triangle</term> <note>original: "orthogonū triangulum"</note> is a semicircle, of which the base bc would be the <term>diameter</term> <note>original: "dimetiens."</note>. Therefore, in whatever units bc is 200,000, ab and ac will be given as the <term>chords</term> <note>original: "subtendentes," literally those which stretch under the arcs.</note> subtending the remaining angles. Consequently, the ratio of the Table <note>original: "Canonem," referring to the trigonometric table provided in previous chapters.</note> will reveal these in units where 360 degrees are equal to two right angles <note>Copernicus is noting that in his system, the internal angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees, or half of a 360-degree circle.</note>. The same will result if bc is given along with one of the sides forming the right angle, which I think is now clearly established.

#### IV.

Now let the acute angle abc be given, along with the sides ab and bc which enclose it. From point a, let a <term>perpendicular</term> <note>A line falling at a 90-degree angle.</note> ad descend to the line bc (extended if necessary), depending on whether it falls inside or outside the triangle. This line ad separates the area into two right-angled triangles, abd and adc. Since the angles in triangle abd are given—for d is a right angle and b is given by hypothesis—the sides ad and bd are therefore given as chords subtending angles a and b, in units where the diameter ab of the circle is 200,000 according to the Table. And by the same ratio by which ab was given in length, ad and bd are similarly given; cd is also given, being the difference by which bc and bd exceed each other. Therefore, in the right-angled triangle adc, with the sides ad and cd being given, the sought-after side ac and the angle acd are also given by the preceding demonstration.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a triangle ABC. A perpendicular line AD is drawn from vertex A to the base line. Point D lies on the extension of line BC to the left, creating two right-angled triangles, ADB and ADC, sharing the side AD.</image-desc>

#### V.

It will happen no differently if the angle b is obtuse. When a perpendicular ad is drawn from point a to the extended straight line bc, it creates a triangle abd of two angles <note>That is, a triangle where the angles are known.</note>. Since the exterior angle abd to the angle abc is given, and d is a right angle, then bd and ad are given in units where ab is 200,000. And since ba and bc have a given ratio to each other, then ab is given in the same units as bd and the whole line cbd. Therefore, in the right-angled triangle adc, since the two sides ad and cd are given, the sought-after side ac is also given, as well as the angle bac with the remaining angle acb, which was being sought.

### VII.

**W**hen all the sides of a triangle are given, the angles are also given. Regarding <term>equilateral</term> <note>original: "Isopleuro."</note> triangles, it is too well known to require explanation that each of its angles is one-third of two <term>right angles</term> <note>In modern terms, 60 degrees (1/3 of 180 degrees).</note>. In <term>isosceles</term> <note>Triangles with two equal sides.</note> triangles, it is also clear. For the equal sides are to the third side as the halves of the diameter are to the chord subtending the arc. Through this, the angle enclosed by the equal sides is given from the Table, in which 360 degrees around the center are equal to four right angles; then the remaining angles at the base are also given as halves of the remainder of two right angles. It remains now to demonstrate this for <term>scalene</term> <note>Triangles where all three sides are of different lengths.</note> triangles, which we shall likewise divide into <term>right-angled triangles</term> <note>original: "orthogonios."</note>. Therefore, let there be a scalene triangle *abc* of given sides, and upon the side which

For the angle *c* must be acute; otherwise, *ab* would be the longest side, contrary to our hypothesis, as can be observed from the 17th theorem of the first book of Euclid and the two following it. Therefore, *bd* and *dc* are given, and there will be right-angled triangles *abd* and *adc* with known sides and angles (as has been frequently repeated). By these, the angles of the sought triangle *abc* are established.

## On Spherical Triangles. Chapter XIV.

We define a convex triangle in this context as that which is contained by three arcs of <term>great circles</term> <note>original: "maximorum circulorum," circles on a sphere whose center is the center of the sphere itself, like the equator on a globe.</note> on the surface of a sphere. The difference and magnitude of the angles, however, are determined by the arc of a great circle described with the point of intersection acting as its <term>pole</term> <note>original: "polo." In spherical geometry, the pole of a circle is the point from which all points on the circle's circumference are at a 90-degree distance.</note>. This arc is the portion intercepted by the quadrants of the circles which form the angle. For whatever ratio the intercepted arc has to the entire circumference, the same ratio the angle of intersection has to four right angles (which we have said contain 360 equal parts).

## I.

If there are three arcs of <term>great circles</term> <note>A circle on the surface of a sphere that shares the same center as the sphere itself, dividing it into two equal halves.</note> of a sphere, of which any two joined together are longer than the third, it is evident that a spherical triangle can be formed from them. For what is proposed here concerning arcs, <term>Euclid</term> <note>A Greek mathematician (c. 300 BCE) known as the "father of geometry."</note> demonstrates in the 23rd proposition of his eleventh book regarding angles; since the ratio of angles and arcs is the same, and great circles are those that pass through the center of the sphere, it is clear that those three sectors of circles, of which the arcs are part, form a <term>solid angle</term> <note>original: "angulum solidum," an angle formed by three or more planes meeting at a single vertex, like the tip of a pyramid.</note> at the center of the sphere. Therefore, what is proposed is manifest.

## II.

Each arc of the triangle must be less than a <term>semicircle</term> <note>original: "hemicyclio," a half-circle of 180 degrees.</note>. For a semicircle creates no angle at the center, but instead collapses into a straight line. Moreover, the remaining two angles, of which there are arcs, cannot enclose a solid at the center, and consequently cannot form a spherical triangle. I believe this was the reason why <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the Greco-Roman astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is refining.</note>, in his explanation of this kind of triangle—especially regarding the figure of a spherical sector—expressly warns that the assumed arcs must not be larger than a semicircle.

## III.

In spherical triangles having a right angle, the <term>chord</term> <note>original: "subtendens," literally the line "stretching under" the arc. In this context, the chord of double the arc is functionally equivalent to twice the sine of the angle.</note> of double the side which is opposite the right angle, to the chord of double one of the sides forming the right angle, is as the diameter of the sphere is to the chord which subtends double the angle contained by the remaining side and the hypotenuse in a great circle of the sphere.

These lines extend to meet an arc DE of a great circle. Points G, I, and K are marked on internal segments, illustrating chords and perpendiculars used in a mathematical proof relating the sides and angles of the triangle.]

I say that the chord of double *AB* to the chord of double *BC* is as the diameter of the sphere to the chord which, in a great circle, subtends double the angle *BAC*. Furthermore, since GB is perpendicular to FD, because angles FGB and GFD are right angles, the angle FDK will be equal to GBI by the tenth proposition of **Euclid's** eleventh book. But the angle at FKD is a right angle, as is GIB by the definition of a perpendicular line. Therefore, the sides of these <term>similar triangles</term> <note>Triangles that have the same shape (equal angles) but may differ in size; their sides are in the same proportion.</note> are proportional: as DF is to BG, so is DK to BI. But BI is half the <term>chord of twice the arc</term> <note>original: "subtendentis duplum." It is clear, therefore, that the chord of twice the arc AB is to the chord of twice BC, as the diameter is to the chord that subtends twice the angle A (or the intercepted arc DE), which was the appropriate thing to demonstrate.

**If the angles of a triangle are given, and one of them is a right angle, the sides are also given.**

Maintaining the same figure used previously, where because angle **c** is given, the circumference <note>In spherical geometry, an "arc" or "circumference" of a great circle represents the measure of an angle at the center of the sphere, used here to define the length of a side.</note> **de** is given, as is the remainder **ef** from the quadrant of the circle. ### VIII.

Furthermore, if two triangles have two sides equal to two sides, each to each, and an angle equal to an angle—whether it be the one that the equal sides encompass, or the one at the base—they will also have the base equal to the base, and the remaining angles equal to the remaining angles. I say that the base BD is also equal to the base EF, and angle B to F, and the remaining angle BDA equal to the remaining CEF. For we will have two triangles AGN and CLM, of which angles G and L are right angles, and GAN equal to MCL, which are the remainders of the equal angles BAD and ECF. Therefore these triangles are mutually equiangular and equilateral. Wherefore, from the equals AD and CE, there also remain DN and ME equal. But it has already been shown that the angle which is under DNH is equal to that under EMK, and those at H and K are right angles; thus the two triangles DHN and EMK will also be of mutually equal angles...

### IX.

In isosceles <note>A triangle with at least two equal sides.</note> triangles on a sphere, the angles at the base are equal to one another. Let there be a triangle <term>ABC</term>, of which the two sides <term>AB</term> and <term>AC</term> are equal. From the vertex <term>A</term>, let a great circle <note>original: "maximus orbis"; the largest possible circle drawn on a sphere, which bisects it into two hemispheres.</note> descend, cutting the base at right angles—that is, passing through the poles—and let it be <term>AD</term>. Since, therefore, in the two triangles <term>ABD</term> and <term>ADC</term>, side <term>BA</term> is equal to side <term>AC</term>, and <term>AD</term> is common to both, and the angles around <term>D</term> are right angles, it is clear by the preceding demonstration that the angles <term>ABC</term> and <term>ACB</term> are equal. Which was to be demonstrated <note>original: "quod erat demonstrandũ" (Q.E.D.).</note>. From this follows a corollary <note>original: "Poriſma"; a deduction or corollary that follows naturally from a proof.</note>: that the arc which falls from the vertex of an isosceles triangle at right angles onto the base will bisect <note>To cut exactly into two equal halves.</note> both the base and the angle contained by the equal sides; and conversely, this is established by the preceding demonstration.

<image-desc>A diagram of a spherical triangle labeled ABC. A vertical arc AD is drawn from the vertex A to the base BC, bisecting the triangle into two symmetrical right-angled spherical triangles.</image-desc>

### X.

Any two triangles on the same sphere having equal sides, each to each, will also have equal angles, each to each respectively. For since three segments of great circles on both sides constitute pyramids <note>In early modern geometry, "pyramids" often refers to the solid angles or the tetrahedral shapes formed by the radii of the sphere meeting at the center.</note> having their vertices at the center of the sphere, their bases are the triangles contained by the planes of the straight lines subtending the arcs of the convex triangles. Those pyramids are similar and equal...

#### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK I.

[The text concludes a proof on the similarity of spherical triangles...]
...are equal, by the definition of equal similar solid figures. Moreover, the ratio of similarity is such that, in whatever way the angles are taken, they have them equal to one another; therefore, the triangles themselves will have angles equal to one another. Specifically, those who define the similarity of figures more generally wish them to be whatever figures have similar inclinations, and in these, angles equal to one another. From which I think it is manifest that, in a sphere, triangles which are equilateral to one another are similar, just as in plane surfaces.

**XI.**
Every triangle, of which two sides have been given together with any angle, is made [known] in its remaining angles and sides. For if the given sides are equal, the angles at the base will be equal; and by dropping an arc from the vertex to the base at right angles, the sought things will easily be clear through the Corollary of the ninth [theorem]. But if the given sides are unequal, as in triangle **ABC**, of which angle **A** is given, along with the two sides which either encompass the given angle or do not encompass it. 

Let them first be the encompassing sides, the given sides **AB** and **AC** themselves; and with the pole being made at **C**, let the arc of a great circle **DEF** be described, and let the quadrants **CAD** and **CBE** be completed, and let the produced **AB** intersect **DE** at point **F**. Thus also in triangle **ADF**, the side **AD** is given, being the remainder of the quadrant from **AC**. Also, angle **BAD** [is given] from **CAB** [being the remainder] of two right angles. For the ratio and dimension of the angles which occur at the intersection of straight lines and planes is the same, and angle **D** is a right angle. Therefore, by the fourth [theorem] of this [book], triangle **ADF** itself will be of known angles and sides. 

And again, in triangle **BEF**, angle **F** is found, and **E** is a right angle by the intersection at the pole, and also side **BF**, by which the whole **ABF** exceeds **AB**. Therefore, by the same Theorem, triangle **BEF** will be of known angles and sides. From which, from **BE** is given **BC**, the remainder of the quadrant and the sought side; and from **EF**, the remainder of the whole **DEF**, which is **DE**, and this is angle **C**; and through the angle which is under **EBF**, the sought angle at the vertex **ABC** is found. But if in place of **AB**, **CB** is assumed, which is opposite the given angle, the same result will follow. For the remainders of the quadrants **AD** and **BE** are given, and by the same argument the two triangles **ADF** and **BEF** are of known angles and sides, as before; from which the proposed triangle **ABC** may be known in its sides and angles, which was intended.

**XII.**

Likewise, through the fourth [theorem] of this [book], **BE** and **BF** are given, from which the other sought sides **AB** and **BC** will be established. 

Otherwise, if one of the given angles were opposite the given side—as for instance, if angle **ABC** is given instead of that which is under **ACB**, the others remaining—it will be established by the same demonstration that the whole triangle **ADF** has given angles and sides, and the particular triangle **BEF** similarly; since on account of angle **F** being common to both, and **EBF** which is at the vertex being [equal] to the given one, and **E** a right angle, it is demonstrated in the preceding that all its sides also are given; from which finally those same things follow which we have said. For all these things are always bound together by a mutual and perpetual link, as befits the form of a globe.

But the whole **BAC** is given. Through the preceding Theorem, therefore, the angles **BAD** and **CAD** will also be given. Then through the fifth [theorem], we shall attain the sides **AB**, **BC**, **AC**, **CD**, and the whole **BC**.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS ON THE REVOLUTIONS
### BOOK SECOND.

[Large historiated initial 'C' showing a figure with a celestial sphere.]

Since in the preceding book we have set forth the three motions of the Earth in sum, by which we promised to demonstrate all the appearances of the stars, we shall do so henceforth by examining each one through its parts and inquiring according to our ability. We shall begin, moreover, from that most known revolution of all, of the time of day and night, which we said is called *nychthemeron* [Gr. νυχθήμερον] by the Greeks, and which we have taken as being most especially and without intermediary appropriate to the terrestrial globe; since from it months, years, and other times of many names arise, just as number from unity. 

Concerning, therefore, the inequality of days and nights, the rising and setting of the Sun, the parts of the zodiac and signs, and that class of things following upon the revolution itself, we shall say a few things: especially since many have written abundantly enough about these, which nevertheless support and agree with our own [conclusions]. And it matters nothing if what they demonstrate through a stationary Earth and a turning world, we—taking the opposite [view]—concur at the same goal; since in those things which are in mutual relation, it happens so that they agree with each other in turn. 

Nevertheless, we shall omit nothing of those things which will be necessary. Indeed, let no one wonder if we still simply name the rising and setting of the Sun and stars, and similar things, but let him know that we speak in the accustomed discourse, which can be received by all, yet always holding in mind that:
> "To us who are carried by the Earth, the Sun and Moon pass by,
> And the turns of the stars return, and again recede." [Referencing Virgil/Poetic tradition]

### On the circles and their names. Chapter I.

We have called the equinoctial circle the greatest of the parallels described about the poles of its daily revolution. But the Zodiac [we have called] the circle through the middle...

***

### PAGE 77
[Original Page 28]
#### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK II.

...middle of the signs, under which the center of the Earth itself travels in its annual revolution. But since the zodiac exists oblique to the equinoctial—according to the mode of the inclination of the Earth's axis to it—through the daily revolution of the Earth it describes two circles touching it on both sides, as the extreme limits of its obliquity, which they call Tropics. For the Sun seems in these to make *tropas* [Gr. τροπάς], that is, conversions, namely winterly and summery. Whence they have been accustomed to call the one which is toward the North the solstitial tropic, and the other towards the South the Brumal [Winter], as was set forth above in the summary narration of the terrestrial revolutions. 

Next follows the circle called Horizon, which the Latins call the *Finientem* [Limit]; for it defines for us the apparent part of the world from that which is hidden, at which all things which set seem to rise, having its center on the surface of the Earth, and its pole at our vertex. But since the Earth exists as incomparable to the immensity of the heaven—especially because even all this which exists between the Sun and Moon cannot, according to our hypothesis, be compared to the magnitude of the heaven—the horizon circle seems to bisect the heaven as if through the center of the world, as we demonstrated from the beginning. Insofar as the horizon is oblique to the equinoctial, it also touches two parallel circles on either side: the Northern of those always apparent, and the Southern of those always hidden; and that one is named Arctic, this one Antarctic, by Proclus and generally by the Greeks, which become larger or smaller according to the mode of the obliquity of the horizon or the elevation of the equinoctial pole. 

There remains the meridian, which passes through the poles of the horizon and also through the poles of the equinoctial circle, and for that reason is erect to both circles; when the Sun has reached it, it shows midday and midnight. But these two circles having their center on the surface of the Earth—I mean the Finitor and the Meridian—follow entirely the motion of the Earth and our sight wherever it may be. For the eye everywhere assumes for itself the center of the sphere of all visible things round about. Consequently, all circles assumed on the Earth refer to similar images of circles in the heaven, as is demonstrated more clearly in Cosmography and regarding the dimensions of the Earth. And these indeed are the circles having proper names, while others can be designated in infinite ways and names.

***

[Original Page: NICOLAUS COPERNICUS]

### On the obliquity of the sign-bearer [ecliptic], and the distance of the tropics, and how they are taken. Chapter II.

[Historiated initial 'S']
The sign-bearing circle [the ecliptic], since it travels obliquely between the tropic and the equinoctial: I now deem it necessary that we experience the distance of the tropics themselves, and likewise the angle of intersection of the equinoctial and sign-bearing circles, how great it may be. For it is necessary to perceive this by sense and by the skill of instruments, for which this [method] especially is held: that a wooden square be prepared, or rather one of another more solid material, stone or metal; lest perhaps the wood, being inconstant by the alteration of the air, might deceive the operator. 

Moreover, let one of its surfaces be most exactly smoothed, and let it have a width sufficient for admitting the divisions, such as if it were of three or four cubits. For with the center taken in one of the angles, a quadrant of a circle is designated for its capacity and is distinguished into 90 equal parts, which are likewise subdivided into 60 minutes, or as many as they can receive. Then at the center a cylindrical gnomon is fixed, best turned [on a lathe], and being erect to that surface, let it project a little, perhaps by the width of a finger, or less. 

With the instrument thus prepared, it is convenient to lay out a meridian line on a pavement spread to the level of the horizon, and as carefully as possible made level through a *Hydroscopium* or *Chorobates* [water-leveling devices], lest it tilt in any direction. For with a circle described in this [pavement] from its center, a gnomon is erected; and observing at some time before noon where the extremity of the shadow touches the circumscribing circle, we shall mark it. We shall do similarly after noon, and we shall bisect the arc of the circle lying between the two marks already noted. In this way indeed, a straight line drawn from the center through the point of division will infallibly indicate the South and North for us. 

To this line, therefore, as a base, the plane of the instrument is erected and fixed to the perpendicular, with the center turned toward the south, so that the line descending exactly from it agrees at right angles with the meridian line. For it happens in this way that the surface of the instrument holds the meridian circle. Hence, on the days of the Solstice and Winter, the meridian shadows of the Sun are to be observed...

***

### PAGE 79
[Original Page 29]
#### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK II.

...to be observed falling through that index or cylinder from the center, applying something about the subject circumference of the quadrant, so that the place of the shadow may be held more certainly; and we shall note as accurately as possible the middle of the shadow in degrees and minutes. For if we do this, the arc which is found marked between the two shadows, the Solstitial and Brumal [Winter], will show us the distance of the tropics and the entire obliquity of the sign-bearer [ecliptic]. By taking half of this, we shall have how much the tropics themselves are distant from the equinoctial; and how great is the angle of inclination of the equinoctial to that circle which is through the middle of the signs [the ecliptic] will become manifest. 

Ptolemy, therefore, detected this interval which is between the already mentioned limits, Northern and Southern, to be of 47 degrees, 42 minutes, and 40 seconds, of which the circle is 360; just as he found it observed before himself by Hipparchus and Eratosthenes. And these are 11 parts of which the whole circle would be 83; and from that, the half-difference, which is 23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds, established the distance of the tropics from the equinoctial circle (where the circle is 360 degrees) and the angle of intersection with the sign-bearer. 

Ptolemy therefore thought this to hold invariably, and that it would remain so forever. But from that time these [values] are found to have continually decreased down to us. For the distance of the tropics has already been found by us and certain others of our contemporaries to be no more than 46 degrees and about 58 minutes; and the angle of intersection 23 degrees, 28 minutes, and two-fifths of one [minute]; so that it is already clear enough that even the obliquity of the sign-bearer is mobile. Of which more [will be said] below, where we shall also show by a probable enough conjecture that it was never greater than 23 degrees 52 minutes, nor will it ever be less than 23 degrees 28 minutes.

### On the arcs and angles of the intersecting circles—the equinoctial, sign-bearer, and meridian—from which are declination and right ascension, and on their computation. Chapter III.

[Historiated initial 'Q' with a face/mask]
What we were saying, therefore, about the Finitor [horizon]—that the parts of the world rise and set from it—this [we say] in the case of the meridian circle...

***

### PAGE 80
[Original Page: NICOLAUS COPERNICUS]

...we say bisects the heaven; which also transmits and separates both the sign-bearer and the equinoctial in the space of 24 hours, by cutting their arcs from the vernal or autumnal intersection; and in turn is separated by them [by] the intercepted arc. And since they are all great circles, they constitute a right-angled spherical triangle; for the angle is right where the meridian cuts the equinoctial through the poles, as has been defined. 

Moreover, they call the arc of the meridian, or of any circle through the poles so intercepted, the **declination** of a segment of the zodiac. But that arc which corresponds from the equinoctial circle, rising together with its peer arc of the zodiac, [they call] the **right ascension**. All which things are easily demonstrated in a convex triangle. 

For let **ABCD** be the circle passing through the poles of the equinoctial and the zodiac simultaneously, which many call the Colure of the solstices. Let the half of the sign-bearer be **ABC**, the half of the equinoctial **BED**, the Vernal intersection at point **E**, the Solstice at **A**, the Winter at **C**. Moreover, let **F** be assumed as the pole of the daily revolution; and from the sign-bearer let arc **EG** be, for example, of 30 degrees, upon which is drawn the quadrant of the circle **FGH**. 

Then it is manifest that in triangle **EGH**, the side **EG** of 30 degrees is given, with the angle **GEH**, since the smallest [obliquity] was 23 degrees 28 minutes [Copernicus uses 24 degrees in some contexts, but here follows his previous measurement] according to the maximum declination **AB**, of which 360 are four right angles; and angle **GHE** is a right angle. Therefore, by the fourth [theorem] of spherical [triangles], the triangle **EHG** itself will be of known angles and sides. Namely, it has been demonstrated that the chord of the double of **EG** is to the chord of the double of **GH** as the chord of the double of **AGE** (or the diameter of the sphere) is to the chord of the double of **AB**, and their halves similarly. Since the half of the double of **AGE** is 100,000 from the center, and that which is under **AB** is 39,822 of the same parts; and **EG** is 50,000 parts [as a sine/half-chord]. 

And since if four numbers are proportional, the product of the means is equal to that of the extremes, we shall have the half-chord of the double of arc **GH** as 19,911 parts; and in the table this same **GH** is 11 degrees 29 minutes, the declination corresponding to segment **EG**. Wherefore also in triangle **AFG**, the sides **FG** of 78 degrees 31 minutes and **AG** of 60 parts are given as the remainders of the quadrants; and angle **FAGE** is a right angle; in the same way the chords of the doubles **FG, AG, FGH, and BH**, or...

### XII.

**F**urthermore, if two angles are given in any way along with some side, the same results will follow. For with the construction of the previous figure remaining <note>Copernicus refers back to the diagram used in Chapter XI, which is repeated here for the reader's convenience</note>, let there be triangle **ABC**, with two angles **ACB** and **BAC** given along with side **AC**, which is adjacent to both angles. Furthermore, if one of the given angles were a right angle, all other things could be determined through reasoning by the fourth [theorem] preceding <note>Theorem IV in this book established how to solve right-angled spherical triangles</note>. However, we wish to distinguish this case where they are not right angles. Therefore, **AD** will be the remainder of the quadrant from **CAD**, and the angle under **BAD** is the remainder of **BAC** from two right angles <note>original: "è duobus rectis"; meaning they are supplementary angles forming a straight line</note>, and **D** is a right angle. Therefore, in triangle **AFD**, the angles and sides are given by the fourth [theorem] of this book. And through the given angle **C**, the arc **DE** is given, and the remainder **EF**, and also the right angle **BEF**, and angle **F** is common to both triangles. Likewise, **BE** and **BF** are given by the fourth [theorem] of this book, from which the remaining sought sides **AB** and **BC** will be established. 

Otherwise, if one of the given angles were opposite to the given side—for example, if angle **ABC** is given instead of **ACB**, while the others remain—the same demonstration will establish the whole triangle **ADF** with its given angles and sides, and similarly the particular triangle **BEF**. For because of angle **F** which is common to both, and **EBF** which is given as a vertical angle <note>original: "ad uerticem"; opposite angles formed by intersecting lines</note>, and **E** being a right angle, it was demonstrated in the preceding sections that all its sides are also given. From these, finally, the same things follow which we have said. For all these things are always linked by a mutual and perpetual connection, as befits the form of a globe.

### XIII.

**F**inally, in a triangle where all sides are given, the angles are given. Let all the sides of triangle **ABC** be given; I say that all the angles are also found. For either the triangle itself will have equal sides, or not. Let them first be equal, **AB** and **AC**. It is manifest that the halves of the chords subtending twice these arcs <term>chords subtending twice the arcs: Copernicus is using the "chord" function, the precursor to the modern sine function ($chord(2\alpha) = 2 \sin \alpha$)</term> will also be equal. # ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK I.

...and its rotation. But through the 3rd proposition of the same book <note>Copernicus refers to Euclid's Elements, Book XI, which deals with solid geometry</note>, angle **DEB** is a right angle in plane **ABD**, and **DEC** is similarly a right angle in plane **ACD**. Therefore, angle **BEC** is the angle of inclination of these planes according to the 4th definition of Euclid’s eleventh book. We shall find this angle in the following way. For when the straight line **BC** has been subtended <note>the "subtended line" is the straight chord connecting the two endpoints of an arc</note>, we will have a <term>rectilinear triangle</term> <note>a triangle made of straight lines on a flat plane, rather than arcs on the surface of a sphere</note> **BEC**. Since its sides are given through the known lengths of their arcs, it will also consist of given angles. Thus we will have the sought angle **BEC**, which is the spherical angle **BAC**, and the remaining angles will be found through the preceding theorems.

But if it should be a <term>scalene</term> <note>a triangle where all three sides have different lengths</note> triangle, as shown in the second figure, it is clear that the halves of the lines subtending double the arcs <note>Copernicus is calculating the equivalent of the modern sine function, which in his time was treated as half the chord of a doubled arc</note> will not touch each other. Because if arc **AC** were greater than **AB**, the half-chord of double **AC** (which we call **CF**) will fall lower. If it were smaller, it would be higher, just as it happens that such lines become closer to or farther from the center according to the 15th theorem of Euclid’s third book. 

Then, if a line **FG** is drawn parallel to **BE**, cutting the line **BD** (the common section of the circles) at point **G**, and **CG** is connected: it is then clear that angle **EFG** is a right angle (namely, equal to angle **AEB**). Also, angle **EFC** is a right angle, since **CF** is the half-chord of double arc **AC**. Therefore, **CFG** will be the angle of the intersection of the circles **AB** and **AC**, which we therefore obtain. For the ratio of **DF** to **FG** is the same as **DE** to **EB**, since triangles **DFG** and **DEB** are similar. 

Therefore, **FG** is given in the same units in which **FC** is also given. Moreover, **DG** is to **DB** in that same ratio; thus **DG** will be given in the units in which **DC** is 100,000 <note>Copernicus uses a standard radius of 100,000 for his trigonometric tables to allow for high precision without using decimals</note>. Furthermore, the angle **GDC** is given through arc **BC**. Therefore, by the second theorem of plane triangles, side **GC** is given in the same units as the other sides of the plane triangle **GFC**. Finally, through the last theorem of plane triangles, we will have angle **GFC**, which is the sought spherical angle **BAC**, and we will then perceive the remaining angles through the 11th theorem of spherical triangles.

From this, the whole angle **EDA**—which contains circumference **AB**—is found, and the remainder **CB** will also be established, which was the goal of the demonstration.

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS
### BOOK TWO.

Since in the preceding book we explained the three motions of the earth in summary, by which we promised to demonstrate all the appearances of the stars, we shall henceforth do this by examining and investigating each part individually as best we can. We shall begin with the best known of all: the revolution of day and night time, which we said is called a **nuchthemeron** <note>original: "νυχθήμερον"; a Greek term for a full 24-hour period consisting of one night and one day</note> by the Greeks, and which we have taken to be most especially and directly suited to the terrestrial globe. For from it arise months, years, and other divisions of time by many names, just as numbers arise from unity. Therefore, concerning the inequality of days and nights, the rising and setting of the Sun, and the parts of the zodiac and the signs, and things of that kind that follow from this revolution, we shall say a few things; especially since many have written quite enough about these, and their accounts agree and coincide with our own. 

It makes no difference if we, taking the opposite view, reach the same goal that they <note>earlier astronomers who believed the Earth was stationary</note> demonstrate by means of a stationary earth and a whirling of the universe, since in things related to one another, it so happens that they agree with each other reciprocally. Nevertheless, we shall omit nothing that will be necessary. Let no one wonder, indeed, if we still simply speak of the rising and setting of the Sun and stars, and similar things, but let them know that we are speaking in the accustomed manner, which can be accepted by everyone, yet always keeping in mind that:

> For us who are carried by the earth, the Sun and Moon pass by,
> And the stars return in their turns, and again they recede.
<note>Copernicus is parodying a famous line from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (3.72), where the land and cities "recede" from the sailors; here, it is the celestial bodies that seem to move because the Earth is carrying us.</note>

### On the circles and their names. Chapter I.

We have called the **equinoctial circle** <term>equinoctial circle</term> <note>the celestial equator; the great circle on the celestial sphere in the same plane as the Earth's equator</note> the greatest of the parallels described by the terrestrial globe around the poles of its daily revolution. But the **Zodiac** passing through the middle of the signs...

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK II.

...the circle of the signs <note>the Zodiac</note>, under which the annual revolution of the center of the Earth itself traces its path. But since the zodiac is oblique <note>tilted</note> to the equinoctial <note>the celestial equator</note>, according to the degree of inclination of the Earth's axis to it, the daily revolution of the Earth describes two circles on either side that touch it at its extreme limits. These limits of its obliquity are called the **Tropics**. Indeed, the Sun appears to make "tropas"—that is, "turnings"—at these points, namely at the winter and summer solstices. For this reason, people have been accustomed to call the northern one the "solstitial tropic," and the other, which is toward the South, the "brumal" <note>winter</note> tropic, as was set forth earlier in the summary account of the terrestrial revolutions. 

Next follows the so-called **Horizon**, which the Latins call the "Finisher" <note>original: "finientem"</note>; for it defines for us the visible part of the world from that which is hidden. For those for whom everything that sets appears to rise, it has its center on the surface of the Earth and its pole at our zenith <note>the point directly overhead</note>. But since the Earth is incomparably small relative to the immensity of the heavens—especially as even this entire distance existing between the Sun and the Moon cannot be compared to the magnitude of the heavens according to our hypothesis—the circle of the horizon appears to divide the heavens into two equal parts as if through the center of the universe, just as we demonstrated from the beginning. To the extent that the horizon is oblique to the equinoctial, it also touches two parallel circles on either side: the northern circle of those stars which are "always visible," and the southern circle of those "always hidden." These are named the **Arctic** and **Antarctic** by Proclus <note>a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and mathematician</note> and most of the Greeks, and they become larger or smaller according to the degree of obliquity of the horizon or the elevation of the equinoctial pole.

There remains the **Meridian**, which passes through the poles of the horizon and also through the poles of the equinoctial circle; it is therefore set upright <note>perpendicular</note> to both circles. When the Sun reaches this circle, it indicates midday and midnight. But these two circles that have their center on the surface of the Earth—I mean the Finisher <note>Horizon</note> and the Meridian—follow the motion of the Earth and our sight entirely. For the eye, everywhere it goes, assumes for itself the center of the sphere of all things visible around it. Consequently, all circles assumed on the Earth reflect their images as similar circles in the heavens, as is demonstrated more clearly in Cosmography <note>the study of the Earth in relation to the universe</note> and regarding the dimensions of the Earth. And these indeed are the circles having specific names, although others can be designated in infinite ways and by infinite names.

Concerning...

He emphasizes that because of the Earth's negligible size relative to the universe, the observer's horizon appears to bisect the heavens perfectly.</summary>

### On the Obliquity of the Zodiac, the Distance Between the Tropics, and How They Are Measured. Chapter II.

**T**he zodiac circle <note>original: "Signifer ergo circulus"; the OCR's "Ignifer" is likely a misreading of the decorative initial 'S'</note> proceeds at an angle between the tropics and the equinoctial <note>the celestial equator</note>. Therefore, I now consider it necessary to determine the distance between the tropics, and likewise the size of the angle of intersection between the equinoctial and the zodiac circles. To perceive this, we must rely on the senses and the skill of instruments. For this purpose, one should prepare a wooden square, or better yet, one made of a more solid material like stone or metal, lest the wood—which can be inconsistent due to changes in the air—might deceive the observer. 

One of its surfaces should be perfectly smoothed and planed, and it should have a width sufficient to accommodate the markings, perhaps three or four cubits <note>a cubit is roughly the length of a forearm, about 18 inches</note>. Taking one of the corners as the center, a quadrant <note>a quarter-circle</note> is drawn to match the size of the square and divided into 90 equal parts <note>degrees</note>, which are themselves subdivided into 60 minutes <note>original: "scrupula"</note>, or as many as the space can receive. 

Next, a <term>gnomon</term> <note>the part of a sundial or instrument that casts a shadow</note> is attached to the center. It should be a perfectly turned cylinder, fixed perpendicular to the surface, and should protrude slightly—perhaps the width of a finger or less. Once the instrument is prepared in this way, it is necessary to lay out a meridian line on a floor leveled to the plane of the horizon. This should be leveled as carefully as possible using a <term>Hydroscope</term> <note>a water-level</note> or a <term>Chorobates</term> <note>a 20-foot long leveling tool described by the Roman architect Vitruvius</note>, so it does not slope in any direction. 

Within a circle drawn on this floor, the gnomon is erected at the center. We will mark the point where the tip of the shadow touches the circumference of the circle at some time before noon. We shall do the same after noon, and then bisect the arc of the circle lying between the two marked points. In this way, a straight line drawn from the center through the point of bisection will infallibly indicate North and South for us. 

The vertical surface of the instrument is then erected upon this line as a base and fixed perpendicularly. The center of the quadrant should face South, so that a plumb line hanging from the center falls exactly at right angles to the meridian line. In this way, the surface of the instrument functions as the meridian circle. From this setup, the noon shadows of the Sun are to be observed on the days of the Summer and Winter solstices...

# BOOK II OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...should be observed through that index or <term>cylinder</term> <note>original: "Kylindrium"</note> falling from the center, using some object placed around the lower circumference of the quadrant so that the position of the shadow may be held more surely; and we will note as accurately as possible the middle of the shadow in degrees <note>original: "partibus"</note> and minutes <note>original: "scrupulis"</note>. For if we do this, the arc that is found marked between the two shadows—that of the Summer Solstice <note>original: "Solsticialem"</note> and the Winter Solstice <note>original: "Brumalem"</note>—will show us the distance between the tropics and the total obliquity of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi"</note>. By taking half of this, we will have the distance of the tropics from the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>the celestial equator</note>, and it will become clear how great the angle of inclination is between the equinoctial and the circle that runs through the middle of the signs <note>the ecliptic or zodiac path</note>.

Ptolemy <note>a Greek-Roman astronomer whose 2nd-century models Copernicus was updating</note> therefore found this interval between the aforementioned Northern and Southern limits to be 47 degrees, 42 minutes, and 40 seconds, where the circle is 360 degrees. He found this to be the same value observed before his time by Hipparchus and Eratosthenes. This is also expressed as 11 parts out of 83 for the whole circle. From this, the half-difference, which is 23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds, established the distance of the tropics from the equinoctial circle (in a circle of 360 degrees) and the angle of intersection with the zodiac.

Ptolemy therefore thought that this remained invariably so and would always remain. But from that time, these values are found to have continually decreased down to our own day. For it has now been discovered by us and some of our contemporaries that the distance of the tropics is no more than 46 degrees and roughly 58 minutes, and the angle of intersection is 23 degrees, 28 minutes, and two-fifths of one minute. Thus, it is now sufficiently clear that the obliquity of the zodiac is also movable. We shall say more about this below, where we will also show, by a fairly probable conjecture, that it was never greater than 23 degrees and 52 minutes, nor will it ever be less than 23 degrees and 28 minutes.

<meta>This page continues the geometric explanation of how the celestial circles—the equator and the ecliptic (the Sun's path)—interact. Copernicus is transitioning from general observations of the Earth's tilt to the specific mathematical ratios used to calculate a star's or the Sun's position in the sky.</meta>

->BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS<-

...do we say it "reaches the meridian" <note>culminates at the highest point in the sky</note>, which also passes through and divides both the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferum"; the path the Sun appears to follow</note> and the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>the celestial equator</note> in the space of 24 hours? It divides them by cutting their circumferences from the vernal or autumnal intersection; and in turn, the circumference intercepted between them is divided by them. Since these are all great circles <note>circles that share the same center as the Earth/Sphere</note>, they form a **right-angled spherical triangle**. Indeed, the angle is a right angle where the meridian cuts the equinoctial through the poles, as has been defined. Now, they call the arc of the meridian—or of any circle passing through the poles—that is intercepted in this way, the **declination** <note>the distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator</note> of the segment of the zodiac. But the arc that corresponds to it on the equinoctial circle, which moves out at the same time as its matching part of the zodiac, they call the **right ascension**. All of these things are easily demonstrated in a convex triangle.

For let circle **ABCD** be the circle passing through the poles of both the equinoctial and the zodiac; most people call this the **Solstitial Colure** <note>the great circle passing through the celestial poles and the solstices</note>. Let **ABC** be the half of the zodiac, **BED** the half of the equinoctial, the vernal intersection <note>the Spring Equinox</note> at point **E**, the Summer Solstice at **A**, and the Winter Solstice at **C**. Let **F** be assumed as the pole of the daily revolution <note>the North Celestial Pole</note>, and on the zodiac let **EG** be an arc of, for example, 30 degrees. Over this, let a quadrant of a circle **FGH** be drawn. 

Then it is clear that in triangle **EGH**, side **EG** is given as 30 degrees, with angle **GEH**. When this angle is at its minimum, it is 23 degrees and 28 minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum"</note>, according to the maximum declination **AB** <note>this refers to the tilt of the Earth's axis</note>, where 360 degrees make four right angles; and angle **GHE** is a right angle. Therefore, by the fourth theorem on spherical triangles, this triangle **EHG** will have its angles and sides given. For it has been demonstrated that the <term>chord</term> <note>original: "subtensa"; a straight line connecting two points on a curve</note> of twice **EG** is to the chord of twice **GH**, as the chord of twice **AGE**—or the diameter of the sphere—is to the chord of twice **AB**. 

Their halves are similar, since the half of the chord of twice **AGE** is 100,000 units from the center, and the half-chord of **AB** consists of 39,822 of those same units. But **EG** is 50,000 units. And since if four numbers are proportional, the product of the means is equal to the product of the extremes, we will have the half-chord of twice the arc **GH** as 19,911 units. In the <term>table</term> <note>original: "canone"; a mathematical table of sines or chords</note>, this gives the arc **GH** as 11 degrees and 29 minutes, which is the **declination** corresponding to the segment **EG**. 

Because of this, in triangle **AFG**, the sides **FG** are given as 78 degrees and 31 minutes, and **AG** as 60 degrees, as they are the remainders of the quadrants. And the angle **FAG** is a right angle. In the same way, the chords of the doubles of **FG, AG, FGH, and BH**, or...

[[image: A geometric diagram of the celestial sphere. A large circle ABCD represents the Solstitial Colure. A horizontal-leaning line BED represents the celestial equator. A diagonal line ABC represents the ecliptic or zodiac path. Point F is the pole at the top. A spherical triangle EGH is formed by these intersections to calculate the Sun's declination and right ascension.]]

Copernicus uses spherical trigonometry and the known tilt of the Earth to show how positions on the zodiac path relate to the celestial equator.</summary>

...or their proportional halves. Since three of these are given, the fourth, **BH**, will also be given as 62 parts and 6 minutes—the right ascension from the point of the solstice—or **HE**, 27 parts and 54 minutes from the vernal equinox. Similarly, from the given sides **FG** (78 parts, 31 minutes) and **AF** of the same (66 parts, 32 minutes) and the quadrant of the circle, we shall have the angle **AGF** as 69 parts, 23 ½ minutes approximately, to which the vertically opposite angle **HGE** is equal. We shall do the same in other cases by this example.

However, one must not be ignorant of the fact that the meridian circle intersects the Zodiac [*signiferum*] at right angles at the signs where it touches the tropics; for it then intersects it through the poles, as we have said. But at the equinoctial points, it makes an angle as much smaller than a right angle as the Zodiac declines from a right angle, so that according to the minimum inclination it is 66 parts and 32 minutes.

It should also be observed that for equal arcs of the Zodiac, which are taken from the equinoctial or tropical points, the angles and sides of the triangles follow as equal. For instance, if we describe the equinoctial circumference **ABC** and the Zodiac **DBE**, intersecting each other at the sign **B** (where the equinox is), and we take equal arcs **FB** and **BG**, and through the poles of the daily motion [we draw] two quadrants of circles **KFL** and **HGM**, there will be two triangles **FLB** and **BMG**, whose sides **BF** and **BG** are equal, and the angles at the vertex **B**, and those around **L** and **M**, are right angles. Therefore, by the 6th [theorem] of spherical [triangles], they have equal sides and angles. Thus the declinations **FL** and **MG** are equal, as are the right ascensions **LB** and **BM**, and the remaining angle **F** is equal to the remaining angle **G**. The same will be evident in arcs taken from a tropical point. For example, when **AB** and **BC** are equal on both sides from the tropical contact **B**: for having drawn the quadrants **DA**, **DB** from the pole **D** of the equinoctial circle, there will similarly be two triangles **ABD** and **DBC**, whose bases **AB** and **BC** and side **BD** (common to both) are equal, and the angles around **B** are right angles. By the 8th [theorem] of sphericals, these triangles will be demonstrated to have equal sides and angles. From this it is manifest that the angles of one quadrant in the Zodiac, and the circumferences set forth, will agree with the remaining...

### PAGE 82

**NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**

...quadrants of the whole circle. Therefore, we shall subjoin an example in the form of a Table [*Canonica descriptione*]. In the first column shall be placed the parts of the Zodiac; in the following place, the declinations corresponding to those parts; in the third place, the minutes by which these differ from and exceed those particular declinations which occur under the maximum obliquity of the Zodiac, the sum of which is 24 minutes. We shall do in a similar manner in the table of ascensions and angles. For it is necessary that all things which follow the obliquity of the Zodiac change according to its change.

Furthermore, in the right ascension, that difference is found to be very small, inasmuch as it does not exceed a tenth part of one "time" [*temporis*], and in an hourly space it effects only a one hundred and fiftieth part. Indeed, the ancients called the parts of the equinoctial circle "times" [*tempora*] which rise together with the parts of the Zodiac; the circle of each of these is 360, as we have often said; but for the sake of distinguishing them, most have named the parts of the Zodiac "degrees" [*gradus*] and those of the equinoctial "times," which we also shall imitate henceforth. Therefore, since this difference is so small that it can rightly be neglected, it was not a burden to add even this. From these, the same things will also be evident in any other obliquity of the Zodiac, if similar parts for each are considered according to the ratio of the excess from the minimum to the maximum obliquity of the Zodiac.

As an example: in an obliquity of 23 parts and 34 minutes, if I wish to know how much declination is due to 30 degrees of the Zodiac taken from the equinox, I find in the Table 11 parts and 29 minutes, and in the difference 11 minutes, which would be added in full in the maximum obliquity of the Zodiac (which was, as we said, 23 parts and 52 minutes). But now it is assumed to be 23 parts and 34 minutes—greater, I say, by 6 minutes than the minimum, which is a fourth part of the 24 minutes by which the maximum obliquity exceeds. Moreover, the parts of the 11 minutes in the same ratio are almost 3; when I add these to the 11 parts and 29 minutes [Note: text says 19, likely OCR error for 29], I will have 11 parts and 32 minutes, by which 30 degrees of the Zodiac, taken from the equinox, will then decline. It will be permitted to do the same in the angles and right ascensions, except that it is always necessary to subtract from the latter, and always add to the former, so that everything may come forth more accurately according to the time.
