**How the declination and right ascension of any star placed outside the circle that is through the middle of the signs [the Ecliptic] may be evident, provided its latitude and longitude are established, and with what degree of the Zodiac it mediates the heavens. Chapter IV.**

These things have been set forth concerning the Zodiac, the equinoctial, and the meridian circle, and their mutual intersections. But for the daily revolution, it is of interest to know not only those things which appear through the Zodiac itself (by which the causes only of the Solar appearance are opened), but also how for those stars which are outside it—both fixed stars and wandering ones, provided their longitude and latitude have been given—their declination from the equinoctial circle and likewise their right ascension may be demonstrated.

Let there be described, therefore, a circle through the poles of the equinoctial and the Zodiac, **ABCD**; let the equinoctial semicircle be **AEC** upon pole **F**, and the Zodiac **BED** upon pole **G**; the intersection of the equinoctial is at sign **E**. From pole **G** through a star let the circumference **GHKL** be drawn; let the given place of the star be at sign **H**, through which a quadrant of a circle **FHMN** descends from the pole of the daily motion. Then it is manifest that the star existing at **H** falls upon the meridian with the two signs **M** and **N**, and the circumference **HMN** itself is the declination of the star from the equinoctial circle, and **EN** is the ascension in the right sphere, which we seek.

Since, therefore, in triangle **KEL**, side **KE** is given, and angle **KEL** and the right angle **EKL** [are given], therefore the sides **KL** and **EL** are given by the fourth [theorem] of sphericals, with the remaining angle **KLE**; thus the whole circumference **HKL** is given. Therefore, in triangle **HLN**, two angles are given, **HLN** and the right angle **LNH**, with side **HL**: therefore, by the same fourth [theorem] of sphericals, the remaining sides **HN** (the declination of the star) and **LN** (which remains from **NE**, the right ascension) are given... Or in another way: if you take the circumference **KE** of the Zodiac as the right ascension of **LE**, **LE** itself will be given in reverse from the Table of right ascensions, and **LK** as the declination corresponding to **LE**, and...

### PAGE 87

**REVOLUTIONS, BOOK II.**

...and the angle **KLE** through the table of meridian angles, from which the rest will be known as already demonstrated. Then, on account of the right ascension **EN**, the parts of the Zodiac **EM** are given, with which the star mediates the heavens with sign **M**.

**On the sections of the Finitor [Horizon]. Chapter V.**

The Horizon circle is of one kind for a right sphere, and another for an oblique sphere. For it is called the horizon of a right sphere when the equinoctial is erected upon it, or [the horizon] is through the poles of the equinoctial circle. We call that of an oblique sphere one to which the equinoctial circle is inclined. Therefore, in a right horizon all things rise and set, and the days are always equal to the nights. For the horizon intersects all parallels described by the daily motion through their middle—namely, through the poles—and there occur those things which we have already explained concerning the meridian. Here we take "day" to be from the rising of the Sun to its setting, not simply from light to darkness as the common people understand it (which is from dawn to the first torch-light), concerning which we shall say more regarding the rising and setting of the signs.

On the contrary, where the axis of the earth is erected toward the horizon, nothing rises or sets, but all things turned in a circle are always in the open or in hiding, unless another motion produces [change], such as the annual motion around the Sun: from which it follows that for a six-month space the day lasts perpetually there, and for the remaining time the night. Nor is there any other distinction than that of winter and summer, since the equinoctial circle there coincides with the horizon.

Furthermore, in an oblique sphere, some things rise and set, and some are always in the open or in hiding; meanwhile, the days and nights become unequal. Where the oblique horizon exists, it touches two parallel circles according to the mode of inclination, of which the one toward the visible pole defines the "always apparent" things, and the opposite one toward the hidden pole defines the "always hidden." Between these limits, the horizon passing through the whole latitude cuts all parallels in the middle into unequal circumferences, except the equinoctial, which is the greatest of the parallels; and greatest circles intersect each other in half. Therefore, the oblique boundary itself divides in the upper hemisphere toward the visible pole the larger circumferences of the parallels from those which are toward the Southern and hidden pole...

[Marginalia: *i*; *polum*]

### PAGE 88

**NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**

...pole, and conversely in the hidden hemisphere, in which the Sun appearing by the daily motion causes the disparity of days and nights.

**What the differences of meridian shadows are. Chapter VI.**

There are also differences of meridian shadows, by which some people are called *Periscii*, others *Amphiscii*, others *Heteroscii*. The *Periscii* are those whom we can call "circum-shadowed" [*circumumbratiles*], obtaining the shadow of the Sun on all sides. These are they whose vertex or pole of the horizon is less distant, or no more distant, from the pole of the earth than the tropic is from the equinoctial. For there the parallels which the horizon touches, being the limits of the always apparent or hidden, are greater than or equal to the tropics. And therefore the summer Sun, standing out among the always apparent, casts the shadows of gnomons in every direction. But where the horizon touches the tropical circles, they themselves become the limits of the always apparent and always hidden. Wherefore the Sun at the solstice is seen to graze the earth at midnight, at which moment the whole Zodiac circle coincides with the horizon, and immediately six signs rise at once, and as many set on the opposite side, and the pole of the Zodiac coincides with the pole of the horizon.

The *Amphiscii*, who cast meridian shadows to both parts [North and South], are those dwelling between both tropics, which space the ancients call the Middle Zone; and because through that whole tract the Zodiac circle stands twice vertically [at the zenith] (as is demonstrated in the second theorem of the *Phaenomena* by Euclid), the shadows of gnomons are twice consumed there, and as the Sun migrates to and fro, the gnomons send the shadow now to the South, now to the North.

The rest of us who dwell between these and those are *Heteroscii*, because we send meridian shadows into only one part, that is, the North. The ancient Mathematicians were accustomed to divide the orb of the earth into seven climates, such as through Meroe, through Syene, through Alexandria, through Rhodes, through the Hellespont, through the middle of the Pontus [Black Sea], through the Borysthenes, through Byzantium, and others through individual parallels, according to the difference and excess of the longest days. Also the length of shadows which they observed by gnomons at midday under the equinoxes and at both turnings of the Sun [solstices], and according to the elevation...

[Marginalia: *nes ele-*]

---

### PAGE 89

**REVOLUTIONS, BOOK II.**

...elevation of the pole, or the latitude of each segment. These things, having partially changed with time, are not exactly the same as they once were, on account of the changeable obliquity of the Zodiac (as we said), which was hidden from the predecessors; or to speak more correctly, on account of the varying inclination of the equinoctial circle to the plane of the Zodiac, upon which those things depend. But the elevations of the pole, or latitudes of places, and the equinoctial shadows agree with those which are found recorded in antiquity; which ought to happen, since the equinoctial circle follows the pole of the terrestrial globe. Wherefore those segments are not defined and designated exactly enough by any accidents of shadows and days, but more correctly by their distances from the equinoctial circle, which remain perpetually. However, that change of the tropics, although existing as very small, allows a small diversity of days and shadows around Southern places; it becomes more evident to those tending toward the North.

Regarding what concerns the shadows of gnomons, it is manifest that for any given altitude of the Sun, the length of the shadow is perceived, and vice versa. Just as if there were a gnomon **AB**, which casts a shadow **BC**, and since the index itself exists perpendicular to the plane of the horizon, it is necessary that it always makes the angle **ABC** a right angle, by the definition of lines perpendicular to a plane. Wherefore if **AC** is connected, we shall have the right-angled triangle **ABC**, and for a given altitude of the Sun, we shall also have that angle which is under **ACB** given. And by the first precept of triangles, the ratio of gnomon **AB** to its shadow **BC** will be given, and **BC** itself in length. Conversely also, when **AB** and **BC** are given, the angle **ACB** will also be established by the third [precept] of plane [triangles], and the elevation of the Sun producing that shadow for the time. In this way, the ancients, in the description of those segments of the terrestrial globe, assigned to each its own lengths of meridian shadows both at the equinoxes and at both solstices [*trope*].

**How the longest day, the latitude of rising, and the inclination of the sphere are demonstrated from one another, and concerning the remaining differences of days. Chapter VII.**

**NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**

Also for any obliquity of the sphere, or inclination of the horizon, we shall demonstrate the longest and shortest day together with the latitude of rising and the remaining difference of days. Moreover, the "latitude of rising" is the arc of the horizon circle intercepted from the solstitial rising to the brumal [winter] rising, or the distance of each from the equinoctial rising.

Let therefore the meridian circle be **ABCD**, and in the eastern hemisphere the semicircle of the horizon **BED**, and of the equinoctial circle **AEC**, whose Northern pole is **F**. Assuming the rising of the Sun under the summer solstice at sign **G**, let the circumference of a great circle **FGH** be described. Since, therefore, the mobility of the terrestrial sphere is performed on the pole **F** of the equinoctial circle, it is necessary for the signs **GH** to agree in the meridian **ABCD**, because parallels are around the same poles, through which all great circles take away similar circumferences from them. Wherefore the same time which is from the rising of **G** itself to midday is also measured by circumference **AEH**, and the remaining subterranean part of the semicircle **CH** from midnight to rising.

Moreover, **AEC** is a semicircle, and **AE** and **EC** are quadrants of circles, since they are from the pole of **ABCD**. Therefore **EH** will be half the difference of the longest day to the equinoctial, and **EG** the latitude between the equinoctial and solstitial rising. Since therefore in triangle **EHG**, the angle **GEH** (the obliquity of the sphere according to circumference **AB**) and the right angle **GHE** are established, with side **GH** (the distance of the summer tropic from the equinoctial), the remaining sides are given by the fourth [theorem] of sphericals: **EH** the half difference of the equinoctial and longest day, and **EG** the latitude of rising.

Therefore, even if with side **GH**, the side **EH** (the difference of the longest and equinoctial day) or **EG** is given: the angle of inclination of the sphere around **E** is given, and likewise **FD**, the elevation of the pole above the horizon. Furthermore, if not the tropic but any other point **G** in the Zodiac is taken, both circumferences **EG** and **EH** will nonetheless be evident. For through the table of declinations set forth above, the circumference of declination **GH** (which concerns that part of the Zodiac) becomes known, and the rest are made clear by the same mode of demonstration. From which it also follows that parts of the Zodiac which are equally distant from the tropic take away the same circumferences of the horizon...

<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s mathematical demonstration of how to calculate the positions of stars and the sun relative to the celestial equator and the ecliptic (the "Zodiac"). It follows the geometric proofs from the previous page by explaining how to use the reference tables (Canons) he has constructed.</meta>

-># NICOLAUS COPERNICUS<-

...will match the quadrants of the entire circle. Since we shall provide an example in the form of a **Table** <note>original: *Canonica descriptione*; Copernicus uses the word "Canon" to refer to a mathematical table or rule</note>. In the first column, we will place the parts of the Zodiac <note>original: *signiferi*; literally the "sign-bearer," referring to the ecliptic path where the constellations of the Zodiac reside</note>. In the following place, we will put the declinations corresponding to those parts. In the third column, the **minutes** <note>original: *scrupula*; literally "small stones," used here for minutes of a degree</note> by which the specific declinations—those occurring under the maximum obliquity <note>the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit</note> of the Zodiac—differ and exceed these; the total sum of these differences is 24 minutes. 

We shall do the same in the table for ascensions and angles. For it is necessary that all things that follow the obliquity of the Zodiac change according to its variation. Furthermore, in **right ascension**, this difference is found to be very small, such that it does not exceed a tenth part of one "time," and in the space of an hour it produces only a 1/150th part. 

<margin>Table</margin>

Indeed, the ancients called the parts of the equinoctial circle "times" <note>original: *tempora*</note> which rise along with the parts of the Zodiac; both circles consist of 360 parts, as we have often stated. But to distinguish between them, most have named the parts of the Zodiac "**degrees**" <note>original: *gradus*</note> and those of the equinoctial "**times**," a practice which we shall also follow from now on. 

Therefore, although this difference is so small that it might deservedly be ignored, we were not reluctant to include it. From these values, the results for any other obliquity of the Zodiac will also be clear, if the proportional parts of the difference between the minimum and maximum obliquity are applied to each value. 

For example, at an obliquity of 23 degrees and 34 minutes: if I wish to know how much declination is due to 30 degrees of the Zodiac measured from the equinox, I find in the **Table** <note>original: *Canone*</note> 11 degrees and 29 minutes [for the minimum obliquity], and a difference of 11 minutes. These 11 minutes would be added in full at the maximum obliquity of the Zodiac, which was, as we said, 23 degrees and 52 minutes. But now the obliquity is set at 23 degrees and 34 minutes; this is 6 minutes greater than the minimum <note>Copernicus is using a range where the minimum is 23° 28' and the maximum is 23° 52'</note>, and 6 minutes is one-quarter of the 24 minutes by which the maximum obliquity exceeds the minimum. Taking the same proportion of the 11-minute difference, we get nearly 3 minutes. When I add these to the 11 degrees and 29 minutes, I will have 11 degrees and 32 minutes, which is the declination of 30 degrees of the Zodiac from the equinox at that time. One may do the same for the angles and right ascensions, except that for the latter one must always subtract the difference, while for the former one must always add, so that everything comes out more accurately according to the time.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

**How the declination and right ascension of any star situated outside the circle of the zodiac <note>original: *signiferi*; the "sign-bearer," referring to the ecliptic or the path of the sun</note>—whose latitude and longitude have been established—may be determined, and which degree of the zodiac reaches the meridian with it. Chapter 4.**

**[[image: Initial H decorated with a human head and floral motifs]]** These things have been explained concerning the zodiac, the celestial equator <note>original: *æquinoctiali*</note>, and the meridian circle, and their mutual intersections. However, for the study of the daily revolution <note>The 24-hour rotation of the heavens.</note>, it is important to know not only those things which appear along the zodiac itself—which reveal the causes of the Solar appearances alone—but also to demonstrate the declination from the celestial equator and the <term>right ascension</term> <note>The distance of a point east of the First Point of Aries, measured along the celestial equator.</note> of those stars which are outside of it, both the fixed stars and the wandering stars <note>original: *errantium*; the planets</note>, provided their longitude and latitude have been given.

Therefore, let a circle **ABCD** be described through the poles of the equator and the zodiac. Let the semicircle of the equator be **AEC** upon the pole **F**, and the semicircle of the zodiac be **BED** upon the pole **G**; let the intersection with the equator be at point **E**. From the pole **G**, let the arc **GHKL** be drawn through a star. Let the given position of the star be at point **H**, through which a quadrant of a circle **FHMN** descends from the pole of the daily motion <note>The celestial pole</note>.

Then it is clear that the star which exists at **H** reaches the meridian <note>original: *meridianum incidit*</note> along with the two points **M** and **N**. The arc **HMN** itself is the declination of the star from the celestial equator, and **EN** is the right ascension in the <term>right sphere</term> <note>The celestial sphere as viewed from the equator, where all stars rise and set vertically.</note>, which are what we seek.

Since, therefore, in the triangle **KEL**, the side **KE** is given, and the angle **KEL** is given, and the angle **EKL** is a right angle, the sides **KL** and **EL** are therefore given by the fourth theorem of spherical triangles, along with the remaining angle **KLE**. Thus, the entire arc **HKL** is given. Consequently, in the triangle **HLN**, two angles are given: **HLN** and the right angle **LNH**, along with the side **HL**. Therefore, by the same fourth theorem of spherical triangles, the remaining sides are given: **HN**, the declination of the star, and **LN**, and the remainder **NE**, which is the right ascension by which the sphere is moved from the equinox to the star.

Or, by another method: If you take the arc **KE** of the zodiac from the preceding sections as if it were the right ascension of **LE**, then **LE** itself will be given, conversely, from the Table of Right Ascensions, and **LK** as the declination corresponding to **LE** itself, and...

[[image: Diagram of intersecting celestial circles with labeled points A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, K, L, M, N. This geometric figure illustrates the intersection of the ecliptic and the equator to find a star's coordinates.]]

<summary>Copernicus provides a geometric proof for calculating the declination and right ascension of stars and planets that do not lie on the ecliptic. By using spherical trigonometry and the poles of the celestial equator and the zodiac, he explains how to find a star's position relative to the daily rotation of the sky.</summary>

<keywords>Nicolaus Copernicus, astronomy, spherical trigonometry, declination, right ascension, ecliptic, celestial equator, fixed stars, planets, celestial coordinates</keywords>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS. Book II.

...and the angle **KLE** is found by the table of meridian angles, from which the remaining elements will be known, as has already been demonstrated. Then, because of the right ascension **EN**, the degrees of the zodiac <note>original: *signiferi*; the "sign-bearer," referring to the ecliptic</note> **EM** are given, at which the star reaches the meridian <note>original: *cælum mediat*; literally "mediates the sky," meaning to culminate at the highest point</note> together with the sign **M**.

**Concerning the sections of the horizon. Chapter 5.**

**[[image: Initial O decorated with a human head]]**The circle of the horizon, however, is of one kind for a "right sphere" <note>An observer at the equator, where the celestial poles lie on the horizon.</note> and of another for an "oblique sphere" <note>An observer at any latitude between the equator and the poles.</note>. For it is called the horizon of a **right sphere** when the celestial equator <note>original: *æquinoctialis*</note> stands perpendicular to it, or when the horizon passes through the poles of the celestial equator. But we call it the horizon of an **oblique sphere** when the celestial equator is inclined toward it. Therefore, in a right horizon, everything rises and sets, and the days are always equal to the nights. For the horizon cuts all the <term>parallels</term> <note>The paths stars take as they rotate around the Earth.</note> described by the daily motion exactly in half—namely, through the poles—and those things occur there which we have already explained regarding the meridian. 

Now, we define "day" here as the time from the rising of the Sun to its setting, not simply from light to darkness as the common people understand it—which is from dawn <note>original: *diluculo*</note> until the first lamps are lit <note>original: *primam facem*</note>—about which we will say more regarding the rising and setting of the zodiacal signs. On the contrary, where the axis of the Earth stands perpendicular to the horizon <note>The North or South Pole.</note>, nothing rises or sets, but everything revolves in a circle and is always visible or always hidden, unless another motion produces a change, such as the annual motion around the Sun. From this it follows that the day lasts continuously for a six-month period, and the night for the remaining time; there is no distinction other than between winter and summer, because the celestial equator coincides with the horizon there. 

Furthermore, in an **oblique sphere**, some things rise and set, while some are always visible or always hidden, and in the meantime, the days and nights become unequal. In this case, the oblique horizon touches two parallel circles according to the degree of its inclination; the one toward the visible pole defines the stars that are always visible <margin>pole</margin>, and conversely, the one toward the hidden pole defines those that are always hidden <margin>i</margin>. Therefore, the horizon, passing through the whole latitude between these limits, cuts all the parallels in between into unequal arcs, except for the celestial equator, which is the largest of the parallels; and the largest circles always bisect each other. Thus, the oblique horizon <note>original: *finiens*</note> itself divides the upper hemisphere toward the visible pole into larger arcs of the parallels than those toward the Southern and hidden pole.

<summary>Copernicus defines the differences between the "right sphere" (equator) and "oblique sphere" (latitudes), explaining how the horizon determines the length of days and which stars remain permanently visible or hidden.</summary>
<keywords>right sphere, oblique sphere, horizon, celestial equator, parallels, daily motion, day and night, poles</keywords>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

**What the differences of noon shadows are. Chapter 6.**

**[[image: Initial S decorated with floral and bird motifs]]**There are also differences in noon shadows, according to which some people are called **Periscii**, others **Amphiscii**, and others **Heteroscii**. The **Periscii** <note>original: *Periscij*; from Greek meaning "shadows all around"</note> are those whom we might call "circular-shadowed," as they receive the Sun’s shadow from all sides. These are the people whose zenith <note>The point directly above an observer.</note> or horizon pole is less distant, or no more distant, from the pole of the Earth than the tropic is from the equator <note>original: *æquinoctiali*</note>. There, the parallels that the horizon touches—which serve as the boundaries for things always visible or always hidden—are larger than or equal to the tropics. Consequently, the summer Sun, remaining in the region of things always visible, casts the shadows of <term>gnomons</term> <note>A gnomon is the part of a sundial that casts a shadow; Copernicus uses it here to refer to a vertical rod used for astronomical measurement.</note> in every direction. But where the horizon touches the tropical circles, these circles themselves become the boundaries of what is always visible and always hidden. Therefore, at the solstice, the Sun is seen to graze the earth at midnight; at that moment, the entire circle of the **zodiac** <note>original: *signifer*; literally the "sign-bearer," referring to the ecliptic, the Sun's annual path</note> coincides with the horizon, and immediately six signs rise together while the opposite six set together, and the pole of the zodiac coincides with the pole of the horizon.

The **Amphiscii** <note>original: *Amphiscij*; from Greek meaning "shadows on both sides"</note>, who cast their noon shadows in both directions, are those living between the two tropics. The ancients called this space the **Middle Zone** <note>Also known as the Torrid Zone.</note>. Because the circle of the zodiac stands directly overhead twice throughout that whole region (as demonstrated in the second theorem of Euclid's *Phaenomena*), the shadows of gnomons vanish there twice; as the Sun moves from one side to the other, the gnomons cast shadows sometimes to the South and sometimes to the North.

The rest of us, who live between these two groups, are **Heteroscii** <note>original: *Heteroscij*; "shadows in one direction"</note>, because we cast our noon shadows in only one direction—that is, toward the North. Ancient mathematicians were accustomed to dividing the world into seven <term>climates</term> <note>Geographical zones defined by the length of the longest day, rather than modern temperature-based climates.</note>, such as through Meroë, Syene, Alexandria, Rhodes, the Hellespont, the middle of the Black Sea <note>original: *Pontum*</note>, the Borysthenes <note>The ancient name for the Dnieper River.</note>, Byzantium, and so on through each parallel, according to the difference and increase of the longest days. They also noted the length of the shadows which they observed by means of gnomons at noon during the equinoxes and both solstices <note>original: *conuersionibus*; "turnings," referring to the Sun's turning points at the tropics</note>, and according to the ele- <margin>vations of</margin>...

# BOOK II OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...the elevation of the pole, or the latitude of each segment. These things, having changed somewhat over time, are not exactly the same as they once were, because of the changing obliquity of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signiferi*; literally the "sign-bearer," referring to the ecliptic, the Sun's annual path.</note>—as we mentioned—which was unknown to the ancients; or to speak more correctly, because of the varying inclination of the <term>equator</term> <note>original: *æquinoctialis circuli*; the celestial equator.</note> to the plane of the zodiac, upon which those things depend. However, the elevations of the pole—or the latitudes of places—and the noon shadows agree with what was recorded in antiquity. This was bound to happen, since the equatorial circle follows the pole of the Earth's sphere. For this reason, those segments are not defined or designated with enough precision by any incidental shadows and days, but more correctly by their distances from the equator, which remain constant. Indeed, that change of the <term>solstices</term> <note>original: *tropicorum*; the turning points of the Sun's path.</note>, though it is very small, allows for a slight variation in days and shadows in southern regions, but it becomes more evident as one moves North. 

Therefore, regarding the shadows of <term>gnomons</term> <note>A gnomon is a vertical rod used as an astronomical instrument; the length of its shadow reveals the Sun's altitude.</note>, it is clear that for any given height of the Sun, the length of the shadow can be determined, and vice-versa. Just as if there were a gnomon **AB**, which casts a shadow **BC**; since the rod itself stands perpendicular to the plane of the horizon, it must always form a right angle **ABC**, by the definition of lines perpendicular to a plane. Therefore, if **AC** is connected, we will have a right-angled triangle **ABC**, and for a given height of the Sun, we will also have the given angle at **ACB**. And by the first rule of triangles, the ratio of the gnomon **AB** to its shadow **BC** will be given, as will the length of **BC** itself. Conversely, when **AB** and **BC** are given, the angle **ACB** and the elevation of the Sun creating that shadow at the time will also be established by the third rule of plane triangles. In this way, the ancients, in their description of those segments of the Earth's globe, assigned the respective lengths of the noon shadows both at the equinoxes and at each <term>solstice</term> <note>original: *trope*; the "turning" of the Sun.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical proofs of Book II, specifically moving from the general theory of shadows and climates to the specific calculation of day lengths and the Sun’s position on the horizon (rising latitude) for any given geographical location.</meta>

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

**[[image: Initial I decorated with two human figures holding branches]]** Thus also, for any <term>obliquity of the sphere</term> <note>This refers to the angle at which the celestial equator meets the horizon, which is determined by the observer's latitude.</note> or inclination of the horizon, we will demonstrate the maximum and minimum day, along with the rising latitude and the remaining difference of days. Now, the <term>rising latitude</term> <note>original: *latitudo ortus*; today known as "amplitude," this is the distance along the horizon between the point where the Sun rises and the true East.</note> is the arc of the horizon circle intercepted between the solstitial and winter rising points, or the distance of each from the equinoctial rising. 

Therefore, let the <term>meridian</term> circle be **ABCD**, and in the eastern hemisphere let the semicircle of the horizon be **BED**, and that of the <term>equinoctial circle</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note> be **AEC**, whose Northern pole is **F**. Assuming the rising of the Sun at the summer <term>solstice</term> <note>original: *conuersione*; literally a "turning," referring to the point where the Sun stops its northward progress and "turns" back toward the equator.</note> is at point **G**, let the arc of a great circle **FGH** be described. 

Since the motion of the terrestrial sphere is performed around the pole **F** of the equatorial circle, it is necessary that the points **G** and **H** coincide on the meridian **ABCD**, because the <term>parallels</term> <note>Lines of latitude on the celestial sphere.</note> are around the same poles, through which all great circles cut off similar arcs from them. For this reason, the same time that is measured from the rising of **G** itself to the meridian is also measured by the arc **AEH**, and the remaining subterranean part of the semicircle **CH** from midnight to dawn. 

Now, **AEC** is a semicircle, and **AE** and **EC** are quadrants of circles, since they are measured from the pole of **ABCD**. Therefore, **EH** will be half the difference of the longest day to the equinoctial day, and **EG** will be the rising latitude between the equinoctial and solstitial rising. 

Therefore, since in triangle **EHG**, there has been established the angle which is under **GEH** (the obliquity of the sphere according to the arc **AB**) and the angle under **GHE** (which is a right angle), along with the side **GH** (the distance of the summer <term>tropic</term> <note>The Tropic of Cancer.</note> from the equator), the remaining sides are also given through the fourth theorem of spherical triangles: **EH**, the half-difference of the equinoctial and longest day, and **EG**, the rising latitude. 

For this reason, even if the side **EH** (the difference of the longest day and the equinoctial) or **EG** were given along with side **GH**, the angle of the inclination of the sphere at **E** is given, and likewise **FD**, the elevation of the pole above the horizon. 

Furthermore, even if not the tropic but any other point **G** in the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signifero*; literally the "sign-bearer."</note> is taken, both arcs **EG** and **EH** will nonetheless be revealed. Since through the "Table of Declinations" set forth above, the arc of declination **GH** is made known (which concerns that specific part of the zodiac), the rest of the demonstration becomes clear in the same way. From this it also follows that the parts of the zodiac which are equally distant from the tropic cut off the same arcs of the horizon...

[[image: A spherical diagram showing the intersection of the meridian (ABCD), the horizon (BED), and the equator (AEC), with the North Pole (F) at the top. A vertical line connects the pole through the solstice point (G) to the equator (H).]]

<meta>This page continues the geometric proof regarding the symmetry of solar declination and its effect on the length of days. The text completes the argument that points on the ecliptic (the Sun’s path) that are equidistant from the equinoxes share the same rising positions and day lengths.</meta>

->REVOLUTIONS, BOOK II.<-

[va]riations from the <term>equinoctial rising</term> <note>The point on the horizon where the Sun rises exactly at the equinox, i.e., due East.</note>, and toward the same directions; and they make the lengths of days and nights mutually equal. This occurs because the same <term>parallel</term> <note>A circle of constant declination, parallel to the celestial equator.</note> contains both degrees of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signiferi*; the "sign-bearer" or the ecliptic circle containing the twelve signs.</note>, since their <term>declination</term> <note>The angular distance of a heavenly body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> is equal and toward the same direction. On the other hand, when equal arcs are taken in either direction from the equinoctial intersection, the <term>rising latitudes</term> <note>The distance along the horizon from the East point to where the Sun rises.</note> are again equal, but in opposite directions; and the lengths of days and nights are exchanged. This is because they describe equal circumferences of the parallels on both sides, just as the signs themselves, being at equal distances from the equinox, have equal declinations from the equinoctial circle. 

For let the circumferences of the parallels be described in the same figure, and let them be **G M** and **K N**, which intersect the 

[[image: A geometric diagram of a celestial sphere contained within a circle. It shows several intersecting arcs and straight lines representing astronomical coordinates. A horizontal line represents the horizon, and a vertical line represents the meridian. Key points are labeled: A, M, and F at the top; B on the far left; D on the far right; E at the center. Interior points and arc intersections are labeled with O, K, G, H, L, and N.]]

horizon **B E D** at points **G** and **K**; let there also be applied from the Southern pole **L** a quadrant of a great circle **L K O**. Since, therefore, the declination **H G** is equal to **K O**, there will be two triangles **D F G** and **B L K**, of which two sides of one are equal to two sides of the other: **F G** is equal to **L K**, and **F D** (the elevation of the pole) is equal to **L B**, and the angles around **B** and **D** are right angles. Therefore, the third side **D G** is equal to the third side **B K**, from which also the remaining rising latitudes **G E** and **B K** are left equal. Since here also the two sides **E G**, **G H** are equal to the two sides **E K**, **K O**, and the angles at the vertex **E** are equal, the remaining sides **E H** and **E O** are consequently equal. When these equal parts are added together, the whole circumference **O E C** is found to be equal to the whole **A E H**. But great circles passing through the poles of the parallels cut off similar circumferences; therefore, **G M** and **K N** will themselves be mutually similar and equal. This was to be demonstrated. 

But all these things can be demonstrated in another way. Having similarly described the meridian circle **A B C D**, let its center be **E**; let the equatorial diameter and common intersection of those circles be **A E C**; let the diameter of the horizon and the meridian line be **B E D**; let the axis of the sphere be **L E M**, the visible pole **L**, and the hidden pole **M**. Let the distance of the <term>summer solstice</term> <note>original: *conuersionis æstiuæ*; literally the "summer turning," when the Sun reaches its highest point and begins to move back toward the equator.</note> be assumed, or let any other declination be **A F**, at which the diameter of the parallel **F G** is drawn, in the common intersection also with the meridian, which will intersect the axis at **κ** <note>The Greek letter kappa.</note> and the meridian line at **N**. Since 

[[image: A circular geometric diagram representing a cross-section of the celestial sphere. A large circle is labeled with points A, B, C, and D at its quadrants, with center E. A horizontal diameter A-C and a vertical diameter B-D intersect at the center. Another diameter L-M is drawn at a diagonal angle. A horizontal chord F-G is drawn in the upper section of the circle. This chord intersects the diagonal diameter L-M at point K and the vertical diameter B-D at point N.]]

<sig>i iij</sig>

<summary>Copernicus uses spherical geometry to prove that positions on the ecliptic equidistant from the equinoxes result in symmetrical day lengths and rising points on the horizon. He begins an alternative demonstration of these principles using a different cross-section of the celestial sphere.</summary>

--- Page 92 ---
<meta>This page continues the geometric proof regarding the calculation of day lengths and rising times based on a star's or the Sun's position. It follows the previous page's introduction of parallel circles and their intersections with the horizon.</meta>

->NICHOLAS COPERNICUS<-

Since, therefore, these lines are parallel—according to the definition by **Posidonius** <note>Posidonius of Rhodes (c. 135–51 BCE) was a Stoic philosopher and scientist; his definition of parallels emphasized that they maintain a constant distance from one another.</note>, which states they neither converge nor diverge but maintain perpendicular lines between them that are everywhere equal—the straight line **KE** will be equal to half the <term>chord</term> <note>original: *subtendentis*; the straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc.</note> of twice the circumference **AF**. Similarly, **KN** will be half the chord of the circumference of the <term>parallel circle</term> <note>A circle on the celestial sphere whose plane is parallel to the equator.</note> whose radius is **FK**. It is by this difference that an <term>equinoctial day</term> <note>A day where light and dark are equal (12 hours each).</note> differs from a day of a different length. This is because all the semicircles in which these common sections exist—that is, those for which they are diameters, such as **BED** of the <term>oblique horizon</term> <note>The horizon as seen from any latitude other than the poles or the equator.</note>, **LEM** of the <term>right horizon</term> <note>The horizon as seen from the equator, where the celestial poles lie on the horizon line.</note>, **AEC** of the equinoctial, and **FKG** of the parallel—are perpendicular to the plane of the circle **ABCD**.

[[image: A circular geometric diagram inscribed with lines and points. A circle is marked with points A (top), C (bottom), B (left), and D (right). A central point E is the intersection of the main axes. A horizontal-ish line segments FG and a diagonal line LM intersect with the vertical axis AC at points K and N respectively. Lines connect various points to illustrate spherical geometry and the relationships between the horizon, the equator, and parallel circles.]]

And the sections they make with each other, according to the 19th proposition of the 11th book of **Euclid’s Elements** <note>Euclid's *Elements* was the foundational textbook for geometry; Book XI deals with three-dimensional (solid) geometry.</note>, are perpendicular to that same plane at points **E**, **K**, and **N**. Furthermore, by the 6th proposition of the same book, they are parallel. **K** is the center of the parallel circle, and **E** is the center of the sphere. Therefore, **EN** is half the chord of twice the circumference of the horizon, by which the rising of the parallel circle differs from the equinoctial rising. 

Since the <term>declination</term> <note>The angular distance of a body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> **AF** is given along with the remainder of the quadrant **FL**, the halves of the chords of twice **AF** (which is **KE**) and of twice **FL** (which is **FK**) will be established in parts where the radius **AE** is 100,000 <note>Copernicus uses a standard radius of 100,000 for his trigonometric calculations, a common practice before the decimal point was standardized.</note>. In the right-angled triangle **EKN**, the angle **KEN** is given according to the elevation of the pole **DL**, and the remaining angle **KNE** is equal to **AEB**, because in an oblique sphere, the parallels are similarly inclined to the horizon. Thus, the sides are given in the same parts where the radius of the sphere is 100,000. 

Consequently, for any parallel where the radius **FK** is 100,000, the line **KN** will also be given as half the chord of the entire difference between the equinoctial day and the parallel day, in units where the parallel circle is likewise divided into 360 degrees. From this, it is clear that the ratio of **FK** to **KN** consists of two ratios: namely, the chord of twice **FL** to the chord of twice **AF** (which is **FK** to **KE**), and the chord of twice **AB** to the chord of twice **DL** (which is **EK** to **KN**), as **EK** is taken as the intermediate between **FK** and **KN**. Similarly, the ratio of **BE** to **EN** is composed of **BE** to **EK** and **KE** to **EN**. 

In this way, I believe that not only the inequality of days and nights, but also the segments of the <term>diurnal motion</term> <note>The apparent daily rotation of the heavens around the Earth.</note> described by the Moon and the stars—provided their declination is given—can be distinguished: those segments above the earth from those below, from which their rising and setting can be easily understood.

<summary>Copernicus uses Euclidean geometry and the definitions of Posidonius to calculate the length of days and the rising times of celestial bodies. He demonstrates that by knowing a star's declination and the local latitude, one can determine its path above and below the horizon.</summary>

<keywords>Euclid's Elements, Posidonius, declination, oblique horizon, right horizon, diurnal motion, chords, trigonometry, celestial sphere</keywords>

->NICHOLAS COPERNICUS<-

## On hours, and the parts of day and night. Chapter VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'E' at the start of the chapter, featuring a classical scene with a seated figure, likely a scholar or astronomer, at a desk with books and instruments.</image-desc>

From these things, therefore, it is clear that if we add the difference of days <note>original: "differentiã dierũ"; this refers to the "ascensional difference" calculated in the previous tables</note> found in the table for a given solar declination <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator.</note> and a specific elevation of the pole <note>geographic latitude</note> to a quadrant of a circle <note>90 degrees</note> for a Northern declination, or subtract it for a Southern one, and double the result, we will have the length of that day. The remainder of the circle provides the space of the night. If we divide either of these by 15 degrees, it will show how many equal hours <term>equal hours</term><note>Our modern system where every hour is exactly 60 minutes long, regardless of the season.</note> that time contains. However, if we take a twelfth part of the total, we will have the duration of a "temporal hour."

These temporal hours <note>original: "horæ temporales"</note> take their names from the day of which they are always a twelfth part. Accordingly, they are found named by the ancients as Solstitial, Equinoctial, and Winter <note>original: "Brumales"</note> hours. In the earliest times, no other hours were in use than these—twelve from sunrise to sunset—while the night was divided into four "watches" or "guards." This use of hours lasted for a long time by the silent consent of all nations. For this reason, water-clocks <term>clepsydrae</term><note>Ancient devices that measured time by the regulated flow of water. To account for temporal hours, these clocks had to be adjusted so the water flowed faster or slower depending on the season.</note> were invented, in which the hours of the varying days were fashioned by the subtraction and addition of dripping water, so that the division of time would not be hidden even under a cloudy sky. 

But later, once equal hours common to both day and night became generally accepted—since they are easier to observe—those older "temporal" hours became so antiquated that if you were to ask any of the common people which is the first, third, sixth, ninth, or eleventh hour of the day, they would have no answer, or at least one that is irrelevant to the matter. Furthermore, different people even count the number of these equal hours differently: some from noon, some from sunset, some from midnight, and others from sunrise, according as it has been established by each city.

## On the oblique ascension of the parts of the zodiac, and how for any rising degree, the degree that culminates is given. Chapter IX.

# BOOK II OF THE REVOLUTIONS

k iij

<meta>catchword: rises</meta>

With the size and differences of days and nights thus explained, the explanation of oblique ascensions follows in its proper order—that is, the times in which the <term>dodecatemoria</term><note>From the Greek *dodekatemorion*, meaning "twelfth part." These are the twelve 30-degree segments of the zodiac.</note>, which are the twelve parts of the zodiac, or any other arcs of that circle, rise above the horizon. For there are no other differences between right and oblique ascensions than those of the equinoctial and varying days, which we have already explained. Furthermore, the twelve signs—taking their beginning from the vernal equinox—borrowed their names from the constellations of the fixed stars, and were called *Aries*, *Taurus*, *Gemini*, *Cancer*, and the rest as they follow in order. 

Therefore, for the sake of greater clarity, let us reproduce the meridian circle *ABCD*, with the equinoctial semi-circle *ABC* <note>the celestial equator</note>, and the horizon *BED*, which intersect each other at point *E*. Let the equinox be assumed at *H*, through which the <term>signifer</term><note>original: "signifer"; literally "the sign-bearer," the common Latin name for the ecliptic circle where the zodiac signs reside.</note> circle *FHL* passes, intersecting the horizon at *L*. Through this intersection, let a quadrant of a great circle *KLM* descend from the equinoctial pole *K*. 

Thus it certainly appears that while the arc of the zodiac *HL* rises, the arc *HE* of the equinoctial rises with it; but in a <term>right sphere</term><note>The view of the heavens from the Earth's equator, where the celestial equator is at a right angle to the horizon.</note> it would rise with *HEM*. The difference between these is *EM*, which we previously demonstrated to be half the difference between the equinoctial and varying day. But what was there added in Northern declination is here subtracted, and conversely added in Southern declination, to the right ascension so that the oblique ascension may be produced. And hence, how long it takes for a whole sign or any other arc of the ecliptic to emerge will become clear by calculating the ascensions from the beginning to the end.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a celestial sphere inscribed within a circle. The outer circle is marked with points A (top), B (left), C (bottom), and D (right). A horizontal line representing the celestial equator is labeled ABC, with H and M marked on it, and E at the center. A diagonal arc FHL represents the ecliptic (signifer). A verticalish arc KLM drops from the pole K through point L to the equator at M. This diagram illustrates the geometric relationship between right and oblique ascensions in spherical astronomy.</image-desc>

From these things it follows that when a certain degree of the ecliptic is given, measured from the equinox, the degree that <term>mediates the heavens</term><note>original: "cælum mediat"; refers to culmination or the "Midheaven," the point where a celestial body reaches its highest point in the sky for that day.</note> is also given. For when point *L* (which is on the ecliptic and currently rising) is given, its declination according to *HL*, its distance from the equinox, and its right ascension *HEM* are also known, as is the entire semi-diurnal arc *AHEM*. Therefore, the remaining arc *AH* is given, which is the right ascension of *FH*; this is also given through the table, since the angle of the intersection *AHF* is given along with the side *AH*, and the angle at *FAH* is a right angle. And so the entire arc of the ecliptic *FHL* between the horizon and the degree mediating the heavens is given. Conversely, if the degree that mediates the heavens were given first—for instance, the arc *FH*—we would also know the degree that...

## On the angle of intersection of the zodiac with the horizon. Chapter 10.

Furthermore, the zodiac <term>signifer</term><note>original: "signifer"; literally the "sign-bearer," the common Latin term for the ecliptic circle containing the twelve signs of the zodiac.</note> circle, being oblique to the axis of the sphere, creates various angles with the horizon. We have already spoken regarding the differences in shadows for those who live between the tropics, where the zodiac rises vertically to the horizon twice [a year]. However, I believe it is sufficient for us to demonstrate only those angles which serve the <term>Heteroscians</term><note>original: "Heterosciis"; from the Greek, referring to people living in the temperate zones whose noon-day shadows always fall in one direction (either always North or always South).</note>, which is to say, ourselves; from these, the universal logic of the angles will be easily understood. I think it is manifest enough that in an <term>oblique sphere</term><note>A view of the heavens from any latitude other than the equator or the poles.</note>, when the equinox or the beginning of Aries is rising, the zodiac circle is more inclined and sinks toward the horizon by as much as the greatest southern declination (which occurs at the beginning of Capricorn) adds to it, while the latter occupies the mid-heaven; and conversely, [the zodiac] is more elevated, creating a larger eastern angle, when the beginning of Libra emerges and the start of Cancer occupies the mid-heaven. This is because these three circles—the <term>equinoctial</term><note>The celestial equator.</note>, the zodiac, and the horizon—converge through the same common intersection at the poles of the meridian circle; the arcs of the meridian intercepted by these circles reveal how great that eastern angle is judged to be. However, so that a path of measurement may also lie open to the other parts of the zodiac: Let the meridian circle again be **abcd**, the half-horizon **bed**, and the half-

An arc AEC curves through the center E. On the left side, another arc is drawn with points labeled F, G, H. The diagram illustrates spherical geometry and the intersection of the zodiac (signifer) with the horizon.</image-desc>

zodiac **aec**, of which any degree you like rises at point **b**. It is our purpose to find how great the angle **aeb** is, according to the standard where four right angles are **360** <note>original: "ccclx"</note> degrees. Since, therefore, the rising point **b** is given, it is also given from the preceding sections which point is at the mid-heaven, as well as the arc **ae** and the meridian altitude **ab**. And because the angle **abe** is a right angle, the ratio of the <term>chord of double</term><note>original: "subtensæ dupli"; a standard pre-trigonometric method of calculation. Therefore, the angle AEB is also given. But if it is not the degree of the Orient [Ascendant] but the degree of the Midheaven that is given, which let be A, nevertheless that angle of the Orient will be measured. For with the pole made at B, let the quadrant of a great circle FGH be described, and let the quadrants EAG and EBH be completed. Since, therefore, the meridian altitude AB is given, and the remainder of the quadrant AF, and the angle FAG from the preceding [demonstrations], and FGA is a right angle; therefore, the arc FG is given, and the remainder GH, which measures the angle of the Orient according to its position. 

Furthermore, it is also manifest here how, for a degree which mediates the heaven [the Midheaven], that degree which is rising is given. For the chord of double GH is to the chord of double AB as the diameter is to the chord of double AE, as in spherical triangles. Of these matters we have also added three examples of tables. The first will be of ascensions in the right sphere, taking the beginning from Aries and with an increment of six parts [degrees] of the zodiac. The second, of ascensions in the oblique sphere, similarly by six degrees from the parallel where the pole is elevated 39 parts [degrees] up to that which has 57 parts, establishing intermediate increments by three degrees. The remaining [table] is of horizontal angles, also by six degrees under the same seven segments. And all these are according to the minimum obliquity of the ecliptic [signifer] of 23 degrees and 28 minutes [scrupula], which corresponds nearly to our own century.

### NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

#### On the use of these tables. Chapter XI.

The use of the tables is now evident from what has been demonstrated. For if, with the known degree of the Sun, we take the right ascension, and add to it fifteen [degree] units of time for any equal hour—rejecting the 360 parts of a whole circle if they exceed it—the remainder of the right ascension will show the degree of the ecliptic [signifer] located at the Midheaven for the proposed hour from noon. Similarly, if you do the same regarding the oblique ascension of your region, you will have the degree of the ecliptic rising at the sunrise assumed. 

Even in the case of any stars which are outside the circle of the signs [the zodiac], whose right ascension is established as we taught above, there are given through these Canons the degrees of the ecliptic which, through the same right ascension from the beginning of Aries, mediate the heaven with them, and through their oblique ascension, which degree of the ecliptic rises with them, as the ascensions and parts of the ecliptic present themselves in the region of the tables. In a like manner, but always through the opposite position, you shall operate regarding the setting. Furthermore, if a quadrant of a circle is added to the right ascension which mediates the heaven, that which is gathered therefrom is the oblique ascension of the Orient. Therefore, through the degree of the Midheaven, that which is rising is also given, and vice versa. There follows the table of the angles of the ecliptic with the horizon, which are taken through the rising degree of the ecliptic; by which it is also understood how much the ninetieth degree of the ecliptic is elevated from the horizon, which is especially necessary to know in solar eclipses.

#### On the angles and arcs of those [circles] which are made through the poles of the horizon to the same circle of the signs. Chapter XII.

It follows that we should set forth the reasoning of the angles and arcs which [occur] in the sections of the ecliptic with those [circles] which pass through the vertex [zenith] of the horizon, in which is the altitude above the horizon. Now, concerning the meridian altitude of the Sun, or of any degree of the ecliptic mediating the heaven, and the angle of the section with the meridian, it has been set forth above, since the meridian circle itself...

--- Page 107 ---
**[Original Page 43]**

...is one of those which pass through the vertex of the horizon. Concerning the angle of the Orient, discourse has already preceded, whose remainder from a right angle is that which the quadrant of a circle through the vertex of the horizon receives with the rising ecliptic. 

It remains, therefore, to see concerning the intermediate sections, repeating the previous figure [A spherical diagram with points A, B, C, D, G, H, E]: let there be the meridian circle with the semicircles of the ecliptic and the horizon, and let any sign of the ecliptic be assumed between the meridian and the rising or setting; and let it be G, through which a quadrant of a circle FGH descends from the pole of the horizon. Since at that hour, the whole arc AGB of the ecliptic between the meridian and the horizon is given, and AG by hypothesis; and similarly AF, on account of the meridian altitude AB being given, along with the meridian angle FAG itself; FG is also given by the demonstrations of spherical [geometry], and the remainder GH, the altitude of G itself, along with the angle FGA, which we were seeking. These things concerning the angles and sections around the ecliptic we have excerpted in passing from Ptolemy, referring ourselves to the general tradition of spherical triangles, in which if anyone wishes to exercise himself, he will be able to find for himself more utilities than those we have just treated by way of example.

#### On the rising and setting of the stars. Chapter XIII.

The risings and settings of the stars also seem to pertain to the daily revolution; not only those simple ones of which we have just spoken, but the modes by which they become morning and evening [events]. Although these occur by the concurrence of the annual revolution, they shall nevertheless be discussed more aptly in this place. The ancient mathematicians separate the true from the apparent. Of the true, indeed, the morning rising is the rising of the star when it emerges simultaneously with the Sun. The morning setting, however, is when the star sets while the Sun is rising, which in the whole intermediate time was called "morning." But the evening rising is when the star emerges as the Sun is setting. The evening setting is when the star sets together with the setting Sun, which in the intermediate time is also called "evening," as that which...

--- Page 108 ---
### NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...is prepared during the day and follows into the night. Of the apparent [risings and settings], the morning rising of a star is when, at dawn and before the rising of the Sun, it first puts itself forward into emergence and begins to appear. The morning setting, however, is when the star is seen to set for the last time as the Sun is about to rise. The evening rising is when in the twilight the star first appears to rise. The evening setting is when after the setting of the Sun the star ceases to appear any longer, and is hidden by the subsequent approach of the Sun, until in the morning rising they put themselves forward in their prior order. 

These things are the same in the fixed stars and in the "loose" [planets] Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. Venus and Mercury, however, make their risings and settings differently; for they are not overtaken by the approach of the Sun as those others are, nor are they uncovered by its departure. But, preceding it, they mingle with the splendor of the Sun and are snatched away. The former [superior planets], making evening rising and morning setting, are not hidden in such a way that they do not spend nearly the whole night with their lights; but these [inferior planets] hide without distinction from setting unto rising, and cannot be seen anywhere. 

There is also another difference: that in the former, the true morning risings and settings are prior to the apparent ones, and the evening ones are posterior, insofar as in the one case they precede the Sun's rising, and in the other they follow its setting. In the inferior [planets], however, the apparent morning and evening risings are posterior to the true ones, while the settings are prior. The manner by which they are discerned can be understood from the aforementioned, where we explained the oblique ascension of any star having a known position, and with which degree of the ecliptic it rises or sets; in which degree or its opposite, if the Sun then appears, the star will effect a true morning or evening rising or setting. 

From these, the apparent [risings/settings] differ according to the brightness and magnitude of each star; for those which excel with greater light have shorter periods of hiding in the solar rays than those which are dimmer. And the limits of occultation and appearance are taken by the subterranean arcs of the circles which pass through the poles of the horizon, between the horizon itself and the Sun. These are nearly 12 degrees for the primary fixed stars: 11 for Saturn, 10 for Jupiter, 11.5 for Mars, 5 for Venus, and 10 for Mercury. In the whole [arc], however, in which the remainder of the daylight yields to the night, which encompasses twilight or dawn, there are 18 degrees of the aforementioned circle; at which degrees, with the Sun removed, even the smaller stars begin to appear. At which distance some take...

--- Page 109 ---
**[Original Page 44]**

...a subterranean parallel subject to the horizon, which they say, when the Sun reaches it, the day begins to break [diescere] or the night is completed. 

When, therefore, we know with which degree of the ecliptic the star rises or sets, and we know the angle of the section of the ecliptic itself in that same part with the horizon: if then we also find between the rising degree and the Sun so many parts of the ecliptic as are sufficient and regard the depth of the Sun below the horizon, according to the prescribed limits of the proposed star, we shall pronounce its first emergence or occultation to occur. But what we set forth concerning the altitude of the Sun above the earth in the preceding demonstration, corresponds in all ways also to its descent under the earth; for they differ in nothing except position. Just as those things which set for the apparent hemisphere rise for the hidden one, all things are reciprocal and easy to understand. Wherefore, let what has been said concerning the rising and setting of the stars, and also concerning the daily revolution of the terrestrial globe, be sufficient.

#### On seeking out the places of the stars, and the canonical description of the fixed stars. Chapter XIV.

After the daily revolution of the globe of the earth has been set forth by us, and those things which follow it, the demonstrations of the annual circuit ought now to follow. But since some of the ancient mathematicians judged that the phenomena of the non-wandering [fixed] stars should come first, as if the first principles of this art. Which opinion we thought should be followed by us, because among the principles and hypotheses we have assumed that the sphere of the non-wandering stars is altogether immobile, to which the wanderings of all the wandering stars [planets] are compared equally. 

But let no one wonder why we have undertaken this order, since Ptolemy in his *Great Construction* [the Almagest] thought that an explanation of the fixed stars could not be made unless the knowledge of the positions of the Sun and Moon had first preceded; and therefore, he judged that those things pertaining to the fixed stars should be deferred until that time. If you understand this concerning the numbers by which the apparent motion of the Moon and Sun is calculated, perhaps the opinion will stand. For Menelaus the Geometer attained many stars and their positions through lunar conjunctions by numbers.

--- Page 110 ---
### NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

But we shall accomplish this much better if, with the support of instruments, we take any star through the diligently examined positions of the Sun and Moon, as we shall soon teach. We are also warned by the vain effort of those who thought the magnitude of the solar year should be defined simply from the equinoxes or solstices, and not even from the fixed stars, in which they were never able to agree even down to our time, so much so that in no part has there been greater discord. 

Ptolemy had noticed this, who when he had weighed the solar year in his own time—not without suspicion of an error which could emerge over time—admonished posterity to search out further certainty of this matter thereafter. It seemed to us worthwhile, therefore, to show how by the skill of instruments the positions of the Sun and Moon are taken—namely, how much they are distant from the vernal equinox or other cardinal points of the world—which thereafter will provide us with conveniences for investigating other stars, by which we may also set before our eyes the sphere of the fixed stars woven with asterisms [constellations] and its image.

By which instruments the distance of the tropics, the obliquity of the ecliptic, and the inclination of the sphere (or the altitude of the equinoctial pole) are taken, has been set forth above. In the same way, we can take any other meridian altitude of the Sun. Which altitude, according to its difference from the inclination of the sphere, will exhibit to us how much the Sun declines from the equinoctial circle; through which declination, thereafter, its position taken from the equinox or solstice will also become manifest in the noon itself. Now, the Sun is seen to traverse nearly one degree in the space of 24 hours; therefore, 2.5 minutes [scrupula] result for an hourly portion. From which, for any other established hour, its position will be easily conjectured.

For observing the positions of the Moon and the stars, another instrument is constructed, which Ptolemy calls an Astrolabe. For two orbs are fashioned, or the quadrilateral margins of orbs, so that namely with flat sides or "jaws" they receive the concave and convex surface at right angles: equal in all respects and similar, appropriate in size, lest by too great a size they become less manageable, although otherwise amplitude grants more than slenderness to the parts to be divided. Let their width and thickness be...

--- Page 111 ---
<meta>This page continues the instructions for constructing and using astronomical instruments to determine the positions of the stars, following the previous discussion on the Sun and Moon's movements.</meta>

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK II.

Let the rings be at least a thirtieth part of the diameter in thickness. They shall therefore be compared and joined to one another at right angles, with their concave and convex surfaces fitting together as if in the roundness of a single globe. Let one of them take the place of the circle of signs <note>The zodiac</note>, and the other the circle that passes through both poles—that is, the poles of the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note> and the zodiac. Therefore, that circle of signs is to be distributed from its sides into 360 equal parts, as is customary, which should be further subdivided according to the capacity of the instrument. In the other circle as well, after measuring out the quadrants from the zodiac, the poles of that same zodiac are to be assigned; and by taking the distance from these according to the measure of the zodiac's obliquity <note>The axial tilt of the Earth, or the angle between the celestial equator and the ecliptic</note>, let the poles of the equinoctial circle also be marked.

Once these are prepared, let two other rings be crafted to move upon those same poles of the zodiac: an outer and an inner ring. These should have a thickness equal to the space between two planes, and their rims should be similar to the others, so arranged that the concave surface of the larger one touches the convex surface of the zodiac, and the convexity of the smaller one touches the concave surface of the zodiac everywhere. This must be done so that their rotation is not hindered, but they allow the zodiac itself, along with its meridian, to pass through easily and move freely among themselves. We shall then skillfully bore holes through these rings at the poles of the zodiac along the diameter and drive in small axles <term>axonia</term><note>Small pins or pivots upon which the rings rotate</note> by which they may be joined and carried. 

The inner ring should also be divided into 360 equal parts, so that in each of its four quadrants, ninety degrees extend to the poles. Within its cavity, yet another ring—the fifth—is to be placed and made rotatable within that same plane. To its rims shall be fixed mounting systems <term>systematia</term> having passages along the diameter and apertures <term>diaugia</term> or viewfinders <term>specilla</term> through which the light of a star may break in and exit, as is customary in a <term>dioptra</term> <note>A sighting tube or alidade used for alignment</note>, along the very diameter of the ring. To this, certain stops <term>offendicula</term> are to be fitted on either side, serving as indicators of the numbers <note>Pointers or cursors</note> for the sake of observing the latitudes on the containing ring.

Finally, a sixth ring is to be employed which receives and supports the whole <term>Astrolabium</term> <note>The armillary sphere being described here</note>, suspended from the fixed points of the equinoctial poles. This is to be placed upon a small column and supported by it, erected perpendicular to the plane of the horizon. With the poles also adjusted to the inclination of the sphere <note>The local latitude</note>, it should hold a position similar to the natural meridian and should not waver from it at all. 

Once the instrument is thus prepared, whenever we wish to obtain the position of any star, in the evening or when the Sun is about to set, and at a time when we also have the Moon in view, we shall align the outer ring to the degree of the zodiac in which...

It describes the precision fitting of six concentric rings, their graduation into degrees, and the sighting mechanisms required for observation.</summary>

--- Page 112 ---
# NICOLAI COPERNICI

...we have then learned through preceding [calculations] the Sun to be, and we shall turn the section of the rings toward the Sun itself, until both of them—namely the zodiac and that outer ring which is through the poles—shadow themselves equally. Then we also turn the inner ring to the Moon, and with the eye placed at its plane where we see the Moon opposite, as if bisected by the same plane, we shall mark the place on the sign-bearer [zodiac] of the instrument; for that will then be the place of the Moon according to the longitude of its appearance. For without the Moon there was no way of comprehending the places of the stars, since she alone of all [celestial bodies] participates in both day and night. 

Then, when night comes on, when the star whose place we seek can now be seen, we adjust the outer ring to the place of the Moon, through which we align the position of the Astrolabe toward the Moon itself, just as we did with the Sun. Then we also turn the inner circle toward the star, until it appears to adhere to the plane of the ring, and is seen through the view-holes which are in the contained small ring. For thus we shall have found both the longitude and the latitude of the star. While these things are being done, whichever degree of the zodiac is at mid-heaven will be set before the eyes, and therefore it will be clearly established at what hours the deed itself was performed. 

Take the example of Ptolemaeus: who, in the second year of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, on the ninth day of Pharmuthi, the eighth month of the Egyptians, in Alexandria, around sunset, wishing to observe the place of the star which is called *Basiliscus* or *Regulus* in the breast of Leo, and having compared the Astrolabe to the now-setting Sun, five equinoctial hours having passed from noon, while the Sun was found in 3 degrees and a half-twelfth [semuncia] of Pisces, he found the Moon following the Sun by 92 and one-eighth degrees by means of the inner circle applied to it; wherefore the place of the Moon was then seen to be in 5 degrees and a sixth of Gemini. And after half an hour, when the sixth hour from noon was completed and the star had already begun to appear, with the fourth degree of Gemini in mid-heaven, he turned the outer ring of the instrument to the already determined place of the Moon, and proceeding with the inner ring, he took the distance of the star from the Moon in the order of the signs as 57 and one-tenth degrees. 

Since, therefore, the Moon was found from the setting Sun in (as has been said) 92 and one-eighth degrees, which terminated the Moon in 5 degrees and a sixth of Gemini. But it was appropriate that within the space of half an hour the Moon had moved through a quarter of one degree—since the hourly portion in the lunar motion takes up half a degree more or less—but on account of the then subtractive parallax of the Moon, it ought to be a little less than a quarter...

[[margin: which]]

***

--- Page 113 ---
[[original page: 46]]

# BOOK II OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...which he defined as approximately one twelfth [*uncia*]: wherefore the Moon had been in 5 degrees and a third of Gemini. But when we treat of the lunar parallaxes, it will appear that the difference was not so great that it could be sufficiently clear that the seen place of the Moon exceeded five degrees of Gemini by more than a third, and scarcely less than two-fifths; to which the 57 degrees with one tenth part being added, they bring together the place of the star in nearly 2 1/2 degrees of Leo [Note: Margin says *m ij Signo*, indicating the 2nd sign after Gemini, i.e., Leo], distant from the summer solstice of the Sun by nearly 32 1/2 degrees, with a northern latitude of a sixth part of a degree. This was the place of *Basiliscus*, through which the approach to the other non-wandering stars was opened. 

This observation of Ptolemaeus was made in the Year of Christ according to the Romans 139, on the 24th day of February, in the first year of the 229th Olympiad. Thus that most eminent man of mathematicians noted how much each of the stars at that time held a place from the vernal equinox, and he set forth the asterisms of the celestial animals. In this he aided our study in no small way, and relieved us of a sufficiently arduous labor, so that we, who have thought that the places of the stars are to be referred not to the equinoxes (which change with time), but the equinoxes to the sphere of the fixed stars, can easily derive the description of the stars from some other immutable principle. This we have chosen to take from Aries, as the first sign, and from its first star, which is in its head, so that thus the same and absolute appearance may always remain for those things which, as if fixed and cohering, once they have taken their seat, place themselves perpetually. 

They were, however, through the wonderful care and skill of the ancients, digested into 48 forms, except those which the circle of always-hidden stars [the Antarctic circle] separated from nearly the fourth climate through Rhodes. And thus the unformed stars remained as unknown to them. For the stars were formed into likenesses for no other reason, according to the opinion of Theon the younger in his exposition of Aratus, than so that such a great multitude of them might be distinguished by parts, and might be designated individually by certain names, an ancient enough custom, since it is established that even in Job certain ones were already named, such as the Pleiades, Hyades, Arcturus, and Orion, and we read of them by name in Hesiod and Homer. 

In the description of them according to longitude, therefore, we shall not use the dodecatemories [twelve-parts/signs] which are derived from the equinoxes and solstices, but the simple and customary number of degrees; in other things we shall follow Ptolemaeus, with a few exceptions which we have found to be either corrupted or otherwise somehow different. To what extent their distance from those cardinal points is clear, we shall teach in the following book.
