### PAGE 147
**THIRD BOOK OF THE REVOLUTIONS OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS.**

#### On the anticipation of the equinoxes and solstices. Chapter I.

Having depicted the appearance of the fixed stars, we must pass on to those things which pertain to the annual revolution, and for that reason we shall first treat of the change of the equinoxes, on account of which the fixed stars are also believed to move. We find, however, that the ancient mathematicians did not distinguish the turning or natural year, which is from an equinox or solstice, from that which is taken from one of the fixed stars. Hence it is that they thought the Olympic years, which they began from the rising of the Dog Star (Sirius), were the same as those from the solstice, the difference of the one from the other not yet being known. **Hipparchus** of Rhodes, however, a man of marvelous sagacity, was the first to notice that these differ from each other; while he observed the magnitude of the year more attentively, he found it to be greater when compared to the fixed stars than when compared to the equinoxes or solstices. Whence he thought that some motion in the order of the signs [prograde] existed in the fixed stars also, but so slow as not to be immediately perceptible. But now by the passage of time it has been made most evident, by which we now discern a far different rising and setting of the signs and stars from the prescription of the ancients. And the twelfth parts (signs) of the circle have receded from the signs of the fixed stars by a sufficiently great interval, which originally agreed with each other both in time and position. Moreover, the motion itself is found to be unequal; wishing to provide a cause for this diversity, they brought forward various opinions. Some thought there was a certain oscillation [libramentum] of the hanging world, such as the motion we find in the planets around their latitudes, and that it would eventually return from certain limits as far as it had proceeded, and they judged its deviation on either side from its midpoint to be no greater than 8 degrees. But this now-antiquated opinion could not stand, especially because it is now clear enough that the head of the constellation Aries has moved more than thrice eight degrees from the vernal equinox.

---

### PAGE 148
**NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**

...it is now clear enough that the head of the starred Aries is distant by more than thrice eight degrees from the vernal equinox, and other stars similarly, while in the meantime through so many centuries no trace of regression has been perceived. Others have thought that the sphere of the fixed stars indeed moves forward, but with unequal steps, yet they defined no certain rule. In addition, there occurred another marvel of nature: that the obliquity of the zodiac [signifer] does not appear as great to us as it did to **Ptolemy**, as we have said. For these reasons, some devised a ninth sphere, others a tenth, by which they thought those things would be brought about; yet they could not provide what they promised. Now also an eleventh sphere had begun to come into the light, which number of circles we shall easily refute as superfluous in the motion of the earth. For as has already been partly explained by us in the first book, the two revolutions—namely, of the annual declination and of the center of the earth—are not altogether equal, since the restoration of the declination clearly anticipates the period of the center by a small amount. From this it must follow that the equinoxes and solstices seem to anticipate [precede], not because the sphere of the fixed stars is carried forward, but rather because the equinoctial circle is carried backward, being oblique to the plane of the zodiac, according to the mode of the deflection of the axis of the terrestrial globe. For it would be more to the point to say that the equinoctial circle is oblique to the zodiac, than the zodiac to the equinoctial, by comparison of the smaller to the larger. For the zodiac is much larger, because [abbrev: *q̇*] it is described by the distance of the Sun and the earth in the annual circuit, while [abbrev: *q̃*] the equinoctial is designated by the daily motion around the axis of the earth, as has been said. And in this manner those equinoctial sections, with the whole obliquity of the zodiac, are seen to advance with the passage of time, while the stars are seen to lag behind. However, the measure of this motion and the reason for its diversity remained hidden to the ancients because its revolution, however great it may be, is still unknown on account of its unexpected slowness, inasmuch as in so many centuries since it first became known to mortals, it has hardly completed a fifteenth part of the circle. Nevertheless, as far as is in our power, we shall make things more certain through those observations which we have received from history up to our own memory.

---

### PAGE 149
**ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.**

#### History of the observations proving the unequal precession of the equinoxes and solstices. Chapter II.

In the first period of 76 years according to **Calippus**, in its 36th year—which was the 30th year from the death of Alexander the Great—**Timochares** of Alexandria, who was the first to take care for the positions of the fixed stars, reported **Spica**, which the Virgin holds, to be distant from the solstitial point by 82 and 1/3 parts, with a Southern latitude of two parts; and that star in the forehead of Scorpio, which is the most Northern of three and the first in the order of the formation of the sign itself, to have had a latitude of one part and 1/3, and a longitude of 32 parts from the Autumnal equinox. And again in the 48th year of the same period, he found Spica of the Virgin at a longitude of 82 1/2 parts from the summer solstice, the latitude remaining the same. **Hipparchus**, however, in the 50th year of the third Calippic period—the 196th year of Alexander—found that which is in the breast of Leo, called **Regulus**, following the summer solstice by 29 1/2 and 1/3 of one part. Then **Menelaus**, the Roman geometer, in the first year of the reign of **Trajan**, which was 99 years from the birth of Christ and 422 from the death of Alexander, reported Spica of the Virgin to be distant by 86 parts and a quarter of a part from the solstice; and that which is in the forehead of Scorpio at 36 parts minus one twelfth of one part from the Autumnal equinox. Following these, **Ptolemy**, in the second year of **Antoninus Pius**, which was the 462nd year from the death of Alexander, learned that Regulus of Leo held 32 1/2 parts from the solstice, Spica 86 1/2 parts, and the aforementioned star in the forehead of Scorpio 36 and 1/3 parts of longitude from the Autumnal equinox, the latitude being in no way changed, just as was expressed above in the Canonical exposition. And these things we have reviewed just as they were reported by them. But after a long time, namely in the 1202nd year from the death of the Alexandrian [Alexander], the observation of **Machometus Aracensis** [al-Battani] followed, to which the greatest trust may be applied; in that year Regulus or the **Basiliscus** of Leo was seen to have reached 44 degrees and 5 minutes [scruples] from the solstice, and that in the forehead of Scorpio 47 parts and 50 minutes from the Autumn...

---

### PAGE 150
**NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**

...from the Autumnal equinox; in all of which the latitude of each always remained the same, so that there should no longer be any doubt on this part. For which reason we also, in the Year of Christ 1525, the first after the second intercalary year, which is the 1849th Egyptian year from the death of Alexander, observed the often-named **Spica** in **Frauenburg**, **Prussia**, and its maximum altitude in the meridian circle seemed to be nearly 27 parts. We found the latitude of Frauenburg to be 54 parts and 19 1/2 minutes [first scruples]. Wherefore its declination from the equinoctial will be established as 8 parts and 40 minutes. Whence its position was revealed as follows. For we have described the meridian circle through the poles of both the zodiac and the equinoctial ABCD, in which the common sections and diameters were AEC of the equinoctial, and BED of the zodiac, whose Northern pole is F and axis FEG. Let B be the beginning of Capricorn, D of Cancer; let the arc BH be taken, which is equal to the Southern latitude of the star, of two parts, and from point H let HL be drawn parallel to BD, which cuts the axis of the zodiac at I and the equinoctial at K. Let there also be taken, according to the Southern declination of the star, an arc of 8 parts and 40 minutes, MA; and from point M, let MN be drawn parallel to AC, which will cut the parallel of the zodiac HIL; let it cut it then at point O, and the straight line OP at right angles will be equal to half the chord of twice the declination AM itself. But indeed the circles whose diameters are FG, HL, and MN are perpendicular to the plane ABCD, and their common sections, by the 19th [proposition] of the 11th book of **Euclid's Elements**, are at right angles to the same plane at points O and I; they themselves, by the 6th [proposition] of the same, are parallel to each other. And since I is the center of the circle whose diameter is HL, therefore OI itself will be equal to half the chord subtending twice the arc in the circle of diameter HL, and similar to that by which the star is distant from the beginning of **Libra**, according to the longitude which we seek. It is found, however, in this way: For the angles which are under OKP and AEB are equal, the exterior to the interior and opposite, and OPK is a right angle. On account of which, OP is to OK in the same ratio as half the chord of twice AB is to BE.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

->SOUTHERN SIGNS<-

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS’S ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK THREE.

## On the Precession of the Equinoxes and Solstices. Chapter 1.

[[image: Historiated initial S showing astronomers observing the heavens]]
**HAVING** depicted the appearance of the fixed stars, we must now pass on to those matters which pertain to the annual revolution. For this reason, we shall first treat the change of the <term>equinoxes</term> <note>The two days of the year when day and night are of equal length.</note>, because of which even the fixed stars are believed to move. We find, however, that the ancient mathematicians did not distinguish the "turning" or natural year—which is measured from an equinox or solstice—from the year measured relative to one of the fixed stars. This is why they thought the <term>Olympic years</term> <note>The four-year cycles used in ancient Greece, which Copernicus notes were traditionally timed by astronomical events.</note>, which they began from the rising of the <term>Dog Star</term> <note>The star Sirius.</note>, were the same as those measured from the solstice, since the difference between the two was not yet known. 

However, Hipparchus of Rhodes, a man of marvelous sagacity, was the first to notice that these differ from each other. While he was observing the length of the year more attentively, he found it to be longer when compared to the fixed stars than when compared to the equinoxes or solstices. From this, he judged that there was some movement in the fixed stars as well, following the sequence [of the zodiac signs], but so slow as to not be immediately perceptible. But now, through the long passage of time, it has become most evident; we now see a far different rising and setting of the constellations and stars from what was recorded by the ancients. Furthermore, the <term>twelfth-parts</term> <note>original: "dodecatemoria." These are the twelve 30-degree segments of the zodiac (Aries, Taurus, etc.).</note> of the circle of signs have receded from the constellations of the fixed stars by a considerable distance, whereas originally they agreed in both position and arrangement. 

Moreover, this very motion is found to be unequal. Those wishing to explain the cause of this variation have brought forward various opinions. Some thought there was a certain <term>oscillation</term> <note>original: "libramentum." This refers to the theory of "trepidation," an old belief that the equinoxes moved back and forth like a pendulum rather than in a continuous circle.</note> of the hanging world, much like the motion we find in the planets regarding their latitudes, and they judged that it would eventually return after moving a certain distance from its limits. They believed its wandering on either side of its midpoint was no more than eight degrees. But this opinion, now outdated, could not stand, especially because it is now quite clear that the displacement exceeds three times eight [24] degrees.

<margin>q iii</margin> **now** <note>This marginal mark "q iii" is a signature used by early printers to keep the pages in the correct order for binding.</note>

<summary>Copernicus introduces the "precession of the equinoxes," explaining how Hipparchus first discovered that the solar year differs from the sidereal year, and notes that the stars' positions have shifted significantly since antiquity.</summary>
<keywords>precession of the equinoxes, Hipparchus, Olympic years, Dog Star, Sirius, zodiac signs, trepidation, solar year, sidereal year</keywords>

--- Page 148 ---
<meta>This page continues Chapter 1 of Book Three, following the introduction of Hipparchus’s discovery that the solar and sidereal years differ. Copernicus now moves into his own explanation for this phenomenon—the precession of the equinoxes—by attributing it to the Earth's motion rather than the movement of the stars.</meta>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS
It is now clear enough that the <term>Head of Aries</term> <note>The "starry" Aries refers to the actual constellation, which in antiquity coincided with the spring equinox but has since shifted.</note> is distant from the vernal equinox by more than twenty-four degrees. Other stars have shifted similarly, and yet in all these centuries, no trace of them moving backward has been observed. Some have believed that the sphere of fixed stars does indeed move forward, but at an irregular pace; however, they have never defined a certain law for this. 

To this is added another marvel of nature: that the <term>obliquity of the zodiac</term> <note>The angle of the Earth's tilt relative to its orbit, which determines the severity of the seasons.</note> does not appear as great to us as it did to Ptolemy, as we have mentioned. To explain these things, some astronomers have devised a ninth sphere, and others a tenth, believing these would account for the movements, yet they could not deliver what they promised. Now even an eleventh sphere has begun to appear in their theories. We shall easily refute such a number of circles as superfluous by using the motion of the Earth. 

As we already partially explained in the first book, there are two revolutions—namely, the annual <term>declination</term> <note>The wobbling or shifting tilt of the Earth's axis.</note> and the movement of the Earth's center—which are not perfectly equal. The resetting of the tilt happens slightly faster than the completion of the Earth's orbital period. Consequently, the equinoxes and solstices appear to move forward (precede). This happens not because the sphere of fixed stars is carried forward, but rather because the <term>equinoctial circle</term> <note>The celestial equator, which is the projection of the Earth's equator into space.</note> moves backward. This circle is tilted relative to the plane of the zodiac, following the way the Earth’s axis deflects. 

Indeed, it is more accurate to say the equinoctial circle is tilted relative to the zodiac than the other way around, if we compare the smaller to the larger. For the zodiac is much larger, as it is defined by the distance between the Sun and Earth in their annual circuit, while the equinoctial circle is defined by the Earth's daily rotation around its own axis. In this way, the intersections of the equinoxes, along with the entire tilt of the zodiac, are seen to shift forward over time, while the stars are left behind. 

The true measure and nature of this variation were hidden from earlier astronomers because the length of its full cycle is still unknown. This is due to its incredible slowness; in all the centuries since it was first noticed by humans, it has barely completed a fifteenth part of a full circle. Nevertheless, to the best of our ability and using the historical observations passed down to us, we shall make these matters more certain.

**History**

<margin>Head of Aries: The starting point of the constellation Aries.</margin>
<margin>Sphere: The transparent shells ancient astronomers believed held the stars and planets.</margin>
<margin>Zodiac: The "sign-bearer," the path the sun appears to follow through the stars.</margin>
<margin>Ptolemy: The Greek-Roman astronomer whose model Copernicus is updating.</margin>
<margin>Earth: The third planet, which Copernicus places in motion.</margin>
<margin>Equinoctial circle: The celestial equator.</margin>
<margin>Axis: The imaginary line around which the Earth rotates.</margin>

<summary>Copernicus argues that the shifting of the stars (precession) and the changing tilt of the Earth are caused by the Earth's own physical wobbling rather than the movement of massive celestial spheres. He criticizes the complexity of contemporary models that added more and more "spheres" to explain these slow changes.</summary>

# BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

## Chapter II. The history of observations proving the unequal precession of the equinoxes and solstices.

**First**, therefore, in the thirty-sixth year of the first 76-year <term>Callippic period</term> <note>A 76-year cycle used by Greek astronomers to synchronize the solar year and lunar months.</note>, which was the thirtieth year after the death of Alexander the Great, Timochares of Alexandria—who was the first to take care in recording the locations of the fixed stars—reported that **Spica**, which the Virgin holds, was at a distance of 82 and 1/3 degrees from the summer <term>solstice point</term> <note>The point in the sky where the sun reaches its highest northern point.</note>, with a southern latitude of two degrees. He also recorded that the star in the forehead of Scorpio (the northernmost of the three and the first in the formation of that sign) had a latitude of 1 and 1/3 degrees, and a longitude of 32 degrees from the autumnal equinox. 

Again, in the forty-eighth year of that same period, he found **Spica** in the Virgin at a longitude of 82 and 1/2 degrees from the summer solstice, while its latitude remained the same. Later, Hipparchus, in the fiftieth year of the third Callippic period (the 196th year after Alexander), found the star in the chest of the Lion called **Regulus** <note>original: "Regulus"; also known as the "Little King" or the heart of Leo.</note> following the summer solstice by 29 and 1/2 plus 1/3 of a degree <note>29 and 5/6 degrees.</note>.

Then Menelaus, the Roman geometer, in the first year of the reign of Trajan (which was 99 years from the birth of Christ and 422 years from the death of Alexander), reported that **Spica** in the Virgin was distant from the solstice by 86 and 1/4 degrees in longitude. The star in the forehead of Scorpio he reported at 35 and 11/12 degrees <note>original: "XXXVI minus uncia"; Copernicus uses the Roman "uncia" (twelfth) to denote 1/12th of a degree.</note> from the autumnal equinox. 

Following these men, Ptolemy, in the second year of Antoninus Pius (the 462nd year after the death of Alexander, as has been said), learned that **Regulus** in Leo occupied 32 and 1/2 degrees from the solstice, **Spica** occupied 86 and 1/2 degrees, and the aforementioned star in the forehead of Scorpio occupied 36 and 1/3 degrees of longitude from the autumnal equinox. In all these cases, the latitude had not changed at all, just as was expressed above in the <term>Canonical table</term> <note>Referring to the standard star catalogs used by ancient astronomers.</note>. We have reviewed these measurements exactly as they were reported by those authors.

After a long time, however—namely, in the 1202nd year after the death of Alexander—the observations of **Al-Battani** <note>original: "Machometi Aracensis"; Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD) was a crucial Arab astronomer whose refined measurements corrected many of Ptolemy's errors.</note> succeeded them, in which one may place the greatest trust. In that year, **Regulus** (or the "Little King") of Leo was at 44 degrees and 5 <term>scruples</term> <note>In this context, a "scruple" refers to a minute of an arc (1/60th of a degree).</note> from the solstice, and the star in the forehead of Scorpio was at 47 degrees and 50 scruples from the autumnal equinox.

<summary>Copernicus lists historical observations from Timochares, Hipparchus, Menelaus, Ptolemy, and Al-Battani to track the changing positions of stars like Spica and Regulus. By comparing these over 1,200 years, he demonstrates that the precession of the equinoxes is not a steady movement but varies in speed.</summary>
<keywords>Timochares, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Al-Battani, Spica, Regulus, precession of equinoxes, star coordinates, Callippic period</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s survey of historical observations of the star Spica. Having previously cited ancient astronomers like Timochares and Hipparchus, he now provides his own contemporary observations from 1525 to calculate how much the star's position has shifted over nearly two millennia.</meta>

# NICOLAI COPERNICI
...seen to have reached from the autumnal equinox. In all these observations, the latitude of each star always remained the same, so that there is no longer any room for doubt on this point. For this reason, in the year of Christ 1525—the first year after the second leap year, which is the year 1849 of the Egyptian calendar from the death of Alexander—we also observed the oft-mentioned **Spica** in Frauenburg <note>original: "Frueburgium"; the Latin name for Frombork, Poland, where Copernicus lived and worked.</note>, Prussia. Its maximum altitude on the <term>meridian circle</term> <note>The imaginary great circle in the sky passing through the celestial poles and the observer's zenith.</note> appeared to be nearly 27 degrees. 

We found the latitude of Frauenburg to be 54 degrees and 19.5 minutes <note>original: "scrup. primorum XIX. s."; Copernicus measured his location's latitude to determine the star's position relative to the equator.</note>. Therefore, its <term>declination</term> <note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> from the equator is established as 8 degrees and 40 minutes. From this, its position was revealed as follows:

We have described the meridian circle ABCD passing through the poles of both the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The "zodiac circle" or the path the sun appears to follow.</note> and the equator. The common sections and diameters are AEC for the equator and BED for the zodiac, whose northern pole is F and axis is FEG. Let B be the beginning of Capricorn and D the beginning of Cancer. 

Now, let the arc BH be taken, equal to the southern latitude of the star (two degrees). From point H, let HL be drawn parallel to BD <note>The diameter of the zodiac.</note>, which cuts the axis of the zodiac at I and the equator at K. Also, let the arc MA be taken according to the southern declination of the star, which is 8 degrees and 40 minutes. From point M, let MN be drawn parallel to AC <note>The diameter of the equator.</note>, which will cut the parallel of the zodiac HIL. Let it intersect at point O; the straight line OP, at right angles, will be equal to half the <term>chord</term> <note>A straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc.</note> subtending twice the declination AM. 

However, the circles whose diameters are FG, HL, and MN are at right angles to the plane ABCD. Their common sections (according to the nineteenth proposition of the eleventh book of **Euclid's Elements**) are at right angles to that same plane at points O and I; these lines are parallel to each other (by the sixth proposition of the same book). And since I is the center of the circle whose diameter is HL, the line OI will be equal to half the chord subtending twice the arc in the circle of diameter HL—that is, the distance by which the star is removed from the beginning of **Libra** according to the longitude we are seeking. 

This is found in the following way: the angles OKP and AEB are equal (the exterior angle to the interior and opposite), and OPK is a right angle. Therefore, the ratio of OP to OK is the same as the ratio of half the chord of twice AE to BE.

->[Diagram of the celestial sphere showing the intersection of the equator and zodiac with the coordinates of the star Spica.]<-

<summary>Copernicus uses his 1525 observations of the star Spica in Frauenburg to calculate its modern position. By comparing his data with ancient records, he geometrically demonstrates the shift in the star's longitude while noting its latitude remains constant.</summary>

to $BE$: and the half-chord of double $AH$ to $HK$, for they comprise triangles similar to $OPK$ itself. But $AB$ is of 23 parts, 28 minutes, and 30 seconds [s. = *semis*], and its half-chord of the double is 39,832 parts, where $BE$ is 100,000; and $ABH$ is of 25 parts, 28 minutes, 30 seconds, the half-chord of the double of which is 43,010 parts; and $MA$ is the half-chord of the double of the declination of 15,069 parts. From these it follows that the whole $HK$ is 107,978 parts, and $OK$ 37,831 parts, and the remainder $HO$ 70,147. But the double $HOI$ subtends a segment of the circle $HGL$ of 176 parts; $HOI$ itself will be 99,939 parts, of which $BE$ were 100,000; and therefore the remaining $OI$ is 29,892 parts. However, insofar as $HOI$ is half of the diameter of 100,000 parts, $OI$ will be 29,810 parts, to which corresponds an arc of approximately 17 parts and 21 minutes, by which distance **Spica Virginis** was away from the beginning of **Libra**, and this was the place of the star itself. Ten years earlier also, namely in the year 1515, we found it to decline by 8 parts and 36 minutes, and its place in 17 parts and 14 minutes of **Libra**. Moreover, **Ptolemaeus** reported this [star] to have declined by only half of one part; its place would therefore have been in 26 parts and 40 minutes of **Virgo**, which seems to be truer by comparison with preceding observations. From this it seems clear enough that in almost the entire time from **Timocharis** to **Ptolemaeus**, in 432 years, the equinoxes and solstices were changed by preceding [precession] for the most part by one degree in every hundred years, a ratio of time always being held to the length of their passage, which was in total 4 parts and one-third of one. For also by observing the summer solstice [aestiuam tropen] at **Basiliscus** [Regulus] of **Leo**, from **Hipparchus** to **Ptolemaeus** in 266 years, 2 degrees and two-thirds passed, so that here too, by comparison of time, it is found to have anticipated by one degree in a hundred years. Furthermore, those [observations] at the first front of **Scorpio** by **Albategnius** himself [compared] to those which **Menelaus** [observed], in the intervening 782 years, since 11 degrees and 55 minutes have passed, in no way will 100 years seem to be attributed to one degree, but rather 66 years. Moreover, from **Ptolemaeus**, in 741 years, only 65 years to one degree. If, finally, the remaining space of 645 years be compared to the difference of 9 degrees and 11 minutes of our observation, one degree will obtain 71 years. From which it is evident that the precession of the equinoxes was slower... [OCR break: *praecessionem*]

--- Page 152 ---
[[Original page: 65v]]

# NICOLAI COPERNICI

...of the equinoxes before **Ptolemaeus** in those 400 years than from **Ptolemaeus** to **Albitegnius**; and this [precession] was also swifter from **Albitegnius** to our times. A difference is also found in the motion of the obliquity. Since **Aristarchus Samius** [found] the same obliquity of the zodiac and the equinoctial as **Ptolemaeus**, of 23 parts, 51 first minutes, and 20 seconds. **Albitegnius**, 23 parts and 26 minutes. **Arzachel Hispanus**, 190 years after him, 23 parts and 34 minutes. And likewise after 230 years, **Prophatius Iudaeus**, smaller by almost two minutes. In our times, however, it is not found to be greater than 23 parts, 28 minutes, and 30 seconds. So that from here also it is manifest that from **Aristarchus** to **Ptolemaeus** there was the minimum motion, but the maximum truly from **Ptolemaeus** itself to **Albitegnius**.

### Hypotheses by which the change of the equinoxes, the obliquity of the zodiac [signiferi], and the equinoctial is demonstrated. Chapter III.

**Since**, therefore, the equinoxes and solstices are changed by an unequal motion, it seems manifest from these things. Of which cause no one perhaps will bring forward a better one than a certain deflection of the axis of the earth and the poles of the equinoctial circle. For that seems to follow from the hypothesis of the motion of the earth. Since it is manifest that the circle which is through the middle of the signs [the ecliptic] remains perpetually immutable, certain latitudes of the fixed stars attesting to this, but the equinoctial is changed. Since if the motion of the earth’s axis simply and exactly agreed with the motion of the center, no anticipation of the equinoxes and solstices would appear at all, as we have said. But since they differ among themselves, but by an unequal difference, it was necessary even for the solstices and equinoxes to precede the places of the stars by an unequal motion. In the same way it happens concerning the motion of declination, which also unequally changes the obliquity of the zodiac, which obliquity, however, would be more rightly granted to the equinoctial. For which cause, two entirely reciprocal motions of the poles, similar to hanging librations [oscillations], must be understood, since the poles and circles in a sphere cohere and agree with one another. There will be, therefore, one motion which changes the inclination of those circles, with the poles...

--- Page 153 ---
[[Original page: 66]]

### REVOLUTIONUM LIB. III.

...poles thus carried up and down around the angle of intersection. Another [motion] which increases and diminishes the solstitial and equinoctial precessions, a commotion being made here and there across [transversally]. These motions we call "librations," because, like hanging things [pendulums], the accelerations occur in the middle between two limits along the same path; around the extremes, they are slowest. Such [motions] for the most part happen around the latitudes of the planets, as we shall see in its place. They also differ in their revolutions, because the inequality of the equinoxes is restored twice under one restoration of the obliquity. Just as in every apparent unequal motion, a certain mean must be understood, so that the ratio of the inequality can be grasped: so surely here also it was necessary to think of mean poles and a mean equinoctial circle; also mean equinoctial intersections and points of conversion [solstices], under which the poles and the terrestrial equinoctial circle, deflecting here and there, yet with fixed limits, make those equal motions appear diverse. And so those two librations concurring with each other bring it about that the poles of the earth in time describe certain lines similar to a twisted wreath [corollae intortae]. But since it is not easy to have explained these things sufficiently with words, and even less, as I fear, will they be perceived by hearing unless they are also seen with the eyes. Let us therefore describe the circle of the signs in the sphere $ABCD$; let its North pole be $E$, the beginning of **Capricorn** $A$, of **Cancer** $C$, of **Aries** $B$, of **Libra** $D$; and through the signs $A$ and $C$, and the pole $E$, let the circle $AEC$ be described. Let the maximum distance of the Northern poles of the zodiac and the equinoctial be $EF$, and the minimum $EG$; and accordingly, in the middle place let there be the pole $I$, upon which the equinoctial circle $BHD$ is described, which may be called the mean; and $BD$ the mean equinoxes. Let all these be carried around pole $E$ with an always equal motion in precedence [westward], that is, against the order of the signs under the sphere of the fixed stars, with a slow motion, as has been said. Now let two reciprocal motions of the terrestrial poles be understood, similar to hanging things, one between the limits $FG$, which will be called the motion of anomaly—that is, the inequality of declination. The other across, from preceding into following, and from following into preceding, which we shall call the anomaly of the equinoxes, twice as swift as the former. These two motions, concurring in the poles of the earth, deflect them in a marvelous way. For first, with the North pole of the earth placed under $F$... [OCR break: *r ij*] ...descri... [OCR break]

Thence proceeding, the pole repeats the following [eastward direction] as far as the extreme limit in $M$, and having returned anew is united in the middle, and again turning into preceding [westward] having traversed the limit $N$, it concludes...

### How a reciprocal motion or motion of libration consists of circular motions. Chapter IV.

**That**, therefore, this motion agrees with the appearances we shall now declare. Meanwhile, however, someone will ask in what way the equality of those librations can be understood, since it was said from the beginning that celestial motion is equal, or composed of equal and circular motions. Here, however, in both cases two motions appear as one under both terms [limits], between which it is necessary for a cessation to intervene. We shall indeed admit that they are doubled, but they are demonstrated from equal [motions] in this way. Let there be a straight line $AB$, which is cut into four parts at points $C, D, E$, and in $D$ let homocentric circles be described in the same plane $ADB$ and $CDE$, and on the circumference of the inner circle let point $F$ be taken anywhere, and with $F$ itself as center, but with interval $FD$, let circle $GHD$ be described, which cuts the straight line $AB$ at point $H$, and let the diameter $DFG$ be drawn. It must be shown that with the two motions of the circles $GHD$ and $CFE$ concurring with each other, the mobile point $H$ crawls back and forth reciprocating along the same straight line $AB$. Which will be the case if $H$ is understood to move in the opposite direction, and twice as much as $F$ itself. Since the same angle which is under $CDF$ at the center of circle $CFE$ and standing on the circumference of $GHD$ itself comprises both circumferences of the equal circles $GH$ double to $FC$, given that at some time in the conjunction of the straight lines $ACD$ and $DFG$ the mobile $H$ was in $G$ coinciding with $A$, and $F$ in $C$. But now the center $F$ is [moving] into the right parts [by angle] $PFC$, and $H$ itself through the circumference $GH$ into the left parts twice as great as $CF$ itself.

[Image: Geometrical diagram showing the generation of linear motion from two circles]

--- Page 156 ---
[[Original page: 67v]]

# NICOLAI COPERNICI

...or conversely. $H$, therefore, will be reclined onto the line $AB$; otherwise it would happen that a part is greater than its whole, which I think is easily understood. Moreover, it has receded from its prior place according to the length $AH$ retracted through the inflected line $DFH$, equal to $AD$ itself, by that interval by which the diameter $DFG$ exceeds the chord $DH$. And in this way $H$ will be led to the center $D$, which will be when the circle $DHG$ is tangent to the straight line $AB$, namely while $GD$ stands at right angles to $AB$ itself, and then it will arrive at the other limit $B$, from which it will return again by a similar reason. It is clear, therefore, from two circular motions, and in this way occurring to each other, that a motion is composed into a straight line, and from equal motions [is composed] a reciprocal and unequal one, which was to be demonstrated. From which it also follows that the straight line $GH$ will always be at right angles to $AB$ itself: for the line will comprise a right angle in the semicircle $DHG$. And therefore $GH$ will be the half-chord of double the arc $AG$, and $DH$ the other half-chord of the double of that which remains from the quadrant of the circle $AG$, because circle $AGB$ is double to $HGD$ itself according to the diameter.

...slower at the circumference. Since therefore the double $DK$ subtends double $BF$, and the double $EG$ double of $AE$: $DK$ and $EG$ are therefore equal; but $AG$, by the seventh [proposition] of the third [book] of **Euclid’s** *Elements*, is smaller than $GE$, it will also be smaller than $DK$. But in equal time they traversed $GA$ and $KD$, on account of the equal arcs $AB$ and $BF$. The motion is therefore slower around the circumference $A$ than around the center $D$. This having been demonstrated: let the center of the earth now be taken at $L$, so that the straight line $DL$ is at right angles to the plane of the hemicycle $ABC$, and through the points $A$ and $C$ let the arc of circle $AMC$ be described at center $L$, and let $LDM$ be drawn in a straight line. There will be, therefore, at $M$ the pole of the hemicycle $ABC$, and $ADC$ the common section of the circles, and let $LA, LC$ be joined, and similarly $LK, LG$, which being extended in a straight line cut the arc $AMC$ at $N$ and $O$. Since therefore the angle which is under $LDK$ is right, the one under $LKD$ is therefore acute. Wherefore the line $LK$ is longer than $LD$; so much more in amblygonial [obtuse] triangles, the side $LG$ is greater than side $LK$, and $LA$ than $LG$ itself. Therefore, at center $L$, with interval $LK$, a circle being described, it will fall outside $LD$ itself; but it will cut the remaining $LG$ and $LA$; let it be described and let it be $PKRS$. And since triangle $LDK$ is less than sector $LPK$; but triangle $LGA$ is greater than sector $LRS$, and therefore the ratio of triangle $LDK$ to sector $LPK$ is less than triangle $LGA$ to sector $LRS$. In turn also triangle $LDK$ will be to triangle $LGA$ in a smaller ratio than sector $LPK$ to sector $LRS$. And by the first [proposition] of the sixth [book] of **Euclid’s** *Elements*, as triangle $LDK$ is to triangle $LGA$, so is the base $DK$ to the base $AG$. But the ratio of sector to sector is as angle $DLK$ to angle $RLS$, or arc $MN$ to arc $OA$. Therefore $DK$ is to $GA$ in a smaller ratio than $MN$ to $OA$. But now we have demonstrated $DK$ to be greater than $GA$; therefore so much more strongly will $MN$ be greater than... [OCR break: *MN, quàm*]

# NICOLAI COPERNICI

...$MN$ [greater] than $OA$, which are understood to be described under equal intervals of time through the poles of the earth, according to the equal arcs of anomaly $AB$ and $BF$, which was to be demonstrated. With the zodiac $BED$ remaining, the true apparent equinoctial will be changed according to the transposition of pole $O$. And similarly, the motion of the apparent equinox of the intersection $L$ itself will be more rapid around the middle, very slow at the extremes, almost proportional to the libration of the poles already demonstrated. ### REVOLUTIONUM LIB. III.

### On the equal motions of the precession of the equinoxes and the inclination of the zodiac. Chapter VI.

**Every** circular motion appearing diverse, however, is turned in four terms: there is where it appears slow as if in the extremes, and where it is moderate as if in the middle. Since from the end of diminution and the beginning of increase, it passes to the moderate; from the moderate it grows into velocity; again from the swift it tends toward the moderate; thence, what is remaining, it returns from equality to the former slowness. By which it is given to be understood in which part of the circle the place of diversity or anomaly was for the time, by which signs also the restoration of the anomaly itself is perceived. As in a quadripartite circle, let $A$ be the place of highest slowness, $B$ increasing moderateness, $C$ the end of increase and beginning of diminution, $D$ decreasing moderateness. Since therefore, as was recited above, from **Timocharis** to **Ptolemaeus** the appearing motion of the precession of the equinoxes was found to be slower than at other times, and because it appeared equal and uniform for some time, as the observations of **Aristyllus**, **Hipparchus**, **Agrippa**, and **Menelaus** in the middle time show, it argues that the apparent motion of the equinoxes was simply slowest, and in the middle time at the beginning of increase, when the ceasing diminution, joined to the beginning increase, by mutual compensation brought it about that the motion meanwhile seemed uniform. Wherefore the observation of **Timocharis** is to be placed in the last part of the circle under $DA$; the Ptolemaic truly will fall in the first quadrant under $AB$. Again, because in the second interval from **Ptolemaeus** to **Machometus Aratensis** [al-Battani], a swifter motion is found than in the third, it declares that the highest velocity—that is, point $C$—passed in the second interval of time, and the anomaly has already arrived at the third quadrant of the circle under $CD$, and in the third interval until our time the restoration of the anomaly is almost completed, and returns to the beginning of **Timocharis**. For if in 1,819 years from **Timocharis** to us we comprise the whole circuit in the 360 parts in which it is accustomed, we shall have, by the ratio of years, for 432 years a circumference of 85 parts and 30 seconds [s.]; for 741 years, 146 parts and 51 minutes; and in the remaining 645 years, the remaining circumference of 127 parts and 39 minutes. These things we have received by obvious and simple conjecture...

--- Page 160 ---
[[Original page: 69v]]

# NICOLAI COPERNICI

...we received by conjecture, but revolving them with a more exact calculation, insofar as they might more accurately agree with the observations, we found that the motion of the anomaly in 1,819 Egyptian years had already exceeded its completed revolution by 21 degrees and 24 minutes, and the time of the period contains only 1,717 Egyptian years, by which ratio the first segment of the circle is given as 90 parts and 35 minutes. The second, 155 parts and 34 minutes. But the third, under the remaining 544 years, will contain 113 parts and 51 minutes of the circle. These things being so established, the mean motion of the precession of the equinoxes also became clear, and that it is 23 degrees and 57 minutes under the same 1,717 years, in which all diversity is restored to its pristine state. Since in 1,819 years we had an apparent motion of almost 25 degrees and 1 minute. Truly, from **Timocharis** in the 102 years by which 1,717 years are distant from 1,819, it was necessary for the apparent motion to have been about 1 degree and 4 minutes, because it is likely to have been somewhat larger then, as if it had required one degree in a hundred years, when the end of the decrease was not yet attained while it was still decreasing. Accordingly, if we take away one degree and a fifteenth [part] from 25 parts and 1 minute, there will remain what we said: in 1,717 Egyptian years, a mean and equal motion equated then to the diverse and apparent [motion], of 23 degrees and 57 minutes, by which the integral and equal revolution of the precession of the equinoxes arises in 25,816 years, in which time approximately 15 circuits of the anomaly with a 28th part are made. To this ratio also the motion of obliquity accommodates itself, the return of which we said was twice as slow as the precession of the equinoxes. For because **Ptolemaeus** reported the obliquity to be 23 parts, 51 first minutes, and 20 seconds, and that in 400 years before him it had been changed very little by **Aristarchus Samius**, it indicates that it [the obliquity] then stood almost at the limit of maximum obliquity: namely when the precession of the equinoxes was also in its slowest motion. But now also, while the restoration of the same slowness approaches, the inclination of the axis passes not likewise into the maximum, but into the minimum, which in the middle time **Machometus Aratensis**, as was said, found to be 23 parts and 25 minutes. **Arzachel Hispanus**, 190 years after him, 23 parts and 34 minutes; and likewise 230 years later, **Prophatius Iudaeus**, smaller by nearly two minutes. What finally concerns our times, we, from frequent observation during 30 years, have found 23 [OCR error says 24] parts, 28 minutes, and almost two-fifths of one minute, from which **Georgius Purbachius** and **Ioannes de Monteregio** [Regiomontanus], who...

--- Page 161 ---
**BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS**

...of the region, who most recently preceded us, differ very little. Wherein it is again most clearly evident that the change in obliquity from Ptolemaeus to 900 years later was greater than in any other interval of time. Since we now have the cycle of the anomaly of precession as 1,717 years, we shall also have the half-period of the obliquity in that time, and its full restoration in 3,434 years. Wherefore, if we divide the 360 degrees [of a circle] by the number of 3,434 years, or 180 degrees by 1,717, the annual motion of the simple anomaly will come out to be 6 minutes, 17 seconds, 24 thirds, and 9 fourths. These, again, distributed through 365 days, yield a daily motion of 1 second, 2 thirds, and 2 fourths.

Similarly, when the mean precession of the equinoxes is distributed through 1,717 years—and it was 24 degrees and 57 minutes—the annual motion will come out to be 50 seconds, 12 thirds, and 5 fourths; and from this, through 365 days, the daily motion is 8 thirds and 15 fourths.

However, so that the motions themselves may be clearer and more readily available when appropriate, we shall set forth Tables or Canons of them by the continuous and equal addition of the annual motion, always carrying over 60 [units] into the previous minutes or degrees if they exceed [that number]; and we have aggregated them up to the order of 60 years for the sake of convenience. For in sixty-year periods, the same appearance of numbers presents itself, with only the denominations of the parts and minutes transposed, so that what were previously seconds become minutes, and so on for the rest. These may be conveniently taken and collected as equal motions for the proposed years through these short tables within at least 3,600 years by a double entry. It is the same for the number of days.

In the calculation of celestial motions, we shall use Egyptian years everywhere, which alone among civil years are found to be equal. For it is necessary for the measure to agree with the measured, which does not quite happen with the years of the Romans, Greeks, and Persians, into which intercalations are made not in one way, but as it pleased each of those nations. But the Egyptian year brings nothing of ambiguity under its fixed number of 365 days, in which are twelve equal months, which they call in order by their own names: **Thoth, Phaophi, Athyr, Chiach, Tybi, Mechyr, Phamenoth, Pharmuthi, Pachon, Pauni, Epiphi, Mesori**; in which are equally contained 6 blocks of sixty days [360 days], and five remaining days, which they call intercalary. Therefore, for the calculation of equal motions, the Egyptian years are the most suitable, into which any other years are easily reduced by the resolution of days.

**Chapter VII: What the maximum difference is between the equal and apparent precession of the equinoxes.**

[Geometric diagram depicting the relationship between the mean and true equinoxes on the celestial sphere]

The mean motions having been thus set forth, it must now be investigated how great is the maximum difference between the equal and apparent motion of the equinoxes, or the diameter of the small circle through which the motion of the anomaly revolves. For when this is known, it will be easy to discern any other differences of these motions. Therefore, since (as related above) between the first [observation] of **Timocharis** and that of **Ptolemaeus** in the second year of **Antoninus**, there were 432 years: in which time the mean motion is 6 degrees, but the apparent was 4 degrees 20 minutes; the difference between these is 1 degree 40 minutes. The motion of the double anomaly was also 90 degrees 35 minutes. It also seemed that in the middle of this time, or thereabouts, the apparent motion reached the point of maximum slowness, at which it is necessary that it coincide with the mean motion, and that the true and mean equinox were in the same section of the circles.

Therefore, by making a twofold distribution of the motion and time, the differences between the diverse and equal motion will be on both sides nine-tenths of one degree, which the circumferences of the anomalous circle contain on both sides at 45 degrees 17 1/2 minutes. These being so established, let the circumference of the zodiac be **ABC**, the mean equinoctial **DBE**, and let **B** be the mean section of the apparent equinoxes, whether of Aries or Libra, and through its poles **DBE** let **BF** descend...

**BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS**

...however, the poles of **IG** and **HK** themselves often exist outside the circle **BF** as the motion of declination mixes in, as was seen in the hypothesis: but on account of the very small distance, which when it is at its maximum does not exceed the 450th part of a right angle, we use them as if they were right angles to the sense [of observation]; for no error will appear because of it. Therefore, since in triangle **IBG**, angle **IBG** is given as 66 degrees 20 minutes—since the remainder from the right angle **DBA** was 23 degrees 40 minutes, the angle of the mean obliquity of the zodiac—and **BGI** is a right angle, and also that which is under **BIG** is nearly equal to **IBD**: and the side **IB** is 50 minutes: therefore side **BG**, the circumference of the distance between the mean and apparent poles, is given as equal to 20 minutes. Similarly, in triangle **BHK**, the two angles **BHK** and **HBK** are equal to the two **IBG** and **IGB**: and side **BK** is equal to side **BI**, and **BH** will also be equal to **BG**, [namely] 20 minutes.

But since all these things concern very small amounts, inasmuch as they do not reach a degree and a half of the zodiac, in which the subtended straight lines are nearly equal to their circumferences, and a difference is scarcely found in the "thirds" [1/216,000th of a circle], we shall commit no error if we use straight lines instead of arcs. Let the portion of the circle of signs be **ABC**, in which the mean equinox is **B**; with this taken as a pole, let a semicircle **ADC** be described, which cuts the circle of signs at points **A** and **C**... It is proposed from these to find the whole **BFA**. It is manifest, therefore, that double **BF** subtends double the segment **DE**; and as **BF** of 7,107 parts is to **AFB** of 10,000 parts, so the 50 minutes of **BF** are to the 70 minutes of **AFB**. Therefore **AB** is given as one degree and 10 minutes; and so great is the maximum difference between the mean and apparent motion of the equinoxes which we were seeking, and which the maximum deflection of the poles, 24 minutes, follows.

**Chapter VIII: On the particular differences of these motions, and their Canonical exposition.**

[Historiated initial ‘C’]

Since, therefore, **AB** is given as 70 minutes, which circumference seems to differ not at all from a straight line subtended according to length, it will not be difficult to exhibit any other particular differences between the mean and apparent motions, which the Greeks call **Prosthaphaereses**, and more recent [writers] call **Equations**, by the subtraction or addition of which the appearances are reconciled. We shall use the Greek term as more appropriate.

If, therefore, **ED** is three degrees, according to the ratio of **AB** to the subtended **BF**, we shall have the Prosthaphaeresis **EF** as 4 minutes. If it is six degrees, there will be 7 minutes; for nine degrees, 11; and so for the rest. We think the same should be done regarding the change of obliquity, where (as we said) 24 minutes have been found between the maximum and minimum, which are completed under the semicircle of the simple anomaly in 1,717 years; and the mean consistency under the quadrant of the circle will be 12 minutes, where the pole of the small circle of this anomaly will be under an obliquity of 23 degrees 40 minutes. And in this manner, as we have said, we shall extract the remaining parts of the difference almost proportional to the aforesaid, as contained in the following Canon.

Although the apparent motions can be composed in various ways through these demonstrations, that method nevertheless pleased more by which each particular Prosthaphaeresis is taken separately, whereby the calculation of the motions is made easier to understand and more closely agrees with the explanations of the things demonstrated. Therefore, we have written a table of 60 rows, increasing by triads [threes] of the degrees of the circle. For thus it will neither occupy a sprawling breadth, nor seem to have a too-compressed brevity, as we shall do in other similar cases. This will have four columns: the first two of which contain the degrees of both semicircles, which we call the "Common Number," because through the simple number the obliquity of the signs of the circle is taken, and when doubled, it serves the Prosthaphaeresis of the equinoxes, the beginning of which is taken from the start of the increase.

***

--- Page 169 ---
**BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS**

In the third place, the prosthaphaereses of the equinoxes will be placed, corresponding to each three-part [triad], to be added to or subtracted from the mean motion, which we begin from the first star of the head of **Aries** at the vernal equinox: subtractive prosthaphaereses in an anomaly smaller than a semicircle (or in the first column); additive in the second and following semicircle.

In the last place are the minutes called the "differences of the proportions of obliquity," ascending to the sum of sixty. Since for the maximum and minimum excess of obliquity we set 60 for the 24 minutes, we arrange parts of a similar ratio for the ratio of the remaining excesses; and therefore at the beginning and end of the anomaly, we place 60. But where the excess reaches 22 minutes, as in an anomaly of 33 degrees, we place 55 in its stead. Thus for 20 minutes, 50, as in an anomaly of 28 degrees, and in this manner for the rest, as is evident in the subjoined formula.

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK III.

### On the examination and correction of those things set forth
### concerning the precession of the equinoxes. Chapter 9.

Now, since we have assumed by conjecture that the beginning of the increase in the nonuniform motion <note>original: "motu differente"; this refers to the "trepidation" or the varying speed at which the equinoxes appear to move.</note> occurred in the middle period—from the 36th year of the first Calippic period <note>The Calippic period was a 76-year cycle used by Greek astronomers; the 36th year of the first cycle corresponds to roughly 295 BCE.</note> to the second year of Antoninus <note>The second year of the reign of Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius, approximately 139 AD.</note>, from which point we begin the motion of the anomaly—it is necessary for us to test whether we have done this correctly and whether it agrees with the observed facts. Let us recall those three observations of the stars: those of Timocharis, Ptolemy, and Muhammad of Raqqa <note>original: "Machometis Aratei," referring to the 9th-century Arab astronomer Al-Battani.</note>. It is clear that in the first interval there were 432 Egyptian years; in the second, 742 years. The mean motion <term>mean motion|the theoretical uniform movement of a celestial body, ignoring periodic speeds up or slows down</term> in the first period of time was 6°, while the nonuniform change was 4° 20', with the double anomaly <note>Copernicus uses a "double anomaly" in his model to describe the oscillating movement of the equinoxes.</note> being 90° 35', subtracting 1° 40' from the mean motion. In the second interval, the mean motion was 10° 21', and the nonuniform change was 11° 30' <note>original: "XI. s." where "s." stands for semis, or half a degree.</note>; the double anomaly was 155° 34', adding 1° 9' to the mean motion.

Now, let the circumference of the zodiac be $A B C$ as before, and let $B$ be the mean vernal equinox. With the pole taken there, let a small circle <note>original: "orbiculus"</note> $A D C E$ be described with a circumference of 1° 10'. Let the mean motion of $B$ itself be understood to move toward $A$, that is, into the preceding signs <note>original: "in praecedentia"; westward, or against the order of the zodiac signs.</note>, and let $A$ be the western limit, where the nonuniform equinox is at its furthest point ahead, and $C$ the eastern limit, where the nonuniform equinox is at its furthest point behind. From the pole of the zodiac, let the line $D B E$ descend through point $B$, which will divide the small circle $A D C E$ into four parts, since they intersect each other at right angles through the poles. When the motion is in the semicircle $A D C$ toward the following signs <note>original: "ad consequentia"; moving in the order of the zodiac signs.</note>, and in the remaining $C E A$ toward the preceding signs, the midpoint of the slowness of the apparent equinox will be at $D$ because of its resistance to the progress of $B$; however, the greatest velocity will be at $E$, where the motions move together in the same direction. 

Let there also be taken the arcs $F D$ and $D G$ before and after $D$, each being 45° 17' 30'' <note>original: "XLV. scrup. XVII. s."</note>. Let $F$ be the first term of the anomaly (that of Timocharis), $G$ the second (Ptolemy), and $P$ the third (Muhammad of Raqqa). Through these points, let the great circles $F N$, $G M$, and $O P$ descend through the poles of the zodiac, all of which in the par— <note>The sentence cuts off here as it reaches the end of the page.</note>

## What the maximum difference is between the sections of the equinoctial and the zodiac. Chapter 10.

In a similar way, we shall prove that the explanations given regarding the change in the obliquity <note>the angle of tilt</note> of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; the ecliptic, or the sun's apparent path</note> and the equinoctial <note>the celestial equator</note> are correct. For we have, for the second year of Antoninus in the records of Ptolemy <note>approx. 139 AD</note>, the simple anomaly <note>the position in the cycle of change</note> calculated as 21 degrees and a quarter [21° 15']. At that time, the maximum obliquity was found to be 24 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds. From that time to our own observation, approximately 1,387 years have passed, during which the position of the simple anomaly is calculated to be 145 degrees and 24 minutes. At this time, the obliquity is found to be 23 degrees, 28 minutes, and nearly two-fifths of a minute [23° 28' 24'']. Using these values, let the arc *abc* of the zodiac be represented—or a straight line in its place due to its small size—and upon it, let there be a semicircle of the simple anomaly with its pole at *b*, as before. Let *a* be the limit of maximum declination <note>the highest point of tilt</note> and *c* the minimum, the difference of which we are seeking. Therefore, let the arc *ae*

Let the perpendicular lines *eg* and *fk* be dropped to the diameter *abc*. Now, the segment *gk* on the arc of the great circle <note>representing the change in tilt on the celestial sphere</note> is known to be 22 minutes and 56 seconds, based on the difference in obliquity from Ptolemy’s time to ours. Furthermore, the line *gb* is half the chord of twice the arc *ed*—or equal to it—being 932 units, where the diameter *ac* is 2000 units. In the same units, *kb* would be half the chord of twice the arc *df*, which is 973 units. This gives the total length of *gk* as 1,905 units, where *ac* is 2000. From this, it is established that the maximum obliquity between the times of Timocharis <note>a Greek astronomer from the 3rd century BC</note> and Ptolemy was 23 degrees and 52 full minutes, and it is now approaching a minimum of 23 degrees <note>Copernicus is observing that the tilt of the Earth is slowly decreasing toward its minimum value in his cycle</note>.

## On establishing the positions of the uniform motions of the equinoxes and the anomaly. Chapter 11.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'H' featuring a human face mask surrounded by foliate scrolls.</image-desc>
**With** all these matters thus explained, it remains for us to establish the positions of the motions of the vernal equinox <note>the spring equinox</note> itself, which are called "roots" <term>radices: the reference points or starting dates used as a baseline for astronomical tables</term> by some, from which calculations are derived for any proposed time. For this matter, Ptolemy established as the ultimate goal the beginning of the reign of Nabonassar <note>a King of Babylon; his reign began in 747 BCE</note> of the Chaldeans, which among historians falls upon Shalmaneser <note>original: "Salmanassar"</note>, king of the Chaldeans. However, we, following more well-known times, have thought it sufficient to begin from the first Olympiad <note>776 BCE</note>, which is found to have preceded Nabonassar by 28 years, taking our start from the summer solstice <note>the longest day of the year</note>, at which time the Dog Star <term>Canicula: the star Sirius</term> rose for the Greeks and the Olympic Contest <note>the Games</note> was celebrated, as Censorinus and other approved authors have recorded. 

From this point, according to a more exact calculation of times, which is necessary in calculating celestial motions, from the first Olympiad to the noon of the first day of the Greek month Hecatombaeon <note>original: "Ecatonbæonos"</note>, until Nabonassar and the noon of the first day of the month Thoth <note>the first month of the Egyptian calendar</note> according to the Egyptians, there are 27 years and 247 days. From here until the death of Alexander [the Great], there are 424 Egyptian years; and from the death of Alexander until the beginning of the years of Julius Caesar, there are 278 Egyptian years and 118.5 days, calculated to the midnight before the Kalends <note>the first day</note> of January, from which Julius Caesar made the beginning of the year established by him. 

He, as High Priest <term>Pont. Max.: Pontifex Maximus, the head of the Roman state religion</term>, instituted that year in his third consulship and that of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. From this year, thus ordered by Julius Caesar, the others thereafter were called Julian; and from Caesar's fourth consulship until Octavian Augustus, for the Romans there were indeed 18 years, likewise from the Kalends of January, although on the 16th day before the Kalends of February <note>January 17</note>, the son of the divine Julius Caesar, Emperor Augustus, was so named by the Senate and other citizens upon the motion of Munatius Plancus <note>Copernicus writes "Numatij"</note>, in his seventh consulship and that of Marcus Vipsanius [Agrippa]. But the Egyptians, because they had come into the power of the Romans two years earlier, after the [defeat] of Antony and Cleo-

### BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...and the downfall of Cleopatra <note>original: "Cleopatræ occasum"</note>, there are 15 years and 246.5 days, at noon on the first day of the month of Thoth <note>the first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note>, which for the Romans was the third day before the Kalends of September <note>August 30th</note>. Therefore, from Augustus to the years of Christ, starting similarly from January, there are 27 years according to the Roman calendar, but 29 years and 130.5 days according to the Egyptians. From this point to the second year of Antoninus <note>Emperor Antoninus Pius</note>, in which Claudius Ptolemy <note>original: "C. Ptole."</note> recorded the positions of the stars he had observed, there are 138 Roman years and 55 days, which adds 34 days to the Egyptian count. Altogether, from the first Olympiad until this time, there are 913 years and 101 days. During this period, the uniform precession <term>antecessio: the slow westward shift of the equinoxes</term> of the equinoxes is 12 degrees and 44 minutes <term>scrupula prima: 'first small parts,' the standard term for minutes of a degree</term>. The simple anomaly <term>anomalia: the irregularity or variation in the speed of celestial motion</term> is 95 degrees and 44 minutes.

However, in the second year of Antoninus, as has been reported, the vernal equinox <note>the spring equinox</note> preceded the first of the stars in the head of Aries <note>the Ram</note> by 6 degrees and 40 minutes. And since the double anomaly was 42.5 degrees, the difference between the uniform and apparent motion was subtractive <note>meaning it must be taken away from the uniform to find the apparent</note> by 48 minutes. When this is restored to the apparent motion of 6 degrees and 40 minutes, it results in the uniform position of the vernal equinox itself being at 7 degrees and 28 minutes. If we add the 360 degrees of a full circle to this and subtract 12 degrees and 44 minutes from that total, we will have the uniform position of the vernal equinox for the first Olympiad—which began at noon on the first day of the month of Hekatombaion <note>original: "Ecatombæonos"</note> among the Athenians—at 354 degrees and 44 minutes. This means it then followed the first star of Aries by 5 degrees and 16 minutes.

In a similar way, if 95 degrees and 45 minutes are subtracted from 21 degrees and 15 minutes of the simple anomaly, there will remain, for that same start of the Olympiads, the position of the simple anomaly at 285 degrees and 30 minutes. Furthermore, by adding the motions calculated over these time intervals—always discarding 360 degrees whenever the sum exceeds them—we will have the following positions or roots <term>radices: the baseline data or "starting numbers" for astronomical tables</term>:
For **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great</note>: uniform motion 1 degree, 2 minutes; simple anomaly 332 degrees, 52 minutes.
For **Caesar** <note>Julius Caesar</note>: uniform motion 4 degrees, 5 minutes; simple anomaly 2 degrees, 2 minutes.
For the position of **Christ**: uniform motion 5 degrees, 32 minutes; anomaly 6 degrees, 45 minutes.
And thus we shall obtain the roots of the motions for any other chosen starting points in time.

## On the computation of the precession of the vernal equinox and the obliquity. Chapter XII.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or astronomer, in a Renaissance style frame.</image-desc>
Whenever we wish, therefore, to determine the position of the vernal equinox <note>the spring equinox; the point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator from south to north</note>, if the years from our chosen starting point to the given time are unequal—such as the Roman years <note>the Julian calendar years, which vary in length due to leap years</note> that we commonly use—we must convert them into equal or Egyptian years <note>the Egyptian calendar used by astronomers consisted of exactly 365 days, making it much easier to calculate long-term celestial cycles</note>. For we use no other years in the calculation of uniform motions than the Egyptian ones, for the reason we have already stated.

Indeed, we shall distribute the number of years into groups of sixty, insofar as it exceeds sixty. When we enter the tables of motions with these groups of sixty, we will pass over the first value that appears in the motions as if it were a surplus; then, starting from the second place (the degrees), we will take the groups of sixty, if there are any, along with the remaining degrees and minutes <term>scrupula: literally 'small pebbles,' used here for minutes or 1/60th of a degree</term> that follow. Next, we will perform a second entry for the remaining years, and from the first place as they lie, we will take the groups of sixty, degrees, and minutes that occur. We shall do the same for days and for groups of sixty days, when we wish to add uniform motions to them using the tables of days and minutes. However, in this context, the minutes of days might not wrongly be ignored—or even the days themselves—due to the slowness of these motions, since in the daily motion we are dealing only with thirds or seconds of minutes <note>Copernicus means the precession moves so slowly—about 1 degree every 70-100 years—that a single day's movement is too tiny to matter for most calculations</note>.

Therefore, when we have aggregated all these values with their root <note>the "root" is the base value or position at a known historical epoch</note>, adding each to each according to their kind, and having rejected groups of six degrees of sixty <note>original: "sex graduum sexagenis," referring to 360 degrees, a full circle</note> if they exceed that amount, we will have the mean position <term>locum medium: the calculated average position of a celestial body, ignoring periodic irregularities</term> of the vernal equinox for the proposed time, by which it precedes the first star of Aries <note>the constellation of the Ram</note>, or the position of that same star following the equinox. In the same way, we shall also find the anomaly <term>anomalia: the angular distance used to calculate the variation in a cycle</term>.

With the simple anomaly itself, we will find the proportional minutes <term>scrupula proportionum: factors used to adjust the calculation for specific positions in an orbit</term> placed in the last column of the table of differences, which we shall set aside. Then, with the double anomaly, we will find the prosthaphaeresis <term>prosthaphaeresim: from the Greek for 'addition and subtraction'; the value added to or subtracted from the mean motion to find the true position</term> in the third row of the same table—that is, the degrees and minutes by which the true motion differs from the mean. If the double anomaly is less than a semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>, we shall subtract that very prosthaphaeresis from the mean motion. But if it has exceeded a semicircle, having more than 180 degrees, we shall add it.

<summary>Copernicus explains how to use his astronomical tables to calculate the precession of the equinoxes, favoring the consistent Egyptian calendar over the Roman one for mathematical accuracy. He details the process of adding "mean motions" to historical "roots" and applying a correction factor known as the prosthaphaeresis.</summary>

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS Book III.

[...add] itself to the mean motion, and whatever is thus collected or remains will contain the true and apparent precession of the vernal equinox <note>the spring equinox; the point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator from south to north</note>, or how far the first star of Aries was then distant from that same vernal equinox. But if you seek the position of any other star, add the number assigned to it in the description of the stars <note>the star catalog</note>.

Since practical matters usually become clearer with examples, let it be our objective to find, for the 16th day before the Kalends of May in the year of Christ 1525 <note>April 16, 1525</note>, the true position of the vernal equinox along with the obliquity <note>the tilt</note> of the zodiac, and how far Spica Virginis <note>the brightest star in the constellation Virgo</note> is distant from that same equinox.

It is clear, therefore, that in 1,524 Roman years <note>Julian years</note> and 106 days from the beginning of the years of Christ to this time, 381 leap days have been intercalated <note>inserted into the calendar</note>. These make, in equal years <note>the 365-day Egyptian years used for calculation</note>, 1,525 years and 122 days. These consist of twenty-five groups of sixty years <note>25 x 60 = 1500</note> and 25 years, and two groups of sixty days <note>2 x 60 = 120</note> along with two days.

In the table of mean motion, twenty-five groups of sixty years correspond to 20 degrees, 55 <term>scrupula prima: "first minutes," or 1/60th of a degree</term>, and 2 <term>scrupula secunda: "second minutes," or 1/3600th of a degree</term>. For the 25 years, there are 20 minutes and 55 seconds. For the two groups of sixty days, there are 16 seconds; the remaining two days are in <term>thirds: 1/216,000th of a degree</term>. All these, combined with the root <note>original: "radice"; the starting value for the era of Christ</note> which was 5 degrees and 32 minutes, total 26 degrees and 48 minutes: the mean precession of the vernal equinox.

Similarly, for the motion of the simple anomaly <note>the irregular variation in the Earth's wobble</note>, twenty-five groups of sixty years have two groups of sixty degrees plus 37 degrees, 15 minutes, and 3 seconds. In 25 years, there are 2 degrees, 37 minutes, and 15 seconds. In two groups of sixty days, 2 minutes and 4 seconds; and in the two days, 2 seconds. These also, with the root which is 6 degrees and 45 minutes, make 2 groups of sixty, 46 degrees, and 40 minutes of simple anomaly. Using this value in the table of differences, I will save the proportional minutes found in the last column for the purpose of finding the obliquity; in this instance, only one is found.

Then, with the double anomaly <note>calculated as twice the simple anomaly</note>, which has 5 groups of sixty, 34 degrees, and 20 minutes, I find the <term>prosthaphaeresis: a correction value added or subtracted to find the "true" position from the "mean" position</term> to be 32 minutes, which is additive because the anomaly is greater than a semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>. When this is added to the mean motion, the true and apparent precession of the vernal equinox results as 27 degrees and 21 minutes. Finally, if I add to this the 170 degrees by which Spica Virginis is distant from the first star of Aries, I will have its position from the vernal equinox, in order of the signs, at 17 degrees [of Libra] <note>Spica is traditionally located at the beginning of the sign of Libra</note>.

and 21 <term>minutes: "scrupula," the 60th part of a degree</term> of Libra, where it was found at nearly the time of our observation.
The tilt of the zodiac and the declinations <note>the angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator</note> follow a ratio such that when the proportional minutes are 60, the excesses are recorded in the Table of Declinations; the differences between the maximum and minimum tilt are added in full to their respective parts of the declinations. In this specific case, however, a single unit of those minutes adds only 24 seconds to the tilt. Therefore, the declinations of the parts of the zodiac circle placed in the Table remain as they are for this present time, because we are now approaching the minimum tilt, whereas at other times the change is more evident. For example, if the simple anomaly <note>the angular distance used to track the cycle of the Earth's wobbling axis</note> were 99 degrees, as it was in the Egyptian year 880 of Christ <note>approximately 880 AD, the era of the astronomer Al-Battani</note>, the proportional minutes calculated through it are 25. But just as 60 minutes relates to the 24 minutes of the difference between maximum and minimum tilt, so 25 relates to 10. When these 10 are added to 28 [minutes], the resulting tilt existing for that time is 23 degrees and 38 minutes. If then I also wished to know the declination of some part of the zodiac—for instance, the third degree of Taurus, which is 33 degrees from the equinox—I find in the Table 12 degrees and 32 minutes, with an excess of 12 minutes. Now, as 60 is to 25, so 12 is to 5. These 5 minutes, added to the parts of the declination, make 12 degrees and 37 minutes for the 33 degrees of the zodiac. In the same way, we can calculate the angles of the intersection of the zodiac and the equator, as well as the right ascensions <note>the position of a star measured eastward along the celestial equator</note>, unless one prefers to calculate them through the logic of spherical triangles—except that one must always add to the former and subtract from the latter, so that all values may come out more precisely for the specific time.

<meta>This page transitions from the specific calculation of stellar declinations to a foundational discussion on the length of the year.
