### BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

...the temporal year must be distinguished from the sidereal year. Indeed, we call the "natural" or "temporal" year that which regulates the four annual seasons for us. The "sidereal" year, however, is that which returns to one of the fixed stars. That the natural year—which they also call the *turning year* <note>original: "annus vertens"</note>—is unequal, is shown by the many observations of the ancients. For Callippus, Aristarchus of Samos, and Archimedes of Syracuse defined it as containing one-quarter of a day beyond 365 whole days, taking the start of the year from the summer solstice in the Athenian manner.

But Claudius Ptolemy, noticing that the apprehension of the solstices is difficult and precise <note>original: "scrupulosam," meaning requiring extreme care</note>, did not trust their observations enough. Instead, he turned to Hipparchus, who left behind records not only of solar solstices but also of equinoxes observed in Rhodes, and reported that the year lacks a small amount of that quarter-day. Later, Ptolemy determined this deficit to be the 1/300th part of a day, in this manner:

He takes the Autumn equinox observed with great accuracy by Hipparchus at Alexandria in the 177th year after the death of Alexander the Great, on the third intercalary day according to the Egyptians, at midnight, which was followed by the fourth intercalary day. Then Ptolemy joins this with the same equinox observed by himself at Alexandria in the third year of Antoninus, which was the 464th year from the death of Alexander, on the ninth day of the Egyptian month Athyr, nearly one hour after sunrise. Therefore, between this observation and that of Hipparchus, there were 285 Egyptian years, 70 days, 7 hours, and one-fifth of an hour, whereas there should have been 71 days and six hours if the turning year had been a full quarter-day beyond the whole days. Thus, in 285 years, it fell short by one day minus a twentieth part of a day. From this, it follows that in 300 years, a whole day is lost.

He also takes a similar estimate from the Vernal equinox. For he remembers that it was noted by Hipparchus in the 178th year of Alexander, on the 27th day of Mechir, the sixth Egyptian month, at sunrise; he himself found it in the 463rd year on the seventh day of the month Pachon, the ninth month according to the Egyptians, one hour and a little more after noon. Likewise, in 285 years, one day was missing minus a twentieth part of a day. Aided by these indications, Ptolemy defined the turning year as 365 days, 14 <term>minutes: "scrupula prima," 1/60th of a day</term>, and 48 <term>seconds: "scrupula secunda," 1/60th of a minute</term>. After these things, Muhammad <note>the astronomer Al-Battani, c. 858–929 AD</note> in Raqqa, Syria...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the length of the solar year, specifically moving from the observations of the ancient Greeks like Ptolemy and Hipparchus to the medieval Islamic astronomer Al-Battani (referred to as Machometus Aratensis) and Copernicus's own contemporary observations in Frombork.</meta>

# NICOLAI COPERNICI

...With no less diligence, in the 1206th year after the death of Alexander, he <note>Referring to Al-Battani, also known as Albategnius, a major 9th-century Arab astronomer</note> observed the Autumn equinox and found that it occurred after the seventh day of the month Pachon, during the following night, at approximately seven and two-fifths hours—that is, four and three-fifths hours before the light of the eighth day. Therefore, comparing this observation of his to that made by Ptolemy in the third year of Antoninus, one hour after sunrise at Alexandria (which is ten degrees <note>original: "partibus"</note> west of Raqqa <note>original: "Arata," Al-Battani's base of observation in modern Syria</note>), he adjusted that same observation to his own meridian at Raqqa, where it ought to have been one hour and two-thirds after sunrise.

Thus, in an interval of 743 equal years, there were 178 extra days, 17 hours, and three-fifths [of an hour], instead of the 185 days and three-quarters <note>original: "dodrantem"</note> that would have accumulated from the addition of the quarter-days. Since there was a deficit of seven days and two-fifths of an hour, it appeared that the 106th part of a day was missing from the quarter-day. Taking the 743rd part of those seven days and two-fifths of an hour—which amounts to 13 <term>minutes of time</term> <note>original: "scrupuli horarij," literally "hourly scruples"</note> and 36 seconds—he subtracted it from the quarter-day and announced that the natural year contains 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes <note>original: "scrup. prima"</note>, and 24 seconds.

We also observed the Autumn equinox in Frombork <note>original: "Fruëburgo," the town in Poland where Copernicus lived and worked</note> in the year of Christ’s birth 1515, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October [September 14]. This was 1,840 Egyptian years after the death of Alexander, on the sixth day of the month Phaophi, half an hour after sunrise. But since Raqqa <note>original: "Areca"</note> is further east than our region by about 25 degrees—which equals two hours minus one-third of an hour—the time between our observation and that of Al-Battani <note>original: "Machometi Aratensis"</note> was 633 Egyptian years, plus 153 days, 6 hours, and three-quarters, instead of 158 days and 6 hours.

Indeed, from that Alexandrian observation of Ptolemy to the same place and time of our own observation, there are 1,376 Egyptian years, 332 days, and half an hour; for we differ from Alexandria by about one hour. Thus, from the time of Al-Battani to ours, in 633 years, five days minus one hour and a quarter would have been lost—or one day for every 128 years. From Ptolemy's time, however, in 1,376 years, nearly 12 days were lost—or one day every 115 years. This proves once again that the length of the year is unequal in both instances.

We have also taken the spring equinox which occurred in the year after the birth of Christ 1516, four hours and one-third [of an hour] after midnight on the fifth day before the Ides of March [March 11]. From that spring equinox of **Ptolemaeus** (taking into account the comparison of the meridian of Alexandria to ours), there are 1,376 Egyptian years, 332 days, 16 hours and one-third, in which it also appears that the distances of the spring and autumn equinoxes are unequal. It is of such great importance that the solar year, taken in this manner, should exist as uniform. For as much as in the autumnal equinoxes between **Ptolemaeus** and us (as has been shown) a hundred and fifteenth part of a day-quadrant was lacking according to the uniform distribution of years, this does not agree with the equinox of **Machometus Aratensis** [Al-Battani] by half a day; nor does that which is from **Machometus Aratensis** to us (where a hundred and twenty-eighth part of a day ought to be lacking from the fourth [quadrant]) harmonize with **Ptolemaeus**, but the number precedes his observed equinox by more than a whole day, and that of **Hipparchus** by more than two days. Similarly, the calculation of **Machometus Aratensis** taken from **Ptolemaeus** transcends the Hipparchian equinox by two days. 

Therefore, the equality of the solar year is more correctly taken from the sphere of the non-wandering stars [fixed stars], which **Thebites** son of **Chora** [Thabit ibn Qurra] first discovered, and [found] its magnitude to be 365 days, 15 first minutes, and 24 seconds—which are 6 hours, 9 first minutes, and approximately 12 seconds—taking the likely argument that in the encounter of equinoxes and solstices the year would seem longer in a slower [motion] than in a faster one, and that by a certain proportion. This could not happen unless there were equality in comparison to the sphere of the fixed stars. Wherefore **Ptolemaeus** is not to be heard in this part, who thought it absurd and irrelevant to measure the annual equality of the Sun against some restitution of the fixed stars, and that it was no more fitting than if someone were to do this from **Jupiter** or **Saturn**. Thus, the cause is at hand why the temporary year itself was longer before **Ptolemaeus**, because after him it was made shorter by a manifold difference. But an error can also occur regarding the *asteroterida* [sidereal] or sidereal year, yet in a small degree, and far less than that which we have already explained; and this is because that same apparent motion of the center of the earth around the Sun also exists as unequal by another double diversity.

Of which...

### PAGE 182
**NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**

Of which differences, the first and simple one has an annual restitution; the other, which varies the first by shifting it, is perceived over a long tract of time. Wherefore the ratio of annual equality is neither simple nor easy to know. For if anyone wished to take it simply according to a certain known distance of some star having a position (which can be done by use of the Astrolabe by means of the Moon, as we explained concerning the **Basiliscus of Leo** [Regulus]), he will not entirely avoid error, unless at that time the Sun, on account of the motion of the earth, either had no *prosthaphaeresis* [correction/equation] then, or obtained a similar and equal one at both boundaries. Unless this should happen, and there were some difference according to their inequality, a uniform circuit will certainly not seem to have occurred in equal times. But if in both boundaries the total diversity were deducted, or applied according to the ratio, the work will be perfect. 

Furthermore, the apprehension of the diversity itself requires knowledge of the preceding mean motion, which we seek for that reason. Nevertheless, so that we may at last come to the resolution of this knot, we find four causes in all for the unequal appearance. The first is the inequality of the prevention [precession] of the equinoxes which we have set forth. The second is that by which the Sun seems to intercept unequal circumferences of the zodiac, which is nearly annual. The third, which also varies this one, and which we shall call the second diversity. The fourth remains, which changes the highest and lowest apsides of the center of the earth, as will appear below. Of all these, only the second was known to **Ptolemaeus**, which alone could not have produced the annual inequality, but being involved with the others, it does so more [significantly]. For demonstrating the difference between the equality and the solar appearance, the most exact ratio of the year does not seem necessary, but it is enough if we should take for the magnitude of the year 365 days with a quadrant in the demonstration, in which that motion of the first diversity is completed. Since that which is so little distant from the whole circle, being subsumed in a smaller magnitude, vanishes entirely. But for the sake of the excellence of order and the ease of teaching, we here set forth the uniform motions of the annual revolution of the center of the earth, which we shall then establish with the differences of equality and appearance through necessary demonstrations.

Concerning the uniform...

#### On the uniform and mean motions of the revolutions of the center of the earth. Chapter XIV.

We have found the magnitude of the year and its equality, which **Thebith Benchora** [Thabit ibn Qurra] produced, to be greater by only one second minute and 10 thirds; so that it is 365 days, 15 first minutes, 24 seconds, and 10 thirds—which are 6 equal hours, 9 first minutes, and 40 seconds—and let its certain equality be manifest toward the sphere of the non-wandering stars. Therefore, when we have multiplied the 360 degrees of one circle by 365 days, and divided the product by 365 days, 15 first minutes, 24 seconds, and 10 thirds, we shall have the motion of one Egyptian year in five sixties of degrees [300°], 59 degrees, 44 first minutes, 49 seconds, 7 thirds, and 4 fourths. And the motion of sixty similar years, having rejected the whole circles, is 5 sixties of degrees, 44 degrees, 49 first minutes, 7 seconds, and 4 thirds. Again, if we divide the annual motion by 365 days, we shall have a daily motion of 59 first minutes, 8 seconds, 11 thirds, and 22 fourths. 

If we add to these the mean and uniform precession of the equinoxes, we shall compose also the uniform motion in temporary [tropical] years: the annual [motion] being 5 sixties [300°], 59 degrees, 45 minutes, 39 seconds, 19 thirds, and 9 fourths; and the daily motion 59 first minutes, 8 seconds, 19 thirds, and 37 fourths. And by that reasoning we can call that motion of the Sun (to use a common word) the "simple uniform" [sidereal], and this one the "composite uniform" [tropical], which we shall also set forth in tables in the same manner as we did concerning the precession of the equinoxes. To these is added the uniform motion of the solar anomaly, concerning which [we shall speak] later.

#### Preliminary theorems for demonstrating the inequality of the apparent solar motion. Chapter XV.

But for the better grasping of the apparent inequality of the Sun, we shall demonstrate yet more clearly that, with the Sun holding the center of the world around which the earth is rotated as if it were the center—if it were, as we have said, that the distance between the Sun and the earth cannot be perceived in comparison to the immensity of the sphere of the fixed stars—the Sun will be seen to move uniformly toward any chosen sign or star of the same sphere. 

For let there be a greatest circle in the world AB in the plane of the zodiac, its center C, in which the Sun stands; and according to the distance of the Sun and the earth CD, toward which the height of the world is immense, let the circle DE be described in the same surface of the zodiac, in which the annual revolution of the center of the earth is placed. I say that toward any sign or star assumed in the circle AB, the Sun will be seen to move uniformly. Let it be assumed, and let it be A, to which the sight of the Sun from the earth (which is at D) is extended as ACD. Let the earth also be moved however much through the circumference DE, and from E, the boundary of the earth, let AE and BE be drawn. Therefore the Sun will now be seen from E in the sign B; and since AC is immense compared to CD, or to its equal CE, AB will also be immense compared to the same CE. 

For let any point F be taken in AC, and let EF be connected. Since, therefore, from the boundaries of the base CE, two straight lines fall outside the triangle EFC to point A, by the converse of the 21st [proposition] of the first book of **Euclid’s Elements**, the angle FAE will be smaller than the angle EFC. Wherefore the straight lines extended into immensity finally comprehend the acute angle CAE, so much so that it can no longer be discerned; and it is this [angle] by which angle BCA is greater than angle AEC, which also on account of such a small difference seem equal, and the lines AC and AE [seem] parallel. And the Sun [appears] toward any sign of the sphere of the stars...

### Scholarly Notes on the Translation:
*   **Machometus Aratensis:** Refers to the 9th-century Arab astronomer Al-Battani, born in Harran (hence "Aratensis").
*   **Thebites Chorae filius:** Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century mathematician/astronomer.
*   **Sexagenis:** Copernicus uses a sexagesimal (base-60) system for his tables. The first column of the motion tables refers to units of 60 degrees.
*   **Prosthaphaeresis:** A technical term in Ptolemaic and Copernican astronomy referring to the "equation of center"—the correction added to or subtracted from the mean motion to find the true position.
*   **Asteroterida:** A Greek-derived term used by Copernicus for the "sidereal" year (measured against the stars).
*   **Anomaly:** The angular distance of a planet (or the Earth, in Copernicus's system) from its apogee or perihelion.

Having established that the solar year is best measured against the fixed stars, he now introduces the specific variables that make the Sun's movement appear irregular from Earth.</meta>

# BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

Of these differences, the first and simple one has an annual restoration; the other, which varies the first by changing it, is perceived over a long stretch of time. Because of this, the calculation of the annual uniformity is neither simple nor easy to understand. For if anyone simply wishes to determine it relative to the known distance of a certain star having a known position (which can be done by using an astrolabe through the mediation of the Moon, as we explained regarding **Regulus** <note>original: "Basiliscum Leonis"</note> in Leo), he will not entirely avoid error, unless the Sun—on account of the motion of the earth—then either has no correction <term>prosthaphaeresis <note>original: "prosthaphaeresim"; the difference between the mean/average motion and the true/apparent motion</note></term>, or happens to have a similar and equal correction at both ends of the observation. Unless this happens, and if there is any difference due to their inequality, a uniform circuit will certainly not seem to have occurred in equal times. But if at both ends the total diversity is deducted or applied according to the ratio, the work will be perfect. Furthermore, the understanding of this diversity itself requires prior knowledge of the mean motion, which is what we are seeking for this reason.

Nevertheless, so that we may eventually come to the untying of this knot, we have found four causes in total for the unequal appearance. The first is the inequality of the precession <term>prevention <note>original: "praeventionis"; referring to the precession of the equinoxes, which Copernicus views as a result of the Earth's wobbling axis</note></term> of the equinoxes, which we have explained. The second is that by which the Sun seems to cross unequal arcs of the zodiac <term>zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"</note></term>, which is an almost annual occurrence. The third, which even varies this second cause, we shall call the "second diversity." The fourth remains, which changes the highest and lowest apsides <term>apsides <note>original: "absides"; the points in an orbit where a celestial body is closest to or farthest from the center of its motion</note></term> of the Earth’s center, as will appear below. 

Of all these, only the second was known to **Ptolemy**; that alone could not have produced the annual inequality, but when entangled with the others, it does so more significantly. To demonstrate the difference between the uniform and apparent solar motion, an extremely exact calculation of the year does not seem necessary; it is enough if we take 365 days and a quarter for the length of the year in the demonstration, in which that motion of the first diversity is completed. Since what is so slightly distant from the whole circle, when subsumed into a smaller magnitude, vanishes entirely. But for the sake of good order and ease of instruction, we here place first the uniform motions of the annual revolution of the center of the Earth, which we shall then establish with the differences of uniformity and appearance through necessary demonstrations.

ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.

### On the uniform and mean motions of the revolutions of the Earth's center. Chapter 14.

**A**lthough Thabit ibn Qurra <note>original: "Thebith Benchorae"; a 9th-century Harranian astronomer and mathematician</note> reported the magnitude of the year and its uniformity, we have found it to be greater by only one second and 10 thirds, so that it consists of 365 days, 15 minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum primorum"; here used for fractions of a day</note>, 24 seconds, and 10 thirds. This equals 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 40 seconds. Its certain uniformity in relation to the sphere of the fixed stars is thus established. Therefore, when we multiply the 360 degrees of a circle by the 365 days of an Egyptian year <term>Egyptian year <note>A year of exactly 365 days, used by ancient astronomers for ease of calculation</note></term> and divide the product by the length of the year—365 days, 15 minutes, 24 seconds, and 10 thirds—we will find the motion of one Egyptian year to be five units of sixty degrees <term>sexagenis <note>units of sixty in a base-60 system; 5 × 60 = 300 degrees</note></term>, plus 59 degrees, 44 minutes, 49 seconds, 7 thirds, and 4 fourths. The motion for sixty similar years, after discarding the full circles, is five units of sixty degrees, 44 degrees, 49 minutes, 7 seconds, and 4 thirds. 

Furthermore, if we divide the annual motion by 365 days, we will have a daily motion of 59 minutes, 8 seconds, 11 thirds, and 22 fourths. But if we add the mean and uniform precession of the equinoxes to these values, we will also calculate the uniform motion in tropical years <note>original: "annis temporariis"; years measured from equinox to equinox</note>. The annual motion for this is five units of sixty degrees, 59 degrees, 45 minutes, 39 seconds, 19 thirds, and 9 fourths; the daily motion is 59 minutes, 8 seconds, 19 thirds, and 37 fourths. 

For that reason, we may call that first motion of the Sun "simple uniform" (to use common terminology), and this latter one "composite uniform." We will set these out in tables, just as we did for the precession of the equinoxes. To these is added the uniform motion of the Sun's <term>anomaly <note>original: "anomaliae"; the angular distance of a planet from its perihelion, used here to calculate the Earth's varying distance from the Sun</note></term>, which we will discuss later.

NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

### Preliminary Theorems for Demonstrating the Inequality of the Apparent Solar Motion. Chapter 15.

[[image: Geometric diagram showing the Earth's annual revolution. A central circle represents the Earth's orbit with center C and points D, E labeled. A larger arc AB represents the stellar sphere. Lines connect points A, B, C, D, E, F.]]

**T**o more clearly understand the apparent variation in the Sun's speed <note>original: "inaequalitatem" <term>inequality: in Renaissance astronomy, this refers to the non-uniform speed or "irregularity" of a celestial body's motion as seen from Earth.</term></note>, we will demonstrate even more plainly that—with the Sun occupying the center of the universe and the Earth revolving around it as its center—if the distance between the Sun and the Earth is considered negligible compared to the vastness of the sphere of fixed stars, the Sun will appear to move uniformly relative to any chosen zodiac sign or star in that sphere.

For let there be a great circle in the universe, AB, in the plane of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi" — the "sign-bearer" or zodiac belt.</note> with its center at C, where the Sun is located. According to the distance between the Sun and the Earth, CD—relative to which the height of the universe is immense <note>original: "immensitatem"</note>—let a circle DE be described in that same plane of the zodiac, representing the annual revolution of the center of the Earth. I say that relative to any chosen sign or star in circle AB, the Sun will appear to move uniformly. 

Let a point be chosen at A, toward which the view of the Sun from the Earth (located at D) is directed along the line ACD. Now, let the Earth move in any way along the circumference DE to a point E, and from the Earth’s position at E, let lines AE and BE be drawn. The Sun will now appear from E to be at the sign B. Since the distance AC is immense compared to CD (or its equal, CE), the distance AB will also be immense compared to CE. Let any point F be taken on AC, and connect EF. Since two straight lines are drawn from the ends of the base CE falling outside the triangle EFC to point A, then by the converse of the 21st theorem of the first book of Euclid's *Elements* <note>Euclid’s Proposition I.21 concerns the properties of triangles. Copernicus uses it here to show that as the distance to the stars (AC) becomes huge, the angle of parallax (the change in perspective) becomes so small it's invisible.</note>, the angle FAE will be smaller than angle EFC. 

Therefore, straight lines extended to such an immense distance will eventually enclose an acute angle CAE so small that it can no longer be perceived. This angle is the difference by which angle BCA is greater than angle AEC; because this difference is so slight, they appear equal, and the lines AC and AE appear parallel. Thus, the Sun toward any sign of the sphere of stars...

<summary>Copernicus provides a geometric proof to explain why the Sun appears to move through the zodiac at a steady rate despite the Earth's own movement, arguing that the stars are so unimaginably distant that the Earth's orbit is effectively a single point by comparison.</summary>
<keywords>heliocentrism, solar inequality, geometry, Euclid's Elements, stellar parallax, zodiac, annual revolution</keywords>

[[original page: 85]]

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.

[...that the centers of the] stars move uniformly, which was to be demonstrated. Moreover, its inequality is demonstrated because the motion of the center and the annual revolution of the Earth is not entirely about the center of the Sun. This can surely be understood in two ways: either by an eccentric circle (that is, one whose center is not the Sun’s), or by an epicycle on a homocentric [circle]. For it is declared by an eccentric in this manner: Let there be an eccentric **ABCD** in the plane of the zodiacal circle [*signifer orbis*], whose center **E** is at a not very small distance from the center of the Sun or of the world, which [center] is **F**; let its diameter through both centers be **AEFD** [abbrev: *utrunque centrum*], and let the apogee be at **A** (which is called the highest apsis [*summa absis*] by the Latins), the place furthest from the center of the world, while **D** is the perigee, which is the nearest and lowest apsis [*infima absis*]. Therefore, since the Earth is carried uniformly in its orbit **ABCD** about center **E**, as has already been said, the motion will appear diverse at **F**. For if equal arcs **AB** and **CD** are taken, and straight lines **BE, CE, BF, CF** are drawn: the angles **AEB** and **CED** will indeed be equal, subtending equal arcs about center **E**. However, the angle **CFD**, which is observed, is greater than angle **CED**, being an exterior angle to the interior; therefore it is also greater than angle **AEB**, which is equal to **CED**. But even the exterior angle **AEB** is greater than the interior angle **AFB**; much more so, then, is angle **CFD** greater than **AFB**. Yet both [motions] produced an equal time on account of the equal arcs **AB** and **CD**. Therefore, the motion will appear uniform about **E**, but unequal about **F**. The same thing may be seen even more simply, because [arc **AB**] is further from the center at **F** than **CD**. For by the seventh [proposition] of the third [book] of Euclid’s *Elements*, the lines by which **AF, BF** are bounded are longer than **CF, DF**, and as is demonstrated in optics, equal magnitudes which are nearer appear larger than those more remote. Thus it is manifest what is proposed concerning the eccentric. And the demonstration is precisely the same if the Earth were at rest at **F** and the Sun moved in the circuit **ABC**, as in Ptolemy and others. The same will also be declared by an epicycle on a homocentric. Let **BCD** be the homocentric, **E** the center of the world in which the Sun also is, and in the same plane let **A** be the center of the epicycle **FG**, and let the straight line **CEAF** be drawn through both centers; let the apogee of the epicycle be **F** and the perigee **I**. It is clear, therefore, that there is equality [y] at **A**...

[[image: An eccentric circle diagram with Earth's orbit and Sun at F.]]

***

--- Page 192 ---
[[original page: unnumbered]]

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...but the inequality of the appearance is in the epicycle **FG**. Since if **A** is moved toward the parts of **B** (that is, in consequence [*in consequentia*]), and the center of the Earth from apogee **F** [is moved] in precedence [*in praecedentia*], it will appear to move more at **B** in the perigee (which is **I**), because the two motions of **A** and **I** were in the same direction; but at the apogee (which is **F**), **B** itself will seem slower, inasmuch as it is moved only by the prevailing motion out of two contrary [motions]; and when the Earth is situated at **G**, it will precede the uniform motion, but at **K** it will follow, and in both cases according to the arc **AG** and **AK**, by which, therefore, the Sun will also be seen to move in different ways.

Whatever is produced by an epicycle can happen in the same way by an eccentric, which the transit of the star in the epicycle describes [as] equal to the homocentric and in the same plane, the center of which eccentric is distant from the center of the homocentric by the magnitude of the semidiameter of the epicycle. This also happens in three ways. For if the epicycle on the homocentric and the star in the epicycle make equal revolutions, but with motions opposing each other, the motion of the star will designate a fixed eccentric, inasmuch as its apogee and perigee occupy immutable seats. Just as if **ABC** were the homocentric, **D** the center of the world, **ADC** the diameter, and let us suppose that when the epicycle was at **A**, the star was in the apogee of the epicycle, which is **G**, and the half of its diameter is in the straight line **DAG**. Let arc **AB** of the homocentric be taken from center **B**, and with a distance equal to **AG**, let epicycle **EF** be described, and let **DB** and **EB** be extended in a straight line; and let arc **EF** be taken in the contrary direction and similar to **AB**, and let the star or Earth be at **F**, and let **BF** be joined; let segment **DK** be taken on line **AD** equal to **BF**. Since, therefore, the angles **EBF** and **BDA** are equal, and for that reason **BF** and **DK** are parallel and equal: if straight lines are joined to equal and parallel straight lines, they are also parallel and equal, by the 34th [proposition] of the first [book] of Euclid. And since **DK, AG** are assumed...

[[image: Diagrams of epicycles and eccentrics.]]

***

--- Page 193 ---
[[original page: 86]]

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.

...assumed equal, let the common [part] **AK** be added; **GAK** will be equal to **AKD**, and therefore also equal to **KF**. Therefore, with center **K** and distance **KAG**, the described circle will pass through **F**, which indeed **F** itself has described by the composite motion of **AB** and **EF** [as] an eccentric equal to the homocentric, and for that reason also fixed. For when the epicycle makes equal revolutions with the homocentric, it is necessary that the apsides of the eccentric so described remain in the same place. 

But if the center of the epicycle and the circumference make unequal revolutions, the motion of the star will no longer designate a fixed eccentric, but one whose center and apsides are carried in precedence or consequence, according as the motion of the star was swifter or slower than the center of its epicycle. Just as if [angle] **EBF** were greater than angle **BDA**, and let [an angle] equal to it be established under **BDM**; it will likewise be demonstrated that in line **DM**, if **DL** is taken equal to **BF**, and with center **L** and distance **LMN** equal to **AD**, the described circle will pass through the star **F**. By this it becomes manifest that arc **NF** is described by the composite motion of the star of an eccentric circle, whose apogee has migrated in the meantime from sign **G** into precedence through arc **GN**. Conversely, if the motion of the star in the epicycle were slower, then the center of the eccentric will follow in consequence, and in the direction in which the center of the epicycle is carried; for instance, if angle **EFB** were less than **BDA**, and [an angle] equal to it [were] under **BDM**, it is manifest that what we have said occurs. 

From all these things, it is clear that the same inequality of appearance is always produced, whether by an epicycle on a homocentric or by an eccentric circle equal to the homocentric, and they differ in no way from each other, provided that the distance of the centers is equal to that which is from the center of the epicycle. Therefore, which of these exists in the heavens is not easy to discern. Ptolemy indeed, where he understood simple inequality and fixed and immutable seats of the apsides (as he thought in the case of the Sun), considered the ratio of the eccentricities [*eccentrotetis*] to suffice. But for the Moon and the other five wandering stars [planets] with double or multiple differences, he accommodated eccentre-epicycles [*eccentrepicyclos*].

***

--- Page 194 ---
[[original page: unnumbered]]

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

From these things, it is also easily demonstrated that the greatest difference between uniform and apparent motion is seen then, when the star appears in the middle position between the highest and lowest apsis, according to the mode of the eccentric; but according to the epicycle, in its point of contact, as in Ptolemy. 

By the eccentric in this manner: Let **ABCD** be [the circle] about center **E**, the diameter **ABC** through the Sun **F** outside the center. Let line **BFD** be drawn at right angles through **F**, and let **BE, ED** be connected. Let the apogee be **A**, the perigee **C**, from which **B [and] D** are the mean appearances. It is manifest that the exterior angle **AEB** encompasses the uniform motion, while the interior **EFB** the apparent, and their difference is angle **EBF**. I say that no angle greater than either of these angles **BD** can be established upon the line **EF** in the circuit. For if points **G** and **H** are taken before and after **B**, let **GD, GE, GF** be joined; likewise **HE, HF, HD**. Since, therefore, **FG**, which is nearer the center, is longer than **DF**, the angle **GDF** will be greater than **DGF**. But those under **EDG** and **EGD** are equal, the equal sides **EG** and **ED** descending to the base. Therefore, angle **EDB**, equal to **EBF**, is greater than angle **EGF**. Similarly, **DF** is longer than **FH**, and angle **FHD** is greater than **FDH**; but the whole **EHD** is equal to the whole **EDH**, for **EH** and **ED** are equal. Therefore the remainder **EDF**, equal to **EBF**, is greater than the remainder **EHF**. Nowhere, therefore, than at points **B** and **D** above the line **EF**, is a greater angle established. Thus the greatest difference of uniformity and appearance consists in the middle position between the apogee and perigee.

## On the Apparent Inequality of the Sun. Chapter XVI.

These things have indeed been demonstrated in general, which can be accommodated not only to solar appearances but also to the inequality of other stars. Now we shall treat those things which are proper to the Sun and the Earth, and first those which we have received from Ptolemy and other ancients, then those which a more recent age and experience have taught us. Ptolemy found that from...

***

--- Page 195 ---
[[original page: 87]]

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.

...from the Vernal equinox to the solstice, 94 ½ days are encompassed; from the solstice to the Autumnal equinox, 92 ½ days. Therefore, according to the ratio of time, the mean and uniform motion in the first interval was 93 degrees 9 minutes [*scrupula*]. In the second, 91 degrees 11 minutes. Let the circle of the year divided in this way be **ABCD**, with center **E**. Let **AB** be taken for the first space of time, 93 degrees 9 minutes; **BC** for the second, 91 degrees 11 minutes. And from **A** let the Vernal equinox be viewed; from **B** the Summer solstice [*estiua conuersio*]; from **C** the Autumnal equinox; and the remainder from **D**, the Winter Solstice [*Bruma*]. Let **AC** and **BD** be connected, which cut each other at right angles at **F**, where we place the Sun. 

Since, therefore, arc **ABC** is greater than a semicircle, and **AB** is also greater than **BC**: Ptolemy understood from these that the center **E** of the circle is contained between lines **BF** and **FA**, and the apogee between the Vernal equinox and the Summer tropic of the Sun. Now let **IEG** be drawn through center **E**, [parallel] to **AFC**, which will cut **BFD** at **L**; and **HEK** to **BFD**, which cuts **AF** at **M**. In this way, the rectangular parallelogram **LEMF** will be established, whose diameter **FE**, extended in a straight line, will indicate the line **FEN**, the greatest distance of the Earth from the Sun, and the place of the apogee at **N**. Since, therefore, arc **ABC** is 184 degrees 20 minutes, its half **AH** is 92 degrees 10 minutes; if it is subtracted from **GB**, it leaves the excess **HB** at 59 minutes. Again, the parts of the quadrants [*HG*] of the circle subtracted from **AH** leave **AG** at 2 degrees 10 minutes. 

The half-chord of double **AG** has 378 parts, of which the radius is 10,000, and it is equal to **LF**. But the half-chord of double **BH** is 172 of the same parts. Therefore, with two sides of the triangle **ELF** given, the hypotenuse **EF** will be 415 of similar parts, almost the twenty-fourth part of the radius **NB**. As **EF** is to **EL**, so is **NB** (the radius) to the half-chord of double **NH**. Therefore, **NH** itself is given as 24 ½ degrees, and according to these parts is the angle **NEH**, to which the angle of appearance **LFE** is also equal. By so great a space, therefore, did the highest apsis precede the Summer solstice of the Sun before Ptolemy. But since **IK** is a quadrant of the circle, from which if...

[[image: Diagram of the eccentricity of the solar orbit.]]

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...from which if **IC, DK** (equal to **AG, HB**) are subtracted, there remains **CD** of 86 degrees 51 minutes, and what remains from **CDA**, **DA** itself is 88 degrees 49 minutes. But to 86 degrees 51 minutes correspond 88 days and an eighth part of a day; to 88 degrees 49 minutes, 90 days and an eighth part of a day (which is 3 hours), in which under the uniform motion of the Earth the Sun was seen to pass from the Autumnal equinox into the Winter solstice, and what is remaining of the year to return from the Winter solstice into the Vernal equinox.

Ptolemy testifies that he found these things no differently than they had been produced before him by Hipparchus. For which reason, he judged that for the remaining time, the highest apsis would remain perpetually 24 ½ degrees before the Summer tropic, and the eccentricity [*eccentroteta*] would remain a twenty-fourth part of the radius, as was said. Now both are found to have changed by a manifest difference. Machometus Aratensis [Al-Battani] noted from the Vernal equinox to the Summer solstice 93 days 35 minutes; to the Autumnal equinox 182 days 37 minutes; from which, according to the prescription of Ptolemy, he elicited an eccentricity of no more than 347 parts, of which the radius is 10,000. Arzachel the Spaniard [Al-Zarqali] agrees with him in the ratio of the eccentricity, but he produced the apogee at 12 degrees 10 minutes before the solstice, which to Machometus Aratensis seemed to be 7 degrees 43 minutes before the same solstice. 

By these indications, it was surely grasped that another difference still remains in the motion of the center of the Earth, which is also proved by the observations of our age. For from the ten and more years in which we have applied our mind to investigating these things, and especially in the year of Christ 1515, we found that from the Vernal to the Autumnal equinox 186 days 5 ½ minutes were completed. And so that we might not be deceived in taking the solstices (which some suspect happened at times to our predecessors), we adopted for ourselves certain other positions of the Sun in this business, which were by no means difficult to observe even beyond the equinoxes, such as the midpoints of the signs of Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius. We found, therefore, from the Autumn equinox to the middle of Scorpio 45 days 16 minutes; to the Vernal equinox 178 days 53 ½ minutes. The uniform motion in the first interval is 44 degrees 37 minutes; in the second, 176 degrees 19 minutes.

With these things so prepared, let circle **ABCD** be repeated. And let **A** be the sign from which the Sun appeared at the Vernal equinox, **B** from where the Autumnal equinox was seen, **C** the middle of Scorpio. Let **AB, CD** be joined, cutting each other at **F** the center of the Sun, and let **AC** be subtended. Since, therefore, arc **CB** is known to be 44 degrees 37 minutes, the angle under **BAC** is given as [it would be] if 360 were two right angles; and the angle **BFC** of apparent motion is 45 degrees where 360 are four right angles; but insofar as they are two right angles, **BFC** itself will be 90 degrees; hence the remainder **ACD**, which is in arc **AD**, is 45 degrees 23 minutes. 

But the whole segment **ACB** is 176 degrees 19 minutes; subtracting **BC**, there remains **AC** as 131 degrees 42 minutes, which with **AD** itself collects arc **CAD** at 177 degrees 5 ½ minutes. Since, therefore, each segment **ACB** and **CAD** is less than a semicircle, it is clear that the center of the circle is contained in the remainder **BD**; let it be **E**, and through **F** let the diameter **LEFG** be drawn, and let **L** be the apogee, **G** the perigee; let **EK** be erected perpendicular to **CFD**. 

But the chords of the given arcs are also given through the Canon [table of chords]: **AC** as 182,494 and **CFD** as 199,934, where the diameter is assumed to be 200,000. For the triangle **ACF** of given angles, the ratio of the sides will be given by the first [book] of plane [trigonometry], and **CF** is 97,967 parts, of which **AC** was 182,494; and on that account the half-excess over **FD**, which is **FK**, is 2,000 of the same parts. And since the segment **CAD** falls short of a semicircle by 2 degrees 54 ½ minutes, the half of its subtended chord, equal to **EK**, is 2,534 parts. Accordingly, in triangle **EFK**, with two sides **FK, KE** given encompassing a right angle, the sides and angles will be given: **EF** is nearly 323 parts, such as **EL** is 10,000; and angle **EFK** is 70 ⅔ degrees where 360 are four right angles. Therefore the whole **AFL** is 96 ⅔ degrees, and the remainder **BFL** is 83 ⅓ degrees. But where **EL** is 60 parts, **EF** will be approximately 1 part 56 minutes. This was the distance of the Sun from the center of the orbit, now having become barely a thirty-first part, which to Ptolemy...

## Demonstration of the First and Annual Solar Inequality with its Particular Differences. Chapter XVII.

Since, therefore, several differences of solar inequality are found, we judge that the one which is annual and better known than the others should be deduced first; and for that reason let circle **ABC** be repeated about center **E** with diameter **AEC**; let the apogee be **A**, perigee **C**, and the Sun at **D**. 

It has been demonstrated, however, that the greatest difference between uniform and apparent motion is in the middle position according to appearance between both apsides; and for that reason let the perpendicular **BD** be erected to **AEC**, which cuts the circumference at point **B**, and let **BE** be joined. Since, therefore, in the right-angled triangle **BDE**, two sides are given (namely **EB**, which is from the center of the circle to the circumference, and **DE**, the distance of the Sun from the center), the angles and angle **DBE** will be given, by which the uniform motion **BEA** differs from the apparent right angle **EDB**. Insofar as **DE** is made larger or smaller, the whole appearance of the triangle is changed. Thus before Ptolemy, angle **B** was 2 degrees 23 minutes; under Machometus Aratensis and Arzachel it was 1 degree 59 minutes; but now it is 1 degree 51 minutes. And Ptolemy had arc **AB** (by which angle **AEB** is taken) as 92 degrees 23 minutes, and **BC** 87 degrees 37 minutes; Machometus Aratensis had **AB** 91 degrees 59 minutes, **BC** 88 degrees 1 minute. Now **AB** is 91 degrees 51 minutes, **BC** 88 degrees 9 minutes. 

Hence the remaining differences also are clear. For having assumed any other arc **AB**, as in the second figure, let the angle under **AEB** be given, as well as the interior **BED**, and the two sides **BE, BD**; the angle **EBD**, the prosthaphaeresis, will be given through the doctrine of plane [triangles], as well as the difference of uniform and apparent motion, which differences must also change on account of the mutation of side **ED**, as has already been said.

## On the Examination of the Uniform Motion in Longitude. Chapter XVIII.

These things have been set forth concerning the annual inequality of the Sun. But it [the motion] is not through a simple difference, as appeared, but one mixed as yet with that which the length of time has revealed. We shall distinguish these from each other hereafter. In the meantime, the mean and uniform motion of the center of the Earth will be rendered in more certain numbers the more it is separated from the differences of inequality and the longer the interval of time by which it is distant. 

That, moreover, will be established in this manner: We have taken that Autumnal equinox which was observed by Hipparchus at Alexandria in the 32nd year of the third Calippic period, which was (as was recited above) the 177th year from the death of Alexander, after the third day of the five intercalary days at midnight, which the fourth day followed. But according as Alexandria follows Cracow in longitude toward the east by nearly one hour, it was nearly one hour before midnight. Therefore, according to the calculation handed down above, the place of the Autumnal equinox under the sphere of the fixed stars was 176 degrees 10 minutes from the head of Aries, and that was the Sun's apparent place; it was distant from the highest apsis by 114 ½ degrees. 

For this example, let the circle **ABC** be designated, which the center of the Earth described about center **D**; let the diameter be **ADC**, and in it let the Sun be taken, which is **E**, with the apogee at **A** and perigee at **C**. Let **B** be where the Autumnal Sun appeared in the equinox, and let straight lines **BD, BE** be connected. Since, therefore, angle **DEB** (according to which the Sun is seen to be distant from the apogee) is 114 ½ degrees, and **DE** was then 415 parts where **BD** is 10,000: the triangle **BDE** becomes [one] of given angles by the fourth [book] of plane [trigonometry], and the angle under **DBE** is 2 degrees 10 minutes, by which angle **BED** [z] differs from...

***

--- Page 200 ---
[[original page: unnumbered]]

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...differs from that which is under **BDA**; but angle **BED** is 114 degrees 30 minutes, so **BDA** will be 116 degrees 40 minutes; and through this, the mean or uniform place of the Sun from the head of Aries of the sphere of the fixed stars is 178 degrees 20 minutes. 

To this we have compared the Autumnal equinox observed by us in Frauenburg [*Frueburgum*] under the same Cracovian meridian, in the year of the birth of Christ 1515, on the 18th day before the Kalends of October [Sept. 14], in the 1840th Egyptian year from the death of Alexander, on the sixth day of Phaophi (the second Egyptian month), a half hour after sunrise. In which the place of the Autumnal equinox, according to the calculation and observations, was in the sphere of the attached stars 152 degrees 45 minutes, distant from the highest apsis (according to the preceding demonstration) by 83 degrees and 20 minutes. 

Let the angle which is under **BEA** now be established as 83 degrees 20 minutes (where 180 are two right angles), and the two sides of the triangle are given: **BD** 10,000 parts and **BE** 323 parts. Through the fourth demonstration of plane triangles, angle **DBE** will be approximately 1 degree 50 minutes. For if a circle circumscribes triangle **BDE**, angle **BDB** [sic, likely BDE] on the circumference will be 166 degrees 40 minutes (where 360 are two right angles), and the chord **BD** 19,864 parts where the diameter is 20,000; and according to the given ratio of **BD** to **DE**, **DE** itself will be given at nearly 642 of the same parts in length, which subtends angle **DBE** at the circumference at 3 degrees 40 minutes, but at the center 1 degree 50 minutes. And this was the prosthaphaeresis and the difference of uniform and apparent motion, which when added to angle **BED** (which was 83 degrees 20 minutes), we shall have angle **BDA** and arc **AB** as 85 degrees 10 minutes, the distance from the apogee equal [to the uniform motion]; and thus the mean place of the Sun in the sphere of the attached stars as 154 degrees 35 minutes. 

Therefore, in the interval of both observations, there are 1,662 Egyptian years, 37 days, 18 first minutes [*scrupula prima*], 45 second minutes [*scrupula secunda*]; and the mean and uniform motion besides the complete revolutions (which are 1,660) is approximately 336 degrees 15 minutes, consistent with the number which we set forth in the tables of uniform motions.

### REVOLUTIONUM LIB. III.

#### Chapter XIX: On the Setting of the Epochs and Principles for the Uniform Motion of the Sun.

[Page 201 / Folio 90]

Therefore, in the time [abbrev: *tpe* → *tempore*] elapsed from the death of Alexander the Great to the observation of **Hipparchus**, there are 176 years, 362 days, and 27.5 [abbrev: *scru. s.* → *scrupula semis*] minutes. In these, the mean motion according to the calculation of parts is 312° 44'. When these have been subtracted from the 178° 20' of **Hipparchus’s** observation adapted to the 360 degrees of the circle, there will remain for the beginning of the years of the deceased Alexander the Great a position at noon on the first day of the month of **Thoth**, the first of the Egyptians, of 225° 37'. And that [abbrev: *Idqꝫ* → *Idque*] under the meridian of **Cracow** and **Frombork** [Fruenburgensi], the place of our observation. From here to the beginning of the Roman years of **Julius Caesar**, in 278 years and 118.5 days, the mean motion after complete [abbrev: *cōpletas* → *completas*] revolutions is 46° 27'. These, added to the numbers of the Alexandrian position, yield the position of **Caesar** at midnight on the Kalends of January, from which the Romans are accustomed to begin their years and days, of 272° 4'. Then, in 45 years and 12 days—or from Alexander the Great in 323 years and 130.5 days—the position of **Christ** arises [abbrev: *cōsurgit* → *consurgit*] at 272° 31'. And since [abbrev: *Cumqꝫ* → *Cumque*] **Christ** was born in the third year of the 194th **Olympiad**, which [abbrev: *q̄* → *quae*] collect from the beginning of the first **Olympiad** 775 years and 12.5 days to the midnight before the Kalends of January, they similarly refer the position of the first **Olympiad** to 96° 16' at noon on the first day of the month **Hecatombaeon**, the anniversary of which day now [abbrev: *nūc* → *nunc*] falls on the Kalends of July according to the Roman years. In this manner, the principles of the simple solar motion are established relative to the sphere of the fixed stars. The composite positions are also made by the addition of the equinoctial precessions [abbrev: *praecessionum*], and like those, the **Olympiad** position is 90° 59', Alexander’s is 226° 38', **Caesar’s** 276° 59', and **Christ’s** 278° 2'. All these are referred, as we said, to the meridian of **Cracow**.

#### Chapter XX: On the Second and Double Inequality Which Occurs Regarding the Sun Due to the Change of the Apsides.

Now a greater difficulty arises regarding the inconstancy of the solar apsis, since **Ptolemy** thought it to be fixed, while others thought it followed the motion of the eighth sphere, according to which [abbrev: *ꝙ* → *quod*] they judged the fixed stars also to move. **Arzachel** was of the opinion that this motion was also unequal, inasmuch as it might even happen to move backward; he took evidence for this from the fact that although **Machometus Aratensis** [Al-Battani], as has been said, found the apogee seven degrees and 44 minutes [abbrev: *scrupula*] before the solstice—which previously under **Ptolemy** in 740 years had progressed by nearly 17 degrees—it seemed to him [Arzachel] after 200 years minus 7 to have retrograded nearly 4.5 [abbrev: *s.* → *semis*] degrees. For this reason, he thought there was some other motion of the center of the annual orbit in a certain small circle, according to which the apogee would deflect forward and backward, and would produce unequal distances of the center of that orbit from the center of the world. A truly fine invention, but not accepted for the reason that it does not generally agree with other comparisons. For example, if the succession of the motion itself is considered in order: that it stood still for some time before **Ptolemy**, that in roughly 640 years it passed through 17 degrees, then in 200 years it returned by 4 or 5 degrees, and for the remaining time until our own it progressed, with no other regression perceived in the whole time, nor several stations which must necessarily intervene between contrary motions. These things can in no way be understood in canonical and circular motion. Wherefore it is believed by many that some error fell into their observations. Both mathematicians were indeed equal in zeal and diligence, such that it is ambiguous whom we should rather follow. I myself confess that in no part is there greater difficulty than in apprehending the Sun's apogee, where we reason out great things from certain minimal and scarcely perceptible details. For around the perigee and apogee, a whole degree changes the prosthaphaeresis [correction] by only two minutes more or less; whereas around the mean apsides, 5 or 6 degrees pass under a single minute [abbrev: *scrupulo*], and thus a slight error can propagate itself immensely.

---

### REVOLUTIONUM LIB. III.

[Page 203 / Folio 91]

**propagate.** Accordingly, even though we placed the apogee at 6° and a half and a sixth [6° 40'] of **Cancer**, we were not content to consider it with horoscopic instruments, unless the eclipses of the Sun and Moon also made us more certain. For if an error lies hidden in them, they undoubtedly detect it. Therefore, what may be most similar to the truth from the general concept of the motion, we can observe to be a consequence, yet [abbrev: *tamẽ* → *tamen*] unequal. For after that station from **Hipparchus** to **Ptolemy**, the apogee appeared in a continuous, orderly, and increasing progress up to the present, except for that error which, as is believed, fell between **Machometus Aratensis** and **Arzachel**, since other things seem to agree. For since the Sun's prosthaphaeresis likewise does not yet [abbrev: *nōdum* → *nondum*] cease to diminish, it seems to follow the same ratio of circulation. And that both inequalities are co-equated under that first and simple [abbrev: *simpliciqꝫ* → *simplicique*] anomaly of the obliquity of the zodiac [signifer], or something similar. To make this clearer, let circle AB be in the plane of the zodiac, with center C and diameter ACB, in which D is the globe of the Sun as if in the center of the world. Around center C another small circle EF is described, which does not enclose the Sun, according to which small circle the center of the annual revolution of the Earth's center is understood to move with a certain slow progress. And when [abbrev: *Cūqꝫ* → *Cumque*] the small circle EF together with line AD is in the order of the signs [consequentia], and the center of the annual revolution through circle EF is in the order opposite the signs [praecedentia], and both [abbrev: *utrunqꝫ* → *utrunque*] move with quite a slow motion, the center of the annual orbit will sometimes be found at the maximum distance, which is DE, sometimes at the minimum, which is DF. There it is in slower motion, here in swifter; and in the middle curvatures of the small circle, it causes that distance of the centers to increase and decrease with time, and the highest apsis to precede and alternately follow that apsis or apogee which occurs [abbrev: *cōtingit* → *contingit*] under line ACD as the mean [abbrev: *mediũ* → *medium*]. For example, if arc EG is taken, and with G as center, a circle equal to AB itself is described, the highest apsis will then be in line DGK, and the distance DG will be less than DE, by the 8th [proposition] of the 3rd [book] of **Euclid**. #### Chapter XXI: How Great is the Second Difference of the Solar Inequality.

Since it has now been seen that this second inequality follows that first and simple anomaly of the obliquity of the zodiac, or its likeness, we shall have its certain differences, if no error of past observers stands in the way. #### Chapter XXII: How the Uniform Motion of the Solar Apogee is Explained Together with the Variable [Motion].

Since therefore the time in which the maximum eccentricity coincided [abbrev: *cōgruebat* → *congruebat*] with the beginning of the first and simple anomaly was the third year of the 178th **Olympiad**, and the 259th year of **Alexander the Great** according to the Egyptians; and therefore the true and mean position of the apogee was at 5.5° of **Gemini**, that is, 65.5° from the vernal equinox. The true precession of that equinox, also then coinciding with the mean, was 4° 38.5', which being subtracted from 65.5°, there remained from the head of **Aries** of the sphere of fixed stars 60° 52' for the position of the apogee. Again, in the second year of the 573rd **Olympiad**, of **Christ** 1515, the position of the apogee was found at 6° and two-thirds of **Cancer**. But since the precession of the vernal equinox according to the calculation was 27° and a quarter, which if they are deducted from 96° 30' and 20' [96° 50'], they leave 69° 25'. It was shown, however, that the first anomaly being then 165° 39', the prosthaphaeresis was 2° 7', by which the true position preceded the mean. Therefore, the mean position of the solar apogee itself appeared as 71° 32'. In the intervening 1580 Egyptian years, therefore, the mean and uniform motion of the apogee was 10° 41'; when these have been divided by the number of those years, we shall have an annual [abbrev: *annuā* → *annuam*] portion of 24" 20''' 14''''.

### On the second and twofold variation which occurs concerning the Sun due to the shift of the apsides. Chapter 20.

**I**ncreasing difficulty now arises regarding the instability of the solar <term>apsis</term> <note>The points in an orbit where a celestial body is furthest from (apogee) or closest to (perigee) the center of motion.</note>. Ptolemy believed this to be fixed, while others thought it followed the motion of the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars; this refers to the slow shift known as the precession of the equinoxes.</note>, according to their belief that the fixed stars also move. <note>Arzachel is the Latinized name of Al-Zarqali, an 11th-century Arab astronomer from Al-Andalus.</note> Arzachel was of the opinion that this motion was also unequal—namely, that it could even move backward. He took his evidence from the fact that <note>Machometus Aratensis is Al-Battani, a 9th-century astronomer.</note> Al-Battani, as has been said, found the apogee to be seven degrees and 44 minutes <note>original: "scrupula"</note> before the summer solstice. Previously, in the 740 years since Ptolemy, it had advanced by nearly 17 degrees; yet to Arzachel, 193 years later <note>original: "after 200 years minus 7"</note>, it seemed to have moved backward by almost four and a half degrees. Because of this, he thought there was some other motion of the center of the annual orbit within a certain small circle, according to which the apogee would deflect forward and backward, and the distances from the center of the orbit to the center of the world would be made unequal. It is indeed a clever discovery, but it is not accepted because it does not generally agree with other observations when compared. For instance, if the sequence of the motion is considered in order: it would have stood still for some time before Ptolemy; then in about 640 years it would have passed through 17 degrees; then in 200 years it would have retreated 4 or 5 degrees; and for the remaining time until our own day it would have progressed. No other regression has been perceived in all that time, nor several "stations" <note>Points where a planet appears to stand still before changing direction.</note> which must necessarily occur between contrary motions. These things cannot be understood at all within the rules of circular and uniform motion. For this reason, many believe that some error occurred in those observations. Both mathematicians <note>Al-Battani and Al-Zarqali.</note> were equal in zeal and diligence, so it is unclear which we should follow. Indeed, I confess that in no part is there greater difficulty than in grasping the Sun's apogee, where we reason about great things through the smallest and barely perceptible details. This is because near the perigee and apogee, a whole degree of movement changes the <term>correction</term> <note>original: "prosthaphaeresis"; the geometric adjustment used to find the true position of a planet from its mean motion.</note> by only two minutes, more or less. However, near the mid-points of the <term>apsides</term>, 5 or 6 degrees pass by for a single minute of error. Thus, a slight error can spread itself immensely for

...to extend. Furthermore, even regarding the fact that we placed the apogee <note>The point in the Sun's path where it is furthest from the Earth.</note> at 6 and 1/2 and 1/6 degrees of Cancer <note>The "sixth part of a degree" equals 10 minutes, so 6° 40' of Cancer.</note>, we were not satisfied to rely solely on time-observing instruments, unless solar and lunar eclipses also made us more certain. For if an error lies hidden in the observations themselves, the eclipses undoubtedly reveal it. Therefore, regarding what is most likely to be true, we can perceive from the overall concept of the motion that it is a consequence, though an unequal one. 

Since the time of that station observed by Hipparchus <note>Hipparchus of Nicea (c. 190–120 BCE), a foundational Greek astronomer.</note> up to Ptolemy, the apogee appeared in a continuous, orderly, and increasing progress until the present day—excepting that error which is believed to have occurred between Al-Battani <note>original: "Machometum Aratensem"</note> and Arzachel <note>Al-Zarqali, an 11th-century astronomer.</note>, as the rest of the data seems to agree. For since the <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>The "equation of center," or the correction added or subtracted to the mean motion to find the actual position of a planet.</note> of the Sun likewise has not yet ceased to diminish, it seems to follow the same ratio of circulation. And both inequalities are equated under that first and simple <term>anomaly</term> <note>An irregularity in motion.</note> of the obliquity of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi"</note>, or something similar.

To make this clearer, let there be a circle **AB** in the plane of the zodiac with center **C**, and diameter **ACB**. Let **D** be the globe of the Sun, as if at the center of the world. Around center **C**, let another very small circle **EF** be described, which does not encompass the Sun. Let it be understood that the center of the annual revolution of the center of the Earth moves along this small circle with a certain slow progress. 

When the small circle **EF**, along with the line **AD**, is moving in <term>prograde</term> <note>original: "consequentia" — moving in the order of the signs of the zodiac.</note>, and the center of the annual revolution is moving through the circle **EF** in <term>retrograde</term> <note>original: "praecedentia" — moving opposite the order of the signs.</note>, and both are moving with an extremely slow motion, the center of the annual orbit will sometimes be found at its maximum distance, which is **DE**, and sometimes at its minimum, which is **DF**. In the former, the motion is slower, and in the latter, faster. In the middle curvatures of the small circle, it causes that distance of the centers to increase and decrease with time, and causes the highest <term>apsis</term> <note>The highest or furthest point of the orbit.</note> to precede and alternately follow that apsis—or apogee—which is situated under the line **ACD** as a mean. 

For example, if the circumference **EG** is taken, and with **G** as the center, a circle equal to **AB** is described, the highest apsis will then be on the line **DGK**, and the distance **DG** will be less than **DE**, according to the 8th proposition of the third book of Euclid. These things are demonstrated in this way through an "eccentric of an eccentric." Through an epicycle

...and also an **epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note> in this manner. Let circle AB be **concentric** <note>Sharing the same center.</note> with the universe and the Sun, and let ACB be the diameter in which the highest **apogee** <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note> occurs. With A as the center, let epicycle DE be described; and again, with D as the center, let a **small epicycle** <note>original: "epicyclium"</note> FG be described, in which the Earth revolves. All of these are in the same plane of the **zodiac** <note>The band of the sky through which the Sun, Moon, and planets appear to move.</note>.

[[image: A complex astronomical diagram showing nested circles and epicycles. A large circle AB with center C represents the main orbit. A smaller circle (epicycle) is centered at point A. Within that, a tiny circle (small epicycle) FG is centered at point D. Various lines (CI, CK, ID) demonstrate the geometric relationships and angles used to calculate the Earth's position.]]

And let the motion of the first epicycle be <term>in the order of the signs</term> <note>original: "in succedentia"; this refers to "direct" motion from West to East.</note> and nearly annual; and that of the second [point], that is D, also annual, but <term>contrary to the order of the signs</term> <note>original: "in praecedentia"; this refers to "retrograde" motion from East to West.</note>. Let the revolutions of both be equal relative to the line AC. Again, let the center of the Earth move from F in the "preceding" direction slightly faster than point D.

From this it is manifest that when the Earth is at point F, it will produce the maximum apogee of the Sun, and at point G the minimum. However, in the middle arcs of this small epicycle FG, it will cause the apogee itself to precede or follow, appearing increased or diminished, larger or smaller. Thus, the motion appears to vary, just as was demonstrated previously regarding the epicycle and the **eccentric** <note>A circular orbit where the center of motion is "off-center" from the Earth or Sun.</note>. 

Now let the arc AI be taken, and at center I let the epicycle be restored, and let the connection CI be extended into a straight line CIK. The angle KID will be equal to the angle ACI because the revolutions are equal. Therefore, as we demonstrated above, point D will describe an **eccentric circle** equal to the concentric circle AB, with its center at L and at a distance CL which is equal to ID. Point F also will describe its own eccentric according to the distance CLM equal to IDF, and G similarly according to the equal distances IG and CN. # THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK III. 92

**Whenever FO [describes] the circumference of the second and its own epicycle, point O will no longer trace an eccentric circle whose center lies on line AC, but rather on a line parallel to DO, such as LP.** Furthermore, if OI and CP are joined, they will also be equal, but smaller than IF and CM, and angle DIO will be equal to angle LCP, according to Euclid’s *Elements*, Book I, Proposition 8 <note>original: "per VIII. primi Euclid." Copernicus uses this geometric principle to prove that the triangles are congruent.</note>. Consequently, the Sun’s **apogee** <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the center of motion—the Sun, in this case.</note> will appear to precede line A within line CP. From this, it is also clear that the same effect occurs through an <term>eccentrepicycle</term> <note>A model that combines an eccentric circle (a circle whose center is not the Earth) with an epicycle (a smaller circle rotating on the edge of a larger one).</note>. For if, on a pre-existing single eccentric circle described by epicycle D around center L, the center of the Earth revolves on the circumference F under the aforementioned conditions—that is, slightly more than an annual revolution—it will introduce another eccentric circle around center P, and exactly the same effects will occur. Since so many different models lead to the same numerical result, I could not easily say which one actually exists, except that the perpetual harmony between the calculations and the observations <note>original: "apparentium," referring to the phenomena seen in the sky.</note> compels us to believe it is one of them.

### How Great the Second Difference of the Solar Inequality Is. Chapter XXI.

[[image: An ornate historiated initial 'C' showing an astronomer or scholar pointing toward a celestial globe or a series of concentric spheres.]]

**S**ince it has now been shown that this second inequality follows the first simple <term>anomaly</term> <note>An "anomaly" is the angle used to track a planet's position along its path. The "simple anomaly" here refers to the long-term cycle of the tilt of the Earth's axis.</note> of the **obliquity of the zodiac** <note>original: "obliquitatis signiferi"; the tilt of the Earth's path (the ecliptic) relative to the celestial equator.</note>, or something similar to it, we will have certain values for its differences—provided no error from past observers stands in the way. We find this simple anomaly in the year of our Lord 1515 was approximately 165 degrees and 39 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula"; small fractions of a degree used for precision.</note>. By calculating backward, we find its starting point <note>original: "principium"</note> was approximately sixty-four years before the birth of Christ. From that time until our own, 1,580 years have accumulated. At that starting point, the maximum **eccentricity** <note>original: "eccentrotes"; the measurement of how far the Sun is from the geometric center of the orbit.</note> was found by us to be 417 parts (where the radius of the orbit is 10,000 parts); however, our current eccentricity, as has been shown, is 323. Now, let AB be a straight line in which B is the Sun and the center of the world. Let the maximum eccentricity be AB, and the minimum be BD. Imagine the description of a small circle whose diameter is AD. Let the arc AC be taken according to the measure of the first simple anomaly, which was 165 degrees and 39 minutes. Therefore, since AB is given as 417 parts, which at the beginning of the simple anom[aly]...

...of the anomaly, that is, it was found at A, and now BC is 323 parts. We will have triangle ABC, with the sides AB and BC given, as well as the single angle CAD, because the remaining arc CD is 14 degrees and 21 minutes <note>original: "scrupula," a term for minutes or small parts of a degree</note> from the semicircle. Therefore, through the proofs for plane triangles, the remaining side AC will be given, as well as angle ABC, which is the difference between the mean and the varying motion of the **apogee**. [[A geometric diagram showing a very acute triangle with its apex at point B. The base of the triangle is part of a small circle at the top, containing points A, E, F, D, C. Lines extend from B to these points. This diagram is used to calculate the solar eccentricity.]]

For through the angle CAD of 14 degrees and 21 minutes, we will have CB as 2498 parts where the diameter of the circle circumscribing the triangle is 20,000. According to the ratio of BC to AB, AB itself is given as 3225 of the same parts, and the side which subtends angle ACB is 341 degrees and 26 minutes. From this, and because the remaining sum is 360 degrees (or two right angles), the angle CBD is 4 degrees and 13 minutes, which is subtended by side AC at 735 parts. Therefore, where AB is 417 parts, AC is found to be nearly 95 parts; because this subtends the given circumference, it will have the same ratio to AD as it does to the diameter. AD is therefore given as 96 parts, of which ADB is 417, and the remaining DB is 321 parts—this is the minimum distance of the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The distance between the center of the Earth's orbit and the actual Sun.</note>. Moreover, the angle CBD, which was found to be 4 degrees and 13 minutes as measured on the circumference, is 2 degrees and 6.5 minutes when measured from the center. This is the subtractive <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>original: "prosthaphaeresis," a Greek-derived term used in astronomy to describe the "equation" or correction added to or subtracted from the mean motion to find the true position.</note> from the uniform motion of AB around the center B. 

Now, let the straight line BE be drawn touching the circle at point E, and with center F being taken, let EF be joined. Since in the <term>right-angled triangle</term> BEF, the side EF is given as 48 parts and BDF as 369 parts (where the radius FBD is 10,000), EF will be 1300 parts. This is half of the chord subtending double the angle EBF, which is 7 degrees and 28 minutes (where 360 degrees equals four right angles). This is the **maximum prosthaphaeresis** between the uniform and apparent motion. From this, the other specific differences can be established. For example, if we take the angle AFE to be 6 degrees, we will have a triangle with given sides BF and FB, along with the angle EFB, from which the correction (prosthaphaeresis) EFB of 41 minutes will result.

### How the uniform motion of the solar apogee is explained along with the variable motion. Chapter 22.

[[image: Historiated initial Q with a figure holding a book.]]

**S**ince, therefore, the time in which the maximum <term>eccentricity</term> <note>original: "eccentrotes"; the distance the center of the orbit is offset from the center of the universe (Earth or Sun).</note> coincided with the beginning of the first and simple <term>anomaly</term> <note>An astronomical term for the angular distance of a planet from its apogee.</note> was the 178th Olympiad, in its third year—which was the 259th year of Alexander the Great according to the Egyptians—the true and mean position of the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth (or Sun).</note> was together at 5 1/2 degrees of Gemini. That is, 65 1/2 degrees from the Vernal Equinox. Furthermore, the true <term>precession of the equinoxes</term> <note>The slow, westward shift of the equinox points along the ecliptic.</note> at that time also coincided with the mean precession at 4 degrees and 38 1/2 minutes. When these are subtracted from the 65 1/2 degrees, there remained 60 degrees and 52 minutes from the head of Aries on the sphere of the fixed stars as the position of the apogee. Again, in the second year of the 573rd Olympiad, which was the year of Christ 1515, the position of the apogee was found at 6 and two-thirds degrees of Cancer. But because the precession of the Vernal Equinox according to the calculation was 27 1/4 degrees, if these are deducted from the 96 degrees and 40 minutes <note>original: "medietate & tertia" (half and a third), referring to 2/3 of a degree or 40 minutes.</note>, they leave 69 degrees and 25 minutes. However, it was shown that since the first anomaly was then 165 degrees and 39 minutes, the correction was 2 degrees and 7 minutes, by which the true position preceded the mean. It therefore became clear that the mean position of the solar apogee was 71 degrees and 32 minutes. Therefore, in the intervening 1,580 Egyptian years, the mean and uniform motion of the apogee was 10 degrees and 41 minutes. When these are divided by the number of those years, we will have an annual portion of 24 seconds, 20 thirds, and 14 fourths. <note>Copernicus is using sexagesimal fractions (60ths) to describe incredibly precise movements: seconds, thirds (1/60th of a second), and fourths (1/60th of a third).</note>
