# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

### On the calculation of the Solar appearance. Chapter XXV.

From these things I think it is now sufficiently clear how the apparent position of the Sun may be calculated for any [abbrev: *quodcunque*] proposed time. For the true position of the Vernal equinox for that time must be sought—that is, its precession—together with its first simple anomaly, as we explained above. Then, the simple mean motion of the center of the Earth (or you may call it the motion of the Sun) and the annual anomaly are obtained through the tables of uniform motions, which are to be added to their established principles. Therefore, with the first and simple anomaly, and [abbrev: *atque*] its number being found in the first or second column of the preceding table, or the one occurring [abbrev: *occurrentem*] closer to it, you will find in the third column the prosthaphaeresis of the annual anomaly, and preserve the following proportional minutes. However [abbrev: *autem*], add the prosthaphaeresis to the annual anomaly if the first [anomaly] was less than a semicircle, or if its number was contained [abbrev: *comprehensus*] under the first column; otherwise, subtract it. For that which [abbrev: *quod*] remains or is the sum will be the adjusted anomaly of the Sun, through which you again take the prosthaphaeresis of the annual orbit, which occupies the fifth column, along with [abbrev: *cum*] the following excess. Indeed, if this excess, through the proportional minutes previously preserved, produces anything, let it always be added to this prosthaphaeresis, and it will become [abbrev: *fietque*] the adjusted prosthaphaeresis itself, which is to be taken away from the mean position of the Sun if the number of the annual anomaly was found in the first column, or was less than a semicircle. But let it be added if it was greater, or occupied the other column of numbers. For that which [abbrev: *quod*] will have been the remainder or the collection [abbrev: *collectumve*] in this manner will determine the true position [abbrev: *locum*] of the Sun taken from the head of the starred Aries; if to this the true precession of the Vernal equinox is finally added, it will immediately show the position of the Sun from the equinox itself in the signs of the zodiac [dodecatemoria] and the degrees of the signs of the circle. But if [abbrev: *quod si*] you wish to achieve this in another way, take the composite uniform motion instead of the simple motion, and do the rest as was said, except that [abbrev: *quod*] for the precession of the equinox, you add or subtract only its prosthaphaeresis, as the matter requires. Thus stands the logic of the Solar appearance [abbrev: *apparentiae*] through the mobility of the earth, agreeing with ancient and more recent observations, by which it is more [abbrev: *etiam*] presumed that the future...

--- Page 213 ---
[[Original Page: 96]]
# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.

...is already foreseen. Nevertheless, we are also [abbrev: *quoque*] not ignorant that [abbrev: *quod*] if anyone thought the center of the annual revolution were fixed like the center of the world, but the Sun were mobile with two motions similar and equal to those which we demonstrated regarding the center of the eccentric, all things would appear as before—the same numbers and [abbrev: *eademque*] the same demonstration—since nothing else would be changed in them except the position itself, especially as pertains to the Sun. For the motion of the center of the Earth would then be absolute and simple around the center of the world [abbrev: *mundi*], with the remaining two being granted [abbrev: *concessis*] to the Sun; and [abbrev: *manebitque*] therefore there will still remain doubt concerning the center of the world, whether it is one of those, as we said at the beginning *amphibolikōs* [ambiguously], that the center of the world is in the Sun or around it. But about this question we shall say more in the explanation of the five wandering stars [planets], which we shall also decide to the best of our ability, thinking it sufficient if we have now adopted certain and by no means [abbrev: *minimeque*] deceptive numbers for the solar appearance.

### On the *nychthēmeron*, that is, the difference of the natural day. Chapter XXVI.

It remains yet to say something concerning the Sun about the inequality of the natural day, which [abbrev: *quod*] time is encompassed by the space of 24 equal hours [abbrev: *horarum*], which indeed [abbrev: *quidem*] we have used until now as the common and certain measure of the celestial motions. Such a day [abbrev: *diem*] others define as the time between two sunrises, such as the Chaldeans and Jewish antiquity; others between two sunsets, such as the Athenians [abbrev: *Athenienses*]; others from midnight to midnight, such as the Romans; others from midday to midday, such as the Egyptians. It is manifest, however, that under that time the proper revolution of the globe of the earth is completed, together with that which is added [abbrev: *adiectionem*] in the meantime by the annual progress according to the apparent motion of the Sun. That this addition is made unequal is shown primarily by the unequal apparent course of the Sun itself, and furthermore because that natural day pertains to the poles of the equinoctial circle, but the annual motion is under the circle of the signs [the zodiac]. For these reasons, that apparent time cannot be a common and certain measure of motion, since day does not agree with day, nor are they mutually consistent in every part; and therefore it was appropriate to choose some mean and equal day among these, by which without doubt the uniformity of motion...

--- Page 214 ---
# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...might be measured. Since, therefore, under the circle of the whole year there are 365 revolutions on the poles of the earth, to which by the daily addition through the apparent progress of the Sun a nearly entire supernumerary revolution is added, it follows that the 365th part of that is what, from the equal motion, completes the natural day. Therefore, we must define and [abbrev: *atque*] separate the equal day from the varying apparent day. We call that the equal day which contains the entire revolution of the equinoctial circle and as much portion besides as the Sun is seen to traverse in that time by equal motion. But we call that the unequal and apparent [abbrev: *apparentemque*] day which encompasses [abbrev: *comprehendit*] the 360 units [times] of the equinoctial of one revolution, and besides that which ascends with the apparent progress of the Sun on the horizon or meridian. Although the difference of these days is very small and not immediately perceived, nevertheless, after several days have been multiplied, it coalesces into evidence. There are two causes of this: both [abbrev: *cum*] the inequality of the solar appearance, and also the unequal ascension of the obliquity of the zodiac [signifer]; the first which exists because of the unequal and apparent [abbrev: *apparentemque*] motion of the Sun. It has already been shown that in the semicircle in which the highest apsis [absis] mediates, there was a deficit toward the parts of the zodiac, according to Ptolemy [abbrev: *Ptolemaeum*], of 4 units [times] with three-quarters of one, and in the other semicircle, in which the lowest apsis was, the same amount was in abundance. Therefore, the total excess of one of the semicircles to the other was 9 and a half units. In the second cause, which is according to sunrise and sunset, the greatest difference occurs between the semicircles of both turnings [solstices], which exists between the shortest and longest day, varying greatly, namely, being peculiar to each [abbrev: *unicuique*] region. But that which occurs from midday or midnight is everywhere contained within four limits. Since from the 16th degree of Taurus to the 14th of Leo, 88 degrees pass through the meridian in nearly 93 units of time, and from the 14th of Leo to the 16th of Scorpio, 92 parts pass in 87 units of time, so that here five units are lacking, and there the same amount is in abundance. Thus indeed in the first segment the collected days exceed those in the second by ten units, which make two parts of one hour; which [abbrev: *quod*] similarly happens in the other semicircle by alternating turns under the remaining diametrically opposite limits. It pleased the Mathematicians...

--- Page 215 ---
[[Original Page: 97]]
# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.

...that the beginning of the natural day be taken not from sunrise or sunset, but from midday or midnight. For the difference [abbrev: *differentia*] taken from the horizon is more complex, as it extends itself to several hours, and furthermore because it is not the same everywhere, but is varied in many ways according to the obliquity of the sphere. But that which pertains to the meridian is the same everywhere and [abbrev: *atque*] simpler. Therefore, the whole difference, which is established from both causes already mentioned—as much because of the unequal apparent progress of the Sun as because of the unequal transit across the meridian—before Ptolemy [abbrev: *Ptolemaeum*] indeed took its beginning of diminution [abbrev: *diminutionis*] from the middle of Aquarius, and by increasing from the beginning of Scorpio, it collected 8 and one-third units of time. Which now, by decreasing from the twentieth degree of Aquarius or near it to the tenth of Scorpio, and by increasing from the tenth of Scorpio to the twentieth of Aquarius, is contracted into seven units of time and 48 minutes [scrupula]. For these things also change over time because of the instability of the perigee and the eccentricity [abbrev: *eccentrotetis*]. To which, if finally the greatest difference of the precession of the equinoxes is compared [abbrev: *comparata*], the total difference of natural days could extend itself beyond ten units of time under some number of years. In which a third cause of the inequality of days has been hidden until now, for the reason [abbrev: *quod*] that the revolution of the equinoctial circle was found to be equal in relation to the mean and [abbrev: *aequalemque*] equal equinox, not to the apparent equinoxes, which, as is sufficiently clear, are not entirely equal. Therefore, ten units of time doubled make one hour with one-third, by which sometimes the longer days can exceed the shorter. These things concerning the annual progress of the Sun and the [abbrev: *caeterarumque*] slower motion of the other stars could perhaps be ignored without manifest error. But because of the speed of the Moon, on account of which an error of half a degree and a third could be committed, they are by no means to be ignored. Therefore, the method of correlating equal time with varying apparent time, in which [abbrev: *quo*] all differences may agree, is this. For any proposed time, one must seek at both limits of that time—I mean the beginning and the end—the mean position of the Sun from the equinox through its mean equal motion, which we called composite, and [abbrev: *atque*] also the true apparent position from the true equinox; and it must be considered [abbrev: *considerandumque*] how many temporal parts passed through the right ascensions...

[Marginalia: B circa]

--- Page 216 ---
# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...around midday or midnight, or were between those which [pass] from the first true position to the second true position. For if they were equal to those degrees which are between both mean positions, then the apparent time assumed will be equal to the mean. But if [abbrev: *quod*] the temporal parts exceeded, let the excess itself be added to the given time; but if they were deficient, let the deficit itself be subtracted from the apparent time. For doing this, from those which will have been collected or [abbrev: *relictamve*] left, we will have the time changed into equality, by taking for any temporal part four minutes of an hour, or 10 seconds of one sixtieth of a day. But if equal time were given, and [abbrev: *nosseque*] you wish to know how much apparent time corresponds to it, the contrary must be done. We had, however, at the first Olympiad [abbrev: *Olympiadem*], the mean position of the Sun from the mean Vernal equinox at midday of the first day of the first month according to the Athenians, Hecatombaeon [abbrev: *Hecatombaeonos*], as 90 degrees and 59 minutes; and from the apparent equinox, 0 degrees and 36 minutes of Cancer. But at the years of Christ, the mean motion of the Sun was 8 degrees and 2 minutes of Capricorn; the true motion 8 degrees and 48 minutes of the same. There ascend [abbrev: *ascendunt*] therefore in the right sphere [abbrev: *sphaera recta*] from 0 deg. 36 min. of Cancer to 8 deg. 48 min. of Capricorn, 188 units and 54 minutes of time, exceeding the distance of the mean positions by 1 unit and 54 minutes of time. Which make 7 and a half minutes of one hour. And so for the rest, by which the course of the Moon can be examined most exactly, concerning which it will be spoken in the following book.

--- Page 217 ---
[[Original Page: 98]]
# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS ON THE REVOLUTIONS
### BOOK FOUR.

Since in the preceding book, to the extent that our mediocrity was able, we explained what seemed to occur because of the motion of the earth around the Sun, and [abbrev: *sitque*] it is our purpose by the same occasion to discern the motions of all the wandering stars, now the course of the Moon interrupts, and [abbrev: *idque*] necessarily so, because through it, which is a partaker of day and [abbrev: *noctisque*] night, the positions of any stars are especially captured and examined; then, because it alone of all of them brings its revolutions, although they are diverse, collectively to the center of the earth, and [abbrev: *sitque*] it is most related to the earth. And therefore, as far as it is in itself, it does not indicate anything concerning terrestrial mobility, except perhaps the daily motion; rather, they believed for that reason that the earth is the center of the world, the common [center] of all revolutions. We indeed, in the explanation of the lunar course, do not differ from the opinions of the ancients in what occurs around the earth. Nevertheless, we shall bring forward other things than those which we received from our elders, and [abbrev: *magisque*] more consistent, by which we shall establish the lunar motion as certain as possible.

### Hypotheses of the lunar circles according to the opinion of the ancients. Chapter I.

The lunar course, therefore, has this [property]: that it does not follow the middle circle of the signs [the ecliptic], but its own inclined [circle], which bisects that one and is in turn bisected by it, from which it migrates into both latitudes. These things behave almost as the solstices [conuersiones] in the annual motion of the Sun; nor is it a wonder, since what a year is to the Sun, this a month is to the Moon. The mean positions of the sections are called "ecliptic," or by others "nodes." And the conjunctions and [abbrev: *oppositionesque*] oppositions of the Sun and Moon happening in these are called "ecliptic."

[Marginalia: B ii uocan-]

--- Page 218 ---
# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...called. For there are no other signs common to both circles besides these, in which eclipses of the Sun and [abbrev: *Lunaeque*] Moon can happen. For in other places the digression of the Moon ensures that the lights [the luminaries] least interfere with one another, but passing by they do not impede themselves. This oblique orbit of the Moon is also carried with those four cardinal points of its own around the center of the earth uniformly, daily by nearly three minutes of one degree, completing its revolution in the nineteenth year. Under this orbit, therefore, and its plane, the Moon is seen to always move in consequence [eastward], but sometimes very little, sometimes very much. For it is as much slower as it is higher [sublimior], but faster as it is closer to the earth. Which could be discerned in it more easily than in any other star because of its proximity. They understood, therefore, that this happened through an epicycle, since the Moon, running around it, in the upper circumference subtracted from the uniformity, but in the lower promoted the same. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that those things which happen through an epicycle can also happen through an eccentric. But they chose the epicycle because the Moon seemed to admit a double diversity. For when it was in the highest or lowest apsis of the epicycle, no difference indeed appeared from the equal motion. But around the contact of the epicycle, not in one way, but far greater in the half-moon [diuidua] waxing and waning than if it were full or new [sitiens], and this by a certain and regular succession. For which reason they thought that the orbit in which the epicycle is moved is not homocentric with the earth, but an eccentric-epicycle [eccentrepicyclum] in which the Moon is carried by that law, so that in all mean oppositions and [abbrev: *coniunctionibusque*] conjunctions of the Sun and Moon, the epicycle is in the apogee of the eccentric, but in the mean quadrants of the circle, in the perigee of the same. They imagined, therefore, two motions equal to each other and contrary at the center of the earth, namely, the epicycle moving in consequence, and the center of the eccentric and its apsides moving in precedence, with the line of the mean Solar position always mediating between both. And in this manner, twice in a month the epicycle runs through the eccentric. So that these things may be subjected to the eyes: Let the oblique circle of the Moon ABCD be homocentric to the earth, dissected into four parts by the diameters AEC and BED, the center of the earth being E; let there be in line AC the mean conjunction of the Sun and Moon, and in the same place and time the apogee of the eccentric, whose center is F and the center of the epicycle...

--- Page 219 ---
[[Original Page: 99]]
# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV.

...MN at the same time. Now let the apogee of the eccentric be moved in precedence, as much as the epicycle moves in consequence, both uniformly around E with equal and monthly revolutions toward the mean conjunctions or oppositions of the Sun; and let the line of the mean position of the Sun AEC be always midway between them, and the Moon again in precedence from the apogee of the epicycle. For they think that the appearances agree with these things thus established. For since the epicycle in the time of half a month completes a semicircle from the Sun, but a whole revolution from the apogee of the eccentric, it follows that in the middle of this time, which is around the half-moon, they are opposed to each other on the diameter BD, and the epicycle becomes the perigee in the eccentric, as in the mark G: where, being made closer to the earth, it produces greater differences of inequality. For equal magnitudes exposed to unequal intervals—the one closer to the eye appears larger. They were therefore at a minimum when the epicycle was in A, but at a maximum in G. Since the diameter MN of the epicycle will have the smallest ratio to line AE, but a greater one to GE than all others which are found in other places, since GE itself is the shortest of all, and AE (or its equal DE) is the longest of those which can be extended from the center of the earth into the eccentric circle.

[Image: Geometrical diagram of the lunar epicycle and eccentric model.]

### On the defect of these assumptions. Chapter II.

The ancients indeed assumed such a composition of circles as if [abbrev: *consencientem*] agreeing with the lunar appearances. But if we weigh the matter itself more diligently, we shall find this hypothesis neither fit enough nor sufficient. Which we can prove by reason and by sense. For while they admit that the motion of the center of the epicycle is uniform around the center of the earth, it must also be admitted that it is unequal in its own orbit, which it describes in the eccentric. Since if, for example, the angle AEB is taken as 45 degrees—that is, half a right angle—and equal to ABD itself, so that the whole BED becomes a right angle, and the center of the epicycle is taken in G...

[Marginalia: B iii & con-]

--- Page 220 ---
# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...and GF is connected, it is manifest that the angle GFD is greater than GEF, the exterior to the interior and opposite. For which reason both the circumferences DAB and DG, described in one time, are dissimilar; so that when DAB is a quadrant, DG, which the center of the epicycle described in the meantime...

[Image: Geometrical diagram showing a circle with points A, B, C, D and internal eccentric point F.]

...is greater than a quadrant of the circle. But it was clear that in both half-moons DAB and DG were a semicircle; therefore, the motion of the epicycle is unequal in its own eccentric which it describes. If it were so, what shall we answer to the axiom: "The motion of the celestial bodies is uniform, and only appears unequal relative to the appearances," if the uniform apparent motion of the epicycle was in reality unequal? And it would happen that it is entirely contrary to the established and assumed principle. But if you say that it moves uniformly around the center of the earth, and that this is enough to maintain uniformity, what sort of uniformity will that be in a foreign circle, in which its motion does not exist, but in its own eccentric? Thus indeed we also wonder at this, that they wish the uniformity of the Moon itself in the epicycle to be understood not in comparison to the center of the earth through the line—namely, EGM—to which the uniformity ought by right to be referred (the center of the epicycle itself consenting), but to some different point, and that the earth is midway between it and the center of the eccentric, and that the line IGH is like an index of the uniformity of the Moon in the epicycle, which also in reality demonstrates this motion to be sufficiently unequal. For the appearances, which partly follow this hypothesis, compel this to be admitted. Thus also, with the Moon running through its epicycle unequally, if we now wish to prove the inequality of appearance from inequalities, one may notice what sort of argument it will be. For what else shall we do but provide an handle to those who disparage this art? Then, experience and sense itself teach us that the parallaxes [abbrev: *parallaxes*] of the Moon do not agree with those which the logic of those circles promises. For parallaxes—which they call "commutations" [abbrev: *commutationes*]—occur because of the evident magnitude of the earth in relation to the proximity of the Moon. Since those straight lines which are extended from the surface of the earth and its center to the Moon did not then appear parallel, but...

[Marginalia: inclina-]

--- Page 221 ---
[[language: Latin]]
[[original page: 100]]

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV. 100

intersect with a manifest inclination in the lunar body, they must necessarily produce a diversity in the lunar appearance, so that it appears in a different place to those looking [contuentibus [1]] at it obliquely from the convexity of the Earth than to those who have viewed the Moon from its center or their own vertex [zenith]. Therefore, such commutations [parallaxes] vary according to the ratio of the lunar distance from the Earth. For by the consensus of all mathematicians, the greatest distance is 64 parts and a sixth, of which the distance from the center of the Earth to the surface is one; but according to their symmetry, the minimum distance ought to have been 33 parts and as many [totidemque [2]] minutes, so that the Moon would approach us by almost half the space, and by consequent reasoning, it was necessary for the parallaxes at the minimum and maximum distance to differ between themselves by almost double. We, however, see that those parallaxes which occur in the halved Moon [dichotomy], as it increases and decreases, even at the perigee of the epicycle, differ very little or not at all from those which happen in eclipses of the Sun and Moon, as we shall teach sufficiently in its proper place. But the body of the Moon itself most clearly declares the error, because [quod [3]] by a similar reasoning it would happen that it appeared twice as large and small according to its diameter. Just as circles are in the double ratio of their diameters, it would appear four times [plerunque [4]] larger in the quadratures when closest to the Earth than when opposite the Sun [at full moon], if it shone full; but since it shines halved, it would nonetheless shine with double the light than it would when existing there as a full moon. Although the opposite of this is manifest of itself, if anyone, not content with simple sight, wishes to experiment by the Hipparchan dioptra or by any other instruments by which the diameter of the Moon may be taken, he will find that it does not differ except as much as the epicycle without that eccentric would require. For that reason, Menelaus and Timochares, in their inquiry into the fixed stars by means of the Moon's position, did not hesitate to always use the same lunar diameter as half of one degree, which is as much as the Moon is usually seen to occupy.

### Another opinion on the motion of the Moon. Chapter III.

It clearly appears, therefore, that there is neither [neque [5]] an eccentric [eccentrum [6]] by which [quem [7]] the epicycle appears larger and smaller, but rather another [alium [8]] arrangement [modum [9]] of circles.

For let there be an epicycle AB, which we shall now call the first and larger [maioremque [10]]; let its center be C, and from the center of the Earth, which is D, let the straight line DC be extended to the highest apsis of the epicycle, and in that center A let another also [quoque [11]] small epicycle [epicyclium [12]] EF be described [describatur [13]], and all these in the same plane of the oblique orbit of the Moon. Now let C be moved in consequence [prograde], but A in precedence [retrograde], and again the Moon from F, the upper part of the same EF, in consequence, that order being observed so that while the line DC is together with the mean position of the Sun, the Moon is always closest to the center C, that is, in the mark E, but in the quadratures and [atque [14]] furthest away in F. In the quadratures, however, it describes the largest according to the distance from the center CF. And so [sicque [17]] again, it will produce smaller differences of equality and appearance there, and larger ones here, under similar but unequal circumferences about the center C. And since [cumque [18]] the center C of the epicycle is always on a circle homocentric to the Earth, it will not exhibit such diverse parallaxes, but only those conforming to the epicycle itself. And the cause will be readily apparent why the lunar body also appears somewhat similar to itself, and [atque [19]] all other things which are discerned concerning the lunar course will happen thus. We shall hereafter demonstrate these things through this hypothesis of ours, although [quanquam [20]] the same things can again be done through eccentrics, as we did concerning the Sun, the proper proportion being observed. We shall begin, however, from the equal motions, as we did above, without which the unequal cannot be discerned. But here no [non [21]] small difficulty exists because of the parallaxes which we have mentioned: for which reason its position is not observable by means of Astrolabes and [atque [22]] any other instruments. But the kindness of nature has provided for human desire even in this part, whereby it may be detected more certainly through its eclipses than by the use of instruments, and without [absque [23]] suspicion of error.

For since the other parts of the world are pure and full of daily light, it is established that night is nothing other than the shadow of the Earth, which tends into a conical figure and [definitque [24]] ends in a point, into which the Moon falling is dimmed, and [atque [25]] being established in the midst of the darkness, it is understood to have arrived at the position opposite the Sun. Nor indeed do Solar eclipses, which [quae [26]] happen by the interposition of the Moon, provide a certain proof [argumentum [27]] of the lunar position. For then it happens that the conjunction of the Sun and Moon is seen by us, which nevertheless, in comparison to the center of the Earth, has either already passed or has not yet occurred, because of the stated cause of commutation [parallax]. And for that reason, we do not perceive the same eclipse of the Sun as equal in magnitude and duration in all lands, nor [neque [28]] similar in its parts. In lunar eclipses, however, no such impediment happens, but they are everywhere similar to themselves. Since the Earth transmits the axis of that dimming shadow through its center from the Sun, and [suntque [29]] for that reason lunar eclipses are most suitable for detecting the course of the Moon by the most certain reasoning.

### On the revolutions of the Moon, and its particular motions. Chapter IV.

From [Ex [30]] the most ancient people, therefore, who took care of this matter so that it might be handed down to posterity in numbers, Meton the Athenian was found, who flourished in the thirty-seventh Olympiad. He declared that in 19 solar years, 235 months are completed, whence that great year was called *enneadecaeteris* (nine-and-ten-year), that is, the nineteen-year Metonic cycle. Which number pleased so much that it was posted [prefigeretur [31]] in the forum at Athens and other more distinguished cities, and it has even [etiam [32]] been commonly received up to the present, because [quod [33]] they think that by it the beginnings and ends of months are established in a certain order. Also that the Solar year of 365 days [dierum [34]] and a quarter is commensurable with the months. Hence that Callippic period of 76 years, in which one day is intercalated ten and nine times, and they named it the Callippic year. But the skill of Hipparchus found that in 304 years a whole day grows in excess, and is then alone verified when the Solar year was a 300th part of a day smaller. Thus also that great year of Hipparchus was named by some.

born, in which 7,600 months were completed. These things were said more simply and by a "coarser Minerva," as they say. When also the restorations of the anomaly and latitude are sought [quaeruntur [35]]. Wherefore the same Hipparchus further investigated those things, namely, having compared the notes which he most diligently [diligentissime [36]] observed in lunar eclipses to those which he received from the Chaldeans: he defined the time in which the revolutions of the months and the anomaly returned together to be 345 Egyptian years, 82 days, and one hour, and in that time 4,267 months and 4,573 circuits of anomaly were completed. When therefore the proposed multitude of days was distributed by the number of months, and [suntque [37]] there are 126,007 days and [atque [38]] one hour, one month is found equal to 29 days, 31 first minutes, 50 seconds, 8 thirds, 9 fourths, 20 fifths. By which reasoning the motion of any time also became clear. For the 360 degrees of one monthly revolution having been divided by the monthly time, the daily course of the Moon from the Sun came forth as 12 degrees, 11 first minutes, 26 seconds, 41 thirds, 20 fourths, 18 fifths. These collected 365 times produce, beyond twelve revolutions, an annual motion of 129 degrees, 37 first minutes, 31 seconds, 28 thirds, 29 fourths. Furthermore, since [cum [39]] 4,267 months to 4,573 circuits of anomaly are in composite numbers with each other, seeing that 17 measures them as a common measure, they will be in the smallest numbers as 252 to 269; in which ratio [ratione [40]] by theorem XV of the fifth book of Euclid, we shall have the lunar course to the motion of anomaly. So that when we have multiplied the motion of the Moon by 269 and [atque [41]] divided the product [confectum [42]] by 252, the annual motion of anomaly will come out indeed [quidem [43]] after the whole revolutions as 13 degrees, 88 [sic: probably 88 degrees total or an error in transcription for 88 minutes] ... 88 minutes, 43 seconds, 8 thirds, 40 fourths, 20 [fifths]; and likewise the daily [motion] as 13 degrees, 3 first minutes, 53 seconds, 56 thirds, 29 fourths. But the revolution of latitude has another ratio [rationem [44]]: for it does not agree under the predefined time [tempore [45]] which [quod [46]] the anomaly restores, but we understand that the latitude of the Moon has returned only then, when [quando [47]] a later eclipse of the Moon was in all things similar and equal to the prior one, namely when on the same side the obscurings of both were equal, in the magnitude in which they occurred and in duration, which [quod [48]] happens when [quando [49]] the distances from the highest or lowest apsis of the Moon were equal; for then it is understood that the Moon passed through equal shadows in an equal time.

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV. 102

Such a return, according to Hipparchus, occurs in 5,458 months, to which 5,924 revolutions of latitude correspond. By which reasoning also the particular motions of latitude in years and days were established like the others. For when we have multiplied the motion of the Moon from the Sun by 5,924 months and divided the product by 5,458, we shall have the motion of the Moon's latitude. In years indeed after [full] revolutions, 168 degrees, 42 first minutes, 46 seconds, 20 thirds, 3 fourths. In days, however, 13 degrees, 13 first minutes, 45 seconds, 39 thirds, 40 fourths. In this way Hipparchus estimated the equal motions of the Moon, to which no one before him approached more closely; nevertheless, subsequent centuries manifested that they were not yet absolute in all numbers. For Ptolemy found the same mean motion from the Sun as Hipparchus, but that the annual motion of anomaly lacked from that [of Hipparchus] 1 second minute, 11 thirds, 39 fourths. But that the annual [motion] of latitude exceeded by 52 thirds, 41 fourths. We, however, after more times have now passed, have found that the mean annual motion of Hipparchus also lacks 1 second minute, 7 thirds, 56 fourths; but only 26 thirds, 55 fourths are lacking from the anomaly. Also, the motion of latitude exceeds by 1 second minute, 2 thirds, 42 fourths. Therefore, the equal motion of the Moon by which it differs from the terrestrial motion will be annually 129 parts [degrees], 37', 22'', 36''', 25''''. Of the anomaly 88 parts, 43', 9'', 7''', 15''''. Of latitude 148 parts, 42', 45'', 17''', 21''''.

### NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

#### Demonstration of the first inequality of the Moon, which occurs at the new and full moon. Chapter V.

We have set forth the uniform motions of the Moon as far [abbrev: *usque*] as they have been able to become known to us to the present. Now the explanation of the inequality must be attempted, which we shall demonstrate by means of [abbrev: *modum*] an epicycle, and first [abbrev: *primum*] that which occurs in the conjunctions and [abbrev: *et*] oppositions of the Sun, concerning which the ancient Mathematicians used admirable ingenuity by means of triads of Lunar eclipses [abbrev: *deliquiorum*]. We shall follow that path thus prepared [abbrev: *praeparatam*] by them for us, and we shall take [abbrev: *capiemusque*] three eclipses diligently [abbrev: *diligenter*] observed by Ptolemy, with which we shall compare three others also [abbrev: *quoque*] noted with no [abbrev: *non*] less diligence, so that the uniform motions already set forth may be examined to see if they are correct. In their [abbrev: *eorum*] explanation, we shall use the mean motions of the Sun and [abbrev: *et*] Moon from the place of the Vernal equinox as if [abbrev: *tanquam*] they were uniform, in imitation of the ancients. For the variation which occurs on account of the unequal precession of the equinoxes is not perceived in so short a time, even ten years [abbrev: *annorum*].

Ptolemy therefore assumes the first eclipse to have occurred in the 17th year of Hadrian the prince, when the twentieth day of the month of Pauni had passed according to [abbrev: *secundum*] the Egyptians [abbrev: *Aegyptios*]; but it was the 133rd year of Christ, on the sixth day of the month of May, or the day before the Nones. And it was [abbrev: *defecitque*] total, the middle time of which was three-quarters [*dodrantem*] of a uniform hour before midnight at Alexandria, but at Fruenburg [Frombork] or [abbrev: *siue*] Kraków it would have been one hour and three-quarters before the middle of the night, which the seventh day followed, with the Sun occupying 14 parts and a quarter of a part of Taurus, but 12° 21' of Taurus according to the mean motion. 

The second he says was in the 19th year of Hadrian, when two days had passed of the month of Chiach, the fourth of the Egyptians [abbrev: *Aegyptiorum*]. It was [abbrev: *autem*] in the year of Christ 134, the 13th day before the Kalends of November, and [abbrev: *et*] it failed from the North by ten-twelfths [*dextantem*] of its diameter, the middle [abbrev: *medium*] of which was one equinoctial hour at Alexandria. At Kraków, however [abbrev: *autem*], it was two hours before the middle [abbrev: *medium*] of the night, the Sun being [abbrev: *existente*] in the 25th degree and a sixth part of the sign of Libra, but by mean motion in 26° 43' of the same [abbrev: *eiusdem*]. 

The third eclipse was also [abbrev: *quoque*] in the 20th year of Hadrian, when 19 days of Pharmuthi, the eighth month of the Egyptians [abbrev: *Aegyptiorum*], had passed. In the year of Christ 135...

--- Page 233 ---
...135, on the 6th of March, when it had passed, the Moon failing again from the North by half [*semisse*] of its diameter, the middle of which was at Alexandria at four equinoctial hours, but at Kraków at three hours after the middle of the night, the morning of which was on the Nones of March. The Sun was also [abbrev: *quoque*] then [abbrev: *tunc*] in the 14th degree and 12th part of Pisces, by mean motion in 11° 44' of Pisces. 

It is clear, moreover, that in the middle interval of time which was between the first and [abbrev: *et*] second [abbrev: *secundam*] eclipse, the Moon traversed as much as the Sun in apparent motion (subtracting, I say, complete circles), 161 parts and 55 minutes [*scrupula*]. And from the second to the third, 137 parts 55 minutes. From these things also which have been set forth in the lunar eclipses [abbrev: *deliquiis*], it will be permitted to test whether the uniform motions of the Moon which [abbrev: *quas*] we have already set forth are correctly held. Also the motion of anomaly, rejecting complete circles, was 9 parts 49 minutes. 

The time, however, which intervened from the 19th year of Hadrian, in the Egyptian month of Chiach, on the second day and [abbrev: *et*] two hours before the middle of the night, which the third day of the month followed, up to the year of Christ 1522, and the fifth day of September at one hour and [abbrev: *et*] a third of one in apparent time, which when it had been equated, are 1,388 Egyptian years, 302 days, 3 hours 34 minutes. Of anomaly indeed according to Hipparchus 9 parts 39 minutes, but according to Ptolemy 9 parts 11 minutes. There are lacking, therefore, from those, 26 minutes to the motion of the Moon, and 38 minutes to the anomaly, which increase in our numbers and agree with those we have set forth.

#### On the second difference of the Moon, and what ratio the first epicycle has to the second. Chapter VIII.

Thus, therefore, the equal motions of the Moon with its first difference have been demonstrated. We must now inquire in what ratio the first epicycle stands to the second, and both to the distance of the center of the earth. Now, the greatest difference is found, as we said, in the mean quadratures, when the Moon is halved [dichotomous], waxing or waning, which extends to seven degrees and two-thirds,

and two-thirds, as the notes of the ancients also maintain. For they observed the time in which the halved Moon had most nearly reached the mean distance of the epicycle, and this around the contact of the line proceeding from the center of the earth, which could easily be perceived through the calculation explained above. And since the Moon itself was then existing around the ninetieth degree of the zodiac [signifer] taken from the rising or setting, they guarded against the error which parallax could introduce into the motion of longitude. For then, the circle which passes through the vertex of the horizon divides the zodiac at right angles, and does not allow any change in longitude, but it falls entirely into latitude. Therefore, by the skill of the Astrolabic instrument, they took the place of the Moon relative to the Sun; when the comparison was made, the Moon was found differing from equality by seven degrees (as we said) and two-thirds of one, instead of five degrees.

Now let the epicycle AB be described, its center being C, and from the center of the earth, which is D, let the straight line DBCA be extended; let the apogee of the epicycle be A, and the perigee B. Let the tangent to the epicycle DE be drawn, and let CE be connected. Therefore, since the maximum prosthaphaeresis is in the tangent, which in this proposal is 7° 40′, which is also the angle BDE, and the angle at CED is right, namely at the contact of circle AB. On this account, CE will be 1334 parts, of which the radius CD is 10,000. But at the full and new Moon, it was far smaller, being approximately 861 of the same parts. Thus, the ratio of these, CG to GE, is established as 1097 to 237, of such parts as CD was ten thousand.

#### On the remaining difference, by which the Moon is seen to move unequally from the highest apsis of the epicycle. Chapter IX.

Through this induction [*epagoge*] it is also given to be understood how the Moon moves unequally in its first epicycle, the greatest difference of which occurs when it is curved into horns, or is gibbous, or exists as a half-full orb. Let that first epicycle be again AB, which the center of the second epicycle describes in a mean way, its center being C, the highest apsis A, and the lowest B. Let a point B [sic, likely E or a variable point] be taken anywhere on the circumference, and let CB be joined. Let CE be to EF as 1097 is to 237; and with center E and distance EF, let the second epicycle be described, and let the straight lines CL and CM be drawn as tangents to it on both sides. And let the motion of the small epicycle be from A toward E, that is, upward in precedence [westward], but the Moon from F to L, also in precedence. It is clear, therefore, that when the motion AE is equal, yet the second epicycle adds to that equality through the course FL the circumference EL, and through MF it subtracts it. Now truly, in triangle CEL, the angle at L is right, and EL is 237 parts, of which CE was 1097. Of such parts, therefore, as CB [the radius] would be ten thousand, EL will be 2160, which by the Canon subtends the angle ECL of 12° 28′, equal to MEF, since the triangles are similar and equal. And such is the maximum difference by which the Moon varies from the highest apsis of the first epicycle. This happens, moreover, when the Moon in its mean motion has stood apart from the line of the mean motion of the earth, before and behind, by 38° 46′. Thus it is indeed manifest that under the mean distance of the Sun and Moon of 38° 46′, and as many degrees from the mean opposition on either side, these greatest prosthaphaereses occur.

#### How the apparent lunar motion is demonstrated from the given equal motions. Chapter X.

All these things having been thus provided, we wish now to show how the apparent and equal motion is discussed from those proposed equal motions of the Moon by a graphic method, taking an example from the observations of Hipparchus, by which the doctrine may be simultaneously proved by experiment. In the 197th year from the death of Alexander, on the seventeenth day of the month Pauni, which is the tenth of the Egyptians, after nine and one-third hours of the day had passed at Rhodes, Hipparchus found by an observation of the Sun and Moon with the Astrolabic instrument that they were distant from one another by 48° and a tenth part, by which the Moon followed the Sun. And since he judged the place of the Sun to be in 11 degrees less a tenth part of Cancer, it followed that the Moon occupied the 29th degree of Leo. At which time also the twenty-ninth degree of Scorpio was rising, with the tenth degree of Virgo mediating the heavens at Rhodes, for which the North pole is elevated 36 degrees. By this argument, it was established that the Moon, being positioned around the ninetieth degree of the zodiac from the setting, admitted no then-perceptible change of vision in longitude. Truly, because this consideration was made at three and one-third hours from the noon of that seventeenth day, which at Rhodes corresponds to four equinoctial hours, they would have been 3 and one-sixth hours at Cracow, according to the distance by which Rhodes is closer to us than Alexandria by a sixth part of an hour. Therefore, from the death of Alexander there were 196 years, 286 days, 3 and one-sixth hours simply; but regularly 3 and one-third hours approximately. In this time, the Sun by its mean motion reached 12° 3′ of Cancer, but in apparent motion 10° 40′ of Cancer, whence it appears that the Moon, according to the truth, was in 28° 37′ of Leo. Now, the equal motion of the Moon according to its monthly revolution was 45° 5′, and the Anomaly from the highest apsis was 333° according to our calculation. With this example proposed, let us describe the first epicycle AB, its center C,

its diameter ACB, which is extended in a straight line to the center of the earth, and let it be ABD. And with center E and distance EF, let the epicycle of the epicycle FG be described. Let the Moon be at point G. Now, let the circumference FG be 90° 10′, by reason of the double of the equal motion from the Sun, which was 45° 5′; and let CG, EG, and DG be connected. Therefore, since two sides of the triangle CEG are given, CE as 1097 parts and EG as 237 (equal to EF), with the angle GEC as 90° 10′, there are given through the demonstrations of plane triangles the remaining side CG as 1123 of the same parts, and the angle ECG as 12° 11′, by which the circumference EI also consists, and the prosthaphaeresis additive to the anomaly. Wherefore, in triangle GDC, two sides are also given: GC as 1123 parts (of which CD is ten thousand), and angle GCD as 165° 11′. From these we shall also have the angle CDG as 1° 29′, and the prosthaphaeresis which was added to the mean motion of the Moon, so that the true distance of the Moon from the mean motion of the Sun was 46° 34′, and its apparent place in 28° 37′ of Leo, distant from the true place of the Sun by 47° 57′, falling short of Hipparchus’s consideration by nine minutes. But lest anyone should suspect either his inquiry or our calculation to have failed on that account, although the difference is slight, we shall show that neither he nor we committed an error, but that it stands correctly in this way. For if we remember that the lunar circle is oblique, which she follows, we shall also admit that in the zodiac it produces some diversity in longitude, especially around the mean places, which are the readings between both the Northern and Southern limits and both ecliptic [intersections], in almost the same way as we explained concerning the inequality of the natural day between the obliquity of the zodiac

--- Page 246 ---
[Original Page: 113]
# OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

of the zodiac and the equinoctial circle. So also, if we transfer the ratios to the orbit of the Moon, which Ptolemy reported to be inclined to the zodiac, we find that in those places it makes a difference in longitude to the zodiac of seven minutes, which doubled will produce 14; and this happens similarly by increasing and decreasing. Since the Sun and Moon are distant by a quadrant of a circle, if the Northern or Southern limit of latitude is in the middle of them, then the intercepted circumference of the zodiac exists larger than the quadrant of the lunar circle by 14 minutes; and conversely in the other quadrants, in which the ecliptic sections are in the middle, the circles through the poles of the zodiac intercept just as much less than a quadrant. So also in the present case. Since the Moon was turning around the middle, which was between the Southern limit and the ascending ecliptic section (which the moderns call the Head of the Dragon), and the Sun had already passed the other descending section (which they call the Tail), it is no wonder if that lunar distance of 47° 57′ in its oblique orbit, compared to the zodiac, increased by at least 7 minutes, without the fact that the Sun also, verging toward its setting, might have applied some subtractive parallax of vision, concerning which more will be said clearly in the explanation of parallaxes. And thus that distance of the luminaries according to Hipparchus, which he had taken by instrument as 48° 6′, agrees with our calculation with admirable consensus and as if by agreement.

#### Canonical exposition of the prosthaphaereses, or lunar equations. Chapter XI.

By this example, therefore, I think the method of discerning lunar courses is generally understood. Since in triangle CEG the two sides GE and CE always remain the same. But according to the angle GEC, which changes continually, we nevertheless discern the remaining side GC with the angle ECG, which is the prosthaphaeresis of the anomaly to be equated. Then also in triangle CDG, when the two sides DC, CG with the angle DCE have been calculated, the angle D around the center of the earth becomes manifest in the same way between the equal and true motion. So that these may be even readier,

--- Page 247 ---
[Original Page: 113 continued]
# REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV.

we shall set forth the Canon of these prosthaphaereses, which will contain six orders [columns]. For after the two common numbers of the circle, in the third place will be the prosthaphaereses which, proceeding from the small epicycle, vary the equality of the first anomaly according to the doubled motion in the months. Then, the following place being left empty for future numbers, we shall pre-occupy the fifth, in which we shall write the prosthaphaereses of the first and greater epicycle, which occur in the mean conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun and Moon, the greatest of which is 4° 56′. In the penultimate place are placed the numbers by which the prosthaphaereses that occur in the halved Moon exceed those former ones, the greatest of which is 2° 44′. But so that the other excesses might also be rated, proportional minutes [scrupula proportionum] have been devised, of which this is the ratio. For they took the parts 2° 44′ as 60, for any other excesses occurring in the contact of the epicycle. Just as in the same example, where we had the line CG as 1123 parts (of which CD is ten thousand), which produces at the contact of the epicycle a maximum prosthaphaeresis of 6° 29′, exceeding that first one by 1° 33′. As 2° 44′ is to 1° 33′, so is 60 to 33; and thus we have the ratio of the excess which occurs in the semicircle of the small epicycle to that which occurs under the given circumference of 90° 18′. We shall therefore write in the table, opposite 90°, 33 minutes. In this way, for each circumference of the same circle pre-assigned in the Canon, we shall find the proportional minutes, to be set forth in the vacant fourth place. Finally, in the last place, we have added the parts of latitude, Northern and Southern, concerning which we shall speak below. For the convenience and use of the operation advised us to place these in this order.

#### On the calculation of the Lunar course. Chapter XII.

The method, therefore, of calculating the lunar appearance is clear from what has been demonstrated, and it is this. We shall reduce the time proposed for which we seek the place of the Moon to equality; through this, we shall deduce the mean motions of longitude, anomaly, and latitude (which we shall also define shortly) in the same way as we did for the Sun, from the given principle of Christ or another, and we shall establish the places of each at the proposed time. Then we shall look for the equal longitude of the Moon, or the doubled distance from the Sun, in the table, noting the prosthaphaeresis occurring in the third column and the proportional minutes that follow. If, therefore, that number with which we entered was found in the first place, or less than 180 degrees, we shall add the prosthaphaeresis to the lunar anomaly; but if it was greater than 180, or in the second place, let it be subtracted from it, and we shall have the equated anomaly of the Moon, and its true distance from the highest apsis. By this, entering the Canon again, we shall take the prosthaphaeresis corresponding to it in the fifth column, and the excess that follows in the sixth column, which the second epicycle increases over the first; the proportional part of which, taken according to the ratio of the minutes found to sixty, is always added to this prosthaphaeresis. And that which has been collected is subtracted from the mean motion of longitude and latitude, provided that the equated anomaly was less than 180 degrees or a semicircle, and it is added if the anomaly itself was greater; and in this way we shall have the true distance of the Moon from the mean place of the Sun, and the equated motion of latitude. Wherefore neither the true place of the Moon will be unknown, whether from the first star of Aries by the simple motion of the Sun, or from the Vernal equinox in a composite way, or by the addition of its precession. Finally, through the equated motion of latitude, we shall have in the seventh and last place of the Canon the parts of latitude by which the Moon has stood apart from the middle circle of the signs [the ecliptic]. Which latitude will then be Northern when the motion of latitude is found in the first part of the table...

--- Page 251 ---
...is found [to be...], that is, if it were less than 90 or greater than 270 degrees; otherwise, it will follow the Southern latitude. And therefore, the Moon will be descending from the North up to 180 degrees, and from there climbing from the Southern limit until it has completed the remaining parts of the circle. Thus, the apparent course of the Moon [*lunaris*] has in some way as many concerns around the center of the Earth as the center of the Earth has around the Sun.

## How the motion of lunar latitude is examined and demonstrated. Chapter XIII.

Now an account must also be given regarding the motion of lunar latitude, which is seen to be more difficult to discover for the reason that it is hindered by more [*pluribus*] circumstances. For as we said before, if two eclipses of the Moon were similar and equal in all respects—that is, with the deficient parts in the same Northern or Southern position, and around the same ecliptic section [node], whether ascending or descending, and if its distance from the Earth or from the highest apsis were equal—since, with these factors thus agreeing, it is understood that the Moon has completed entire circles of its latitude in true motion. For since the shadow of the Earth is conical, and if a right cone is cut by a plane parallel to the base, the section is a smaller circle at a greater distance from the base and a larger one at a smaller distance, and likewise equal at an equal distance; thus indeed the Moon at equal distances from the Earth passes through equal circles of the shadow, and represents equal disks of itself to our sight. Hence it is that [*quod*] the Moon itself, projecting by equal parts toward the same side, according to an equal distance from the center of the shadow, makes us certain of equal latitudes; from which it must follow that it is distant from the same ecliptic connection [node] by equal intervals when it has returned to its prior place of latitude. This is especially true if the location also agrees on both sides, for the approach and recession of the Moon or of the Earth changes the entire magnitude of the shadow, though only by a small amount...

[Margin: F iij]

--- Page 252 ---
# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...however, a small amount that can scarcely be grasped. Therefore, the greater the time that mediates between both [observations], the more defined we can have the motion of the Moon’s latitude, as was said regarding the Sun. But since it is rare to find two eclipses agreeing in these conditions, they certainly have not occurred for us at present. Nevertheless, we have noticed that there is another way through which this can be achieved. Since, while other conditions remain, if the Moon should also fail [be eclipsed] in different parts, and around opposite sections [nodes], it will then signify that the Moon in the second eclipse has arrived at a place diametrically opposite to the place of the first, and besides entire circles, has described a semicircle. This will seem to satisfy the investigation of this matter.

We have found, therefore, two eclipses related in nearly these ways. The first in the seventh year of Ptolemæus Philometor, which was the 150th year of Alexander, after 27 days had passed (as Claudius [Ptolemy] says) of the month Phamenot, the seventh of the Egyptians, in the night which the 28th day followed; and the Moon failed from the beginning of the eighth hour until the end of the tenth hour, in the nocturnal temporal hours of Alexandriæ, at most seven digits of the lunar diameter from the North around the descending section. Therefore, the middle time of the eclipse was (he says) two temporal hours from midnight, which make two and one-third equinoctial hours, since the Sun was in the sixth degree of Taurus; but at Cracouia it would have been one hour and one third. 

We observed the second under the same meridian of Cracouia, in the year of Christ 1509, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, with the Sun in the 21st degree of Gemini; the middle of which was after noon of that day at 11 equinoctial hours and three-fifths of one hour, in which nearly eight digits of the lunar diameter failed from the Southern part around the ascending section. Therefore, from the beginning of the years of Alexander, there are 149 Egyptian years, 206 days, 14 1/3 hours at Alexandriæ, but at Cracouia 14 hours and one third, according to the appearance, but strictly examined 14 1/2 hours. At which time the place of the equal anomaly according to our calculation, agreeing nearly with Ptolemæus, was 163 degrees 33 minutes, and the prosthaphæresis was 1 degree 23 minutes, by which the true place of the Moon was less than the equal [mean] place. 

To the second eclipse, from the same...

--- Page 253 ---
### REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV

...established principle of Alexander, there are 1832 Egyptian years, 295 days, 11 hours, 45 minutes in apparent time; but in equated time 11 hours 55 minutes, whence the mean motion of the Moon was 182 degrees 18 minutes; the place of the anomaly 159 degrees 55 minutes, but equated 161 degrees 14 minutes; the prosthaphæresis, by which the mean motion was less than the apparent, was one degree 14 minutes. It is clear, therefore, that in both eclipses the distance of the Moon from the Earth was equal, and the Sun was at apogee in both cases nearly, but the difference in the eclipses was one digit. 

Because the diameter of the Moon usually occupies nearly half a degree, as we shall show later, its twelfth part for one digit will be 2 1/2 minutes, with which nearly half a degree in the oblique orbit of the Moon around the ecliptic sections corresponds; by this amount in the second eclipse the Moon was further from the ascending section than in the first from the descending section, whereby it is very clear that the true motion of the latitude of the Moon, after completed revolutions, was 179 1/2 degrees. But the lunar anomaly between the first and second eclipse adds 21 minutes to the equality, by which the prosthaphæreses exceed each other. We shall have, therefore, the equal motion of the latitude of the Moon after whole circles as 179 degrees 51 minutes. Moreover, the time between both eclipses was 1683 years, 88 days, 22 hours, 35 minutes in apparent time, which agreed with the equal time. In which time, with equal revolutions completed, twenty-two thousand five hundred seventy-seven times, there are 179 degrees 51 minutes. These agree with our [tables], which we have already set forth.

## On the places of the anomaly of the latitude of the Moon. Chapter XIIII.

In order that we may also fix the places of this course at the presumed principles [epochs], we have assumed here also two lunar eclipses, not at the same section [node], nor diametrically and in opposite parts as in the preceding, but at the same parts, North or South. But with all other...

--- Page 254 ---
# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...conditions preserved, as we said, according to the Ptolemaic prescription, by which we shall obtain our proposal without error. 

The first eclipse, therefore, which we also used in investigating other motions of the Moon, was that which we said was observed by C. Ptolemæus in the nineteenth year of Adrianus [Hadrian], after two days of the month Chiach had passed, before the middle of the night by one equinoctial hour at Alexandriæ, but at Cracouia two hours before the middle of the night which the third day followed; and the Moon failed in the very middle of the eclipse in nine-twelfths [*dextante*] of the diameter, that is, ten digits from the North, while the Sun was in 25 1/10 of Libra, and the place of the lunar anomaly was 64 degrees 38 minutes, and its subtractive prosthaphæresis was 4 degrees 20 minutes around the descending section. 

We also observed another with great diligence at Rome, in the year of Christ 1500, after the Nones of November, two hours from the middle of the night which dawned on the eighth day before the Ides of November. But at Cracouia, which follows the East by five degrees, it was two hours and one-third of an hour after the middle of the night, while the Sun was in 23 1/6 of Scorpio; ten digits again failed from the North. There are collected, therefore, from the death of Alexander, 1824 Egyptian years, 84 days, 14 hours, 20 minutes in apparent time, but in equal time 14 hours 16 minutes. Therefore, the mean motion of the Moon was in 173 degrees 16 minutes. The lunar anomaly was 293 degrees 40 minutes, equated 291 degrees 35 minutes. The additive prosthaphæresis was 4 degrees 28 minutes. 

It is manifest, therefore, that the Moon even in both these eclipses had a distance from its highest apsis nearly equal, and the Sun was in both cases around its middle apsis, and the magnitude of the shadows was equal, which declare that the latitude of the Moon was Southern and equal, and thereafter that the Moon itself had equal distances from the sections, but here ascending, there descending. There are, therefore, in the middle of both eclipses 1366 Egyptian years, 358 days, 4 hours, 20 minutes in apparent time; but equally 4 hours 24 minutes. In which the mean motion of latitude is 159 degrees 55 minutes. Let there be now the oblique circle of the Moon, whose diameter AB is the common section of the zodiac [signiferi], let the Northern limit be at C, the Southern at D, and the descending...

## Construction of the parallactic instrument. Chapter XV.

That the maximum latitude of the Moon, according to the angle of the section of its orbit and the zodiac, is five parts (of which the circle is 360), fortune did not grant us the opportunity of testing that C. Ptolemæus had, due to the impediment of lunar parallaxes [*commutationum*]. For he at Alexandriæ, for which the Northern pole is raised 30 degrees 58 minutes, observed how much the Moon was to approach the summit [zenith] of the horizon at most, namely while it was in the beginning of Cancer and at the Northern limit, which could already be known beforehand by numbers. He found then through a certain instrument, which he calls parallactic, manufactured for detecting the parallaxes of the Moon, its minimum distance from the summit to be only two degrees and an eighth of a part, around which if any parallax had occurred, it was necessary for it to have been very slight in such a short interval. 

Therefore, with two degrees and an eighth part subtracted from 30 degrees 58 minutes, there remain 28 degrees 51 1/2 minutes, which exceed the maximum obliquity of the zodiac (which was then 23 degrees 51 minutes 20 seconds) by nearly five whole degrees; which latitude of the Moon is found to agree with other details even until now. 

The parallactic instrument, moreover, consists of three rules, two of which are equal in length to at least four cubits, and the third somewhat longer. This [the third] and one of the prior ones are joined at the extremities, the others by skillful perforation and axles or pins fitting into these, so that being movable in the same surface in those joints, they do not wobble at all. Moreover, on the longer rule from the center of its joint, let a straight line be carved through its whole length, from which, according to the distance of the joints taken as exactly as possible, an equal [distance] is taken. Let this be divided into a thousand equal small parts, or into more if possible, and let this division be extended into the rest...

--- Page 257 ---
### REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV

...according to the same parts, until the whole becomes 1414 parts, which subtends the side of a square inscribable in a circle whose radius would be a thousand parts. For the rest that remains from this rule, it will be permitted to cut it off as superfluous. On the other rule also, from the center of the joint, let a line be described equal to those thousand parts, or to that which exists between the centers of the joints, and let it have viewing apertures [*specilla*] fixed into its side, as is customary in a dioptra, through which the sight passes, so arranged that the passages themselves do not deviate at all from the line marked along the length of the rule, but are equally distant. 

Provided also that the line itself, with its end extended to the longer rule, can touch the divided line, and in this way let an isosceles triangle be made by the function of the rules, the base of which will be in the parts of the divided line. Then some pole, very well squared and smoothed, is erected and fixed, to which this instrument is attached at the rule in which both ligaments [joints] are, by certain hinges, in which (just as would befit a door) it can be revolved. In such a way, however, that the straight line which is through the center of the joints of the rule always corresponds to a plumb line, and stands at the summit [zenith] of the horizon as an axis. 

Therefore, when someone seeks the distance of any star from the summit of the horizon, when he has held the star itself correctly sighted through the apertures of the rule, with the rule with the divided line applied below, he will understand how many parts subtend the angle that exists between the sight and the axis of the horizon—of which parts the diameter of the circle would be 20 thousand—and he will have through the Canon [table] the sought circumference of the great circle between the star and the summit.

## On the parallaxes of the Moon. Chapter XVI.

With this instrument, as we said, Ptolemæus discovered the maximum latitude of the Moon to be five degrees. Then he turned himself to perceiving its parallax [*commutationem*], and says he found it at Alexandriæ to be one degree 7 minutes, while the Sun was in 5 degrees 28 minutes of Libra; the mean distance of the Moon from the Sun was 78 degrees 13 minutes. The equal [mean] anomaly was 262 degrees 20 minutes. The motion of latitude was 354 degrees 40 minutes; the additive prosthaphæresis was 7 degrees 26 minutes...

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...26 minutes, and therefore the place of the Moon was 3 degrees 9 minutes of Capricorn. The equal motion of latitude was 2 degrees 6 minutes. The Northern latitude of the Moon was 4 degrees 59 minutes. Its declination from the equinoctial was 23 degrees 49 minutes. The latitude of Alexandria was 30 degrees 58 minutes. He says the Moon was seen in nearly the meridian circle through the instrument to be 50 degrees 55 minutes from the summit of the horizon, that is, more than one degree and 7 minutes than the computation required. 

By which, according to the opinion of the ancients concerning the eccentric and epicycle, he demonstrates that the distance of the Moon from the center of the Earth then was 39 parts 45 minutes, of which the radius from the center of the Earth is one part; and those things which then follow the ratio of their circles, namely that the Moon at its maximum distance from the Earth (which they say is in the apogee of the epicycle under a new and full moon) has those same 64 parts 10 minutes, or a sixth of one [part]; but at the minimum (which in quadratures and the half-moon, being at perigee in the epicycle) only 33 parts 33 minutes. From this he also rated the parallaxes which happen around ninety degrees from the summit: the minimum as 54 minutes 34 seconds; the maximum as one degree 44 minutes, as it is permitted to see in more detail what he constructed concerning these. 

But it is now in the open for those wishing to consider it, that these things are far otherwise, as we have experienced in many ways. We shall, however, review two observed things, by which it is again declared that our hypotheses concerning the Moon are so much more certain than theirs as they more closely agree with the appearances and leave nothing of doubt. 

In the year, I say, from the birth of Christ 1522, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, five equal hours and two-thirds passed from noon around the setting of the Sun, at Fruenburgum [Frombork] we took through the parallactic instrument in the meridian circle the center of the Moon from the summit of the horizon, from which we found its distance to be 82 degrees 50 minutes. There were, therefore, from the beginning of the years of Christ up to this hour, 1522 Egyptian years, 284 days, 17 hours, and two-thirds of an hour according to appearance. But in equated time, 17 hours 24 minutes. Wherefore the apparent place of the Sun according to calculation was in the 13th degree 29 minutes of Libra. The equal motion of the Moon from the Sun was 87 degrees 6 minutes. The equal anomaly was 357 degrees...

## The distance of the Moon from the Earth, and what ratio they have in parts, of which that which is from the center of the Earth to the surface is one: a demonstration. Chapter XVII.

From these things it will now appear how great the lunar distance is from the Earth, without which a certain account of the parallaxes cannot be assigned, for they are mutually dependent; and it will be declared in this way. Let the great circle of the Earth be AB, its center C. In which also let another circle be described, to which the Earth has a notable magnitude, and let it be DE, and D the pole of the horizon, and in E the center of the Moon, so that its known distance from the summit A is DE. Since, therefore, the angle DAE in the first observation was 82 degrees 50 minutes, and ABC [was] 50 minutes, which were of the parallax: we have the triangle ACE with given angles, therefore also with given sides. For on account of the given angle CAE, side CE will be 99219 parts (of which the diameter of the circle circumscribing triangle ABC would be 100,000), and AC 1454 such parts, which are in CE nearly sixty-eight times, of which AC (which is from the center of the Earth) would be one part. And this was the distance of the Moon from the center of the Earth in the first consideration.

But in the second, the apparent angle DAE was 81 degrees 55 minutes, but the calculated ACE was 80 degrees 55 minutes, and the remainder which is under AEC was 60 minutes. Therefore, side EC is 99006 parts and AC 1747, of which the diameter of the circle circumscribing the triangle would be 100,000; and thus the distance of the Moon CE was 56 parts 41 minutes, of which the AC from the center of the Earth is one part. 

Let the greater epicycle of the Moon now be ABC, whose center is D, and let the center of the Earth E be taken, from which a straight line EBDA is drawn, so that it is the apogee A, and perigee B. Moreover, let the circumference ABC be taken as 242 degrees 10 minutes, according to the calculated equality of the lunar anomaly, and with the center made in C, let the second epicycle be described according to FGK, whose circumference FGK is 194 degrees 12 minutes of the doubled distance of the Moon from the Sun, and let DK be connected, which subtracts from the anomaly...

Therefore, the angles of triangle KDB are given in parts where 180 are two right angles; the ratio of the sides is also given: DE as 91,821 parts and EK as 86,310 parts, where the diameter of the circle circumscribing the triangle KDB itself would be 100,000; but where DE is 100,000, KE will be 93,998 parts. And yet it was shown above [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] that DF was also 8,600 such parts, and the whole DFG 13,340. Therefore, according to this given ratio, when EK is, as has been shown, 56 parts, 41 minutes (where the radius of the Earth is one), it follows [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] that DE of the same parts is 60, 18 minutes; and DF is 5 parts, 11 minutes; DFG is 8 parts, 2 minutes. Just as the whole EDG, extended into a straight line, is 68 1/3 parts, the maximum altitude of the half-moon [*Lunae diuiduae*]; also, with DG subtracted from ED, there remain 52 parts, 17 minutes, for its minimum distance. Thus also the whole BDF, which occurs at full and new moon, will be a maximum altitude of 65 1/2 parts, and with DF deducted, a minimum of 55 parts, 8 minutes. Nor indeed ought it to move us [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] that others think the maximum distance of the full and new Moon to be 64 parts, 10 minutes; especially those to whom the parallaxes [*commutationes*] of the Moon could not have become known except in part, due to the arrangement of their locations. But for us, so they might be perceived more fully, the greater proximity of the Moon to the horizon was granted, around which it is established that the parallaxes themselves are completed; and yet, despite this difference, we do not find the parallaxes to differ by more than one minute.
