**Chapter XVIII. On the diameter of the Moon and of the terrestrial shadow, in the place of the Moon’s passage.**

According to the distance of the Moon from the Earth, the apparent diameters of the Moon and the shadow also vary; wherefore it pertains to speak of these as well. And although the diameters of the Sun and Moon are correctly taken through the dioptra of Hipparchus, he nonetheless thinks this is achieved much more certainly through some partial eclipses [*defectus*] of the Moon, in which the Moon has stood equally distant from its highest or lowest apsis [*abside*], especially if then also the Sun has accommodated itself in the same way, so that the circle of the shadow, which the Moon has passed through on both sides, is found to be equal, unless [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] the eclipses themselves are in unequal parts. For it is manifest [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] that the difference of the eclipsed parts, and the latitude of the Moon compared to each other, shows how much the diameter of the Moon subtends of the circumference around the center of the Earth; having perceived this, the semi-diameter of the shadow is soon also understood. Which will become clearer by an example: as if in the middle of a prior eclipse, three digits [note: *digiti*] or inches of the Moon’s diameter were eclipsed, having a latitude of 47 prime minutes and 54 seconds; in another, ten digits, with a latitude of 29 prime minutes and 37 seconds. For the difference of the obscured parts is seven digits, [and the difference] of latitude is 18 prime minutes, 17 seconds; to which 12 digits are proportional at 31 [minutes], 20 [seconds], subtending the diameter of the Moon. It is clear, therefore, [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] that the center of the Moon in the middle of the first eclipse exceeded the shadow by a quarter of its diameter, in which there are 7 prime minutes and 50 seconds of latitude; if these are taken away from 47 prime minutes, 54 seconds of the total latitude, there remain 40 prime minutes, 4 seconds for the semi-diameter of the shadow. Just as in the other eclipse, in which, above the latitude of the Moon, [which was] 10 prime minutes, 27 seconds, the shadow occupied [it] for a third of the lunar diameter; when [these] have been added to 29 prime minutes, 37 seconds, they likewise make 40 prime minutes, 4 seconds for the semi-diameter of the shadow. Thus indeed in the opinion of Ptolemaeus, while the Sun and Moon are conjoined or opposed at the maximum distance from the Earth, the diameter of the Moon is of prime minutes

[Catchword: primorum]

***

### PAGE 263

**ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV.**

31 and a third; such as he also confesses to have found for the Sun through the dioptra of Hipparchus; but [he estimated the diameter] of the shadow to be one part, 31 prime minutes and a third, and he thought these were to each other as 13 to 5, [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] which is as a double ratio plus three-fifths [*duplum superpartiens tres quintas*].

**Chapter XIX. How the distance of the Sun and Moon from the Earth, their diameters, the shadow in the place of the Moon’s passage, and the axis of the shadow may be demonstrated simultaneously.**

Since indeed the Sun makes some parallax, which, although it is slight, is not so easily perceived, except [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] that these things cohere with each other—namely, the distance of the Sun and Moon from the Earth, their diameters, the passage of the Moon through the shadow, and the axis of the shadow—which therefore reveal each other in resolutory demonstrations. First, we shall indeed review the dogmas of Ptolemaeus concerning these, and how he demonstrated them, from which we shall elicit what shall seem most true. He assumes the apparent diameter of the Sun to be 31 prime minutes and a third, which [note: *q̃* → *quae*] he uses without distinction. To this he makes equal the diameter of the full and new Moon when it is at apogee, which [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] he says is at a distance of 64 parts and 10 minutes, where half the diameter of the Earth is one. From these he demonstrated the rest in this manner. Let the circle of the solar globe be ABC, through its center D; the terrestrial circle at its maximum distance from the Sun be EFG, through its center which [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] let be K; let the straight lines touching both be AG and CB, which being extended meet at the point [*mucronem*] of the shadow, as at sign S; and through the centers of the Sun and Earth DKS, let there also be drawn AK, KC; and let AC and GE be connected, which ought to differ very little from the diameters on account of their immense distance. Let there be taken on DKS equal parts LK, KM, according to the distances which the Moon makes at apogee when full and new, according to his opinion, 64 parts and 10 minutes, of which EK is one part; let QMR be the diameter of the shadow under the same passage of the Moon, and NOL the diameter of the Moon at right angles to DK itself; and let LOP be extended. The first proposal is to find the ratio of DK to KE. Since therefore angle NKO was 31 minutes and a third, of which 360 parts are four right angles,

**Chapter XXI. On the apparent diameter of the Sun and its parallaxes.**

Since indeed the same magnitudes appear smaller when more remote than when nearer, it happens for that reason that the Sun, Moon, and the Earth's shadow vary, according to their unequal distances from the Earth, no less than the parallaxes. All of which are easily discerned from the aforesaid at any other elongation. First, indeed, this is manifest in the Sun. For since we have demonstrated that the Earth is 10,323 parts distant from it at the most remote point (where the radius of the annual revolution's orbit is 10,000), and 9,678 parts at the nearest remaining diameter. In those parts, therefore, where the highest apsis is 1179 (where the Earth's radius is one), the lowest will be of 1105 of the same parts, just as the mean is 1142 parts. Therefore, when we have divided 100,000 by 1179, we shall have 848 parts, subtending in a right-angled triangle the minimum angle of 2 prime minutes, 55 seconds, of the maximum parallax which happens around the horizon. Similarly, having divided a million by 1105 parts of the minimum distance, there result 905 particles, subtending an angle of 3 prime minutes, 7 seconds, of the maximum parallax of the lowest apsis. Moreover, it has been shown [note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] that the diameter of the Sun is 5 parts, 27 minutes, where the diameter of the Earth is one part, so that at the highest apsis it appears as 31 prime minutes, 48 seconds. For the parts 1179 are proportional to 5 parts, 27 minutes; and as 200,000 of the circle's diameter to 9245, which subtend 31 prime minutes, 48 seconds. ### On the diameter of the Moon and the Earth's shadow, at the place of the Moon's crossing. Chapter 18.

**B**ecause the apparent diameters of the Moon and the shadow also vary according to the Moon's distance from the Earth, it is pertinent to speak of these matters as well. And although the diameters of the Sun and Moon are correctly captured through the <term>dioptra</term> <note>A classical astronomical sighting instrument used for measuring altitudes or the angular diameters of celestial bodies.</note> of Hipparchus, it is nonetheless judged that this is achieved with much greater certainty through certain partial <term>eclipses</term> <note>original: *defectus*</note> of the Moon. In these instances, the Moon should be at an equal distance from its highest or lowest <term>apsis</term> <note>original: *abside*. The points in an orbit where a body is closest to or farthest from the center of motion.</note>, especially if the Sun has also positioned itself in the same way, so that the circle of the shadow—which the Moon passes through in both cases—is found to be equal, unless the eclipses themselves occur in unequal parts. For it is manifest that the difference between the obscured parts and the latitude of the Moon, when compared to each other, shows how much of the circumference around the center of the Earth the diameter of the Moon subtends; once this is perceived, the semi-diameter of the shadow is also soon understood.

This will become clearer by an example. Suppose that in the middle of a first eclipse, three <term>digits</term> <note>original: *digiti*. A traditional unit for measuring eclipses; the diameter of the celestial body is divided into 12 digits or "inches" (*unciae*).</note> or twelfths of the lunar diameter were obscured, with the Moon having a latitude of 47 minutes and 54 seconds. In a second eclipse, ten digits were obscured, with a latitude of 29 minutes and 37 seconds. The difference in the obscured parts is seven digits; the difference in latitude is 18 minutes and 17 seconds. To these, 12 digits are proportional to 31 minutes and 20 seconds, which subtend the diameter of the Moon. It is clear, therefore, that the center of the Moon in the middle of the first eclipse exceeded the shadow by a quarter of its diameter, in which there are 7 minutes and 50 seconds of latitude. If these are taken away from the 47 minutes and 54 seconds of the total latitude, there remain 40 minutes and 4 seconds for the semi-diameter of the shadow. Just as in the other eclipse, in which the shadow occupied a third part of the lunar diameter beyond the latitude of the Moon (being 10 minutes and 27 seconds), when these are added to the 29 minutes and 37 seconds, they likewise produce 40 minutes and 4 seconds for the semi-diameter of the shadow. Indeed, according to the opinion of Ptolemy, while the Sun and Moon are joined or in opposition at their maximum distance from the Earth, the diameter of the Moon is

of the first <note>original: *primorum*. Catchword for the next page.</note>

By these same units, LK is 64 parts and 10 minutes, or KB is one part. And according to the fact that the ratio of LO to MR is as 5 is to 13, MR will be 45 minutes and 38 seconds in the same units. Now, because LOP and MR are at equal intervals and are parallel to KE itself, LOP and MR together will therefore be double KB. After rejecting <note>meaning: subtracting</note> MR and LO from that total, there remained OP, being 56 minutes and 49 seconds. However, according to the second theorem of the sixth book of Euclid, the proportions of EC to PC, KC to OC, and KD to LD are in the same ratio as KB to OP; that is, 60 minutes to 58 minutes and 48 seconds. Similarly, LD is given as 56 minutes and 49 seconds, where the whole DLK would be one part; and the remainder KL is therefore 3 minutes and 11 seconds. However, insofar as KL was 64 parts and 10 minutes (where EK is one), then the whole distance KD will be 1210 parts. Now it has become clear that MR, in such units, was 45 minutes and 38 seconds. Since the ratio of KE to MR and KMS to MS is established, then for the whole KMS, KM itself will be 14 minutes and 22 seconds; and by division <note>original: *diuisim*. A geometric method of comparing ratios by subtracting the denominator from the numerator.</note>, where KM was 64 parts and 10 minutes, the whole length of the shadow axis KMS will be 268 parts. Thus indeed thought Ptolemy. But others after Ptolemy, because they found that these things did not sufficiently agree with the appearances <note>i.e., observed data</note>, set forth certain other things concerning them. They confess, nonetheless, that the maximum distance of the Full and New Moon from the Earth is 64 parts and 10 minutes. They grant that the apparent diameter of the Sun at <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the Sun's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth.</note> is 31 minutes and a third; they also grant that the diameter of the shadow at the place of the Moon’s crossing is as 13 to 5, just as Ptolemy himself did. Nevertheless, they deny that the apparent diameter of the Moon is then greater than 29 and a half minutes, and for that reason, they set the diameter of the shadow at one part and 16 minutes with nearly <term>three-quarters</term> <note>original: *dodrante*. An ancient Roman term for 3/4.</note>. From these values, they think it follows that the distance of the Sun at apogee from the Earth is 1146 parts, and the axis of the shadow is 254 parts, where the radius of the Earth is one,

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

Therefore, the diameter of the Earth is to the diameter of the Moon as seven is to two—that is, a ratio of three and a half <note>original: *tripla sesquialtera*. In classical mathematics, "sesquialtera" refers to the ratio 3:2 or 1.5; when combined as "triple sesquialtera," it signifies 3.5 or 7/2.</note>. When this ratio is cubed <note>original: *triplata*. ### On the Apparent Diameter of the Sun and its Parallaxes. Chapter XXI.

**S**ince, in truth, the same magnitudes appear smaller when they are farther away than when they are closer, it happens because of this that the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth's shadow vary according to their unequal distances from the Earth, no less than their <term>parallaxes</term> <note>original: *commutationes*. Parallax is the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points; here, it refers to the difference in the Sun's position as seen from the Earth's surface versus its center.</note> do. All these things are easily discerned from the previous statements for any other distance.

First, indeed, this is manifest in the Sun. For we have demonstrated that the Earth's farthest distance from the Sun is 10,323 parts (where the radius of the annual revolution's orbit is 10,000 parts), and at the other end of the diameter, it is 9,678 parts at its closest. In those units where the radius from the center of the Earth is one, the highest <term>apsis</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of attraction.</note> is 1,179 parts; the lowest is 1,105 parts; and the middle distance is 1,142 parts. 

Therefore, when we have divided 100,000 by 1,179, we obtain 84.8 parts, which, in a <term>right-angled triangle</term> <note>original: *orthogonio*</note>, subtend the smallest angle of 2 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: *scrupulis primorum*. A "first small part" or 1/60th of a degree.</note> and 55 <term>seconds</term> <note>original: *secundorum*. A "second small part" or 1/3600th of a degree.</note> of maximum parallax occurring at the horizon. Similarly, by dividing 1,000,000 by 1,105 (the distance at the lowest apsis), there result 905 parts, which subtend an angle of 3 minutes and 7 seconds for the maximum parallax at the lowest apsis. 

It has been shown, however, that the diameter of the Sun is 5 parts and 27 minutes (where the Earth's diameter is one part), so that at the highest apsis it appears as 31 minutes and 48 seconds. For the ratio of 1,179 parts to 5 parts and 27 minutes is the same as the ratio of 200,000 (the diameter of a circle) to 9,245, which subtends 31 minutes and 48 seconds. It follows that at the minimum distance of 1,105 parts, the diameter appears as 33 minutes and 54 seconds. The difference between these values is 2 minutes and 6 seconds. ### On the Unequally Apparent Diameter of the Moon and its Parallaxes. Chapter XXII.

**A** greater diversity of both appears in the Moon, as it is the closest celestial body. For the most remote half-moon, the parallax is 50 minutes and 18 seconds. For the full and new moon at its farthest, it is 51 minutes and 24 seconds. For the closest full and new moon, it is 62 minutes and 21 seconds; and for the closest half-moon, it is 65 minutes and 45 seconds. From these, the apparent diameters of the Moon are also clear. ### On the Reason for the Variation of the Earth's Shadow. Chapter XXIII.

**W**e have already shown that the ratio of the diameter of the shadow to the diameter of the Moon is as 403 to 150. Thus, the greatest difference is 14 minutes and 8 seconds. The Earth's shadow also varies during any given transit of the Moon because of the Earth's unequal distance from the Sun, in this manner: Let the straight line DKS be repeated, as in the preceding figure, passing through the centers of the Sun and the Earth, along with the lines of tangency CES, with DC and KE joined.

### A Tabular Exposition of the Specific Parallaxes of the Sun and Moon in the Circle passing through the Zenith. Chapter XXIV.

**N**ow it will no longer be uncertain how to determine the individual parallaxes <note><term>parallax</term>: the apparent shift in a celestial body's position when viewed from the surface of the Earth compared to its "true" position as seen from the Earth's center.</note> of the Sun and Moon. In the same plane, let DE be the circle of the Moon and FG the circle of the Sun. Let the line CDF pass through the zenith, and CEG be the line in which the true positions of the Sun and Moon are understood to be; let the lines of sight AG and AE be connected to those positions. Therefore, the parallaxes of the Sun are determined by the angle AGC, and those of the Moon by the angle AEC. The difference in position between the Sun and Moon is the angle GAE, which remains as the difference between the angles AGC and AEC.

Let us now take the angle ACG <note>This represents the altitude or "zenith distance" of the planet or star.</note>, to which we wish to compare those parallaxes. Let it be, for example <note>original: *verbi gratia*</note>, 30 degrees. It is clear from the demonstrations of plane geometry <note>original: *triangulorum planorum*</note> that when we set the line CG at 1,142 parts—where AC <note>The radius of the Earth.</note> is one—the angle AGC, by which the true altitude of the Sun differs from the observed altitude, will be one and a half minutes. When, however, the angle ACG is 60 degrees, AGC will be 2 minutes and 36 seconds. The other values will be revealed in a similar way. We have organized the Table itself into nine columns <note>original: *ordines*. Literally "orders" or "rows," but here referring to the vertical columns of the table.</note>. In the fifth, the minimum parallaxes which occur when the Moon is at its half-phase <note>original: *dividua*. Referring to the first or last quarter moon.</note> and at its furthest point from Earth (apogee); these are less than the parallaxes that follow at the full and new moon. The sixth column will contain those parallaxes produced by the full or "thirsty" Moon <note>original: *sitiens Luna*. The minutes that follow are the differences by which the parallaxes occurring when the Moon is at its half-phase and closest to us exceed the ones near to them. Finally, the remaining two spaces that are left over are reserved for the "proportional minutes." By these, the parallaxes can be calculated between these four limits. Let **AB** be the first epicycle of the Moon, the center of which is **C**; and once the center of the Earth **D** is taken, let the straight line **DBCA** be drawn. At the apogee **A**, with a center established, let a second epicycle **EFG** be described. Moreover, let the arc **EG** be taken as 60 degrees, and let **AG** and **CG** be connected. Since, therefore, in the preceding [sections] straight lines were demonstrated of 5 parts [and] 11 minutes [*scrupulorum*], of which the radius of the Earth is one; of which also **DC** is 60 parts [and] 18 minutes; and of these same, **EF** is 2 parts [and] 51 minutes. Therefore, in the triangle **ACG**, the sides **GA** of 1 part [and] 25 minutes and **AC** of 6 parts [and] 36 minutes are given, with the angle **CAG** contained by them. Therefore, through the [principles] demonstrated for plane triangles, the third side **CG** of the same [units] will be 6 parts [and] 7 minutes. Therefore, the whole [line] **DCG** brought into a straight line, or **DCL** equal to it, will be 66 parts [and] 25 minutes. But **DCE** was 65 ½ parts. There remains, therefore, the excess **EL** of approximately 55 ½ minutes. And through this given ratio, when **DCE** is 60 parts, **EF** of the same will be 2 parts [and] 37 minutes, [and] **EL** [will be] 46 minutes. Insofar, therefore, as **EF** is 60 minutes, the excess **EL** will be approximately 18 [minutes]. We shall mark these in the seventh place of the Table [*Canon*] in the region of 60 degrees. Similarly, we shall show [the same] around the perigee **B**, in which the second epicycle **MNO** is repeated with the angle **MBN** of 60 degrees; for the triangle **BCN** will be formed, as before, from given sides and angles, and similarly the excess **MP** [will be] approximately 55 ½ minutes, of which the radius of the Earth is one. But since **DBM** is 55 parts [and] 8 minutes of the same, which if it were established as 60 parts, such [a line] **MBO** would be 3 parts [and] 7 minutes, and the excess **MP** 55 minutes. As 3 parts and 8 minutes is to 55 minutes, so is 60 to approximately 18, and the same as before; yet they differ by a few seconds. In this way we shall also proceed in the other [cases], with which we shall complete the eighth column of the Table. If, in place of these, we used those things which were set forth in the Table of Prosthaphaereses, we would by no means commit an error, for they are almost the same, and it deals with the smallest things.

# On the calculation of the parallax of the Sun and Moon. Chapter XXV.

[Decorative Initial M] We shall also briefly set forth the method of calculating the parallaxes of the Sun and Moon through the Table. For we shall take the occurring parallaxes in the table through the doubled distance from the zenith of the Sun or Moon. Of the Sun indeed simply; but of the Moon in its four limits, and with the motion of the Moon, or its doubled distance from the Sun, the first proportional minutes, with which we shall take the proportional parts of the excess of both the first and last term to 60, which we shall always subtract from the next following parallax [*commutatione*], and the latter [minutes] we shall always add to that which is in the penultimate limit; and we shall have two rectified parallaxes of the Moon in the apogee and perigee, which the minor epicycle increases or diminishes. Then, with the lunar anomaly, we shall take the last proportional minutes, by which we shall also take a proportional part from the difference of the parallaxes recently found, which we shall always add to the first examined parallax, which is in the apogee, and the sought parallax of the Moon will come forth for the place and time, as in the example. Let the distance from the zenith of the Moon be 54 parts, the mean motion of the Moon 15 parts, the adjusted anomaly 100 parts. I wish to find from these through the Table the lunar parallax: I double the parts of the distance, they become 108, to which in the Table corresponds the excess between the first and second limit, 1 minute [*scrupulum*] [and] 48 seconds; the parallax of the second term 42 minutes [and] 50 seconds; the parallax of the third limit 50 minutes [and] 49 seconds. The excess of the third and fourth [limit] 2 minutes [and] 46 seconds; which I note individually. The doubled motion of the Moon makes 30 parts; with this I find the first proportional minutes [as] five, by which I take the proportional part to 60; and they are 9 seconds from the first excess; these I subtract from the 42 minutes 50 seconds of parallax, there remain 42 minutes 41 seconds. Similarly from the second excess, which was 2 minutes 46 seconds, the proportional part is 14 seconds, which I add to the 50 minutes 49 seconds of the second parallax; they become 51 minutes 13 seconds. Now the difference of these parallaxes is 8 minutes 32 seconds. After this, with the adjusted anomaly, I take the extreme proportional minutes, which are 34; and through these I take the proportional part of the difference 8 minutes 31 seconds [sic], and it is 4 minutes 50 seconds.

---

### PAGE 276

[[original page: 127 verso]]
### NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

Which I add to the first adjusted parallax, and 47 minutes 31 seconds are collected; and this will be the sought parallax of the Moon in the circle of altitude.

# How parallaxes of longitude and latitude are distinguished. Chapter XXVI.

[Decorative Initial D] Parallax is distinguished into longitude and latitude simply, or that which is between the Sun and Moon, through the circumferences and angles of the circles intersecting each other, the zodiac [*signiferi*] and that which is through the poles of the horizon. Since it is manifest that when this circle rests upon the zodiac at right angles, it effects no parallax of longitude, but all passes into latitude, the circle of latitude and altitude being the same. But where it happens conversely that the zodiac stands upright to the horizon, and becomes the same as the circle of altitude, then if the Moon were free of latitude, it admits no other than a parallax of longitude. But if distracted in latitude, it will not escape some parallax [*commutationem*] of longitude. For example, if **ABC** is the zodiacal circle, which stands upright to the horizon, and **A** is the pole of the horizon. Therefore the orb **ABC** itself will be the same as the circle of altitude of the Moon lacking latitude, whose place were **B**, and its whole parallax **BC** will be in longitude. But when it also has latitude, once the circle **DBE** is described through the poles of the zodiac, taking the latitude of the Moon **DB**, or **BE**, it is manifest that side **AD**, or **AE**, will not be equal to **AD** [sic], nor will the angle which is under **D** or **E** be a right angle, since **DA**, **AE** are not circles through the poles of **DBE** itself, and the parallax will participate in something of latitude, and all the more so the closer the Moon is to the zenith. For with the same base **DE** of the triangle **ADE** remaining, the shorter sides **AD**, **AE** will contain sharper angles at the base. And the more the Moon stands away from the zenith, the more those angles will become similar to right angles. Now let the circle of altitude of the Moon **DBE** be oblique to the zodiac **ABC**, not having latitude, as in the ecliptic section, which is

[Geometric Diagram: Triangle A-D-E with altitude B-C.]

---

### PAGE 277

[[original page: 128]]
### ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.

which is **B**. Moreover, the parallax in the circle of altitude is **BE**, and let the circumference **EF** of the circle be drawn through the poles of **ABC** itself. Since therefore in triangle **BEF**, the angle which is under **EBF** is given, as shown above, and that at **F** is a right angle, and side **BE** is given. Therefore, through the demonstrated [principles] of spherical triangles, the remaining sides **BF**, **FE** are given; the latter of latitude, the former of longitude, corresponding to **BE** itself. But since **BE**, **EF**, **FB** differ by a small and insensible amount from straight lines due to their brevity, we shall not err if we use the right-angled triangle as if it were rectilinear, and for that reason the calculation will become easy. It is more difficult when the Moon has latitude. For let the zodiac **ABC** be repeated, to which the orb through the poles of the horizon **DB** falls obliquely, and let **B** be the place of the Moon’s longitude, with northern latitude **FB**, or southern **BE**. From the zenith of the horizon, which is **D**, let the circles of altitude **DEK**, **DFC** descend upon the Moon itself, in which the parallaxes are **EK**, **FG**. For the true places of the Moon according to longitude and latitude will be in signs **E**, **F**, but the visible ones in **K**, **G**, from which let circumferences be drawn at right angles to the zodiac **ABC** itself, which are **KM**, **LG**. Since therefore the longitude and latitude of the Moon are established with the latitude of the region, two sides **DB**, **BE** and the angle of intersection **ABD** will be known in triangle **DEB**, and with the right angle the whole **DBE**; for that reason also the remaining side **DE**, with angle **DEB**, will be given. Similarly in triangle **DBF**, when the two sides **DB**, **BF** are given with angle **DBF**, which is the remainder of that which is under **AB**... [garbled OCR] it will also give **DF** with angle **DFB**. Therefore the parallax **EK** and **FG** of both circumferences **DE**, **DF** is given through the Table, and the true distance of the Moon from the zenith **DE** or **DF**. Similarly also the visible [distance] **DEK**, or **DFG**. And in triangle **EBN**, once the intersection of **DE** with the zodiac is made at point **N**, angle **NEB** is given and **NBE** is a right angle, with base **BE**; the remaining angle which is under **BNE** will also be known, with the remaining sides **BN**, **NE**. Similarly also in the whole triangle **NKM**, from the given angles at **M**, **N**, and the whole side **KEN**, the base **KM** will be established. And this is the visible southern latitude of the Moon, whose excess over **BE** is the parallax of latitude, and the remaining side **NBM** is given, from which **NB** having been taken away, the parallax of longitude **BM** remains. Just as also in the northern triangle **BFC**, when side **BF** is given with angle **BFC**,

[Geometric Diagrams: Spherical triangles and intersecting arcs showing longitude/latitude corrections.]

---

### PAGE 278

[[original page: 128 verso]]
### NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

and right angle **B**, the remaining sides **BLC** and **FGC** are given, with the remaining angle **C**, and by the subtraction of **FG** from **FGC**, the given side **GC** remains in triangle **GLC**, with two angles **LCG** and **CLG** being a right angle; for that reason the remaining sides **GL**, **LC** are given, and then that which remains from **BC**, and that is **BL** the parallax of longitude, and **GL** the visible latitude, whose parallax is the excess of the true latitude **BF**. Nevertheless, as you see, that calculation has more labor than fruit, since it is concerned with the smallest things. For it will be sufficient if we use **ABD** for angle **DCB**, and **DBF** for **DEB**, and simply, as before, use the mean **DB** for the circumferences **DE**, **EF**, neglecting the lunar latitude; nor for that reason will an error appear, especially in regions of the Northern tract, but in very Southern parts, where **B** happens to reach the zenith of the horizon with a maximum latitude of five degrees, and the Moon being closest to the Earth, the difference is almost six minutes. Moreover, in solar eclipses [*eclipticis Solis coniunctionibus*], in which the latitude of the Moon cannot exceed one and a half degrees, it can be only one and three-quarters minutes. From these things, therefore, it is manifest that in the eastern quadrant of the zodiac, the parallax of longitude is always added to the true place of the Moon, and in the other quadrant it is always subtracted, so that we may have the visible longitude of the Moon. And the visible latitude [is found] through the parallax of latitude: since if they were in the same [direction], they are joined together; if in different [directions], the smaller is subtracted from the larger, and what remains is the visible latitude of that part toward which the larger declines.

# Confirmation of those things which have been set forth concerning the parallaxes of the Moon. Chapter XXVII.

[Decorative Initial Q] Therefore, that the parallaxes of the Moon thus set forth are conformable to appearances, we can affirm by several other experiments, such as this one which we had at Bologna on the seventh day before the Ides of March after sunset, in the year of Christ 1497. For we observed that the Moon

---

### PAGE 279

[[original page: 129]]
### ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.

was about to occult the bright star of the Hyades, which the Romans call Palilicium [Aldebaran]; having waited for this, we saw the star applied to the dark part of the lunar body, and already hiding between the horns of the Moon in the fifth hour of the night, but closer to the Southern horn by about a third of the latitude or diameter of the Moon. And since the star, according to calculation, was in 2 degrees and 52 minutes of Gemini with a Southern latitude of five and one-sixth degrees, it was manifest that the center of the Moon according to sight preceded the star by half a diameter, and for that reason its visible place in longitude was 2 parts [and] 36 minutes. In latitude, approximately 5 parts [and] 2 minutes. Therefore, from the beginning of the years of Christ there were 1497 Egyptian years, 76 days, 23 hours at Bologna; but at Kraków, which is more eastern by about 9 degrees, 24 hours [and] 36 minutes, to which the equation adds 4 minutes; for the Sun was in 28 ½ parts of Pisces. Therefore, the mean motion of the Moon from the Sun was 74 parts. The adjusted anomaly was 111 parts [and] 10 minutes. The true place of the Moon was 3 parts [and] 24 minutes of Gemini, the Southern latitude 4 parts [and] 35 minutes. For the true motion of latitude was 203 parts [and] 41 minutes. At that time also at Bologna, the 26th degree of Scorpio was rising, with an angle of 59 ½ parts; and the Moon was 84 parts from the zenith of the horizon, and the angle of intersection of the circles of altitude and the zodiac was approximately 29 parts. The parallax of the Moon [was] one part: of longitude 51 minutes, of latitude 30 minutes; which agree very well with the observation, so that no one should doubt that our hypotheses and the things produced from them are correctly established.

# On the mean conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun and Moon. Chapter XXVIII.

[Decorative Initial E] From those things which have been said thus far concerning the motion of the Moon and Sun, the method of investigating their conjunctions and oppositions is opened. For at a time near to that which we estimated this or that would be, we shall seek the mean motion of the Moon, which if we find to have already completed the circle, we understand it to be a conjunction; in a semicircle

---

### PAGE 280

[[original page: 129 verso]]
### NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

a full [Moon]. But since that presents itself more rarely, the distance between them must be considered, which when we have divided by the daily motion of the Moon, we shall know by how much time it preceded the other, or is to be, according as we had more or less in the motion. For this time, therefore, we shall seek the motions and places, by which we shall calculate the true new moons and full lunations, and we shall distinguish their ecliptic conjunctions from others, as we shall indicate below. Once we have these established, it will be permitted to extend them to any other months, and to continue them for several years through the Table of twelve months, containing the times and mean motions of the anomaly of the Sun and Moon, and the latitude of the Moon, to be joined each to each to those formerly found even as equals. But to the anomaly of the Sun we shall add [the amount] truly, so that we may have it adjusted immediately; nor indeed in one or several years will its diversity be felt due to the slowness of its beginning, that is, of the highest apsis.

What remains are the proportional minutes <term>proportional minutes: "scrupula proportionum"; these are interpolation factors used to calculate values between the "middle limits" of an orbit</term>, which are within the middle limits, namely between the second and third. Let the first epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle</term> be marked as **AB** at the Full and New Moon, its center being **C**; let **D** be taken as the center of the Earth, and let the straight line **DBCA** be extended. Also, let an arc **AE** of 60 degrees be taken from the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</term> **A**. ### BOOK IV OF THE REVOLUTIONS

# On the calculation of the parallax of the Sun and Moon. Chapter 25.

We shall also briefly explain the method of calculating the parallaxes <note>Parallax is the displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</note> of the Sun and Moon by means of the Table <note>original: "Canonem" — referring to the mathematical table of values provided in the preceding chapters.</note>. Indeed, by doubling the distance from the zenith <note>original: "a uertice" — the point in the sky directly above the observer.</note> of the Sun or Moon, we will find the corresponding parallaxes in the table. For the Sun, this is done simply; for the Moon, however, we look at its four limits, and with the motion of the Moon—that is, its doubled distance from the Sun—we find the first proportional minutes <note>original: "scrupula proportionum" — small units of arc used to adjust values based on ratios.</note>. With these, we will take the proportional parts (out of 60) of the difference between the first and last terms. We will always subtract these parts from the next following parallax <note>original: "commutatione" — another term for parallax, literally meaning a 'change' or shift.</note>, and always add the subsequent ones to the value found in the second-to-last limit.

By this method, we will have two rectified parallaxes of the Moon, one at its farthest point from Earth <note>original: "apogaeo" — apogee.</note> and one at its nearest point <note>original: "perigaeo" — perigee.</note>, which the smaller epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; Copernicus uses these to account for the varying distances of the planets.</note> increases or decreases. Then, using the adjusted lunar anomaly <note>original: "anomalia" — the position of the Moon within its own orbital cycle.</note>, we take the final proportional minutes. By these, we also take a proportional part of the difference between the parallaxes we just found; we always add this to the first investigated parallax (the one at apogee), and the result will be the required parallax of the Moon for that specific place and time, as shown in the following example.

Let the distance of the Moon from the zenith be 54 degrees, the mean motion of the Moon be 15 degrees, and the adjusted anomaly be 100 degrees. I wish to find the lunar parallax from the Table using these figures. I double the degrees of distance, making 108. In the Table, the difference between the first and second limit corresponds to 1 minute and 48 seconds <note>original: "scrup. primum unu, secunda XLVIII"</note>. The parallax of the second term is 42 minutes and 50 seconds; the parallax of the third limit is 50 minutes and 49 seconds. The difference between the third and fourth is 2 minutes and 46 seconds; I note these down individually.

The doubled motion of the Moon makes 30 degrees. With this, I find the first proportional minutes to be 5. Using these, I take a proportional part (relative to 60) from the first difference, which is 9 seconds. I subtract these from the 42 minutes and 50 seconds of the parallax; 42 minutes and 41 seconds remain. Similarly, for the second difference, which was 2 minutes and 46 seconds, the proportional part is 14 seconds. I add these to the 50 minutes and 49 seconds of the second parallax, making 51 minutes and 13 seconds. The difference between these two parallaxes is 8 minutes and 32 seconds. After this, with the adjusted anomaly, I take the final proportional minutes, which are 34. Through these, I take the proportional part of the 8 minute 31 second difference <note>The text here says 8' 31", though the previous sentence calculated it as 8' 32"; such minor discrepancies are common in early astronomical manuscripts.</note>, which is 4 minutes and 50 seconds.

<note>Vocabulary: **parallax** (apparent shift), **Table/Rule** (mathematical reference), **anomaly** (orbital position), **shift** (parallax), **proportional** (ratio-based), **apogee** (farthest point), **perigee** (nearest point).</note>

Copernicus demonstrates how to interpolate between values to find a precise measurement for the Moon's apparent shift in the sky.</summary>

# How the parallaxes of longitude and latitude are resolved. Chapter 26.

**D**istinguishing the parallax into longitude and latitude is done simply—whether it is the parallax between the Sun and Moon or otherwise—by using the circumferences and angles of the intersecting circles: the <term>zodiac <gloss>original: "signifer," meaning the "sign-bearer"</gloss></term> and the circle passing through the poles of the horizon <note>This refers to the vertical circle of altitude.</note>. For it is clear that when this circle [of altitude] sits at right angles to the zodiac, it produces no parallax in longitude; instead, the entire shift passes into latitude, since the circle of latitude and the circle of altitude are the same.

But when, conversely, it happens that the zodiac stands perpendicular to the horizon and becomes identical with the circle of altitude, then if the Moon were to have no latitude <note>Meaning the Moon is sitting exactly on the ecliptic line.</note>, it would experience no parallax other than that of longitude. However, if the Moon is shifted into latitude [away from the ecliptic], it will not escape having some change in its longitude.

For example, let **ABC** be the circle of the zodiac standing perpendicular to the horizon, and let **A** be the pole of the horizon <note>The zenith, or the point directly above the observer.</note>. Therefore, the circle **ABC** itself will be the same as the circle of altitude for a Moon that lacks latitude. If the Moon's position is at **B**, its entire shift <note>original: "commutatio" — used here as a synonym for parallax.</note> **BC** will be in longitude. 

But when the Moon also possesses latitude, we describe a circle **DBE** through the poles of the zodiac. Taking the latitude of the Moon as **DB** or **BE**, it is clear that the side **AD** or **AE** [in the diagram] will not be equal to **AB**. Nor will the angle at **D** or **E** be a right angle, since **DA** and **AE** are not circles passing through the poles of the circle **DBE**. Thus, the parallax shift will involve some latitude, and all the more so the closer the Moon is to the vertex <note>The zenith.</note>. For while the base **DE** of the triangle **ADE** remains the same, the shorter sides **AD** and **AE** will enclose more acute angles at the base. And the further the Moon is from the vertex, the more these angles will become like right angles.

Now, let the circle of altitude of the Moon **DBE** be oblique <note>Tilted at an angle.</note> to the zodiac **ABC**, for a Moon having no latitude, as in an ecliptic section, which is...

->[[image: A geometric diagram. Point A is at the top (the zenith). A vertical line drops down to point B and continues to C. A horizontal line crosses through B, with point D on the left and point E on the right, forming a cross shape within a triangular framework.]]<-

<summary>Copernicus explains how to calculate the components of parallax, showing that the apparent shift of the Moon depends on the angle between the zodiac and the observer's horizon. He uses geometric triangles to demonstrate how a single vertical shift is divided into changes in longitude and latitude.</summary>

...which is at point **B**. The parallax in the <term>circle of altitude <gloss>a vertical circle reaching from the point directly overhead to the horizon</gloss></term> is **BE**, and let arc **EF** of a circle be drawn through the poles of the <term>zodiac <gloss>original: "signifer"</gloss></term> **ABC**. Therefore, since in triangle **BEF**, the angle at **EBF** is given (as shown above), and the angle at **F** is a right angle, and side **BE** is also given, then by the laws of spherical triangles, the remaining sides **BF** and **FE** are given. **FE** represents the parallax in latitude and **BF** the parallax in longitude, corresponding to the total shift **BE**. 

But because **BE**, **EF**, and **FB** differ from straight lines by such a tiny and imperceptible amount due to their shortness, we will not error if we use this right triangle as if it were a flat, <term>rectilinear <gloss>made of straight lines</gloss></term> triangle; this makes the calculation easy. <note>Copernicus is explaining a common mathematical shortcut: when dealing with very small portions of a sphere, the surface is "flat enough" to use simpler plane geometry instead of complex spherical trigonometry.</note>

The calculation is more difficult when the Moon already possesses its own latitude. Let the zodiac **ABC** be represented again, which the <term>oblique circle <gloss>the circle of altitude</gloss></term> **DB** intersects through the poles of the horizon. Let **B** be the Moon's position in longitude, with its latitude being **FB** to the North, or **BE** to the South. From the <term>vertex of the horizon <gloss>the zenith, or the point directly overhead</gloss></term>, which is **D**, let the circles of altitude **DEK** and **DFC** descend upon the Moon itself; in these circles, the <term>parallaxes <gloss>original: "commutationes"</gloss></term> are **EK** and **FG**. 

The true positions of the Moon in longitude and latitude will be at points **E** and **F**, but the seen (apparent) positions will be at **K** and **G**. From these points, let arcs **KM** and **LG** be drawn at right angles to the zodiac **ABC**. Now, when the longitude and latitude of the Moon are established along with the latitude of the region <note>Meaning the observer's geographic latitude on Earth.</note>, two sides of the triangle **DEB** (**DB** and **BE**) will be known, as well as the angle of intersection **ABD**, and the total angle **DBE** (including the right angle). Therefore, the remaining side **DE** and the angle **DEB** will be given. 

Similarly, in triangle **DBF**, since the two sides **DB** and **BF** are given along with the angle **DBF** (which is what remains of the right angle at **AB**), it will also give the side **DF** along with the angle **DFB**. Thus, for both arcs **DE** and **DF**, the parallax (**EK** and **FG**) is found through the <term>Table <gloss>original: "Canon"</gloss></term> of Parallaxes, as is the true distance of the Moon from the zenith (**DE** or **DF**). The same applies to the seen distances **DEK** or **DFG**. 

Furthermore, in triangle **EBN**, created by the intersection of **DE** with the zodiac at point **N**, the angle **NEB** is given, and **NBE** is a right angle; with the base **BE** known, the remaining angle **BNE** will be known, along with the remaining sides **BN** and **NE**. Likewise, in the whole triangle **NKM**, from the given angles at **M** and **N** and the whole side **KEN**, the base **KM** will be established. This is the Moon's apparent Southern latitude; the amount by which it exceeds **BE** is the parallax of latitude. Additionally, the remaining side **NBM** is given; when **NB** is subtracted from it, the remainder **BM** is the parallax of longitude. Just as in the Northern triangle **BFC**, when the side **BF** is given with the angle **BFC**...

Points are labeled with letters (D, E, F, G, K, L, M, N) to correspond with the geometric proof in the text.]]

### BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...and **B** being a right angle, the remaining sides **BLC** and **FGC** are given, along with the remaining angle **C**. By subtracting **FG** from **FGC**, the side **GC** remains given in triangle **GLC**. Since the two angles **LCG** and **CLG** are right angles, the remaining sides **GL** and **LC** are also given. Consequently, what remains from **BC** is **BL**, which is the <term>parallax in longitude <gloss>original: "commutatio longitudinis"</gloss></term>, and **GL** is the <term>apparent latitude <gloss>the latitude as it appears to an observer on Earth's surface rather than from its center</gloss></term>, the parallax of which is the difference from the true latitude **BF**. 

Nevertheless, as you see, this calculation, which is worked out for the smallest details, involves more labor than benefit. For it will be sufficient if we use angle **ABD** in place of **DCB**, and **DBF** in place of **DEB**, and simply use the mean **DB** as we did before for the arcs **DE** and **EF**, neglecting the lunar latitude. No perceptible error will arise from this, especially in the Northern regions. Only in the far Southern parts, where **B** might reach the <term>zenith <gloss>the point directly overhead</gloss></term> while at its maximum latitude of five degrees and with the Moon at its closest point to the Earth, would the difference be nearly six minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum". In astronomical measurement, a minute is 1/60th of a degree.</note>. 

In <term>solar eclipses <gloss>original: "eclipticis Solis coniunctionibus"</gloss></term>, where the Moon's latitude cannot exceed one and a half degrees, the difference can be only one and three-quarters minutes <note>original: "scrupuli unius & dodrantis". A "dodrans" is a Roman term for three-quarters.</note>. From these things, therefore, it is manifest that in the eastern quadrant of the <term>zodiac <gloss>original: "signiferi", literally the "sign-bearer"</gloss></term>, the parallax in longitude is always added to the true position of the Moon, and in the other quadrant it is always subtracted, so that we may have the apparent longitude of the Moon. We find the apparent latitude through the parallax in latitude: if they are in the same direction, they are added together; if in different directions, the smaller is subtracted from the larger, and the result is the apparent latitude in the direction of the larger value.

# Confirmation of the explanations regarding the parallaxes of the Moon. Chapter XXVII.

**Q**uince then, we can affirm that the parallaxes of the Moon set forth in this way are in accordance with the <term>appearances <gloss>the actual observed positions in the sky</gloss></term> through many other experiments. One such experiment is the observation we made at Bologna on the seventh day before the Ides of March <note>March 9th</note>, after sunset, in the year of Christ 1497. For we observed that the Moon... <note>This is a famous early observation by Copernicus where he watched the Moon occult (pass in front of) the star Aldebaran, proving the Moon's distance and size were not as Ptolemy had claimed.</note>

<meta>This page continues Copernicus's application of lunar theory to specific observations. [[original page: 129]]

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV.

The Moon was about to hide the bright star of the <term>Hyades <gloss>a star cluster in the constellation Taurus</gloss></term>, which the Romans call Palilicium <note>original: "Palilicium". Today this star is known as Aldebaran.</note>. Having waited for this, we saw the star close to the dark part of the lunar body, and already disappearing between the horns of the Moon in the fifth hour of the night, specifically closer to the Southern horn by about a third of the Moon's latitude or diameter. And since the star, according to calculation, was at 2 degrees and 52 minutes of **Gemini** with a Southern latitude of five degrees and a sixth <note>original: "sextantis", meaning one-sixth of a degree, or 10 minutes.</note>, it was clear that the center of the Moon, according to sight, preceded the star by half a diameter. Therefore, its apparent position in longitude was 2 degrees 36 minutes, and in latitude almost 5 degrees 2 minutes. It was, therefore, 1,497 Egyptian years, 76 days, and 23 hours from the beginning of the years of Christ at Bologna; but at Krakow, which is further East by about 9 degrees, it was 24 hours and 36 minutes. To this, the <term>equation of time <gloss>original: "aequalitas", the adjustment between apparent solar time and mean time</gloss></term> adds 4 minutes, for the Sun was at 28 and a half degrees of **Pisces**. Therefore, the mean motion of the Moon from the Sun was 74 degrees; the adjusted anomaly was 111 degrees 10 minutes. The true position of the Moon was 3 degrees 24 minutes of **Gemini**, with a Southern latitude of 4 degrees 35 minutes. For the true motion in latitude was 203 degrees 41 minutes. At that same time in Bologna, the 26th degree of **Scorpio** was rising, at an angle of 59 and a half degrees; the Moon was 84 degrees from the <term>zenith <gloss>original: "uertice horizontis", the point directly overhead</gloss></term>, and the angle of intersection of the circles of altitude and the <term>zodiac <gloss>original: "signiferi"</gloss></term> was almost 29 degrees. The parallax of the Moon was 1 degree in longitude 51 minutes, and 30 minutes in latitude. These values agree closely with the observation, so that no one should doubt that our hypotheses and the things produced from them are correct.

For at whatever time we estimate one or the other will occur, we shall seek the mean motion of the Moon. If we find that the Moon has already completed a full circle, we understand a conjunction has occurred; if it is at a semicircle...

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

### Chapter XXIX. On investigating the true conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun and Moon.

When we have obtained, as has been said, the time of the mean conjunction or opposition of these stars along with their motions, the true distance between them, by which they precede or follow one another, is necessary for finding the true [times]. For if the Moon is ahead of the Sun at the [mean] conjunction or opposition, it is clear that the true one will occur; if the Sun has already passed the true one which we seek. These things are made manifest from the prosthaphaeresis of each. Since if there are none, or if they are equal and of the same affection—that is, if both are additive or both subtractive—it is clear that at the same moment the true conjunctions or oppositions coincide with the mean ones. If, however, they are unequal, the excess itself indicates their distance, and that the star whose excess is additive or subtractive precedes or follows. But when they are in different directions, the one whose prosthaphaeresis was subtractive precedes by so much more; and these joined together collect their distance. Upon this, we shall estimate in how many whole hours it can be traversed by the Moon, taking two hours for each degree of distance. For instance, if they are at a distance of about 6 degrees, we shall assume 12 hours for them. For this interval of time thus established, we shall seek the true elongation of the Moon from the Sun, which we shall easily accomplish as long as we know that the mean motion of the Moon is completed by one degree and one scruple in just under two hours. Indeed, the hourly motion of the anomaly and its true motion around the new and full Moon is almost 50 scruples, which in six hours will collect a mean motion of 3 degrees and as many scruples, and a true progress of the anomaly of five parts; with these we shall consider in the Table of lunar prosthaphaereses the difference between the prosthaphaereses themselves, which we shall add to the mean motion if the anomaly was in the lower part of the circle, or subtract if in the upper. For that which has been added or left is the true motion of the Moon in the assumed hours. If, therefore, this motion is equal to the previously existing distance, it is sufficient. Otherwise, having multiplied the distance by the number of estimated hours, we shall divide by this motion, or if we have divided the simple distance by the accepted true hourly motion...

# REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV.

...the true difference of time in hours and scruples between the mean and true conjunction or opposition will result. This we shall add to the time of the mean conjunction or opposition if the Moon was prior to the Sun (or to the place diametrically opposite the Sun), or we shall subtract it if it was posterior, and we shall have the time of the true conjunction or opposition. Although we admit that the inequality of the Sun also adds or subtracts something, it is rightly to be neglected, since in the whole tract, even at the greatest elongation which extends beyond seven degrees, it cannot complete one scruple; and this method of assessing lunations is more certain. For those who rely solely on the hourly motion of the Moon, which they call the hourly excess, are sometimes deceived and are frequently compelled to repeat the calculation. For the Moon is changeable even from hour to hour and does not remain similar to itself. Therefore, at the time of the true coitus [conjunction] or opposition, we shall arrange the true motion of latitude for the purpose of learning the latitude of the Moon itself, and the true place of the Sun from the Vernal equinox—that is, the sign—by which the place of the Moon is also understood to be the same, or opposite. And since time of this kind is understood to be mean and uniform for the meridian of Cracow, we shall reduce it to apparent time through the method delivered above. But if we wish to establish these for any other place than Cracow, we shall consider its longitude, and for each individual degree of its longitude we shall take 4 scruples of an hour, and for each scruple of longitude 4 second scruples of an hour, which we shall add to the Cracovian time if the other place is further east, and subtract if it is further west; and that which remains or is collected will be the time of the conjunction and opposition of the Sun and Moon.

### Chapter XXXI. How great the eclipse of the Sun and Moon shall be.

After we have known that the Sun or Moon will fail [be eclipsed], we shall also easily know how great their eclipse shall be. In almost the same way also in a lunar eclipse, except that for the visible latitude, we use its simple [true] latitude, which having been taken from half the diameters of the Moon and the shadow, there remains the failing part of the Moon, provided the latitude...

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK FIVE.

HITHERTO we have completed the revolutions of the Earth around the Sun, and of the Moon around the Earth. We now approach the motions of the five wandering stars [planets], the order and magnitudes of whose orbits the mobility of the Earth itself connects with a wonderful harmony and a certain symmetry, as we reviewed summarily in the first book, while we were showing that the orbits themselves had their centers not around the Earth, but rather around the Sun. It remains, therefore, for us to demonstrate all these things individually and more evidently, and to satisfy our promises as much as we are able, especially by employing the apparent experiments [observations] which we have received both from the ancients and from our own times, by which the calculation of their motions may be held more certain. These five stars are named in Plato's *Timaeus* each according to its species: Saturn as *Phaenon*, as if you were to say "shining" or "appearing," for it is least hidden from the others and emerges more quickly when obscured by the Sun. Jupiter from its splendor is *Phaëton*. Mars is *Pyrois* from its fiery brilliance. Venus is sometimes *Phosphorus* [Greek], sometimes *Hesperus* [Greek], that is Lucifer and Vesperugo [Morning Star and Evening Star], according as it shines in the morning or evening. Finally, Mercury is *Stilbon* from its glittering and vibrating light. These are also carried in longitude and latitude with a greater difference than the Moon.

### Chapter I. On their revolutions and mean motions.

Two motions of longitude appear in them which differ very much. One is on account of the motion of the Earth which we have spoken of. The other is proper to each. It was not wrongly decided to call the first the motion of commutation [parallax], since it is the one which makes the stations, progressions, and regressions appear...

***

### PAGE 289
**[Original page: 134]**

# REVOLUTIONS, BOOK V.

...to appear in all of them; not because the planet is thus distracted—it which always proceeds by its own motion—but because it thus appears by way of commutation, which the motion of the Earth effects according to the difference and magnitude of their orbits. It is clear, therefore, that the true places of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars then only become visible to us when they happen at sunset [*akronyktai*], which occurs almost in the middle of their regressions. For they coincide then in the middle place of the Sun in a straight line, stripped of that commutation. Furthermore, in Venus and Mercury there is another reason. For they are then hidden, being under the rays [*hypaugi*], and they show only the wanderings they make from the Sun on this side or that, so that they are never found without this commutation. There is, therefore, for each planet its own private revolution of commutation—I mean the motion of the Earth relative to the planet—which they explain among themselves. For we say the motion of commutation is nothing else but that in which the motion of the Earth exceeds their equal motion, as in Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars; or is exceeded by it, as in Venus and Mercury. But since such periods of commutation are found unequal by a manifest difference, the ancients knew that the motions of those stars were also unequal, and had apsides of the circles to which their inequality would return, and they thought those had perpetual seats in the sphere of the fixed stars. By this argument, the entrance was opened for learning their mean motions and equal periods. For when they had the place of some star recorded according to a certain distance from the Sun and a fixed star, and after an interval of time they found the star itself had arrived at the same place with a similar distance from the Sun, the planet was seen to have traversed all inequality and to have returned through all things to its prior state with the Earth. And thus, through the time which intervened, they calculated the number of whole and equal revolutions, and from them the particular motions of the star. Ptolemy reviewed these circuits under a number of solar years, as he admits to have received from Hipparchus. But he wishes solar years to be understood as those which are taken from the equinox or solstice. But it has now become clear that such years are not at all equal; for that reason we shall use those which are taken from the fixed stars, by which also more corrected motions of these five stars have been restored by us, just as in this our time we...

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

### On Investigating the True Conjunctions and Oppositions of the Sun and Moon. Chapter 29.

**W**hen we have obtained, as has been said, the time of the mean conjunction or opposition of these stars along with their motions, the true distance between them—by which they precede or follow one another—is necessary in order to find the true moments of these events. For if the Moon is ahead of the Sun at the time of a mean conjunction <note>original: "coniunctione"</note> or opposition, it is clear that the true event is yet to come; likewise, it is clear if the Sun has already passed the true point we are seeking. These things become manifest from the *prosthaphaeresis* <term>prosthaphaeresis: from Greek terms meaning 'addition and subtraction'; it is a mathematical correction used to find the 'true' position of a planet by accounting for the irregularity of its orbit compared to its 'mean' or average speed</term> of both bodies. 

Since if these corrections are zero or equal, and of the same kind—that is, if both are additive <note>original: "adiectiuae"</note> or both subtractive <note>original: "ablatiuae"</note>—it is clear that the true conjunctions or oppositions coincide with the mean ones at that same moment. But if they are unequal, the difference itself indicates their distance, and whether that body whose correction is additive or subtractive precedes or follows the other. But when they are in opposite directions <note>i.e., one is additive and the other subtractive</note>, the one whose correction was subtractive will precede by that much more, and these values joined together determine the distance between them. 

Based on this distance, we will estimate how many whole hours it might take the Moon to cross that gap, taking two hours for every degree of distance. For example, if they are at a distance of about 6 degrees, we will assume 12 hours for them. Therefore, for this interval of time thus established, we seek the true elongation of the Moon from the Sun. We will do this easily provided we know that the mean motion of the Moon is completed at one degree and one scruple <term>scruple: a 'scrupulus' is a small division, here representing 1/60th of a degree (a minute of arc)</term> every two hours. However, the hourly motion of the anomaly <term>anomaly: the position of a planet in its elliptical or epicyclic path relative to its furthest or nearest point from the center</term>, and the true motion itself near the full and new Moon, is about 50 scruples. These will amount in six hours to a uniform motion of 3 degrees and the same number of scruples, and a true progression of five parts of the anomaly. 

By these values, we will consider the difference between the corrections themselves in the Table of Lunar Prosthaphaereses, which we will add to the mean motion if the anomaly is in the lower part of the circle, or subtract if it is in the upper part. For whatever is the sum or remainder is the true motion of the Moon in the hours assumed. If this motion is equal to the previously existing distance, it is sufficient. Otherwise, having multiplied the distance by the number of estimated hours, we will divide by this motion, or by the simple true hourly motion received...

# BOOK IV OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...divide the simple distance, the true difference of time in hours and minutes between the mean and true conjunction or opposition will result. We shall add this to the time of the mean conjunction or opposition if the Moon was ahead of the Sun, or ahead of the point diametrically opposite the Sun; or we shall subtract it if the Moon was behind. We will then have the time of the true conjunction or opposition. Although we admit that the Sun’s own inequality <note>original: "Solis inaequalitas"; this refers to the Sun's varying apparent speed throughout the year which causes it to deviate from its "mean" or average position</note> adds or subtracts something, it is rightly disregarded; for in the entire span, even at the greatest elongation, which extends over seven degrees, it cannot even total one minute. This method of calculating lunations <term>lunation: the period of time between two successive New Moons, averaging about 29.5 days</term> is more certain. Those who rely solely on the hourly motion of the Moon—which they call the "hourly excess" <note>original: "superationem horariam"; the amount by which the Moon's speed exceeds the Sun's speed per hour</note>—are sometimes deceived and are often forced to repeat their calculations. For the Moon is changeable even from hour to hour, and does not remain consistent with itself.

Therefore, for the time of the true conjunction <note>original: "coitus"; literally "coming together" or "meeting," referring to the New Moon</note> or opposition, we will calculate the true motion of latitude to learn the latitude of the Moon itself, and the true position of the Sun from the Vernal Equinox—that is, the zodiac sign—which also tells us the position of the Moon, whether it is at the same point or opposite. And since time of this sort is understood as mean and uniform time relative to the meridian of Cracow <note>Cracow was the primary reference point for Copernicus’s tables, as he conducted his work in the Kingdom of Poland</term>, we shall reduce it to apparent time <note>the time shown on a sundial, as opposed to "mean time" which assumes every day is exactly 24 hours</note> by the method handed down above. 

If we wish to set these times for any other place than Cracow, we will consider its longitude; for every degree of longitude we take 4 minutes of an hour, and for every minute of longitude 4 seconds of an hour. We add these to the Cracow time if the other place is further east, and subtract if it is further west; the remainder or sum will be the time of the conjunction or opposition of the Sun and Moon.

### Chapter XXXII. On Foretelling How Long the Eclipse Will Last.

[[image: decorative drop cap R]] **I**t remains to see how long the eclipse will last. Here it should be noted that we use the arcs <note>original: "circumferentiis"</note> that occur between the Sun, the Moon, and the shadow as if they were straight lines, because of their smallness, by which they seem to differ in no way from a straight line. Therefore, having taken the center of the Sun or the shadow at point A, and the line BC for the passage of the Moon, whose center at the moments of contact with the Sun or shadow is B at the beginning of the incidence <term>incidence: the start of the eclipse when the bodies first touch</term> and C at the end of the clearing <term>clearing: the end of the eclipse when the bodies finally separate; original: "expurgationis"</term>, let AB and AC be connected, and let a perpendicular AD be dropped to BC itself. It is manifest that when the center of the Moon is at D, it will be the midpoint of the eclipse; for AD is the shortest of the lines descending from A, and BD

[[image: Geometric diagram showing a right-angled triangle with vertex A, base BC, and height AD. Points B and C represent the start and end of the eclipse, while D is the midpoint.]]

is equal to DC, since AB and AC are also equal. Both of these [AB and AC] consist of the half-diameters of the Sun and Moon in a solar eclipse, or of the Moon and the shadow in a lunar eclipse; and AD is the true or visible latitude of the Moon at the midpoint of the eclipse. Therefore, when we have subtracted the square produced from AD from the square of AB, the square of BD remains: thus, the length of BD will be given. When we have divided this by the true hourly motion of the Moon during its eclipse (or the visible hourly motion in a solar one), we will have the time of half the duration. But since the Moon frequently makes a stay <note>original: "moram"</note> in the midst of the darkness—which happens when half the sum of the diameters of the Moon and the shadow exceeds the latitude of the Moon by more than its [the Moon's] diameter, as we have said—therefore, when we have placed B as the center of the Moon at the beginning of the total

**obscuration**

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

of the obscuration, where the Moon touches the surrounding shadow on the inside, and F at the other contact, where it first emerges. By connecting AB and AF, it will be demonstrated in the same way as before that BD and DF are the halves of the stay in darkness <note>original: "morae in tenebris"; refers to the duration of totality in a lunar eclipse</note>, because AD is the known latitude of the Moon, and AB (or AF) is the radius of the shadow plus the radius of the Moon. Therefore, BD or DF will be established, and by dividing these by the true hourly motion of the Moon, we will have the time of the half-stay that was sought.

However, it must be noted here that as the Moon moves in its own orbit, it does not cross segments of the length of the zodiac <term>zodiac: the "circle of signs" or the ecliptic path of the Sun</term> that are exactly equal to those in its own orbit, even when measured by the circles passing through the poles of the zodiac. Yet the difference is extremely small; in the total distance of 12 degrees from the ecliptic intersection <note>original: "ecliptica sectione"; the node where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path</note>—within which the limits of solar and lunar eclipses almost always fall—the arcs of these orbits do not differ from each other by more than two minutes <note>original: "scrup."; scruples or minutes of arc, where 60 minutes equal 1 degree</note>, which would amount to only one-fifteenth of an hour. 

For that reason, we often use one in place of the other as if they were the same. Likewise, we use the same latitude for the Moon at the beginning and end of the eclipse as we do for the middle of the eclipse, even though the latitude of the Moon itself is always increasing or decreasing. Because of this, the periods of incidence <term>incidence: the time from first contact to the start of totality</term> and clearing <term>clearing: the time from the end of totality to final contact</term> are

-> SUN | MOON <-

not perfectly equal, but the difference is so slight that it would seem a waste of time to investigate it more precisely. In this way, the times, durations, and magnitudes of eclipses have been explained according to their diameters. 

But since it is the opinion of many that the eclipsed parts should be determined not by diameters but by surface areas—for it is surfaces, not lines, that fail—let ABCD be the circle of the Sun or the shadow, with its center at E. Let the lunar circle be AFCG, with its center at I, which intersect each other at points A and C. Let the straight line BEIF be drawn through both centers, and let AB, BC, IA, IC, and AKC be connected at right angles to AF itself. We wish to investigate from these how great the obscured surface ADCG was, or how many digits <note>original: "unciarum"; literally 'ounces,' here used to mean the 12 units of area of the disk</note> it is of the whole plane of the Sun's or Moon's disk. Therefore, since the diameter AB and AI of each circle is given from the above, and also the distance of the centers, or the lunar latitude EI, we have a

# BOOK IV OF THE REVOLUTIONS

The triangle $AEI$ has sides of given lengths, and therefore the angles are also given through the methods demonstrated previously; triangle $EIC$ is similar and equal to it. Therefore, the circumferences $ADC$ and $AGC$ will be given in terms of parts in which the total circumference of a circle is 360. Furthermore, Archimedes of Syracuse, in his *On the Measurement of the Circle*, revealed that the ratio of the circumference to the diameter is less than three and one-seventh <note>original: "triplam sesquiseptimam"; the ratio 22/7 or approximately 3.1428</note>, but greater than three and ten-seventy-firsts <note>original: "triplam superpartientem septuagesimas primas decem"; the ratio 223/71 or approximately 3.1408</note>. Between these two, Ptolemy assumes a middle value such that the ratio of the circumference to the diameter is 3, 8 first minutes, and 30 second minutes to 1 <note>original: "trium scrup. prima VIII. secunda XXX."; this is the sexagesimal (base-60) representation 3;8,30, which equals 3.14166</note>. By this ratio, the circumferences $AGC$ and $ADC$ will be revealed in the same units as their diameters, or $AE$ and $AI$. The areas contained under $EA$ and $AD$, and under $IA$ and $AG$, are equal to the <term>sectors: the "pie-slice" areas of a circle</term> $AEC$ and $AIC$, respectively. 

Furthermore, for the <term>isosceles: a triangle with two equal sides</term> triangles $AEC$ and $AIC$, the common base $AKC$ and the perpendicular heights $EK$ and $KI$ are given. Therefore, the area produced by $AK$ and $KG$ is known, which is the area of triangle $AEC$; similarly, the area produced by $AK$ and $KI$ is known for triangle $ACI$. When both triangles are subtracted from their respective sectors, the <term>segments: the area of a circle between a chord and the arc</term> of the circles $AFC$ and $ACD$ will remain. The sum of these segments constitutes the total area $ADCG$ which we were seeking. 

Moreover, the entire area of the circle—whether contained by $BE$ and $BAD$ in a solar eclipse, or by $FI$ and $FAG$ in a lunar eclipse—is given. Thus, it will be manifest how many <term>inches: "digits" or unciae, used as units to measure the depth and area of an eclipse</term> the area $ADCG$ contains, representing the portion missing from the whole circle of either the Sun or the Moon.

Let these remarks concerning the Moon suffice for now, as these matters have been treated more extensively by others. We are indeed hurrying on to the revolutions of the remaining five stars <note>original: "quinque siderum"; referring to the five known planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, which will be discussed in the following books.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK FIVE

**H**itherto, we have completed our account of the revolutions of the Earth around the Sun and of the Moon around the Earth. We now approach the motions of the five <term>wandering stars</term> <note>original: "errantium stellarum"; the word "planet" comes from the Greek word for "wanderer."</note>, the order and magnitudes of whose orbits are connected by the mobility of the Earth itself with a wonderful harmony and a certain symmetry. We summarized this in the first book when we showed that these orbits have their centers not around the Earth, but rather around the Sun. It remains, therefore, for us to demonstrate all these things individually and more clearly. We shall fulfill our promises as far as we are able, especially by applying the observations which we have received both from the ancients and from our own times, by which the logic of these motions may be established with greater certainty. 

In Plato’s *Timaeus*, these five stars are each named according to their appearance: Saturn is called *Phaenon*, as if you were to say "shining" or "appearing," for it is least hidden by the others and emerges more quickly after being concealed by the Sun. Jupiter is called *Phaëton* from its splendor. Mars is *Pyrois* from its fiery brightness. Venus is sometimes called *Phosphorus* <note>original: "φωσφόρος"</note> and sometimes *Hesperus* <note>original: "ἕσπερος"</note>—that is, the Light-bringer and the Evening Star—depending on whether it shines in the morning or the evening. Finally, Mercury is called *Stilbon* from its sparkling and vibrating light. These planets also travel in longitude and latitude with greater variation than the Moon.

### Chapter 1: On their revolutions and mean motions.

**B**oth of the motions in longitude appear quite different in these planets. One occurs because of the motion of the Earth, which we have already discussed. The other is the specific motion belonging to each planet. We have chosen to call the first one the <term>motion of commutation</term> <note>original: "motum commutationis"; this refers to the apparent change in a planet's position caused by the Earth's own movement—what we now call "parallax."</note>, not without reason, since it is this motion which produces the appearances of stations, progressions, and regressions in all of them. 

<summary>Copernicus introduces Book V, shifting focus to the five known planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury). He explains that their apparent movements, including retrograde motion, are actually caused by the Earth's own orbital motion around the Sun.</summary>

<keywords>planets, wandering stars, heliocentrism, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, commutation, planetary motion, Plato's Timaeus</keywords>
