# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK V

...it appears to be, not because the planet is actually pulled off course—for it always moves forward with its own motion—but because it appears so by way of <term>parallax</term> <note>original: "commutationis." Copernicus uses this term to describe the apparent displacement of a planet's position caused by the Earth's own movement in its orbit.</note>, which is caused by the motion of the Earth due to the difference in the size of those orbits. It is clear, then, that the true locations of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars only become visible to us when they are <term>at sunset</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀκρονύκται" (akronyktas); this refers to the "acronychal" rising of a planet, when it rises in the East just as the Sun sets in the West.</note>, which happens nearly in the middle of their <term>regressions</term> <note>original: "repedationum." This is retrograde motion, where a planet appears to move backward in the sky.</note>. For at that time, they align with the mean position of the Sun in a straight line, and are stripped of that parallax. 

Furthermore, in the case of Venus and Mercury, the logic is different. For they are hidden when they are <term>under the sun's rays</term> <note>original: "hypaugi." This refers to a planet being so close to the Sun in the sky that it is lost in the Sun's glare.</note>, and they show only the excursions they make to either side of the Sun, so they are never found without this parallax. Therefore, each planet has its own private "revolution of parallax"—I mean the motion of the Earth relative to the planet, which they unfold between themselves. For we say the motion of parallax is nothing other than that in which the uniform motion of the Earth exceeds their motion (as in the case of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars) or is exceeded by it (as in the case of Venus and Mercury). 

Since these periods of parallax are found to be unequal by a manifest difference, the ancients recognized that the motions of those stars were also unequal, and that they had <term>apsides</term> <note>original: "absides." These are the points in an orbit where a planet is at its maximum or minimum distance from the center of its motion.</note> of their circles to which their inequality returned; they believed these points had fixed positions in the sphere of the fixed stars. By this argument, the way was opened to learning their <term>mean motions</term> <note>The average, steady rate of a planet's motion, ignoring temporary speed-ups or slow-downs.</note> and uniform periods. For when they had a record of a planet's location at a certain distance from the Sun and a fixed star, and after an interval of time found the star had returned to the same place with a similar distance from the Sun, the planet seemed to have completed its full cycle of inequality and returned in all respects to its prior state relative to the Earth. 

Thus, through the time that passed, they calculated the number of whole and uniform revolutions, and from these, the specific motions of the star. Ptolemy reviewed these circuits using the number of solar years, as he admits he received them from Hipparchus <note>Hipparchus (c. 190–120 BCE) was a Greek astronomer whose observations formed the basis for much of Ptolemy's work.</note>. However, he intends "solar years" to mean those measured from the equinox or solstice. But it has already become clear that such years are not perfectly uniform; therefore, we shall use those years measured from the fixed stars <note>Copernicus is distinguishing between the "tropical year" (seasons) and the "sidereal year" (relative to stars), preferring the latter for greater precision.</note>, by which more corrected motions of these five stars have been restored by us, just as we have found in our own time—

...we find that some of them have fallen short or exceeded in this manner. For **Saturn**, the Earth completes fifty-seven revolutions—which we have called the motion of <term>parallax</term> <note>original: "commutationis." This is the apparent movement of a planet caused by the Earth's own motion around the Sun.</note>—in 69 of our solar years, plus one day, approximately 7 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupulis primis." In the sexagesimal (base-60) system used in astronomy, these are "first small parts" or minutes.</note>, and 18 <term>seconds</term> <note>original: "secundis." These are "second small parts."</note>. During this time, the planet completes two circuits in its own proper motion, with the addition of approximately 1 degree, 5 minutes, and 50 seconds.

**Jupiter** is overtaken by the Earth 65 times in 71 solar years, minus 5 days, 54 minutes, and 14 seconds; in this time, the planet revolves six times, falling short by 5 degrees, 42 minutes, and 32 seconds.

For **Mars**, the revolutions of parallax are 37 in 79 solar years, 2 days, 24 minutes, and 45 seconds. In this period, the planet completes 42 circuits in its own motion, adding 2 degrees, 21 minutes, and 44 seconds.

**Venus** overtakes the motion of the Earth five times in 8 solar years, minus 2 days, 26 minutes, and 44 seconds. Indeed, through this time it circles the Sun 13 times, minus 2 degrees, 24 minutes, and 29 seconds.

Finally, **Mercury** makes 145 periods of parallax in 46 solar years, with the addition of one day and 25 minutes, by which it also exceeds the motion of the Earth, with which it returns around the Sun 191 times, with the addition of 21 minutes and 53 seconds.

Therefore, for each planet, there is a single circuit of parallax as follows:
- For **Saturn**: 378 days, 5 minutes, 32 seconds, and 42 <term>thirds</term> <note>original: "tertiis." These are "third small parts," or 1/60th of a second.</note>.
- For **Jupiter**: 398 days, 54 minutes, 3 seconds, and 58 thirds.
- For **Mars**: 779 days, 56 minutes, 14 seconds, and 55 thirds.
- For **Venus**: 583 days, 55 minutes, 17 seconds, and 50 thirds.
- For **Mercury**: 115 days, 52 minutes, 38 seconds, and 53 thirds.

When these values are resolved into the degrees of a circle and multiplied by 365, and we have divided them by the number of their own days and minutes, we shall have the annual motion:
- For **Saturn**: 347 degrees, 32 minutes, 3 seconds, 9 thirds, and 4 fourths.
- For **Jupiter**: 329 degrees, 25 minutes, 8 seconds, 15 thirds, and 6 fourths.
- For **Mars**: 168 degrees, 28 minutes, 30 seconds, 36 thirds, and 4 fourths.
- For **Venus**: 225 degrees, 1 minute, 45 seconds, 3 thirds, and 40 fourths.
- For **Mercury**: after three revolutions, 54 degrees, 57 minutes, 23 seconds, 6 thirds, and 30 fourths. Of these

--- Page 302 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the specific motion tables of Mercury in Book V to a theoretical discussion in Chapter 2 of the same book. While the previous page provided numerical data for Mercury's synodic cycles, this page explains the classical (Ptolemaic) geometric models used to account for planetary irregularities before Copernicus introduces his own system.</meta>

->NICHOLAS COPERNICUS<-

# Demonstration of the uniformity and appearance of the stars, according to the opinion of the ancients. Chapter 2.

Since their mean motions <note>Mean motion is the average speed of a planet, calculated as if it moved in a perfect, unvarying circle.</note> behave in this way, let us now turn to their apparent inequality. The ancient mathematicians, who held that the Earth was immobile, imagined for Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus a system of eccentric-epicycles <note>A model where a planet moves on a small circle (epicycle), which in turn moves along a larger circle (eccentric) whose center is not the Earth.</note>, and furthermore another eccentric relative to which the epicycle would move uniformly, as would the planet within its epicycle.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating planetary motion. It features a system of circles and points along a central vertical axis. The primary circle has points labeled A (at the top) and B (at the bottom). Along the vertical diameter, points are labeled from top to bottom: A, F, C (the center of the main circle), E, D (the center of the Earth/universe), B, and G. To the upper left, a smaller circle (an epicycle) is drawn with center H. Lines connect point C and point E to the epicycle, intersecting it at points I, K, L, and M. The diagram is used to explain the movement of planets through eccentrics and epicycles.</image-desc>

This is as if there were an eccentric circle AB, whose center is C, and a diameter ACB, upon which sits the center of the Earth D, so that the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion (here, the Earth)</term> is at A and the perigee <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the center of motion</term> is at B. If the distance DC is cut exactly in half at point E, and from that center a second eccentric FG is described equal to the first, and within this, at any point H, an epicycle IK is designated, and a straight line IHC is drawn through its center, and similarly a line LHME. 

Furthermore, let the eccentrics be understood as inclined to the plane of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; the "sign-bearer," or the path of the sun through the constellations.</note>, and the epicycle to the plane of the eccentric, because of the latitudes <note>The north-south deviation of a planet from the ecliptic path.</note> produced by the planet; but here they are treated as if they were in a single plane for the sake of the demonstration’s convenience. They say, therefore, that this entire plane moves around point D, the center of the zodiac <note>original: "orbis signorum"</note>, along with points E and C, according to the motion of the fixed stars. By this, they wish it to be understood that these points have fixed seats in the sphere of the non-wandering stars. They also say that the epicycle moves in order <note>original: "in consequentia"; meaning in the sequence of the zodiac signs, from West to East.</note> along the circle FHG, but stays aligned with the line IHC, about which the star also revolves uniformly within the epicycle IK itself. 

It is clear, however, that the uniform motion of the epicycle ought to be measured relative to E, the center of its deferent <note>The "deferent" is the large circle that carries the smaller epicycle.</note>, and the planet's revolution relative to the line LME. They concede, therefore, that even in this case, the uniformity of circular motion can occur around a "foreign" center <note>Copernicus is critiquing the "equant" point (E), where motion looks uniform from a point that is not the actual center of the circle. To Copernicus, this violated the laws of physics.</note> and not its own center. They claim this happens even more so in the case of Mercury. But we have already sufficiently refuted this regarding the Moon. These and similar issues provided us with the occasion to think about the mobility of the Earth and other ways by which uniformity and the principles of the art might be preserved, and the explanation for the apparent inequality be made more consistent.

<summary>Copernicus describes the complex Ptolemaic system of eccentrics, epicycles, and equant points used by ancient astronomers to explain planetary motion. He critiques these models for failing to maintain true uniform circular motion, citing this as a primary motivation for his proposal that the Earth moves.</summary>

## General demonstration of the apparent inequality due to the motion of the earth. Chapter 3.

Therefore, since there are two causes by which a planet's uniform motion appears unequal—both because of the motion of the earth and also because of its own proper motion—we shall explain both of these in general, and separately by a visual demonstration, so that they may be better distinguished from one another, beginning with the one that is mixed with all of them due to the motion of the earth. And first regarding Venus and Mercury, which are enclosed within the earth's circle <note>Copernicus refers here to the earth's orbital path around the sun.</note>. Let there be, then, an eccentric circle AB from the Sun, which the center of the earth describes in its annual circuit, according to the method handed down above; let the center be C. Now, however, let us assume as if the planet had no other inequality except this—which will be the case if we make a circle DE concentric <note>original: "homocentrum"</note> with AB, whether it be for Venus or Mercury, which must be inclined to AB because of latitude <note>Latitude in astronomy refers to the distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic.</note>. But for the sake of a more convenient demonstration, let them be thought of as if they were in the same plane; and let the earth be taken at point A, from which lines of sight <term>uisus: literally "sight" or "vision," here referring to the visual rays or lines of sight from the observer on Earth</term> AFL and AGM are drawn, tangent to the planet's circle at points F and G, and ACB is the common diameter of both.

Therefore C, and the line ACB itself, will appear to be moved according to the mean motion of the Sun, since the eye is carried at A. And where the subtractive motion of the Earth exceeds the additive motion of the star—especially around point A—the star will seem to be left behind by the Earth and move toward the preceding <note>In astronomy, "preceding" means moving westward (retrograde), opposite to the "following" or eastward (prograde) direction of the zodiac.</note> signs, and it will make a station there where the difference between these contrary motions is least to the sight. Thus it is manifest again that all those things happen through the single motion of the Earth, which the ancients sought to explain through the individual epicycles <note>original: "epicyclia." But since the motion of the star is not found to be uniform (contrary to the opinion of Apollonius and the ancients), as revealed by the Earth's revolution in relation to the star, the planets are therefore not carried in a concentric circle <note>original: "homocentro"</note>, but in another way, which we shall also demonstrate immediately.

## In What Ways the Proper Motions of the Wandering Stars Appear Unequal. Chapter IV.

Since their proper motions in longitude <term>longitude: the position of a heavenly body measured along the ecliptic (the Sun's apparent path) from a starting point, usually the spring equinox</term> follow nearly the same pattern—except for Mercury, which is seen to differ from them—they will all be treated together in this four-part discussion. A separate place has been assigned to Mercury.

While the ancients <note>Referring to astronomers like Ptolemy who used a single eccentric circle with an "equant" point to explain changing speeds.</note> assumed a single motion in two eccentrics <note>An "eccentric" is a circular orbit whose center is not the Earth.</note> (as was reviewed), we believe there are two equal motions from which the apparent inequality is composed. This can be achieved either by an eccentric on an eccentric, or by an epicycle on an epicycle <note>An "epicycle" is a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle called a "deferent."</note>, or even by a mixture of an eccentric and an epicycle. These configurations can produce the same inequality, as we demonstrated earlier regarding the Sun and the Moon.

Now, if the first epicycle moves forward <note>Original: "in consequentia," referring to motion in the order of the zodiac signs (West to East).</note>, and the second moves just as much in the opposite direction, upon which the planet finally revolves with a doubled motion, the same results we have already described will occur. Since the other planets do not follow this same change exactly, a certain difference must necessarily follow in them, which, although very slight, is nonetheless perceptible in Mars and Venus. Therefore, we shall now demonstrate from observations that these hypotheses are sufficient for the appearances, beginning first with Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. In these cases, the most important and difficult task is to find the location of the **apogee** <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note> and the distance $CD$, since all other elements are easily demonstrated through them. In this process, we shall use nearly the same method we employed for the Moon. Specifically, we will compare three ancient solar **oppositions** <note>The alignment where a planet is directly opposite the Sun from the Earth's perspective.</note> with an equal number of new ones. The Greeks call these "acronychal risings" <note>Original: "acronychias," referring to a planet rising exactly as the sun sets.</note>; we call them the "extremes of night," namely when the planet falls on the straight line of the mean motion of the Sun and is opposite to the Sun. At this point, the planet is stripped of all that variation which the motion of the Earth introduces. Indeed, such locations are captured from observations using **astrolabic instruments** <note>A reference to the armillary sphere or similar sighting tools used to measure celestial coordinates.</note>, as explained above. The calculation of the Sun is also applied until it is established that the planet has reached the point directly opposite it.

## On Three Other More Recently Observed Oppositions of Saturn. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'C' depicting a seated male figure in a scholarly robe, gesturing with his hand as if in discourse or teaching.</image-desc>

However, since the calculation of Saturn's motion handed down by Ptolemy differs not a little in our own times, and it could not be immediately understood where the error lay hidden, we were compelled to employ new observations. From these, we have once again obtained three of the planet’s <term>acronychal</term><note>original: "acronychijs"; a planet's "nightly extremes," or oppositions, occurring when it is directly opposite the Sun from the Earth's perspective.</note> positions. The first was in the year of Christ **1514**, on the <term>third day before the Nones of May</term><note>May 5th.</note>, at one and one-fifth hours before midnight; in this instance, Saturn was found at **205** degrees **24** minutes. The second was in the year of Christ **1520**, on the <term>third day before the Ides of July</term><note>July 13th.</note> at noon, at **272** degrees **25** minutes. The third was also in the year **1527**, on the <term>sixth day before the Ides of October</term><note>October 10th.</note>, six and two-fifths hours after midnight, at **7** minutes of one degree from the <term>horn of Aries</term><note>The starting point of the zodiacal circle.</note>.

Between the first and second observations, therefore, there are **6** Egyptian years, **70** days, and **33** minutes <note>Refers to fractions of a day in astronomical time.</note>. In this time, the apparent motion of Saturn was **78** degrees **1** minute. From the second to the third, there are **7** Egyptian years, **89** days, and **46** minutes, and the apparent motion of the star is **86** degrees **42** minutes. The <term>mean motion</term><note>The theoretical uniform speed of the planet, as opposed to its varying apparent speed.</note> in the first interval was **75** degrees **39** minutes; in the second, it was **88** degrees **29** minutes. 

Therefore, in the investigation of the <term>highest apsis</term><note>The apogee, or the point in the orbit furthest from the center.</note> and the <term>eccentricity</term><note>original: "eccentrotetis"; the measurement of how far the circular orbit is offset from the center.</note>, we must first proceed according to the rule of Ptolemy, as if the star moved in a simple <term>eccentric</term><note>A circular path whose center is not the same as the Earth's center.</note>. Although this is not sufficient, by being brought closer to the problem in this way, we reach the truth more easily. 

Let the circle be **ABC**, representing the path in which the planet moves uniformly. Let **A** be the sign of the first opposition, **B** the second, and **C** the third. Let the center of the Earth be taken as **D**, to which are connected lines **AD**, **BD**, and **CD**. Let any one of these be extended in a straight line to the opposite side of the circumference, such as **CDE**, and let **AB** and **BE** be joined. 

Since, therefore, the angle **BDC** is given as **86** degrees **42** minutes—where two right angles at the center are **180** degrees—the remaining angle **BDE** will be **93** degrees **18** minutes. But where **360** degrees equal two right angles <note>Copernicus is using a geometric convention where he doubles the degree count for calculations involving chords and arcs, a common practice in Renaissance trigonometry inherited from Ptolemy.</note>, it will be **186** degrees **36** minutes. And **BED**, following the circumference **BC**, is **88** degrees **29** minutes. Therefore, the remaining angle, which is **DBE**...

Let the great circle of the Earth, <term>RST</term>, now be set out with <term>E</term> as its center, whose diameter <term>SET</term> is compared to the line of mean motion <term>CD</term>, with the angles <term>FDC</term> and <term>DES</term> made equal to one another. Furthermore, the angle <term>PES</term>, or the arc <term>RS</term>, is the circumference by which the angle <term>FDC</term> differs from <term>DEP</term> (the angle of equality from the apparent position), which was demonstrated to be 5 degrees 31 minutes. When these are subtracted from a semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>, they leave the arc <term>RT</term> as 174 degrees 29 minutes, which is the distance of the star from the apogee <note>the farthest point from Earth</note> of the orbit, which is <term>T</term>, as if from the mean position of the Sun. 

And so we have it demonstrated that in the year of Christ 1527, on the sixth day before the Ides of October [October 10th], at six and two-fifths hours, the motion of Saturn’s anomaly from the highest apsis of the eccentric was 125 degrees 18 minutes. The motion of commutation <note>the planet's displacement due to the Earth's movement</note> was 174 degrees 29 minutes. And the position of the highest apsis was at 240 degrees 21 minutes from the first star of Aries in the sphere of the fixed stars.

### On the examination of Saturn’s motion. Chapter 7.

It has been shown that at the time of the last of Ptolemy’s three observations, Saturn was at 174 degrees 44 minutes according to its motion of commutation <note>original: "commutationis"; the apparent motion caused by the Earth’s own orbit, which we now call parallax</note>. The location of the highest apsis <note>the point in the orbit furthest from the center</note> of the eccentric was at 226 degrees 23 minutes from the head of the starry Aries <note>the vernal equinox, the fixed starting point of the zodiac</note>. It is clear, therefore, that in the time between both observations <note>Ptolemy's and Copernicus's</note>, Saturn completed 1,344 full revolutions of its equal commutations, minus one-quarter of a degree. 

There are, moreover, from the 20th year of Hadrian, on the 24th day of the Egyptian month Mesury, one hour before noon, until the year of Christ 1527, on the 6th day before the Ides of October, at six hours, the time of this observation: 1,392 Egyptian years, 75 days, and 48 minutes <note>original: "scrup."; here referring to sixty-unit fractions of a day</note>. If we wish to calculate the motion itself from the tables <note>original: "ex canone"; the standardized astronomical reference tables</note> for this duration, we will similarly find five sixty-unit blocks <note>original: "sexagenas"; 5 times 60, equaling 300 degrees</note>, 59 degrees, and 48 minutes, which are the remainder beyond the 1,324 full revolutions of commutation. Therefore, the values that have been set forth concerning the mean motions of Saturn are correct. 

During this same time, because the simple motion of the Sun is 82 degrees 30 minutes, and subtracting 359 degrees 45 minutes from this, there remain 82 degrees 45 minutes of Saturn’s mean motion, which now increases into its 47th revolution, agreeing with the calculation. Meanwhile, the location of the highest apsis of the eccentric has also advanced 13 degrees and 58 minutes against the sphere of the fixed stars; Ptolemy believed this point to be fixed in the same way <note>i.e., stationary relative to the stars</note>, but it now appears that it moves by nearly one degree in one hundred years.

During this time, the motion of Saturn’s commutation is 328 degrees 55 minutes. When this is subtracted from the 174 degrees 44 minutes <note>of Ptolemy's observation</note>, it leaves 205 degrees 49 minutes for the position

And for the era of Caesar, after 278 years and 118 and a half days, the motion is 247 degrees and 20 minutes, establishing a position of 35 degrees and 21 minutes at midnight on the Calends of January.

### On the commutations of Saturn, which arise from the annual orbit of the Earth, and how great its distance is. Chapter 9.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicting a bearded man in robes sitting outdoors in a landscape with a building and trees in the background.</image-desc>

The equal motions of Saturn in longitude, together with the apparent motions, have been demonstrated in this way. For the other appearances that occur to it are "commutations," arising, as we have said, from the annual orbit of the Earth. Just as the size of the Earth creates parallaxes <note>an apparent change in the position of an object when viewed from different points</note> relative to the Moon’s distance, so too does that orbit in which the Earth annually revolves around the five wandering stars <note>original: "quinque errantes stellas"; the five planets known since antiquity: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>; but because of the size of the orbit, these effects are far more evident. Such commutations, however, cannot be understood unless the altitude <note>the distance from the center</note> of the star is first known. It is possible to discover this through any single observation of commutation. 

We had such an observation regarding Saturn in the year of Christ 1514, on the sixth day before the Calends of March <note>February 24, 1514</note>, five equinoctial hours <note>standard 60-minute hours, as opposed to seasonal hours that varied with daylight</note> after the preceding midnight. For Saturn was seen in a straight line with the stars that are in the forehead of Scorpio—namely the second and third stars—which, having the same longitude, are at 209 degrees of the sphere of the fixed stars. Therefore, Saturn's position was also made clear through those same stars. From the beginning of the years of Christ until this hour, there are 1,514 Egyptian years, 77 days, and 13 minutes <note>original: "scrup."; here meaning sixty-unit fractions of a day</note>, and therefore according to...

According to this ratio, when Saturn is at its apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from Earth</term>, its altitude is 9 parts 42 minutes relative to the radius of Earth’s orbit (taken as 1 part); at its perigee <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to Earth</term>, it is 8 parts 39 minutes. 

From this, it can now be clearly established that Saturn's largest commutations [parallaxes] occur in the manner we explained regarding the Moon's small variations. For Saturn, these are 5 degrees 55 minutes when it is at its apogee, and 6 degrees 39 minutes when it is at its perigee. They differ from each other by 44 minutes, which occurs when the lines coming from the star [planet] touch the Earth's orbit. By this example, the specific differences in Saturn's motion are found, which we shall later set forth together for all five of these planets.

### Verification of the uniform motion of Jupiter. Chapter XII.

It was also seen above that in the last of the three flares of the height of night considered by Ptolemy, the star of Jupiter was in its mean motion at 4 degrees, 58 minutes, with an anomaly of parallax of 182 degrees, 47 minutes. ## On the star of Venus. Chapter XX.

The motions of the three superior [planets]—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—which encircle the Earth having been explained, it now occurs to speak of those which the Earth itself circles. And first concerning Venus: which admits a demonstration of its motion easier than those others, and more evident [Note: *euidentiorēm-q[ue]* → *euidentioremque*], provided that the necessary observations of certain places are not lacking. Since if its greatest distances from the mean place of the Sun on either side, morning and evening, are found to be equal to each other, we already hold for certain that in the middle of those two places of the Sun is the highest or lowest apsis of the eccentric of Venus. These are distinguished by the fact that such equalities of digressions [elongations] become smaller around the apogee, and larger in the opposite [perigee]. Finally, in other places, through the differences of those [elongations] by which they exceed one another, it is perceived without doubt how much the orbit of Venus is distant from the highest or lowest apsis, as well as its eccentricity, just as these things were most clearly handed down by Ptolemaeus; so that there would be no need to repeat them individually, except insofar as they are applied to our hypothesis of terrestrial mobility from the same considerations of Ptolemaeus. ## On Mercury. Chapter XXV.

By what modes Venus is bound to the motion of the earth, and under what ratio the equality of its circles lies hidden, has been shown; there remains Mercury, which without doubt will offer itself to the same assumed principle. Although it wanders in more involvements [convolutions] than that [Venus], or any of the above-mentioned. This much is certainly established by the experience of ancient observers, that [Note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] in the sign of Libra Mercury makes its smallest digressions from the Sun, and larger in its opposite, as is right. Yet it does not [make] the greatest in this place, but in certain others, such as in Gemini and Aquarius, especially in the time of Antoninus, according to the opinion of Ptolemaeus, which happens in no other star. The ancient mathematicians, believing the cause of this thing

[[margin: believing]]

**OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**

believing that the earth is immobile, and that Mercury moves in its great epicycle through an eccentric, when they noticed that [Note: *ꝙ* → *quod*] a single and simple eccentric could not satisfy these appearances—even granting that the eccentric itself moved in a center not its own, but another's—they were forced moreover to admit that the same eccentric carrying the epicycle moved in a certain other small circle, such as they admitted concerning the eccentric of the Moon; and so with three centers existing, namely one of the eccentric carrying the epicycle, another of the small circle, and a third of its (which the more recent call the equant) circle, they conceded that the epicycle is carried equally only around the center of the equant, having passed over the two prior [centers]; which was most foreign to the true center and its ratio, and to both pre-existing centers. Nor indeed did they think that the appearance of this star could be preserved by any other ratio, as is declared more diffusely in the Ptolemaic construction. But so that even this last star may be vindicated from the injury and opportunities of detractors, and so that it may be apparent that its equality is no less than that of the others preceding it under the mobility of the earth, we shall assign to it also an eccentric of an eccentric, in place of that which antiquity supposed to be an epicycle. But in a certain different way than in Venus, and nonetheless a certain epicycle may be moved in the eccentric itself, in which the star is carried not according to the circumference, but according to its diameter up and down, which can happen even from equal circular motions, as was set forth above concerning the precession of the equinoxes. Nor is it a wonder, since even Proclus in the exposition of the Elements of Euclid confesses that a straight line can be described by several motions. By all of which its appearances will be demonstrated; but so that the hypothesis may be more clearly understood, let the great orbit of the earth be AB, its center C, the diameter ACB, in which with center D assumed between the signs BC, however with the distance of a third part CD let a small circle EF be described, so that F is the maximum distance from C itself, and E the minimum. Let the orbit HI be an eccentric-eccentric, being an eccentric-epicycle. it follows that Mercury, by its own motion, does not always trace the same path around the circumference of a circle. Instead, depending on its distance from the center of its orbit, it varies greatly: the path is smallest at point $\kappa$ (kappa), largest at point $\lambda$ (lambda), and reaches a middle state through point $\iota$ (iota). This is almost the same manner that can be observed in the <term>epicycle of the epicycle<note>A complex geometric model where a small circle (epicycle) moves along the edge of another small circle, which in turn moves along a larger one. However, while the Moon moves along a circumference, Mercury moves along a diameter in a <term>reciprocal motion<note>Also known as "libration." How this occurs, we have already demonstrated regarding the <term>precession of the equinoxes<note>Copernicus used a similar 'libration' model in Book 1 to explain the slow, oscillating shift of the Earth's axis over centuries.</note></term>. This hypothesis satisfies all the observed appearances of Mercury, as will become clear from the records of observations by Ptolemy and others.

## On the position of the highest and lowest apsides of Mercury. Chapter XXVI.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial O, containing a crescent moon with a face and a starry sky background inside a square border.</image-desc>
For Ptolemy observed Mercury in the first year of <term>Antoninus<note>Antoninus Pius, the Roman Emperor (reigned 138–161 AD). Ptolemy’s ancient observations often use the years of a ruler's reign as a chronological anchor.</note></term>, after sunset on the 20th day of the month <term>Epiphi<note>The eleventh month of the ancient Egyptian calendar, used by Ptolemy for his records.</note></term>, while the planet was at its maximum evening distance from the mean position of the Sun. In our current calculation of time, this was the year 137 AD, on the 188th day, at 42.5 minutes past noon at <term>Krakow<note>Krakow was a major center of astronomical study where Copernicus was educated; he frequently calculated his astronomical tables relative to its geographical meridian.</note></term>. At this time, the mean position of the Sun, according to our calculations, was at 63° 50’, and the star was seen through the instrument at 7° of <term>Cancer<note>original: "Cancri"</note></term>. However, after subtracting the <term>precession of the equinoxes<note>The slow shift of the stars' positions relative to the spring equinox. Copernicus corrects ancient data to a "fixed" starting point to make them comparable to observations from his own time.</note></term>—which was then 6° 40’—it was clear that Mercury’s position was at 90° 20’ from the beginning of <term>Aries<note>original: "Arietis"</note></term> in the sphere of fixed stars, and its maximum distance from the mean Sun was 26.5°. He took another observation in the fourth year of Antoninus, in the early morning of the 19th day of the month <term>Phamenoth<note>The seventh month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note></term>. This was nearly 140 years, 67 days, and 12 minutes after the beginning of the years of Christ. ### On the more recent observations of the motions of Mercury, Chapter XXX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring an ornate frame with architectural and floral motifs, enclosing a small figure or scene.</image-desc> Indeed, the ancients showed us this way of examining the course of this star, but they were aided by a clearer sky—namely where the Nile, as they say, does not breathe out such vapors as our Vistula does. For to us, inhabiting a more frozen region, nature has denied that convenience, where the tranquility of the air is rarer, and furthermore, due to the great <term>obliquity of the sphere<note>Because Copernicus lived in Poland (a high latitude), the angle of the celestial sphere makes Mercury stay very close to the horizon, often lost in the thick air or twilight.</note></term>, the sky rarely permits one to see Mercury. For even at its maximum distance from the Sun, if it is in Aries or Pisces, it does not rise into our view; nor, conversely, does it set in Virgo or Libra. Furthermore, it does not show itself in any way in Cancer or Gemini when there is only the twilight of night or dawn, and never truly during the night, unless the Sun has retreated into a good portion of Leo. For these reasons, this star has tortured us with many detours and much labor so that we might scrutinize its wanderings. We have therefore borrowed three positions from those which were carefully observed at Nuremberg. The first was by Bernard Walther, a disciple of <term>Regiomontanus<note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg, a famous 15th-century astronomer whose work was vital to Copernicus.</note></term>, in the year of Christ 1491, five equal hours after midnight on the <term>fifth Ides of September<note>September 9th.</note></term>. ...of Virgo, with a northern latitude of 1 degree and five-sixths <note>Original: "part. i. medietate & tertia" — one plus a half plus a third equals 5/6 of a degree, or 50 minutes.</note>. At that time, the star was at the beginning of its morning occultation <note>This refers to the planet disappearing into the glare of the rising sun.</note>, while during the preceding days its morning visibility had been continuously decreasing. There were, therefore, from the beginning of the Christian era, 1491 Egyptian years, 258 days, 12 and a half minutes. The mean simple position of the Sun was 149 degrees and 48 minutes. But from the Vernal Equinox, it was at 26 degrees and 47 minutes of Virgo; from which the distance of Mercury was approximately 13 and a quarter degrees.

The second observation was in the year of Christ 1504, five days before the Ides of January <note>January 9th</note>, at 6 and a half hours after midnight, while the meridian at Nuremberg was at 10 degrees of Scorpio. It was observed by **Johannes Schöner**, to whom the star appeared at 3 and a third degrees of Capricorn, with a northern latitude of 45 minutes. Now, according to calculation, the mean position of the Sun from the Vernal Equinox was at 27 degrees and 7 minutes of Aquarius, which Mercury preceded in the morning by 23 degrees and 42 minutes.

A third observation was also made by the same **Johannes** in the same year, 1504, 15 days before the Kalends of April <note>March 18th</note>. He found Mercury at 26 degrees and one-tenth of a degree of Aries, with a northern latitude of almost 3 degrees, while the meridian at Nuremberg was at 25 degrees of Cancer. This was measured using <term>armillary spheres<note>A model of the celestial sphere with metal rings representing the principal circles (like the equator and ecliptic), used for determining coordinates.</note></term> compared against the same star of the <term>Palilicium<note>Original: "pallalitiij". A traditional name for the bright star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus.</note></term>, at 7 and a half hours after noon. At that time, the mean position of the Sun from the Vernal Equinox was 5 degrees and 39 minutes of Aries, from which Mercury, appearing in the evening, was 21 degrees and 17 minutes from the Sun.

Therefore, from the first position to the second, there are 12 Egyptian years, 125 days, 3 minutes, and 45 seconds. In this time, the simple motion of the Sun is 120 degrees and 14 minutes, and the <term>anomaly of commutation<note>The planet's position on its epicycle, which determines its apparent distance from the Sun as seen from Earth.</note></term> for Mercury is 316 degrees and 1 minute. In the second interval, there are 69 days, 31 minutes, and 45 seconds; the mean simple position of the Sun is 68 degrees and 32 minutes, and the mean anomaly of commutation for Mercury is 216 degrees.

From these three observations, therefore, we wish to examine the courses of Mercury for the present time. In these, we believe it must be granted that the proportions of the circles have remained as they were in Ptolemy’s time until now, since in other respects the good authors of the past are not found to have erred in this area. If, along with these, we also establish the position of the <term>apsis<note>The point in an orbit where the planet is at its maximum or minimum distance from the center of motion.</note></term> of the <term>eccentric<note>A circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth.</note></term>, nothing further would be required for the apparent motion of this star as well. We have assumed the location of the highest apsis to be at 211 and a half degrees—that is, at 28 and a half degrees of the sign of Scorpio—for it was not possible to accept a lower value without contradicting the observations. In this way, indeed, we shall have the anomaly of the eccentric...

<summary>Copernicus details three specific observations of Mercury from 1491 and 1504 (recorded by Johannes Schöner) to calculate the planet's modern orbital elements. He concludes by establishing the position of Mercury's highest apsis in the sign of Scorpio.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury, Johannes Schöner, observational astronomy, Sun, Scorpio, Capricorn, Aquarius, Aries, Cancer, armillary spheres, Palilicium, anomaly of commutation, apsis, eccentric orbit</keywords>

Hence also the angle **cef** is 2 parts and a half. However, so that we may know how much the orbit (of which the center is F) has increased from the apogee or perigee through the motion of approach and withdrawal [*accessus et recessus*], let a small circle be set out, divided into four by the diameters LM and NR at center O, and let the angle POM be taken as double the angle **acb**, namely 123 parts and a half. And from point P let a perpendicular be drawn to LM, which shall be PS. Therefore, according to the given ratio, OP—or LO, which is equal to it—is to OS as 10000 to 8349, and 190 to 105, which together constitute LS as 295 parts, of which **ac** is 10000.

Truly, in that ancient consideration in the 21st year of Ptolemy Philadelphus, in the dawn of the 19th day of the first month Thoth according to the Egyptians, the position of the highest apsis of the eccentric was, in Ptolemy’s opinion, at 182 parts 20 minutes in the sphere of the fixed stars; and the equal anomaly of commutation at 211 parts 47 minutes. Moreover, the time between this most recent and that ancient observation is 1768 Egyptian years, 200 days, 33 minutes, in which time the highest apsis of the eccentric moved under the sphere of the non-wandering stars [fixed stars] by 28 parts 10 minutes; and the motion of commutation, beyond the integral revolutions which are 5570, [was] 257 parts 51 minutes. Since in 20 years 64 periods are nearly completed, which in 1760 years total 5544 periods, and in the remaining 8 years and [200] days, 16 revolutions.

### On Establishing the Positions of Mercury. Chapter XXXI.

Since, therefore, from the beginning of the years of Christ until the last observation there are 1504 Egyptian years, 87 days, 48 minutes, in which the motion of the anomaly of commutation of Mercury is 63 parts 13 minutes, the integral revolutions having been rejected; when these are subtracted from 109 parts 38 minutes, there remain 46 parts 24 minutes, the position of the anomaly of commutation of Mercury at the beginning of the year of Christ. From which, again, to the beginning of the first Olympiad there are 775 Egyptian years, 12½ days, in which 95 parts 3 minutes are counted after the integral revolutions. When these are deducted from the position of Christ, one revolution having been borrowed, there remains for the first Olympiad the position of 311 parts 21 minutes. To this also, at the death of Alexander, in 451 years 247 days, by a calculation made, the position arrives at 213 parts 3 minutes.

### On a Certain Other Account of Approach and Withdrawal. Chapter XXXII.

However, before we depart from Mercury, it pleased us to review yet another mode, no less credible than the former, through which that approach and withdrawal can occur and be understood. For let there be a circle GH KP divided into four at center F, in which also a small homocentric circle LM is inscribed; and again, at center L, with a distance LFO equal to FG or FH, [let there be] another circle OR. Let it be posited that this whole form of circles...

...is carried around center F in consequence, with its sections GFR and HFP, daily by about 2 parts 7 minutes—namely, by as much as the motion of commutation of the star exceeds the motion of the Earth in the zodiac—from the apogee of the eccentric of the star, which meanwhile fulfills the remainder from sign G by its own motion through the circle OR of commutation, nearly similar to the terrestrial motion. Let it also be assumed that in this same annual revolution, the center of the orbit OR carrying the star is carried by a motion of libration through the diameter LFM, twice as great as that which we previously posited in reciprocating, as was said above. With these things thus constituted, when we have posited that the Earth moves by mean motion against the apogee of the center of the star, and at that time the center of the orbit carrying the star is at L, but the star itself is at sign O, which then at the minimum distance from F will describe the smallest circle by the motion of the whole, of which [the radius] shall be FO, and so on. So that when the Earth is around the mean apsides, the star falling into sign H, according to the maximum distance from F, will describe the greatest windings, namely according to the circle of which the center is F. For then the deferent which is OR will coincide with the circle GH on account of the unity of the center at F. Hence, with the Earth proceeding into the parts of the perigee, and with the center of orbit OR in the other of the extremes, which is M, it also raises the orbit itself above GK, and the star at R will again fall into the minimum distance from F, and that which happened at the beginning will happen to it. For here three revolutions concur, mutually equal: namely, that of the Earth to the apogee of the eccentric orbit of Mercury; the libration of the center along the diameter LM; and that of the planet from the line FG into the same [line]. From these, only the motion of the sections GH, KP differs from the apsis of the center, as we have said. Thus indeed, nature played around this star with such admirable variety, which she nevertheless confirmed by a perpetual, certain, and immutable order. But it must be noted here that in the mean spaces of the quadrants GH, KP, the star does not pass through without a difference in longitude, since the intervening diversity of centers will necessarily produce some prosthaphaeresis; but the instability of that center stands in the way. For if, for example, while the center remained at L, the star should proceed from O, it would admit the greatest difference around H, according to the measure...

...of the eccentricity FL. But it follows from the assumptions that the star, having progressed from O, begins indeed and promises the difference which the distance of the centers FL is bound to produce. But as the mobile center approaches the middle F, it is more and more withdrawn from the promised diversity, and it is frustrated to such an extent that around the middle sections HP it vanishes entirely, where the maximum was to be expected. And nonetheless, as we confess, having also been made small, it is hidden under the rays of the Sun, and it is not discerned in the East or the West as a morning or evening star, entirely under the windings of the circle. And indeed, we did not wish to pass over this mode, which is no less reasonable than the former, and which will come into use very clearly regarding the departures of latitudes.

### On the Tables of the Prosthaphaereses of the Five Wandering Stars. Chapter XXXIII.

[Note: *Decorative initial H*] These things concerning the motion of equality and appearance of Mercury and the rest of the wandering stars have been thus demonstrated and set out in numbers, by whose examples the way will lie open for calculating the differences of motions for any other places. And for this use we have prepared Canons, proper to each, of six orders, and of 30 rows, by triads of degrees as we are accustomed. First, two orders will have common numbers, both of the anomaly of the eccentric as well as of the commutations. The third [contains] the collected prosthaphaereses of the eccentric—the whole differences, I say, which fall between the equal and diverse motion of those orbits. Fourth, the proportional minutes, which are sixtieths, by which the commutations are increased or diminished on account of the greater or lesser distance of the Earth. Fifth, the prosthaphaereses themselves, which are the commutations occurring from the great orbit at the highest apsis of the eccentric of the planet. Sixth and last, the excesses by which those [commutations] that occur at the lowest apsis of the eccentric exceed [the others]. And these are the Canons.

X [Note: *Signature mark*] **Saturn**

**Vocabulary:** *prosthaphæresis* (correction), *anomalia* (anomaly), *eccentrus* (eccentric), *commutatio* (commutation/parallax), *scrupula* (minutes/scruples).

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...10,000 [parts], <note>The "parts" refer to a standardized radius used in Renaissance trigonometry, where the radius of the main circle is 10,000.</note> by which the star <note>Copernicus uses "star" (*stella*) to refer to the planet Mercury.</note> is made more distant from the center. When these [parts] have been added to the 3,573 parts of the minimum distance, they sum to 3,868. With this [distance] currently at hand, let a circle H G be described around the center F; join E G and E F, and let them be extended into the straight lines E F H. Since, therefore, the angle CEF is shown to be 2 1/2 degrees, and also angle GEC (the observed distance of the morning star from the mean Sun) is 13 1/4 degrees, the whole angle FEG will therefore be 15 3/4 degrees. <note>original: "part. XV. cum dodrante." A "dodrans" is a Latin term for three-quarters.</note>

But also, the ratio of side EF to FG in the triangle EFG is as 10,371 to 3,868. Since the angle is given, this ratio also shows us that the angle EGF is 49 degrees 8 minutes. For this angle, the remaining exterior angle will be 64 degrees 53 minutes; when these are subtracted from a full circle, they leave 295 degrees 7 minutes for the true <term>anomaly of commutation</term>. <note>The anomaly of commutation refers to the planet's position on its epicycle, representing its synodic motion relative to the Sun.</note> If you add the angle CEF to this, the mean and uniform [anomaly] will come out as 297 degrees 37 minutes, which is what I was seeking. 

If to this [value] we add 316 degrees 1 minute, we will have the uniform anomaly of commutation for the second observation equal to 253 degrees 38 minutes, which we shall also show to be certain and consistent with the observation. 

For let us set the angle ACB for the measure of the second anomaly of the eccentric at 58 degrees 29 minutes. Then, in triangle CEI, two sides are given: IC is 736, where EC is 10,000, and the angle ECI is 121 degrees 31 minutes. Therefore, the third side EI is 10,404 of the same parts, and the angle CEI is 3 degrees 28 minutes. 

Similarly, in triangle CIF, since angle EIF is 118 degrees 3 minutes and side IF is 211 1/2 (where EI is 10,404), the third side EF will be 10,505 such parts. The angle IEF will be 61 minutes, and the remaining angle FEC will therefore be 2 degrees 27 minutes. This is the <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>A geometric correction or "equation" used to bridge the difference between the mean motion and the actual observed position.</note> of the eccentric, which, when added to the mean motion of commutation, yields a true anomaly of 256 degrees 5 minutes. Now let us also take the epicycle of approach <note>The "approach and withdrawal" (*accessus et recessus*) refers to the libration or linear oscillation Copernicus used to explain Mercury's changing orbital distance.</note> in...

This will now be confirmed a third time, if we set the angle A C B at 127 degrees 1 minute, or the following angle B C E at 52 degrees 59 minutes. # NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

If we take the circumference of the true <term>commutation</term> <note>The "commutation" refers to the planet's position on its secondary circle (epicycle), which in Copernicus's system represents the Earth's motion relative to the planet.</note> B G to be 112 degrees 10 minutes, and we connect G to F, the resulting angle G F E will be 67 degrees 50 minutes. This angle is enclosed by the given sides: G F is 3,815 units and E F is 9,440 units. From these, the angle F E G is determined to be 23 degrees 50 minutes. After subtracting the <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>original: "prosthaphaeresi"; this is a technical term for the geometric correction or "equation" used to find the difference between a planet's mean and true position.</note> of E F, there remains the angle C E G, which is 21 degrees 18 minutes. This is the apparent distance between the evening star <note>Mercury, when visible after sunset.</note> and the center of the Great Orb <note>The "Great Orb" (Orbis Magnus) is Copernicus's term for the Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note>, which is almost exactly the distance found through the original observation.

These three positions, agreeing so perfectly with the observations, testify without a doubt that the position of the highest <term>apsis</term> <note>The "highest apsis" or apogee is the point in the orbit furthest from the center of motion.</note> of the eccentric is exactly what we assumed: 211 degrees 30 minutes relative to the sphere of the fixed stars in our own time. Furthermore, it is now certain that the following values are correct: the uniform anomaly of commutation was 297 degrees 37 minutes in the first position; 253 degrees 38 minutes in the second; and 109 degrees 38 minutes in the third—which was the result we were seeking.

In that ancient observation made in the 21st year of Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>A ruler of Egypt (3rd century BCE); Copernicus relies on his records preserved by the astronomer Ptolemy.</note>, at dawn on the 19th day of the first month, Thoth, according to the Egyptians, the position of the highest apsis of the eccentric was—in Ptolemy's opinion—at 182 degrees 20 minutes relative to the sphere of the fixed stars. The uniform anomaly of commutation was at 211 degrees 47 minutes. 

The time elapsed between this most recent observation and that ancient one is 1,768 Egyptian years, 200 days, and 33 minutes <note>In this context, "minutes" of a day refer to a fraction of a 24-hour period, common in astronomical calculations.</note>. During this interval, the highest apsis of the eccentric moved 28 degrees 10 minutes under the sphere of the fixed stars. The motion of commutation (beyond the complete revolutions, which number 5,570) was 257 degrees 51 minutes. This is consistent with the fact that in 20 years they complete...

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK 5

Consequently, in 5,568 years, 200 days, and 33 minutes <note>The term "minutes" (original: "scrupulis") here refers to astronomical fractions of a day or a degree, where 60 minutes make one whole unit.</note>, after 5,570 revolutions, there have increased 257 degrees and 51 minutes. By this amount, the observed positions—the ancient one and our own—differ, and these also agree with the numbers we have set forth in the tables. Furthermore, when we compare the 28 degrees and 10 minutes by which the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion.</note> of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit whose center is offset from the center of the universe (the Sun, in Copernicus's system).</note> moved during this time, it will be seen that the motion was one degree every 63 years, provided that the motion was uniform.

### On Establishing the Positions of Mercury. Chapter 31.

Therefore, since from the beginning of the years of Christ to the final observation there are 1,504 Egyptian years <note>The Egyptian year is a fixed calendar used by ancient astronomers consisting of exactly 365 days.</note>, 87 days, and 48 minutes, during which the motion of the <term>anomaly of commutation</term> <note>This refers to the planet's position on its secondary circle, representing the Earth's motion relative to the planet.</note> of Mercury is 63 degrees and 13 minutes, after rejecting the complete revolutions. When these are subtracted from 109 degrees and 38 minutes, there remains 46 degrees and 24 minutes: the position of the anomaly of commutation of Mercury at the beginning of the year of Christ. From that point, going back to the beginning of the first <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used as a chronological marker by the Greeks; the first Olympiad began in 776 BCE.</note>, there are 775 Egyptian years and 12.5 days. In this interval, 95 degrees and 3 minutes are counted after the complete revolutions. When these are deducted from the position at the time of Christ (by borrowing one full revolution), there remains the position for the first Olympiad: 311 degrees and 21 minutes. By a similar calculation for the period up to the death of <term>Alexander</term> <note>Alexander the Great, whose death in 323 BCE served as a common era for astronomical tables.</note> in 451 years and 247 days, the position is determined to be 213 degrees and 3 minutes.

### On Another Account of the Approach and Retreat. Chapter 32.

Before we depart from Mercury, it has pleased us to review yet another method, no less credible than the former, by which that <term>approach and retreat</term> <note>original: "accessus ac recessus"; this refers to the linear oscillation or "libration" of Mercury toward and away from the center, which Copernicus modeled using small circles.</note> can be performed and understood. Let there be a circle G H K P divided into four parts with center F. Within it, let a small <term>homocentric</term> <note>A circle sharing the same center as another circle.</note> circle L M be inscribed. Again, with center L and at a distance L F O equal to F G or F H, let there be another circle O R. Now, let it be assumed that this entire configuration of circles...

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

...of the circles <note>The text continues from the previous page describing the components of the planetary model.</note> is carried around center F in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia"; this refers to moving in the same direction as the zodiac signs, or counter-clockwise from a northern perspective.</note>, with its sections G F R, and H F P, daily by about 2 degrees and 7 minutes. This is the amount by which the motion of the star's <term>commutation</term> <note>The motion of the planet on its epicycle, or in this context, the relative motion between the planet and the Earth.</note> exceeds the Earth's motion in the zodiac, relative to the apogee of the star's <term>eccentric</term>. Meanwhile, the star completes the remainder of the motion from sign G through its own circle of commutation O R, which is almost similar to the Earth's motion.

It should also be assumed that in this same annual revolution, the center of the circle O R which carries the star is moved by a motion of <term>liberation</term> <note>A back-and-forth oscillation along a straight line, which Copernicus uses to explain variations in orbital distance.</note> along the diameter L F M. This motion is twice as great as the one we previously established for the reciprocating motion, as stated above.

With these things so established, when we have placed the Earth moving by mean motion toward the apogee of the star’s center, and at that time the center of the circle carrying the star is at L, but the star itself is at sign O, it will then—at its minimum distance from center F—describe the smallest circle through the motion of the whole, of which the radius is F O, and so on for the positions that follow. 

So it is that when the Earth is around the middle <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit where the planet is either closest to (perigee) or furthest from (apogee) the center.</note>, the star falls into sign H. At this point, being at its greatest distance from F, it will describe the largest windings <note>original: "anfractus"; referring to the complex, looping path the planet appears to take.</note>, namely according to the circle whose center is F. For then the carrying circle O R coincides with the circle G H because their centers unite at F. 

From this point, as the Earth proceeds toward the perigee and the center of circle O R moves to the other extreme, which is M, the circle itself is raised above G K. The star at R then falls back into the minimum distance from F, and the situation returns to how it was at the beginning.

For here, three revolutions coincide and are equal to one another: 
1. The Earth’s motion to the apogee of Mercury’s eccentric orbit.
2. The <term>liberation</term> of the center along the diameter L M.
3. The motion of the planet from the line F G back to the same. 

The only thing that differs from these is the motion of the sections G H and K P from the apse of the center, as we have said. Truly, nature has played with such wonderful variety around this star, yet she has confirmed it with a perpetual, certain, and immutable order.

But it must be noted here that in the middle spaces of the quadrants G H and K P, the star does not pass through without a difference in longitude. Since the shifting of the centers intervenes, it will necessarily produce some <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>original: "prosthaphæresim"; a mathematical correction added or subtracted to the mean motion to find the true position of a celestial body.</note>, but the instability of that center stands in the way. For if, for example, the center remained at L and the star proceeded from O, it would admit the greatest difference around H, according to the degree of its <term>eccentricity</term> <note>original: "eccentrotetis"; the measure of how much the orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>.

# BOOK V OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...of the eccentricity F L. But from these assumptions, it follows that the star, having set out from point O, begins and promises the difference <note>Meaning a deviation or variation in its path.</note> which the distance of the centers F L is meant to produce. However, as the moving center approaches the midpoint F, this promised variation is subtracted more and more, and is frustrated to such an extent that around the midsections H and P it vanishes entirely, precisely where the greatest variation was expected. Nevertheless, as we must admit, even when this variation occurs, it is small and hidden under the rays of the Sun <note>The astronomical phenomenon of "combustion," where a planet is too close to the Sun to be seen.</note>. Thus, it is not perceived in either the East or the West as a morning or evening star, being completely hidden within the windings of the circle. We did not wish to omit this model, as it is no less reasonable than the previous one, and it will be used most clearly when we discuss the departures in latitude <note>Copernicus is referring to the planet's movement north or south of the ecliptic plane.</note>.

### Chapter XXXIII. Regarding the tables of corrections for the five wandering stars.

[[image: Decorative initial 'H' featuring a man's face.]] THESE things concerning the uniform and apparent motion <note>original: "motu aequalitatis & apparentiae"; "uniform" refers to the theoretical constant speed, while "apparent" refers to how we see it from Earth.</note> of Mercury and the other wandering stars <term>planets</term> have been thus demonstrated and set forth in numbers. By these examples, the way will be open to calculate the differences of motions for any other positions. For this purpose, we have prepared Tables <note>original: "Canones"; in this context, it refers to mathematical tables or "canons" of calculation.</note> specific to each planet, consisting of six columns and 30 rows, progressing by triads of degrees <note>Increments of 3 degrees, a common practice in Renaissance astronomical tables to save space.</note>, as is our custom. 

In the first two columns, we will have the common numbers for both the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>The angle of the planet from its furthest point (apogee) on its main circle.</note> and the <term>commutations</term> <note>The variation caused by the Earth’s own movement around the Sun.</note>. The third column contains the "collected corrections" of the eccentric—that is, the total differences that occur between the uniform and the non-uniform motion of those orbits. The fourth column contains the <term>proportional minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula proportionum"; these are fractions (sixtieths) used to adjust the calculations based on the Earth's distance from the planet.</note>, by which the commutations are increased or decreased due to the greater or lesser distance of the Earth. The fifth column contains the corrections themselves, which are the commutations occurring at the highest apogee of the planet's eccentric caused by the great orbit <note>The Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note>. The sixth and last column contains the "excesses" by which those commutations occurring at the lowest apogee exceed the others. And these are the Tables:

--- Page 378 ---
# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

### How the positions of these five stars are calculated in longitude. Ch. XXXIIII.

**P**erceived thus through these Canons [tables] as set forth by us, we shall calculate the positions of these five wandering stars [planets] in longitude without difficulty. For in all of these, the method of calculation is nearly the same; however, in this the outer planets [Saturn, Jupiter, Mars] differ somewhat from Venus and Mercury. First, therefore, let us speak of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. Their calculation is such that for any proposed time, the mean motions are sought—namely, the simple motion of the Sun and the commutation [parallax] of the planet—by the method previously handed down. Next, the place of the highest apsis [apogee] of the eccentric of the planet is subtracted from the simple place of the Sun, and from that which remains, the anomaly of commutation [is subtracted]; what then remains is the anomaly of the eccentric of the star, whose number we shall seek among the common numbers in either of the first [two] rows of the table; and conversely, in the third column, we shall take the equation of the eccentric and the subsequent scruples of proportions. We shall add this equation to the anomaly of commutation and subtract it from the anomaly of the eccentric if the number by which we entered was found in the first series; and conversely, we shall subtract it from the anomaly of commutation and add it to the anomaly of the eccentric if it held the second row; and that which has been collected or left behind will be the equated anomalies of commutation and the eccentric, while the scruples of proportions are preserved for the use soon to be mentioned. Furthermore, we shall seek the anomaly of commutation thus equated also among the earlier common numbers, and in the corresponding fifth column, we shall take the prosthaphaeresis of commutation with its excess placed at the end; from this excess we shall take the proportional part according to the number of scruples of proportions, which we shall always add to the prosthaphaeresis, and it will compute the true commutation of the planet, to be subtracted from the equated anomaly of commutation if it be less than a semicircle, or added if in a larger semicircle. For thus we shall have the true and apparent distance of the star from the mean place of the Sun in precedence [retrograde], which when we have rejected it from the Sun, the sought position of the star will be left...

***

--- Page 379 ---
[[original page: 179]]

# BOOK V OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...relative to the sphere of the fixed stars. To which, finally, if the precession of the equinoxes be applied, it will determine its position from the vernal section [the vernal equinox]. In Venus and Mercury, we use for the anomaly of the eccentric that which exists from the highest apsis to the mean position of the Sun; through which anomaly we equate the motion of commutation and the eccentric anomaly itself, as has already been said. But the prosthaphaeresis of the eccentric, together with the equated parallax, if they be of one affection or type, are simultaneously added to or subtracted from the mean position of the Sun. If, however, they be of different types, the smaller is subtracted from the larger, and with that which remains, let it be done as we just said, according to the additive or ablative property of the larger number, and the apparent position of the one sought will emerge.

### On the stations and retrogradations [repedationibus] of the five wandering stars. Ch. XXXV.

**A**lso pertaining to the account of the motion which is according to longitude, it seems, is the knowledge of their stations, regressions, and retrogradations: where, when, and of what magnitude they occur. Concerning these matters, Mathematicians have treated not a few things, especially Apollonius of Perga. But in a manner as if with only one inequality, and that by which the stars themselves moved with respect to the Sun, which we have called commutation, on account of the motion of the great orbit of the Earth. Similarly in the other three outer ones, whose motion is slower than the velocity...

FURTHERMORE, if the orbits on which the stars are carried were homocentric to the Great Orbit, those things which the demonstrations promise would easily be established, the ratio of the speed of the star to the speed of the sight remaining always the same; but they are eccentric, and from this the motions are diverse according to appearance. **NICOLAUS COPERNICUS ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK SIX.**

WHAT power and effect the assumed revolution of the Earth would have in the apparent motion in longitude of the wandering stars, and into what order it compels all those things (certain and necessary indeed), we have indicated as far as we were able. It remains that we be occupied concerning the transits of those stars by which they diverge in latitude, and that we show how in these also the same mobility of the Earth exercises its command and has prescribed laws for them even in this part. Moreover, this part of the science is necessary, because the digressions of these stars produce no small difference concerning their rising and setting, their appearances, occultations, and other things which were set forth generally above. Nay, their true places are then said to be known when the longitude together with the latitude from the circle of the signs [the zodiac] shall be established. Therefore, those things which the ancient Mathematicians thought they had demonstrated here also through the stability of the Earth, we are about to do the same through its assumed mobility, perhaps with greater brevity and more fittingly.

**General exposition concerning the digression in latitude of the five wandering stars. Chapter I.**

THE ancients found twofold expansions of latitude in all these [planets], corresponding to the twofold inequality of the longitude of each of them. One occurring by occasion of the eccentric orbits, the other according to the epicycles—in place of which epicycles we have accepted the one Great Orbit of the Earth, already often repeated. Not that the orbit itself in any way declines from the plane of the zodiac once and for ever maintained, since they are the same, but because the orbits of those stars are inclined toward this [plane] by...

[[Vocabulary: latitude, longitude, zodiacal, digressions]]

### PAGE 386

[[Original page: verso of 182]]

**NICOLAI COPERNICI**

...by an obliquity that is not fixed. Which variety indeed is regulated according to the motion and revolutions of the Great Orbit of the Earth. Since, truly, the three superior planets—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—are carried in longitude by certain other laws than the remaining two, so also in the motion of latitude they differ not a little. They [the ancients] scrutinized first, therefore, where and how great were their extreme limits of Northern latitude, which Ptolemy found in Saturn and Jupiter about the beginning of Libra; in Mars, however, about the end of Cancer, almost at the apogee of the eccentric. In our times, however, we have found these Northern limits: for Saturn in 7 degrees of Scorpio, for Jupiter in 27 of Libra, for Mars in 27 of Leo, according as the apogees have also been shifted up to us. For the inclinations and the hinges [cardines] of the latitudes follow the motion of those orbits; between these limits, through the quadrants of the circles according to the equated or apparent distances, they seem to make no departure of latitude at all, wherever the Earth may then happen to be. In these middle longitudes, therefore, they are understood to be in the common section [nodes] of their orbits with the zodiac, not otherwise than the Moon in the ecliptic sections, which Ptolemy here calls nodes: the ascending node from which the star enters the Northern parts, and the descending node where it migrates into the Southern. Not that the Great Orbit of the Earth, remaining always in the same plane of the zodiac, brings any latitude to them, but all digression of latitude is from them [the planets' orbits], which varies most in places other than these, to which [the star] approaching the Earth (when they are seen opposite the Sun and acronychal), they always run out with a greater departure than in any other position of the Earth: in the Northern hemicycle toward the North, in the Southern toward the South; and that by a greater difference than the access and recess of the Earth requires. By which occasion it is known that the inclination of those orbits is not fixed, but is that which is changed by a certain motion of libration commensurable with the revolutions of the Great Orbit of the Earth, as will be said a little below. Venus, however, and Mercury seem to run out in certain other ways, yet with a certain law observed toward the mean, extreme, and lowest apsides. For in the mean longitudes, namely when the line of the mean motion of the Sun shall stand apart by quadrants from the highest or lowest apsis of them, and the stars themselves shall be away from the same line of mean motion by quadrants of their orbits [in] evening...

...evening or morning [appearances], they found no departure in them from the circle of signs, by which they understood them then to be in the common section of the circles of the signs and the zodiac [Note: likely "orbits and zodiac" intended], which section passes through their apogees and perigees. And therefore, being superior or inferior with respect to the Earth, they then make manifest egressions. The greatest, truly, in the greatest distance from the Earth, that is, about the evening emergence or morning occultation, where Venus is seen most Northern, Mercury Southern. And alternately in the place nearer to the Earth, when as evening stars they are occulted, or as morning stars they emerge: Venus is Southern, Mercury Northern. Vice versa, with the Earth existing in the place opposite to this, and in the other mean apsis (namely while the anomaly of the eccentric was 270 parts [degrees]), Venus appears in a greater distance from the Earth as Southern, Mercury Northern; and about the place nearer the Earth, Venus is Northern, Mercury Southern. In the conversion of the Earth to the apogees of these stars, Ptolemy found for the morning Venus a Northern latitude, for the evening an Austral [Southern] one. That also, in turn, for the morning Mercury an Austral, for the evening a Northern. These are similarly converted in the opposite place of the perigee, so that Venus the Morning Star [Lucifer] is seen Southern, the Evening Star [Vesperugo] Northern, but the morning Mercury Northern, the evening Southern. And yet in both these places they found the Northern departure of Venus always greater than the Southern, and the Southern of Mercury greater than the Northern. By which occasion they reasoned that there was a twofold latitude in this place, and three in total. The first, which is in the mean longitudes, they called Inclination. The second, which is in the highest and lowest apsis, Obliquity. And the remainder joined to this, Deviation—for Venus always Northern, for Mercury Southern. Between these four limits they are mixed in turn, and alternately increase and decrease, and yield to each other, for all of which we shall assign fitting occasions.

Both, however, are commensurable with the revolutions of the Earth, but not in one way. For the first libration has this [property]: that once the Earth has revolved to their apsides, the motion of the libration itself revolves twice, having as a permanent axis the section which we said [passes] through the apogees and perigees, so that as often as the line of the mean motion of the Sun is in their perigee or apogee, the greatest angle of the section occurs. In the mean longitudes, however, always the least.
