--- Page 382 ---
<meta>This page continues the geometric proof from the previous page (180 recto), where Copernicus is establishing the mathematical criteria for the "stations" of planets—the points where they appear to stop and reverse direction (retrograde motion) from our perspective on Earth.</meta>

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

...our sight has traversed the opposite space of that which lies between the lines EF and EL. It is evident that in the same amount of time that the arc GF has moved the star in <term>retrograde motion</term> <note>original: *praecedentia*; the apparent backward or westward movement of a planet</note> relative to our sight under the smaller angle FEG, the movement of the Earth has pulled it back into <term>direct motion</term> <note>original: *consequentia*; the standard eastward movement of a planet</note> under the larger angle FEL. Thus, the star, having been left behind while still under the angle GEL and falling back, does not yet seem to have come to a <term>station</term> <note>The point where a planet appears to stop moving against the stars</note>.

It is manifest, however, that the opposite will be demonstrated by the same means. If, in the same diagram, we set half of GK to GE in the same ratio as the motion of the Earth has to the velocity of the planet; and if we take the arc GF toward the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth</note> from the straight line EK, then with KF connected to form the triangle KEF (in which GE is designated as greater than EF), the ratio of KG to GE will be less than the ratio of the angle FEG to the angle FKG. Likewise, half of KG to GE has a smaller ratio than the angle FEG has to double the angle FKG—that is, to the angle GDF in turn, as was previously demonstrated. 

And it will be gathered by the same logic that the angle GDF has a smaller ratio to the angle FEG than the velocity of the star has to the velocity of our sight <note>Meaning the Earth's orbital speed</note>. Therefore, while they maintain the same ratio, if the angle GDF is made larger, the star will complete a greater step in retrograde motion than the forward progression requires. 

From these proofs, it is also clear that if we assume the arcs FC and CL to be equal, the **second station** will be at point L. If indeed the line ELM is drawn, the ratio of half of LM to LE will also be the same as the ratio of the Earth's velocity to the star's velocity, just as half of BF was to FE. Therefore, the points F and L will encompass both stations, and they will define the entire arc FCL as retrograde, and the remainder of the circle as progressive.

It also follows that at those distances where the line DC does not have a greater ratio to CE than the velocity of the Earth has to the velocity of the star, it will not be possible to draw another straight line in a ratio equal to this, nor will the star seem to stop or move in retrograde. For when the straight line DC is assumed in the triangle DEG—being smaller than EG—the angle CEG will have a smaller ratio to CDG than the line DC has to CE. But the ratio of DC to CE is not greater than the velocity of the Earth to the velocity of the star; therefore, the angle CEG will also have a smaller ratio to CDG than the velocity of the Earth has to the velocity of the star. Where this occurs, the star **will move forward**...

<summary>Copernicus uses geometric triangles and orbital velocity ratios to define the "stations" of planets, proving how the Earth's motion creates the illusion of a planet stopping or moving backward (retrograde).</summary>

### How the times, places, and arcs of the retrogressions are determined. Chapter 36.

[[image: A geometrical diagram featuring a large circle with points A, B, and C on the circumference and D at the center. Point E sits outside the circle. A line segment connects E, F, D, and A. Another line connects E to B and C. This represents the geometric relationship between the Earth's orbit and an external planet.]]

Furthermore, if the orbits on which the wandering stars <note>original: *sidera erratia*; the planets</note> are carried were <term>concentric</term> <note>original: *homocentri*; sharing the same center</note> with the Great Orbit, the things promised by these demonstrations would be easily established, as the ratio of the star's speed to the speed of our sight would always remain the same. However, the orbits are <term>eccentric</term> <note>original: *eccentri*; having a center that does not coincide with the center of the Earth's orbit</note>, and consequently, their movements appear diverse. For this reason, we must take the distinct and adjusted movements wherever their differences in velocity occur, and use those in our demonstrations, rather than simple and uniform movements—unless the star happens to be near its mean longitudes, where it appears to be carried in its orbit with a median motion.

We shall demonstrate this using the example of Mars, which will make the <term>retrogradations</term> <note>original: *repedationes*; the apparent backward motion of a planet against the stars</note> of the remaining planets clearer. Let ABC be the Great Orbit in which our sight [the Earth] travels. Let the star be at point E, from which a straight line ECDA is drawn through the center of the orbit, as well as line EFB. Let the ratio of half of BF to EF be the same as the ratio of the adjusted velocity of the star to the velocity of our sight (by which it surpasses the star). 

Our goal is to find the arc FC, which is half of the retrogradation, or the arc ABF, so that we may know how far the star is from the point of greatest distance AB when it begins its <term>station</term> <note>The point where a planet appears to stop moving before changing direction</note>, as well as the angle contained under FBC. From these, we shall predict the time and place of such a phenomenon. Let us place the star near the middle <term>apsis</term> <note>original: *absida*; the point in an orbit where a planet is at its median distance from the center</note> of the eccentric orbit, where the motion of longitude and the <term>anomaly</term> <note>original: *anomaliae*; the irregularities or deviations in a planet's predicted uniform motion</note> differ little from uniform motions. Since, therefore, in the case of the star Mars, its median motion is...

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

...will be 1 part, 8 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: *scrupula*; literally "scruples," referring to minutes of arc</note>, and 7 seconds. This is half of line $BF$, insofar as the motion of <term>commutation</term> <note>The perceived change in position of a planet caused by the Earth’s own motion</note>—that is, the motion of our sight—relative to the mean motion of the star is calculated to be 1 part. Thus, $BF$ is a straight line, such that the whole $EB$ consists of 3 such parts, 16 minutes, and 14 seconds; and the rectangle contained under $BE$ and $EF$ is also 3 parts, 16 minutes, and 14 seconds. 

Now, we have demonstrated that $DA$, which is from the center of the orbit, is 6580 where $DE$ is 10000. But where $DB$ is 60, $DA$ will be 39.29, and the whole $AB$ is to $EC$ as 99.29 is to 20.31. The rectangle contained by them is 2041.4, which is understood to be equal to the rectangle under $BE$ and $EF$. Therefore, following the proportions generated from the <term>parabola</term> <note>Copernicus likely refers here to the geometric method of Apollonius</note>, by dividing 2041.4 by 3.16.14, we obtain 624.4, the square root of which is 24.58.52. This is the value of $EF$ in those parts where $DE$ was set at 60. However, where $DE$ is 10,000, $EF$ will be 4163, while $DF$ is 6580. 

Therefore, in the triangle $DBE$, since the sides are given, we find that angle $DEF$ is 27 degrees and 15 minutes; this is the angle of the planet’s <term>regression</term> <note>original: *regressionis*; the backward or retrograde motion of the planet in the sky</note>. We also find angle $CDF$, the anomaly of commutation, to be 16 degrees and 50 minutes. Since the star appears on line $EF$ at its first station, and the star is <term>acronychal</term> <note>original: *acronychtus*; the moment a planet is directly opposite the Sun, rising exactly at sunset</note> at line $EC$, if the star did not move eastward <note>original: *in consequentia*; in the order of the zodiac signs</note>, the circumference $CF$ would encompass the 16 degrees and 50 minutes of the discovered regression—namely 27 degrees and 15 minutes—under angle $AEF$. 

But according to the established ratio of the star's speed to the speed of our sight, 16 degrees and 50 minutes of commutation anomaly corresponds to approximately 19 degrees, 6 minutes, and 39 seconds of the star's longitude. When these are subtracted from 27 degrees and 15 minutes, there remain 8 degrees and 8 minutes from one of the stations to the acronychal point, spanning nearly 36 and a half days, during which those 19 degrees, 6 minutes, and 39 seconds of longitude are completed. Consequently, the total regression is 16 degrees and 16 minutes, completed over 73 days. 

These things are demonstrated for the mean distances of the <term>eccentric</term>, and are shown similarly in other locations, but one must always use the specific velocity of the star according to its position, as we have said. Accordingly, the same method of demonstration is evident for Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, as well as for Venus and Mercury—provided that we take the sight-line through the star or the star through the sight-line. These phenomena are indeed reversed in the orbits that the Earth surrounds <note>the inner planets, Mercury and Venus</note> compared to those that surround the Earth <note>the outer planets</note>. Therefore, let these remarks suffice, so that we do not repeat the same song over and over. 

Yet, since the variable motion of the star according to our sight and the ambiguity of the stations bring no small difficulty—from which the theorem of Apollonius does not release us—I do not know if it would not be better for someone to seek the stations simply and directly from their position. This would be done in the same way we seek the <term>conjunction</term> of an acronychal star with the line of the Sun’s mean motion, or the meeting of any stars, by using the known numbers of their motions to find where they join. We leave this to the preference of the reader.

**End of the Fifth Book of the Revolutions.**

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK SIX.

<note>The initial letter **Q** is large and ornate, featuring a stylized human face and classical motifs.</note> **W**e have indicated, as far as we were able, what power and effect the assumed revolution of the Earth has regarding the apparent motion in <term>longitude</term> <note>The position of a celestial body measured East-West along the ecliptic</note> of the wandering stars <note>original: *errantium siderum*; the planets</note>, and into what certain and necessary order that revolution forces all these things. It remains for us to occupy ourselves with the passages of those stars by which they digress in <term>latitude</term> <note>The position of a celestial body measured North-South relative to the ecliptic plane</note>, and to show how, in these matters as well, the same mobility of the Earth exercises authority and has prescribed laws for them in this part too. Moreover, this part of the science is necessary because the <term>digressions</term> <note>The deviation of a planet from the ecliptic plane</note> of these stars cause no small difference regarding their rising and setting, their appearances and disappearances, and other phenomena which were generally explained above. Furthermore, their true locations are only said to be known when their longitude is established together with their latitude relative to the <term>circle of signs</term> <note>original: *signorum circulo*; the Zodiac</note>. Therefore, what the ancient mathematicians believed they demonstrated here through the stability of the Earth, we shall do the same through its assumed mobility, perhaps with greater brevity and more appropriately.

### A general explanation of the digression in latitude of the five wandering stars. Chapter I.

<note>The initial letter **D** is ornate, decorated with botanical motifs.</note> **T**he ancients found a two-fold expansion in latitude for all these planets, corresponding to the two-fold inequality of the longitude of each. One occurs by occasion of the <term>eccentric orbits</term> <note>Orbits whose center does not coincide with the center of the universe/Earth</note>, and the other by means of <term>epicycles</term> <note>Small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger ones</note>. In place of these epicycles, we have accepted the one "Great Orbit" of the Earth, as we have already often repeated. It is not that this orbit itself in any way declines from the plane of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signiferi*; the "sign-bearer" or ecliptic plane</note> once it has been established for all eternity, since they are the same, but that the orbits of those planets are inclined to this plane obliqu— <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the word is likely *oblique* (obliquely).</note>

<summary>Copernicus introduces Book VI, shifting focus from planetary longitudes to latitudes. He argues that the Earth's motion explains the complex North-South movements of the planets more efficiently than the ancient models of stationary Earth and epicycles.</summary>

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

...pted <note>completing the word "assumed" from the previous page; original Latin: *assumpta*</note> with an obliquity that is not fixed. This variation is regulated according to the motion and revolutions of the great orbital circle of the Earth. Since, indeed, the three superior planets—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—are carried in longitude by certain laws different from the remaining two [Venus and Mercury], they also differ significantly in their motion in latitude. Therefore, they <note>astronomers of the past</note> first investigated where and how great the extreme limits of their northern <note>original: *Boreae*</note> latitude were. Ptolemy found these for Saturn and Jupiter near the beginning of Libra, but for Mars near the end of Cancer, almost at the apogee of its <term>eccentric</term> <note>An orbital path that is not centered exactly on the Sun</note>. In our own times, however, we have found these northern <note>original: *Septentrionales*</note> limits to be: for Saturn, in the 7th degree of Scorpio; for Jupiter, in the 27th degree of Libra; and for Mars, in the 27th degree of Leo, just as the apogees have also shifted down to our time. 

For the inclinations and the pivotal points <note>original: *cardines*</note> of their latitudes follow the motion of those orbital circles. Between these limits—through the quadrants of the circles according to the <term>equated</term> <note>calculated or adjusted for irregularities</note> or apparent distances—they seem to make no departure in latitude at all, wherever the Earth happens to be at that time. In these middle longitudes, therefore, they are understood to be at the common intersection of their orbits with the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signifero*</note>, not unlike the Moon in its ecliptic intersections, which Ptolemy here calls **nodes**: the **ascending node**, from which the star enters the northern parts, and the **descending node**, by which it passes into the southern <note>original: *Austros*</note> parts. 

It is not that the great orbital circle of the Earth, always remaining in the same plane of the zodiac, brings any latitude to them; rather, all deviation in latitude comes from the planets themselves. This deviation varies most in places other than these [the nodes]. As the Earth approaches them—when they appear opposite the Sun and are <term>acronychal</term> <note>rising at the moment of sunset and visible all night</note>—they always deviate with a greater departure than in any other position of the Earth. In the northern hemisphere they move toward the North, and in the southern toward the South, and this occurs with a greater difference than the approach and retreat of the Earth alone would require. On this account it has been recognized that the inclination of those orbits is not fixed, but changes by a certain motion of <term>libration</term> <note>a slow, swinging oscillation back and forth like a pendulum</note> commensurable with the revolutions of the Earth’s great orbital circle, as will be explained a little further below. 

Venus and Mercury, however, appear to deviate in certain other ways, yet following a fixed law observed in relation to their middle, highest, and lowest <term>apsides</term> <note>the points in an orbit closest or furthest from the center</note>. For in their middle longitudes—namely, when the line of the Sun’s mean motion is at a distance of a quadrant from their highest or lowest apsis, and the stars themselves are a quadrant’s distance from that same line of mean motion on their own orbits, whether in the evening...

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK VI.

...whether as morning or evening stars, they found no departure from the circle of signs <note>original: *orbe signorum*; refers to the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path</note> in them. By this, they understood that these planets were then at the common intersection of the orbits of the signs and the zodiac <note>original: *signiferi*</note>, which intersection passes through their apogees and perigees. Therefore, whether they are higher or lower with respect to the Earth, they make their departures manifest at those times. Indeed, at the greatest distance from the Earth—that is, around the evening emergence or the morning occultation—Venus is seen at her most Northern <note>original: *Borea*</note>, and Mercury at his most Southern <note>original: *Austrinus*</note>. Conversely, in the position closer to the Earth, when they are hidden in the evening or emerge in the morning, Venus is Southern and Mercury is Northern. In turn, when the Earth is in the opposite position and at the other middle <term>apsis</term> <note>The points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the center of motion</note>—namely, when the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its apogee</note> of the eccentric is 270 degrees—Venus appears Southern at her greater distance from the Earth, and Mercury Northern; but near the location closer to the Earth, Venus is Northern and Mercury Southern. Furthermore, at the transition of the Earth to the apogees of these stars, Ptolemy found a Northern latitude for Venus when she is a morning star, and a Southern one when she is an evening star. Likewise, for Mercury, he found a Southern latitude as a morning star and a Northern one as an evening star. These are similarly reversed at the opposite position of the perigee, so that Venus as <term>Lucifer</term> <note>The Morning Star</note> is seen as Southern, and as <term>Vesperugo</term> <note>The Evening Star</note> as Northern; but Mercury as a morning star is Northern, and as an evening star is Southern. Yet, in both of these positions, they found the Northern departure of Venus to be always greater than the Southern, and the Southern departure of Mercury to be greater than the Northern. On this occasion, they reasoned that there is a double latitude in this location, and three in total. The first, which occurs at the middle longitudes, they called **Inclination**. The second, which occurs at the highest and lowest apsides, they called **Obliquity**. And the third, joined to this, they called **Deviation**—which is always Northern for Venus and Southern for Mercury. Between these four limits, these motions are mixed together; they alternately increase and decrease and give way to one another. We shall assign appropriate causes for all of these.

# OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...variable but regular. For in Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, the angle of intersection receives a certain libration <note>original: *librationem*; a slow oscillation, like the motion of a balance scale</note> along that intersection as an axis, similar to what we demonstrated regarding the precession of the equinoxes. However, this is a simple libration, commensurable <note>proportionate in scale</note> with the motion of commutation <note>original: *motui commutationis*; the planet's synodic motion, or its position relative to the Sun as seen from Earth</note>, under which it increases and decreases within a fixed interval. 

So it is that whenever the Earth is closest to the planet—namely, at the acronychal <term>rising</term> <note>original: *acronychto*; when the planet is in opposition to the Sun and rises exactly as the Sun sets</note>—the maximum inclination of the planet's orbit occurs; in the opposite position, the minimum; and in the middle, a mean inclination. Thus, when the planet is at the limit of its greatest Northern or Southern latitude, its latitude appears much greater when in proximity to the Earth than at its greatest distance. 

And although the unequal distance of the Earth alone could be the cause of this variation—following the rule that closer objects appear larger than more remote ones—the latitudes of these stars increase and decrease by a greater difference than can be explained by distance alone. This cannot happen unless their orbits also oscillate <note>original: *librentur*</note> in their obliquity <note>tilt or angle</note>. But as we have said before, in things that oscillate, it is necessary to take a certain mean between the extremes. 

To make these things clearer, let there be the "Great Circle" <note>the Earth's orbit around the Sun</note> which is in the plane of the zodiac <note>original: *signiferi*; the ecliptic</note> **ABCD**, having center **E**. To this, let the planet’s orbit be inclined, which shall be **FGKL**, representing the mean and permanent declination <note>the angle of the orbit's tilt</note>. Its Northern limit of latitude is **F**, the Southern is **K**; the descending node <note>original: *nodus*; the point where the planet's path crosses the Earth's orbital plane from North to South</note> of the section is **G**, and the ascending node is **L**. The common section is **BED**, which extends into the straight lines **GE** and **DL**. These four limits indeed do not change, except according to the motion of the <term>apsides</term> <note>the points in an orbit where the planet is nearest or farthest from the center of motion</note>. 

Let it be understood, however, that the motion of the star in longitude is not carried along the plane of the circle **FG** itself, but along another circle **OP**, which is oblique <note>tilted</note> to **FG** and homocentric <note>sharing the same center</note> with it, and which intersects it in the same...

# BOOK VI OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...GB and DL are a straight line. Therefore, while the star is carried under the orbit OP, and occasionally coinciding with the plane FK by the motion of libration <note>original: *librationis*; a rocking or oscillating motion like a balance scale</note>, it migrates into both parts [North and South], and because of this, it makes the latitude appear variable. For let the star first be at its greatest Northern latitude under the sign O, closest to the Earth, which is located at A; the latitude of the star will then increase according to the angle OGF of the greatest inclination of orbit OGP. Because the motion of this approach and retreat is commensurable <note>proportional or synchronized</note> by hypothesis to the motion of commutation <note>original: *motui commutationis*; the planet's position relative to the Sun as seen from Earth</note>, if the Earth is then at B, O will coincide with F, and the latitude of the star will appear smaller in that same place than before. It will appear much smaller still if the Earth is at the sign C, for O will migrate to the extreme and opposite part of its libration, and will leave only as much as remains from the libration that subtracts from the Northern latitude—namely, from an angle equal to OGF. From then on, through the remaining semicircle CDA, the Northern latitude of the star (which is around F) will increase until it returns to the first sign A, from which it departed. 

The same process and manner will apply to a southern star positioned around the sign K, taking the start from the Earth's motion. But if the star is at either node G or L, whether it is acronychal <term>rising</term> <note>rising at sunset, when the planet is opposite the Sun</note> or hidden under the Sun, no latitude of the star will be perceived even though the orbits FK and OP are then at their greatest inclination to each other, since the star would be occupying the common section <note>the "hinge" or intersection line</note> of the orbits. From these things, I believe it is easily understood how the Northern latitude of a planet decreases from F to G, and the Southern latitude increases from G to K, which then vanishes entirely at L and passes into the North. 

And those three superior planets behave in this way. Venus and Mercury differ from them in their latitudes, just as they do in longitude, because they have the common sections of their orbits located through their apogees <term>apogaea</term> <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the center</note> and perigees <term>perigaea</term> <note>the point in an orbit closest to the center</note>. Their greatest inclinations are directed toward the mean apsides <note>the points halfway between the furthest and closest points of the orbit</note>, and like the superior planets, these inclinations are changeable by a libration <note>original: *libramento*</note>. However, these planets undergo an additional libration unlike the former one. Both, nevertheless, are commensurable with the revolutions of the Earth, but not in the same way. For the first libration has this property: when the Earth has revolved once to the planets' own apsides, the motion of the libration itself has revolved twice. Its axis remains fixed, having the section we mentioned through the apogees and perigees, so that whenever the line of the mean motion of the Sun is in their perigee or apogee, the greatest angle of section occurs. In the middle longitudes, however, the angle is always at its minimum.

<summary>Copernicus explains how the "libration" or oscillating tilt of planetary orbits creates variable latitudes, noting that while superior planets follow one pattern, Venus and Mercury follow a distinct, doubled cycle of oscillation tied to the Earth's movement.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical geometric explanation of planetary latitudes, shifting focus from the general theory to the specific complex motions (librations) of the inferior planets, Venus and Mercury, as they relate to the Earth's position and the Sun's mean motion.</meta>

# OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

The second libration <note>original: *libratio*; a swinging or oscillating motion like a balance scale</note>, however, coming upon this first one, differs from it in this respect: because it has a movable axis, it ensures that when the Earth is positioned at the middle longitude, the planet—whether Venus or Mercury—is always on the axis, which is to say, in the common section of this oscillation. It is most deviant, however, when its apogee <note>the point in the orbit farthest from the Sun</note> or perigee <note>the point in the orbit closest to the Sun</note> faces the Earth. At those times, Venus is always inclined toward the North, as has been said, and Mercury toward the South; even though, according to the first and simple inclination, they ought to have lacked any latitude at that time.

For example: when the mean motion of the Sun is at the apogee of Venus, and Venus itself is in the same place, it is clear that according to the simple "inflection" <note>the first component of latitudinal tilting</note> and the first libration, she would have admitted no latitude at all, being in the common section of her orbit with the plane of the Zodiac. But the second libration imposes its greatest "deviation" <note>original: *deuiationem*; a specific latitudinal shift unique to the inferior planets</note> upon her, having its section or axis along the transverse diameter of the eccentric orbit, which cuts the line passing through the highest and lowest apsides <note>the points of greatest and least distance</note> at right angles. If, however, at that same time she is in either quadrant and near the middle apsides of her orbit, then the axis of this libration will coincide with the line of the mean motion of the Sun. Venus herself will then add the greatest deviation to her Northern "reflection" <note>original: *reflexioni*; another component of latitude related to the tilting of the orbital plane</note>, while it will subtract from the Southern reflection

[[image: Geometrical diagram showing the Earth's orbit (the "Great Circle") and the smaller, tilted orbital planes of an inferior planet. Labels A, B, C, and D mark the Earth's positions; F, G, K, and L mark points on the planet's eccentric orbit.]]

and leave it smaller. In this way, the libration of the deviation is measured according to the motion of the Earth.

To make this even easier to understand, let us look again at the Great Circle <note>the Earth's orbit</note> ABCD. Let the eccentric orbit <note>an orbit whose center is offset from the center of the system</note> of Venus or Mercury, which is oblique <note>tilted</note> to the circle ABC, be FGKL according to the equal inclination. Let their common section be FG, passing through the apogee of the orbit at F and the perigee at G. <summary>Copernicus describes the "second libration" or oscillation of the orbits of Venus and Mercury, explaining why they show latitude even when they should theoretically be on the ecliptic plane. He uses a geometric model to show how these deviations are synchronized with the Earth's movement and the Sun's mean position.</summary>

#### Chapter III. How great the inclination of the orbits of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars is.

After the hypotheses of the digressions of the five planets have been set forth, we must descend to the facts themselves and distinguish individual cases; and first, how great the inclinations of the individual circles are, which we calculate through that great circle which passes through the poles of the inclined circle and is described at right angles to that [circle] which passes through the middle of the signs [the ecliptic], toward which the transitions in latitude are considered. For once these are perceived, the way to knowing the latitudes of each will be opened, beginning again from the three superior [planets]. In the Southern extreme limits of their latitudes, according to the Ptolemaic exposition, the departures are evident: for Saturn at acronyctous [opposition], 3 degrees 5 minutes (*scrupula*); for Jupiter, 1 degree 7 minutes; for Mars, 7 degrees. But in the opposite places—namely, while they are in conjunction with the Sun—Saturn [has] 2 degrees 2 minutes; Jupiter, 1 degree 5 minutes; Mars, only 5 minutes; so that it almost touches the circle of the signs, insofar as it was possible to notice from the latitudes which he observed regarding their occultations and emergences.

### How Great the Inclination of the Orbs of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars Is. Chapter III.

In triangle **E F D**, since the ratio of sides **E F** to **F D** is given, along with angle **E F D**, we will obtain the given exterior angle **D F B**, representing the minimum Southern inclination. From here, by taking the difference of each declination, we obtain the total <term>libration<note>original: *librationem*; a periodic rocking or swaying motion of the orbital plane</note></term> of the eccentric to the zodiac. From these angles of inclination, we also calculate the opposite Northern latitudes, specifically the angles **A F C** and **E G C**. If these agree with observations, they will signify that we have not erred. 

We shall provide an example using Mars, because it wanders into latitude more than all the others. Ptolemy noted its maximum Southern latitude as nearly 7 degrees, and this occurs at Mars' <term>perigee<note>original: *perigaeo*; the point in the orbit closest to the Earth</note></term>. This will also reveal to us angle **C G E**, the Northern latitude, as nearly 6 minutes.

# BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

So that these things can be distinguished individually, we shall begin with that which they call <term>declination</term> <note>original: *declinatio*; here referring to the North-South divergence of a planet's path from the ecliptic or "zodiac" line</note>, as it is a simpler treatment. Indeed, it happens to the Sun alone that it is sometimes separated from the others, because around the middle longitudes and around the nodes, according to the examined motions of longitude through the <term>quadrants</term> <note>original: *quadrantes*; quarters of a circle, or 90-degree sections</note> of the circles, the Earth is positioned relative to the <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the center</note> and <term>perigee</term> <note>the point in an orbit closest to the center</note> of the planet. In this proximity to the Earth, they found the parts of the Southern or Northern latitude in **Venus** to be 6 degrees and 22 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: *scrupula*; small units of measurement where 60 minutes make up 1 degree</note>; and in **Mercury**, 4 degrees and 5 minutes. 

However, at the greatest distance of the Earth <note>at the planet's apogee</note>, they found for **Venus** 1 degree and 2 minutes, and for **Mercury** 1 degree and 45 minutes. By these figures, the angles of inclination in this position become manifest through the published Tables of Equations. In that location, at the highest distance from the Earth, 1 degree and 2 minutes for Venus, and at the lowest distance, 6 degrees and 22 minutes, correspond on both sides to a circumference of the orbit of approximately 2 and a half degrees. For Mercury, indeed, the upper distance of 1 degree and 45 minutes and the lower distance of 4 degrees and 5 minutes requires a circumference of its orbit of 6 degrees and a quarter. 

Consequently, the angle of inclination of the orbits is 2 degrees and 30 minutes for **Venus**, and 6 degrees and a quarter for **Mercury**, of which 360 degrees make up four right angles. By these angles, the particular latitudes in that position—which are the latitudes of declination—can also be explained, as we shall now demonstrate, first for Venus. 

For let the underlying circle of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signifer*; literally the "sign-bearer," the path the Sun appears to take through the constellations</note> be represented, and let **A B C** be the common section of the flat plane through the center. Let **D B E** be the common section of the surface of the orbit of Venus. Let the center of the Earth be **A**, and the center of the planet's orbit be **B**, and let the angle **A B E** be the inclination of the orbit to the zodiac. With the orbit **D F E G** described around center **B**, let the diameter **F B G** be joined at right angles to the diameter **D E**. 

Let it be understood that the plane of the orbit is so related to the assumed upright plane that the lines drawn at right angles to **D E** in that plane are parallel to each other and to the plane of the zodiac, and in this plane alone is **F B G**. Our purpose is to find, from the given straight lines **A B** and **B C** and the given angle of inclination **A B E**, how far the planet has moved in latitude. For example:

For example, when the planet is 45° distant from the point **E** <note>original: *signo*; here referring to a specific point or mark on the orbital diagram</note>, which is the point closest to the Earth. We have chosen this specific position, following the lead of Ptolemy, so that it may be seen whether the <term>inclination</term> <note>the tilting of the planet's orbit relative to the Earth's path</note> of the orbit brings any variation in the longitude of Venus or Mercury. Such differences ought to be seen most clearly around the midpoints between the boundaries **D, F, E,** and **G**. This is especially true because a star positioned at these four boundaries produces the same longitudes it would without any declination, as is self-evident. 

Let us therefore take the arc **EH**, as stated, to be 45°. Let the perpendiculars be drawn: **HK** to the line **BE**, and **KL** and **HM** to the underlying plane of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>original: *signifer*; literally the "sign-bearer," referring to the zodiac or the Sun's apparent path</note>. Let **HB, LM, AM,** and **AH** be joined. We shall have a quadrilateral **LKHM** that is both a parallelogram and a rectangle, because **HK** is perpendicular to the plane of the ecliptic. Indeed, the angle **LAM** represents the <term>equation</term> <note>original: *longitudinis prosthaphaeresis*; the geometric adjustment needed to find the true position from the mean position</note> of longitude, and it encompasses the side itself; whereas the transition in latitude is the angle under **HAM**, since **HM** also falls perpendicular to the same plane of the ecliptic. 

Therefore, since the angle **HBE** is given as 45°, **HK** will be half the chord subtending twice **EH**, which is 7,071 units where **BE** is 10,000 <note>Copernicus uses a standard radius of 10,000 for his trigonometric calculations, similar to how we use 1.0 today</note>. The remaining sides of the same parts will be **KL** at 308 and **BL** at 7,064. 

But since the ratio of **AB** to **BE** from what was previously shown is approximately 10,000 to 7,193, the remaining lines in those same units will be: **HK** at 5,086; **HM** (which is equal to **KL**) at 221; and **BL** at 5,081. From this, the remaining segment **LA** is 4,919. Now, in the triangle **ALM**, since the sides **AL** and **LM** (which is equal to **HK**) are given, and the angle **ALM** is a right angle, we shall have the hypotenuse **AM** at 7,075 and the angle **MAL** at 45° 58'. This is the <term>parallax</term> <note>original: *prosthaphaeresis, sive commutatio*; the difference between the planet's position as seen from the Earth versus the center of the orbit</note> or the "great change" of Venus according to the calculation. 

Similarly, in the triangle where the sides **AM** (7,075) and **MH** (equal to **KL**) are given, the angle **MAH** will be 1° 47', which is the latitude of declination. If it is not too much trouble to weigh <note>original: *trutinare*; to balance on a scale or examine carefully</note> what variation this inclination of Venus brings to the longitude, let us take the triangle **ALH**, understanding **LH** to be the diagonal of the parallelogram **LKHM**. It is 5,091 units where **AL** is 4,919. Since the angle **ALH** is a right angle, the hypotenuse **AH** is calculated as 7,079. Given the ratio of the sides, the angle **HAL** will be 45° 58'. But **ALM** was shown to be 45° 57'. Therefore, it increases by only 2 minutes <note>original: *scrupula*; small units of measurement</note>, which was what was to be demonstrated.

By a similar reasoning, we shall demonstrate the latitudes of declination through a description similar to the previous one, in which the arc **E H** is set at 45 degrees. For since the angle under **E A K** is the greatest of all, the line **K E** will have a greater ratio to **E A** than either **H D** or **L F** have to their respective lines **D A** and **F A**. But as **E K** is to **E N**, so is **H D** to **D M**, and **L F** to **F A**; for the angles they subtend are equal, as we have said, and those around **M N O** are right angles. Therefore, **E N** to **E A** has a greater ratio than either **M D** or **O F** to their respective lines **D A** and **F A**. And again, because the angles under **D M A**, **E N A**, and **O F A** are right angles, the angle under **E A N** is therefore greater than the angle **D A M**, and greater than all others formed in this manner. 

From this it is manifest that the differences between the equations of longitude that arise from this <term>inclination</term> <note>original: *obliquatione*; the tilting of the orbital plane</note> are at their maximum when they are determined at the greatest transition around point **E**. For because of the equal angles subtended by **H D**, **K E**, and **L F**, they are proportional to **H M**, **K N**, and **L O**. And since the same ratio of these lines to their excesses remains, it follows that the excess of **E K** and **K N** has a greater ratio to **E A** than the remaining ones have to their counterparts like **A D**. From this it is also manifest that whatever ratio the maximum equation of longitude has to the maximum transition of latitude, the same ratio will exist between the equations of the segments of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>a circular orbit where the Earth is not exactly at the center</note> in longitude and the transitions of latitude. This is because as **K E** is to **E N**, so also are all lines similar to **L F** and **H D** to those similar to **F O** and **D M**, which was the very thing to be demonstrated.

### Chapter VII. What the angles of inclination are for both planets, Venus and Mercury.

Having noted these things, let us see how great an angle is contained within the <term>inflection</term> <note>the "bending" or tilting of the planet's orbital plane relative to the Earth's path</note> of the planes of both planets. Recalling what was said before: that between the maximum and minimum distance, each of them [the planets] becomes for the most part more Northern or Southern by five degrees, in opposite directions according to the position of the orbit. In fact, the transition or difference of Venus makes a manifest departure of five degrees at the <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in the orbit farthest from the Earth</note> and <term>perigee</term> <note>the point in the orbit closest to the Earth</note> of the eccentric, while that of Mercury [is more] by more than half a degree...

However, the maximum prosthaphaeresis of Venus is 46 degrees, and of Mercury about 22. Ptolemaeus, however, as far as possible everywhere shortcutting, seeing that [abbrev: *quòd*] both [abbrev: *utraqꝫ*] types of these latitudes increased and decreased proportionally according to themselves in total and in all their parts, in the manner of lunar latitude. #### On the third kind of latitude of Venus and Mercury, which they call deviation. Chapter VIII.

[Historiated Initial: A scholar with an instrument.]

With these things also thus set out, it remains still to say something about the third motion of latitude, which is the deviation. This, the ancients, who [abbrev: *q̃*] hold that the earth is in the center of the world, think [abbrev: *exiſtimãt*] occurs by the declination of the eccentric together [abbrev: *cũ*] with the epicycle [abbrev: *epicycli*] about the center of the earth, especially when the epicycle is situated in the apogee or perigee. In Venus, by [abbrev: *ꝑ*] a sixth [sextantem] of a part, always in the North [Borea]. In Mercury, truly by [abbrev: *ꝑ*] three-fourths [dodrantem] always in the South [Austro], as we said before. Nor is it sufficiently clear whether they wished such an inclination [abbrev: *inclinatiõẽ*] of the orbits to be always equal and the same [abbrev: *eandẽqꝫ*], for their numbers indicate this, while they command that a sixth part of the proportional minutes always be taken for [abbrev: *ꝑ*] the deviation of Venus, and three-fourths for Mercury. Which does not have a place unless there remained the same...

[margin note: 532]

### REVOLUTIONS BOOK VI. 192 [PAGE 405]

...the same angle of inclination always remained, as the ratio of those minutes which they base themselves on requires. Moreover, even with the same angle remaining, it could not be understood how this latitude of those stars could leap back from the common section into the same latitude which it recently left, unless you say it occurs by the mode of refraction of light, as in optics. But here we are dealing with motion, which is not instantaneous, but is by its own nature commensurable [abbrev: *cõmenſurabilis*]. 

It is necessary, therefore, to admit that a libration is present in them, which makes the parts of the circle be changed into different directions, such as we explained. Which it is also necessary to follow, so that their numbers differ by 1/5 of a degree in Mercury. Wherefore it ought to seem less a wonder if, according to our hypothesis also, this latitude is variable and not so simple, yet not producing an apparent error, which can be discerned thus in all its differences [abbrev: *differẽtijs*]. 

For let [abbrev: *em̃*] there be in the underlying plane at right angles to the zodiac a common section in which **A** is the center of the earth, **B** the center of the orbit, at the maximum or minimum distance of the earth, which let be **C D F**, as if [abbrev: *tanq̃*] through the poles of the inclined orbit itself. And since in the apogee and perigee, that is, when the center of the orbit is in **A B**, the star exists in maximum deviation wherever it may be, according to a circle parallel to the orbit: and let **D F** be the diameter of the parallel to **C B E**, the diameter of the orbit, of which the common sections are posited as right to the plane **C D F**. Moreover, let **D F** be bisected in **G**, and **G** itself will be the center of the parallel; and let **B G**, **A G**, **A D**, and **A F** be joined; and let us place under angle **B A G** the angle which comprises a sixth of one degree in the highest deviation of Venus. 

In the right-angled triangle **A B G** at **B**, we have the ratio of sides **A B** to **B G** as 10000 to 29; but the whole **A B C** is 17193 of the same parts, and the remaining **A B** [is] 2807, which also subtends [abbrev: *ſubtẽdiũ*] half of the double of **C D**, and **B F** are equal to **B G** itself. Therefore, the angles **C A D** will be 6 minutes, and **E A F** nearly 15 minutes, differing from that which is under **B A G**—there by only 4 minutes, here by 5—which are generally neglected on account of their smallness. Therefore, the apparent deviation of Venus, with the earth situated in its apogee and perigee, will be slightly greater or less than 10 minutes, in whatever part of its orbit the star may be.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical demonstration of planetary latitudes for Venus and Mercury from the previous page, specifically calculating the angles of inclination (obliquity) and the resulting corrections (prosthaphaeresis) using geometry.</meta>

# OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

In the maximum slanting <term>obliquation: the tilting of a planet's orbit relative to the ecliptic</term>, the correction for parallax <term>prosthaphaeresis: a geometric adjustment used to calculate the difference between mean and true positions</term> is about 3 minutes. Moreover, it was clear that at the mean apsis <note>the middle distance in the orbit</note>, the angle of inclination of the orbits was 2 ½ degrees; here, however, it has increased by almost a whole degree, which that first motion of libration <note>original: "librationis"; an oscillating, back-and-forth motion used by Copernicus to explain gradual changes in orbital tilt</note>, of which we spoke, has added.

[A geometric diagram showing a circle with points A (representing Earth), B (the center), and points C, D, E, F, G, which define the lines of sight and the perpendiculars used to calculate the orbital tilt.]

In the case of Mercury, the proof is conducted in the same way. For where the radius from the center of the orbit is 3,573 parts, the maximum distance of the orbit from the earth is 10,948, and the minimum is 9,052; the mean between these is 10,000 parts. The line **A B** also has the same ratio to **B D** as 10,000 has to 3,573. We will therefore have the third side of the same triangle, **A D**, as 9,340 parts. And since as **A B** is to **A D**, so is **B D** to **D F**, then **D F** is 3,337 in length. Since the angle of latitude **D A G** is set at 2 ½ degrees <note>original: "II. s.", where 's' stands for 'semis' or 'half'</note>, **D G** will be 407 where **D F** is 3,337.

Thus, in triangle **D F G**, given the ratio of these two sides and the right angle at **G**, we will find the angle **D F G** to be approximately 6 degrees. This is the angle of inclination or obliquity of Mercury's orbit from the plane of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi", the circle of signs</note>. But around the middle longitudes or quadrants, the angle of inclination itself was shown to be 6 degrees and 15 minutes; therefore, 45 minutes have now been added by the first motion of libration.

Similarly, for the purpose of examining the angles of correction and their difference, it may be noted—after it has been shown that the straight line **D G** is 407 parts where **A D** is 9,340 and **D F** is 3,337—that if we subtract the square of **D G** from the squares of **A D** and **D F**, the remainders are the squares of **A G** and **F G**. We will therefore have the length of **A G** as 9,331 and **F G** as 3,314. From these is derived the angle of correction **G A F** as 20 degrees and 48 minutes, while the angle **D A F** is 20 degrees and 56 minutes. The angle resulting from the slanting is deficient from this by about 8 minutes.

It still remains for us to see whether such angles of obliquation and latitudes at the maximum and minimum distances of the orbit are found to be consistent with those received from observations. For this reason, let us again assume in the same description first the ratio for Venus at its maximum distance from the orbit: **A B** to **B D** is 10,208 to 7,193. Since the angle at **A D F** is a right angle, **A D** will have a length of 7,238 parts; and through the ratio of **A B** to **A D**, as **B D** is to **D F**, **D F** will be in length... <note>The calculation continues on the following page.</note>

<summary>Copernicus uses geometric proofs to calculate the varying orbital inclination (obliquity) of Mercury and Venus, accounting for the "libration" or oscillation of their orbital planes. He concludes that Mercury's tilt increases by 45 minutes from its mean state due to this motion.</summary>

# BOOK VI OF THE REVOLUTIONS, 191

...length 5102, but the angle of the **obliquity** <term>obliquity: the tilting or inclination of the planet's orbital plane relative to the Earth's path</term> **D F G** was found to be 3 degrees 29 minutes <note>original: "part. III. scru. XXIX"</note>. The remaining side **D G** will be 309, where **A D** is 7238. Therefore, where **A D** is 10,000, **D G** will be 427, from which it is concluded that the angle **D A G** is 2 degrees 27 minutes at the greatest distance from the earth. 

But at the minimum distance, since the radius of the orbit **B D** is 7193, then **A B** <note>the distance from the Earth to the center of the planet's orbit</note> is 9792, to which the perpendicular **A D** is 6644. Similarly, as **A B** is to **A D**, and **B D** to **D F**, the length of **D F** is given as 4883 parts. But the angle **D F G** is set at 3 degrees 29 minutes; therefore, **D G** is given as 297 parts, where **A D** is also 6644. Because of these given sides of the triangle, the angle **D A G** is given as 2 degrees 34 minutes. 

However, neither 3 minutes nor 4 minutes <note>the difference between the mean and extreme calculations</note> are large enough to be captured by the precision of **astrolabic instruments** <term>astrolabic instruments: complex circular tools, like the armillary sphere, used by Renaissance astronomers to measure the coordinates of stars and planets</term>. Therefore, the value that was thought to be the maximum latitude of deflection in the star Venus holds up well.

Let us likewise take the maximum distance of the orbit of Mercury—that is, the ratio of **A B** to **B D** as 10,948 to 3573. By demonstrations similar to the previous ones, we calculate **A D** to be 9452 parts and **D F** to be 3085. But here also we have the angle of obliquation <note>tilting</note> **D F G** produced as 7 degrees. Thus the line **D G** is 376 parts, where **D F** is 3085, or **A D** is 9452. Therefore, in the right-angled triangle **D A G** with the sides given, we will have the angle **D A G** as approximately 2 degrees 17 minutes <note>original: "part. II. scru. XVII. proxime"</note>, representing the maximum digression <note>variation</note> in latitude. 

At the minimum distance, the ratio of **A B** to **B D** is set at 9052 to 3573. Because of this, **A D** is 8317 of those parts, and **D F** is 3283. Since the ratio of **D F** to **D G** is set at 3283 to 400 because of the same obliquity, **A D** is also 8317 parts; from which the angle **D A G** is 2 degrees 45 minutes.

The variation in latitude <note>original: "digressio"</note> therefore differs from that which follows the mean ratio—which here also was assumed to be 2 ½ degrees—by 13 minutes at the **apogee** <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from the Earth</term> at minimum, and by 15 minutes at the **perigee** <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the Earth</term> at maximum. For the purposes of calculation, we shall use a **quadrant** <note>here meaning one-fourth of a degree, or 15 minutes</note> of one degree following the mean ratio, which does not differ significantly from observations in either direction. 

Having demonstrated these things, and also because the **prosthaphaereses** <term>prosthaphaeresis: a geometric correction used to convert a planet's mean (average) position into its true, observed position</term> of the maximum longitude have the same ratio to the maximum shift in latitude, we will have all the numbers of the latitudes at hand for the remaining sections of the orbit. These latitudes occur due to the obliquity of the orbits of Venus and Mercury. But those values are collected only in the mean way between the apogee and perigee, as we said, of which the maximum latitude was shown to be 2 ½ degrees.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

However, the maximum [elongation] of Venus is 46 degrees, and of Mercury approximately 22 degrees. We now have the **prosthaphaereses** <term>prosthaphaereses: geometric corrections added or subtracted to reconcile the difference between a planet's mean (average) position and its true (observed) position</term> recorded in the tables of unequal motions for each section of the orbits. Therefore, by however much each of these is less than the maximum, we will take a similar proportional part for both stars from those 2.5 degrees <note>original: "II. s. partibus"; the 's' stands for 'semis' or half</note>. We will assign this value to the Table to be set forth below with its own numbers. In this way, we will have explained each of the particular latitudes of **obliquation** <term>obliquation: the tilting of the planet's orbital plane relative to the Earth's path</term> that occur when the Earth is at the highest and lowest **apsis** <term>apsis: the point in an orbit where a planet is closest or furthest from the center of its motion</term>, just as we have also set forth the latitudes of the **declinations** <term>declinations: the distance of a celestial object north or south of the celestial equator</term> at the middle quadrants and middle longitudes. 

Whatever occurs between these four limits can indeed be explained with the subtlety of the mathematical art from the proposed hypothesis of circles, though not without labor. However, **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus was updating</note>, being as concise as possible everywhere, saw that both types of these latitudes increased and decreased proportionally according to their whole and in all their parts, much like the lunar latitude. Therefore, by taking twelve parts of any value—because its maximum latitude is five degrees, which is the 1/12th part of 60—he established **proportional minutes** <note>original: "scrupula proportionum"</note> from them. He thought these should be used not only for these two stars [Venus and Mercury], but also for the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, as will be made clear below.

## Concerning the third type of latitude for Venus and Mercury, which they call deviation. Chapter VIII.

**With** <note>The letter 'Q' in the original Latin 'Quibus' is a historiated initial showing a scholar looking through an instrument at the stars.</note> these things thus explained, it remains to say something about the third motion in latitude, which is the **deviation** <term>deviation: a specific component of the planet's latitudinal motion that shifts it slightly from its expected path</term>. Those predecessors who hold that the Earth is at the center of the world <note>geocentrists</note> believe this is caused by the inclination of the **eccentric** <term>eccentric: a circular orbit whose center is slightly offset from the Earth</term> together with the **epicycle** <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle</term> around the center of the Earth, specifically when the epicycle is positioned at the **apogee** <note>the furthest point</note> or **perigee** <note>the closest point</note>. In Venus, this is by one-sixth of a degree <note>10 minutes of arc</note>, and is always toward the North <note>original: "Borea"</note>. For Mercury, however, it is by three-quarters [of a degree] <note>45 minutes of arc</note>, always toward the South <note>original: "Austro"</note>, as we have said before. Yet it is not sufficiently clear whether they intended such an inclination of the orbits to be always equal and the same; for their numbers indicate this when they command that one-sixth of the proportional minutes should always be taken for the deviation of Venus, and three-quarters for Mercury. This does not hold true unless the same [inclination] remains...

the angle of inclination would always be the same, just as the ratio of those minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum"; in astronomy, these are minutes of a degree</note> requires, upon which they are based. Indeed, even if the angle remained the same, it could not be understood how this latitude of those stars could leap back from the common section suddenly into that same latitude which it had just left, unless you were to say it happens by means of the refraction of light, as in optics. But here we are dealing with motion, which is not instantaneous, but by its own nature is **commensurable** <note>original: "commensurabilis"; meaning it can be measured in relation to time</note>. It must therefore be admitted that a **libration** <term>libration: a slow, pendulum-like oscillation where the orbital plane tilts back and forth</term> exists in them, which causes the parts of the circle to be exchanged in opposite directions, as we have explained. It follows necessarily that their numbers differ by the fifth part of one degree in the case of Mercury. For this reason, it should seem less surprising if, according to our hypothesis as well, this latitude is variable and not so simple; yet it does not produce an error that is apparent, as can be discerned in all the **differences** <note>original: "differentiis"</note> in this way.

For let there be a common section in a plane perpendicular to the **zodiac** <note>original: "signiferum"; literally the "sign-bearer"</note>, in which **A** is the center of the Earth, and **B** is the center of the orbit at its greatest or least distance from the Earth, which is **C D F**, as if through the poles of the inclined orbit itself. And since in the apogee and perigee <term>apogee and perigee: the points in an orbit where a planet is furthest from and closest to the Earth, respectively</term>—that is, when the center of the orbit is at **A B**—the star is at its maximum deviation wherever it may be, according to a circle parallel to the orbit: let **D F** be the diameter of the parallel to **C B E**, the diameter of the orbit, of which the common sections are assumed to be perpendicular to the plane **C D F**. Let it cut **D F** into two equal parts at **G**, and **G** itself will be the center of the parallel; and let **B G**, **A G**, **A D**, and **A F** be joined; and let us set the angle **B A G** to be the angle that contains a sixth part of one degree [10 minutes] in the total deviation of Venus. 

Therefore, in the triangle **A B G**, with the right angle **B**, we have the ratio of the sides **A B** to **B G** as 10,000 to 29; but the whole **A B C** consists of 17,193 of those same parts, and the remaining **A B** <note>Copernicus likely means the line segment to the center</note> is 2,807, which also subtends half of the double of **C D**, and **B F** is equal to **B G**. Therefore, the angles **C A D** will be 6 minutes, and **E A F** approximately 15 minutes, differing from the angle **B A G** by only 4 minutes in the former case and 5 minutes in the latter, which are generally ignored because of their smallness. Therefore, the apparent deviation of Venus, when the Earth is positioned at its apogee and perigee, is slightly greater or less than 10 minutes, in whatever part

The angle beneath **C A D** will have 33 minutes <note>original: "scrup."; abbreviations for "scrupula," which in astronomy are minutes of a degree</note>, while **E A F** will have nearly 70 minutes. Therefore, twelve minutes are lacking in the former, and fifteen minutes are in excess in the latter; yet these differences are almost entirely lost beneath the rays of the Sun before Mercury emerges into our view. For this reason, the ancients <note>original: "prisci"; referring to astronomers like Ptolemy</note> followed only its apparent deviation, as if it were a simple matter.

If anyone, however, is not at all weary of the labor and wishes to follow those paths hidden beneath the Sun by exact reasoning, we shall show how that is done in this manner. We shall do this, for example, in the case of Mercury, because it produces a more notable deviation than Venus.

Let **A B** be a straight line in the common section of the star’s orbit and the **zodiac** <note>original: "signiferi"; literally the "sign-bearer"</note>, while the Earth is sought at the **apogee** or **perigee** <term>apogee and perigee: the points in an orbit farthest from and closest to the Earth, respectively</term> of the star’s orbit. Now let a circle **D E F** be described around center **C**, parallel to the **eccentric** <term>eccentric: a circular orbit where the Earth is not exactly at the center</term> orbit at a distance of **C B**, in which parallel circle the star is then understood to produce its greatest deviation. Let its **diameter** <note>original: "dimetiens"</note> be **D G F**, which ought also to be in relation to **A B**, and let both lines be in the same plane, perpendicular to the orbit of the star.

Therefore, let an arc <note>original: "circumferentia"</note> **E F** be taken, for example, of 45 degrees, for which we are investigating the star’s deviation; and let the perpendiculars **E G** be drawn to **C F**, and **E K** and **G K** be drawn to the underlying plane of the orbit. In triangle **A K E**, since the two sides **A K** and **K E** are given and they encompass the right angle at **K**, the angle **K A E** is also given. This angle corresponds to the deviation at the circumference **E F** which we were seeking, and it differs very little from what has been observed. We shall do the same for the other positions and for Venus, and we will record these values in the Table to be added below. 

Having set these things out, we will adapt the "sixtieths" or proportional minutes <term>proportional minutes: a mathematical tool used to scale a maximum value (like a maximum latitude) to a specific point in time or orbit</term> for the deviations between these limits for both Venus and Mercury. For let circle **A B C** be the eccentric orbit of Venus or Mercury, and let **A C** be the nodes <note>original: "nodi"; the points where the planet's path crosses the ecliptic</note> of this motion in latitude, and **B** the line of maximum deviation. With **B** as the center, let a small circle **D F G** be described, whose diameter **D B F** is positioned across the orbit, through which the libration <term>libration: an oscillating or "swinging" motion, here used to describe how the planet's tilt appears to change</term> of the deviation occurs. 

Since it was established that when the Earth is at the **apogee** or **perigee** of the star’s eccentric orbit, the star itself produces the maximum deviation (specifically at point **F**), and the circle carrying the star then touched the small circle at **F**. Now, let the Earth be at any distance from the apogee or perigee of the star’s eccentric orbit. According to this movement, let a similar arc of the small circle be taken, which shall be **F G**. The circle **A G C**, which carries the star, will also cut the small circle's diameter at **B**. 

Let the star be at point **K**, and the arc **E K** will be similar to arc **G F** according to our hypothesis. Let the line **K L** also be drawn perpendicular to circle **A B C**. Our goal is to find the magnitude of **K L** (the distance of the star from circle **A B C**) using **F G**, **E K**, and **B E**. Since the arc **F G** is given, the straight line **B G** will be given, as a straight line differs very little from a circular one <note>Copernicus is using a common Renaissance approximation for very small angles</note>. Similarly, **E F** will be known in the same parts as the whole **B F**, and the remainder **B E** will also be known. 

But **B F** is to **B E** as the chord of double **C E** <note>original: "subtensa dupli CE"; a standard trigonometric calculation of the era, equivalent to a sine function</note> is to the chord of double **C K**, and as **B E** is to **K L**. If, therefore, we set both **B F** and the radius from center **C E** to 60, we will also have **B E** in those same units. When **B E** is multiplied by itself and the product divided by 60, we will have **K L**, the proportional minutes for the arc **E K** where it is located. We have assigned these values to the fifth and final place in the Table, as follows.

### OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS
#### On the calculation of the latitudes of the five wandering stars. Chapter IX.

The method of calculating the latitudes of the five wandering stars [planets] by means of these tables is as follows. Since in Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars we shall compare the differentiated—or equated—eccentric anomaly to the common numbers: specifically, that of Mars as it shall be; that of Jupiter, however, after first making a subtraction of 20 degrees; and that of Saturn indeed with 50 degrees added. We shall therefore note those which occur in the row of the sixtieths, or proportional scruples [minutes], placed in the last position. Similarly, through the differentiated anomaly of commutation [parallax], we shall take the proper latitude adjacent to each [planet's] own number: first indeed and Northern, if the proportional scruples were in the upper [part], which happens while the eccentric anomaly has less than 90 or more than 270 [degrees]. But [we take] the Southern and the following latitude if the proportional scruples be in the lower [part], that is, if there had been more than 90 or less than 270 degrees in the eccentric anomaly by which entry is made. If, therefore, we multiply either of these latitudes by its own sixtieths, there will result the distance from the circle of the signs [the zodiac] toward the North or South, according to the denomination of the assumed circles. 

But in Venus and Mercury, three latitudes are to be assumed first through the differentiated anomaly of commutation—those occurring for declination, obliquation, and deviation—which should be marked separately; except that in Mercury a tenth part of the obliquation is to be rejected [subtracted] if the eccentric anomaly and its number be found in the upper part of the table, or let just as much be added if in the lower, and the remainder or the sum from these should be preserved. Their denominations, however, whether they be Northern or Southern, are to be distinguished. For if the differentiated anomaly of commutation were in the apogee semicircle, that is, less than 90 or more than 270, and the anomaly of the eccentric also less than a semicircle: Or again, if the anomaly of commutation were in the perigee circumference, namely, more than 90 and less than 270, and the eccentric anomaly greater than a semicircle, the declination of Venus will be Northern, and that of Mercury Southern. If, however, while the anomaly of commutation exists in the perigee circumference, the eccentric anomaly were less...

[[catchword: minor (trans: less)]]

***

### PAGE 413
[[language: Latin]]
[[original page: 196]]

### OF THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK VI.

...less, or the anomaly of commutation in the apogee part, and the eccentric anomaly more than a semicircle, the declination of Venus will be conversely Southern, and that of Mercury Northern. In the obliquation indeed, if the anomaly of commutation is less than a semicircle, and the eccentric anomaly apogeal, or the anomaly of commutation greater than a semicircle, and the eccentric anomaly perigeal, the obliquation of Venus will be Northern, and that of Mercury Southern; these also are exchanged [under opposite conditions]. 

The deviations, however, always remain Northern for Venus and Southern for Mercury. Furthermore, with the differentiated eccentric anomaly, the proportional scruples common to all five [planets] are to be taken, although they are ascribed to the three superior ones; let these be assigned to the obliquation, and the last [ones] to the deviation. After these things, with 90 degrees added to the same eccentric anomaly, [one takes] the common proportional scruples which occur again with that sum, applying [them] to the latitude of declination. All these being thus placed in order, let each of the three set-forth latitudes be multiplied by its respective proportional scruples, and they will come forth as the latitudes themselves, all examined [adjusted] for the place and time. Finally, so that we may have the sum of the three latitudes in these two stars: if they were all of one name [sign], they are added together; if not, at least two which are of the same name are joined, and according to whether they be greater or smaller, they should be subtracted from the third latitude of a different [name] from each other, and the prevailing latitude sought will remain.

**The end of the sixth and final book of the Revolutions.**

### AT NUREMBERG BY
### JOHANNES PETREIUS, IN THE YEAR

### NICOLAUS COPERNICUS
#### On the calculation of the latitudes of the five planets. Chapter 9.

**T**he method for calculating the latitudes of the five wandering stars <note>original: "stellarum erraticarum"; a common Renaissance term for the planets</note> by means of these tables is as follows. For Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, we will compare the adjusted <term>anomaly of the eccentric</term> <note>original: "anomaliam eccentri discretam"; this refers to the planet's position along its own orbital path, corrected for irregularities</note> to the common numbers: for Mars, we use its own value as it is; for Jupiter, however, after first subtracting 20 degrees; and for Saturn, after adding 50 degrees. We will then note the <term>proportional minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula proportionum"; these are fractions of a degree based on a scale of sixty, used to adjust values</note>—also called "sixtieths"—found in the final column of that row. 

Similarly, by using the adjusted <term>anomaly of parallax</term> <note>original: "anomaliam commutationis"; the apparent displacement of the planet caused by the Earth’s own motion</note> specific to each planet, we will find the corresponding latitude. We take the first value, the Northern latitude <note>original: "Boream"</note>, if the proportional minutes are in the upper part of the table—which occurs when the anomaly of the eccentric is less than 90 degrees or more than 270 degrees. We take the Southern <note>original: "Austrinam"</note> and the following latitude if the proportional minutes are in the lower part; that is, if the anomaly of the eccentric used to enter the table was more than 90 degrees or less than 270 degrees. If we then multiply either of these latitudes by its respective "sixtieths" <note>proportional factors</note>, the result will be the distance from the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>original: "circulo signorum"; literally the "circle of signs" or the path of the Sun</note> toward the North or South, according to the designation of the circles we have assumed.

But for Venus and Mercury, we must first determine three separate latitudes based on the adjusted anomaly of parallax: the <term>declination</term>, the <term>obliquation</term>, and the <term>deviation</term>. These are to be recorded separately, with the exception that for Mercury, one-tenth part of the obliquation is subtracted if the anomaly of the eccentric and its number are found in the upper part of the table, or that same amount is added if it is found in the lower part; the resulting remainder or sum is then kept. 

We must also distinguish their directions, whether they be North or South. If the adjusted anomaly of parallax is in the <term>apogeal</term> semicircle <note>the part of the orbit furthest from the Sun</note>—that is, less than 90 degrees or more than 270 degrees—and the anomaly of the eccentric is also less than a semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>; or again, if the anomaly of parallax is in the <term>perigeal</term> circumference <note>the part of the orbit closest to the Sun</note>—namely, more than 90 and less than 270 degrees—and the anomaly of the eccentric is greater than a semicircle, then the declination of Venus will be North and that of Mercury will be South. If, however, the anomaly of parallax is in the perigeal circumference and the anomaly of the eccentric is less
minor <note>catchword: smaller</note>

<summary>This page provides the mathematical instructions for using Copernicus's tables to calculate the latitudes of the five known planets, explaining how to adjust for their specific orbital positions (anomalies).</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Chapter 9 of Book VI, providing the final technical instructions for calculating the latitudes of Venus and Mercury. It marks the completion of the entire work, ending with the 1543 Nuremberg colophon.</meta>

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK VI.

...is smaller, or if the <term>anomaly of parallax</term> <note>original: "commutationis anomalia"; the apparent shift in position due to the Earth's motion</note> is in the apogean part <note>the part of the orbit farthest from the Earth</note> and the anomaly of the eccentric is more than a semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>, then the <term>declination</term> <note>the first component of latitude</note> of Venus will be Southern, and that of Mercury, Northern. In the case of <term>obliquation</term> <note>the second component of latitude, involving the tilting of the orbital plane</note>, however, if the anomaly of parallax is less than a semicircle and the anomaly of the eccentric is in the apogean part—or if the anomaly of parallax is more than a semicircle and the anomaly of the eccentric is in the perigean part <note>the part of the orbit closest to the Earth</note>—then the obliquation of Venus will be Northern and that of Mercury, Southern; these conditions are also reversed in the opposite cases. The <term>deviations</term> <note>the third and smallest component of latitude, unique to the inner planets</note>, however, always remain Northern for Venus and Southern for Mercury. 

Furthermore, using the adjusted anomaly of the eccentric, one should take the <term>proportional minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula proportionum"; fractions used to scale the values in the tables</note> which are common to all five planets—even though they are specifically assigned to the three outer planets—and apply them to the obliquation, using the last set for the deviation. After this, by adding 90 degrees to that same anomaly of the eccentric, one finds the common proportional minutes that occur with that sum and applies them to the latitude of declination. With all these values arranged in order, each of the three latitudes described is multiplied by its own respective proportional minutes, and the result will be the final examined values for that specific place and time. 

Finally, to obtain the sum of the three latitudes for these two stars <note>Venus and Mercury</note>, if they are all of the same name <note>meaning they are all Northern or all Southern</note>, they are added together. If not, the two that share a name are joined; then, depending on which is larger or smaller, the third latitude of a different name is subtracted from them. The result that remains is the <term>predominant</term> <note>original: "praepollens"</note> latitude sought.

**The end of the sixth and final book of the Revolutions.**

1.  **Page 421** represents a *tabula rasa* or flyleaf, typically used to protect the text block from the cover. The Latin terms *vacuum*, *charta*, and *folium* are standard codicological descriptors for an unwritten leaf.
2.  **Page 422** describes the posterior cover of the volume. The term *tegmen* refers to the outer covering, while *corium* specifies the material (leather). *Ligamentum* in a Renaissance or Medieval context refers specifically to the structural elements (cords, thongs, or adhesive) that bind the quires to the boards. 
3.  The "blind-tooled" decoration mentioned in the image description refers to *impressio caeca*, a common technique in Renaissance binding where patterns are stamped into the leather without the use of gold leaf or pigment.
